0.title: Jesus Is Better: The Letter to the Hebrews
0.overview:
The message. Hebrews tells tired believers not to go back. God has spoken many times and in many ways, “but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (1:2), and everything that came before was a promise, a picture and a shadow of him. Jesus is better than the angels, Moses, Aaron’s priesthood and the old sacrifices, because he is what they pointed to. To turn from him is to leave the real thing for its shadow. So the letter does not demand more willpower; it opens their eyes to Christ and calls them to hold fast to him to the end.

Background: the writer. Hebrews does not name its author, and the honest answer to who wrote it is that we do not know. Origen, the great third-century scholar who knew the church’s tradition as well as anyone, concluded that only God knows. The writer knew Timothy (“our brother Timothy has been released”, 13:23), so he probably moved in Paul’s circle. He wrote polished Greek and argued from the Greek Old Testament with great skill. Apollos, eloquent and “competent in the Scriptures” (Acts 18:24), is a strong guess; Barnabas, Luke and Priscilla have also been proposed.

Did Paul write it? For centuries much of the church counted it as Paul’s, and its theology runs as deep as any of his letters. But the style is far more polished than anything Paul wrote, and the writer says the gospel, “declared at first by the Lord”, “was attested to us by those who heard” (2:3), when Paul insisted he received his gospel from Christ himself (Galatians 1:12). This commentary holds that the writer was probably not Paul and is best left unnamed. The church received Hebrews because it bears the marks of God’s word, not because of a name on it. With no author to look at, we have to look at the one he wrote about.

The first readers. The letter was written to a particular congregation (13:24), probably largely of Jewish believers steeped in the Old Testament and its sacrifices. Where they lived is uncertain. “Those who come from Italy send you greetings” (13:24) probably means Italians abroad greeting home, which points to Rome, and the first writer known to quote Hebrews was Clement of Rome, in the 90s. Their faith had cost them. In “the former days” they had been “publicly exposed to reproach and affliction”, had stood by those in prison and “joyfully accepted the plundering of your property” (10:32–34); if they lived in Rome, that may recall the year when Claudius expelled Jews from the city (Acts 18:2). But they had “not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood” (12:4). Now they were weary: some had stopped meeting with the church (10:25), and they had grown “dull of hearing” (5:11). The pull was back to the synagogue: an old, respected faith, tolerated by Rome, with a visible priesthood and without the shame of a crucified Messiah.

When it was written. Probably in the 60s, before AD 70. The writer argues from the Old Testament tabernacle, but speaks of priests and sacrifices as still going on (8:4; 10:1–3, 11), and a letter arguing that the old system was “ready to vanish away” (8:13) would hardly have left out the destruction of the temple if it had already happened. If the church was in Rome, the lack of martyrdom (12:4) may place it before Nero’s persecution of AD 64. The readers were being drawn back to a temple still standing; within a few years it was gone.

A sermon written down. Hebrews calls itself a “word of exhortation” (13:22), the Greek phrase used of a synagogue sermon in Acts 13:15. It begins like a sermon and ends like a letter, and moves back and forth on purpose between teaching about Christ and urging the hearers to act. The five warning passages (2:1–4; 3:7–4:13; 5:11–6:20; 10:26–39; 12:25–29) are not interruptions to the argument; they are what the argument is for. Each argues that if neglecting the word spoken through angels and Moses brought judgment, turning from the Son brings worse. They grow sharper as the letter goes on. They are real warnings and God’s means of keeping his people; those who finally fall away had shared the church’s blessings without being born again, and the writer is confident of better things for his readers (6:9; 10:39).

How the book makes its case. The controlling word is “better” (Greek kreittōn), used thirteen times. Chapters 1–2 show the Son better than the angels: God’s final word, “the radiance of the glory of God” (1:3), who became like his brothers to make propitiation for their sins (2:17). Chapters 3–4 show him better than Moses, and offer a better rest than Joshua gave. From 4:14 to 7:28 he is the better high priest, after the order of Melchizedek, appointed by oath and living for ever, pausing in 5:11–6:20 to shake the hearers awake. Chapters 8–10 show the better covenant promised in Jeremiah 31, the better sanctuary in heaven, and the better sacrifice, offered once for all; the Day of Atonement is the background throughout. From 10:19 teaching turns to exhortation: draw near, hold fast, do not shrink back. Chapter 11 calls the witnesses of faith, who “desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one” (11:16). Chapter 12 sets out the race, the Father’s discipline, and Sinai contrasted with Mount Zion. Chapter 13 shows the life of those who belong to a kingdom “that cannot be shaken” (12:28): love, hospitality, faithfulness, contentment, and bearing Christ’s reproach.

Where it leads: to Christ. Hebrews is one of Scripture’s clearest guides to how the Old Testament points to Christ. The law has “but a shadow of the good things to come” (10:1); tabernacle, priests and the blood of goats and bulls were God-given and temporary, and find their substance in him. The old high priest entered the Most Holy Place yearly and came out to do it all again. Christ entered heaven itself with his own blood, and “when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God” (10:12). His work is finished; his care is not: “he always lives to make intercession for them” (7:25), a high priest who “in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (4:15). He “suffered outside the gate” (13:12), and the readers who feared losing the camp of their old faith are told to go out to him.

For us. Every generation feels the same pull: when following Christ grows costly or dull, to settle for something familiar, visible or respectable. Hebrews answers by showing us Jesus, and by giving us one another: “exhort one another every day, as long as it is called ‘today’” (3:13). We have “a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul” (6:19), a throne of grace we may approach with confidence (4:16), and a Saviour who “is the same yesterday and today and forever” (13:8). So we run, “looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith” (12:2), for “here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come” (13:14). Whatever the pressure, hold fast to Jesus. He is enough.

1.title: The Majesty on High: God Has Spoken His Final Word
1.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 is the opening of the sermon and the foundation of everything in it. Before the writer urges his weary hearers to hold on, he shows them who it is they are holding on to.

The message. God has spoken his last and fullest word, and that word is a person: his Son, the heir and maker of all things, the radiance of God’s glory, who made purification for sins and sat down at God’s right hand. He is not the highest of God’s messengers but God’s own Son, worshipped by the angels, addressed as God, the Lord who made the heavens and will outlast them. To leave him is not to go back to something older and safer; it is to turn away from God at the very moment he has spoken most clearly.

Why it was said. The first readers were being drawn back to a faith whose law had come through angels (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19), with a visible priesthood and without the shame of a crucified Messiah (see the introduction). So the writer begins not with what they should do but with who Jesus is, and he answers from the Scriptures they already loved.

How the chapter makes its case. One long sentence in Greek (vv. 1–4) sets the prophets beside the Son and makes seven statements about him, from creation to the throne, ending with the claim that he is far above the angels. Then seven Old Testament quotations prove it (vv. 5–14). The Father calls him Son and King and commands the angels to worship him (vv. 5–6). Angels are servants, as passing as wind and fire, but the Son is addressed as God on an everlasting throne (vv. 7–9) and as the Lord who laid the earth’s foundation and remains when it wears out (vv. 10–12). He sits at God’s right hand, while the angels are sent out to serve the heirs of salvation (vv. 13–14).

Where it leads. At the centre of the chapter stands one phrase: “After making purification for sins, he sat down” (v. 3). The one through whom the ages were made stooped to wash sinners clean, and then took his seat because nothing was left to do. The letter will come back again and again to that seated priest-king (8:1; 10:12; 12:2). And the chapter ends with a surprise: the angels who surround his throne are sent out for the sake of his people, ordinary believers the world overlooks.

For us. Every age has its own version of the pull to go back: to something more impressive, more familiar or more respectable than plain trust in Christ. This chapter does not scold; it shows us the Son. Whatever you are tempted to set beside him ranks below him, and if you have him, there is nothing higher to reach for.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — God Has Spoken by His Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s final word is his Son, and the Son is greater than every messenger who came before him. The writer sets the prophets, through whom God spoke in pieces, beside the Son, in whom God has spoken fully and last (vv. 1–2a). Seven statements then show who this Son is: heir and maker of all things, the radiance and exact imprint of God, the one who upholds the universe, who made purification for sins and sat down at God’s right hand (vv. 2b–3). So he stands as far above the angels as a son’s name is above a servant’s (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology:
Radiance and Imprint

God has not changed speaker; he has spoken finally, in a Son. Verse 3 holds together what the church later had to defend (see the note on v. 3). And, having made purification for sins, he sat down.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jewish Christians under pressure were thinking of going back to what was partial.

Now: The way out of an old attachment is not to call it worthless but to see what it was pointing at.

verseByVerse.quote: Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God truly spoke through the prophets, but in pieces, and every piece was preparing for the one who would come. The writer honours the old revelation even as he shows that it was waiting for its fulfilment.

A letter with no greeting. Hebrews has no name, address or greeting. It opens like a sermon, which is almost certainly what it is (13:22; on the writer and the first readers, see the introduction). The writer does not introduce himself, because he does not intend to be the subject: the first word of substance is God, and the first thing said about God is that he spoke.

At many times and in many ways. The opening words in Greek are deliberate music: polymerōs kai polytropōs. The first means in many parts, piece by piece: a law here, a psalm there, a prophecy centuries later. The second means in many manners: a voice from a burning bush, a dream, a vision, a still small voice, a prophet told to marry an unfaithful wife and live the sermon in his own home. Both describe revelation that was real and incomplete: God truly spoke, but in instalments, and no single prophet ever held the whole.

God spoke to our fathers by the prophets. The idols of the nations had mouths and could not speak (Psalm 115:5); the living God broke the silence and addressed the creatures he had made. The prophets were men carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:21), so that what they said, God said. “To our fathers” makes that history the readers’ own family story, and the writer does not begin by criticising what they are drawn back to. He affirms it: God really did speak there.

Fragments waiting for a face. The argument of Hebrews is never that the old was wrong. It is that the old was partial, and that going back to a partial thing after the whole has arrived is the tragedy. Nor were the fragments random: the Spirit of Christ in the prophets testified beforehand to his sufferings and glories (1 Peter 1:10–11). Every piece was part of one portrait, and the prophets died without seeing the face. Whatever divides the old covenant from the new, it is not a change of speaker.

The God who would not stop talking. God did not have to speak at all. He could have left the world in the dark it chose, groping after him among idols with painted mouths. Instead he kept speaking, through a thousand years of prophets who were mocked, ignored and killed, and every fragment was true, and every fragment was a promise. The God who would not stop talking to a people who would not stop running is the God who, at the end, sent the Word himself.

Do I still need the Old Testament if God has spoken in his Son? Yes, very much. The Son did not replace the prophets; he fulfilled them, and you cannot understand the fulfilment without the promise. Jesus taught his disciples from Moses and all the Prophets the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27), and this letter can hardly say a sentence about Christ without quoting the Old Testament. The sacrifices, the priesthood, the tabernacle and the psalms are the vocabulary Hebrews uses to explain the cross. Read the Old Testament as a true word from God that is still speaking, and ask in each passage what it was preparing the world to see in Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: The author of Hebrews is not named; Paul, Barnabas, Apollos and others have been suggested. It was written to Jewish Christians tempted to turn back from Christ, probably before the temple fell in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s final word is not another message but his own Son, the maker of all things and the heir of them all. In him God has said all that he will say before the end.

In these last days. The prophets spoke of the last days as the time of the Messiah (Isaiah 2:2; Hosea 3:5). In the New Testament the whole stretch from Christ’s first coming to his return is the last days (Acts 2:17). The final era has begun.

By his Son. The Greek has no word for “his” or “the”: literally “in Son”. The stress falls on the kind of messenger. Before, servants carried the message; now the messenger is the message. The prophets had the word of God; the Son is the Word of God (John 1:1, 18). That is why nothing can come after him: in him God has not sent more words about himself but shown us himself. To know what God is like, you need not guess or wait for another prophet: the way Jesus welcomes sinners, touches lepers and weeps at a grave is the way God is. Whoever sees him sees the one who sent him (John 12:45).

Seven statements in a single arc. Seven statements about the Son run through verses 2 and 3: heir, creator, radiance, imprint, sustainer, purifier, enthroned. They move from the end of history to its beginning, into the being of God, down into the dirt of human sin and back to the throne: the whole story of Christ in one sentence.

The heir of all things. In the ancient world the son, above all the firstborn, inherited his father’s estate. Everything that exists is the Son’s inheritance, as God promised his King: “Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage” (Psalm 2:8).

Through whom he created the world. The heir of all things is the one through whom all things were made (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16). He did not inherit an estate somebody else built; he made it and received it back, so the inheritance is not a promotion but a homecoming. “World” is aiōnas, literally the ages: the prophets lived inside a history the Son had made. And the one who hung the stars and set the calendar running came into his own estate as a baby in a manger and was treated by the tenants as an intruder.

What it does not mean. “Appointed heir” does not mean the Son was not always divine or that he earned his status. As the eternal Son he has always been Lord. But having become man and finished his work, he was appointed heir as the God-man, God and man in one person.

If God’s word is final, how does he guide me today? Through the word he has already given, opened to you by his Spirit: a complete Bible, able to make you wise for salvation and equip you for every good work (2 Timothy 3:15–17). Within what Scripture commands, he guides by wisdom, the counsel of mature believers, ordinary providences and desires he has shaped in you. Test any impression by the word and hold it loosely; never treat it as a voice from God that you must obey. To hear God speak today, open what he has said.

Is it narrow to say that God’s final word came in one man? Only if Christians had picked Jesus as their favourite teacher. The claim is not that we found God but that God came looking for us, and if God is personal, he is free to speak as he chooses: the question is not whether the claim sounds modest but whether it is true. Hebrews points to a life, a death and an empty tomb (2:3–4; 13:20). And see whom it humbles. If the final word is a gift, nobody reached it by being cleverer or more religious than anyone else. The sceptic and the churchgoer stand in the same place: both need to listen.

Where Christians differ: is revelation still ongoing? Some charismatic teaching expects ongoing prophetic revelation alongside Scripture; some liberal theology sees revelation continuing through human experience. This commentary’s view: God’s speaking in the Son is final. The apostles and their associates recorded and explained it in the New Testament, and with them the canon closed (Jude 3; Revelation 22:18–19). God still illumines his word by his Spirit and guides us providentially, but he gives no new revelation equal to Scripture, which alone is sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17). The apostles and prophets were the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20), and a foundation is laid once. Many charismatic brothers agree that nothing they call prophecy may add to Scripture or share its authority, and this commentary honours their longing to hear God, even while it believes the gifts of new revelation ceased with the apostles.

parallels.desc: I will make the nations your heritage

verseByVerse.quote: He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power. After making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son is God’s own glory shining out and his exact likeness, who holds all things in being; he stooped to make sinners clean, then sat down because the work was done.

The radiance of the glory. “He is” is present tense: what he eternally is. “Radiance” (apaugasma) is the light streaming from a source. There was never a moment when the sun existed and its light had not yet begun, and the radiance is not a lesser substance; it is the sun, reaching you. So is the Son to the Father. And “glory” (doxa) is the visible splendour of God’s being, which Moses begged to see (Exodus 33:18–23) and the disciples beheld in the Word made flesh (John 1:14).

The exact imprint. Charaktēr (which gives us character) is the die for stamping coins, or the impression it leaves: not a rough likeness but an exact match. “Nature” (hypostasis) here means God’s very being (the church later used the word for “person”). To see the Son is to see the Father (John 14:9; Colossians 1:15).

Both truths in one clause. The two images hold together what the church later defended at Nicaea. Radiance: he is not a second God, any more than light is a second sun. Imprint: he is truly distinct, as a coin is distinct from the die. One in nature, distinct in person. The great errors about Christ have had to cut one of these words out of the verse, making the Son a lesser being, or making Father and Son one person wearing two masks.

He upholds the universe. Not like Atlas in the Greek myth, holding a weight still: the verb means bearing something forward toward an end. The Son is conducting creation somewhere, by speaking, the same means by which it was made (Colossians 1:17). If he fell silent, it would stop. Every atom in your body exists this morning because he has not stopped speaking it into being.

Purification for sins. Then the sentence turns, and the turn is the whole gospel: the one who carries the universe stooped to deal with dirt. Sin makes us not only guilty but unclean, unfit to come near a holy God, as a man covered in mud is unfit for a king’s table. To purify is to remove guilt and stain together, so that the cleansed sinner may draw near to God (9:14; 10:22). On the Day of Atonement purification was made by blood (Leviticus 16:30), and had to be made again the next year. Christ made it by his own blood, once for all (9:12–14, 26).

He sat down. Priests in the tabernacle stood at their work every day (10:11), and among all the furniture Exodus lists there is no chair for them: the work was never finished. Christ sat down because his was (10:12). A seated priest is a priest with nothing left to do. The right hand is the place of honour, authority and power (Psalm 110:1), and “the Majesty on high” is a reverent Jewish way of naming God without pronouncing his name.

Prophet, priest and king. Here is the seed of what theology later called Christ’s threefold office: he has spoken as prophet (v. 2), made purification as priest, and sat down as king. In Israel the offices were kept apart; when King Uzziah went into the temple to burn incense he was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). The Son holds them all.

Silent before Pilate. The light of God’s own glory took a body that could be struck, and the Word that holds every atom in place was silent before Pilate. The radiance was hidden in the darkness of Golgotha so that sinners stained past cleaning could be made clean, and then that light rose and took the throne. The face we will see there is the exact imprint of the Father, and it is turned toward us in welcome.

What it does not mean. “Sat down” does not mean Christ is inactive; he reigns and intercedes (7:25). It means his atoning work is finished.

If he made purification once for all, why do I still feel dirty? Because the conscience is slow to believe good news. The purification rests on what Christ did, not on what you sense. When guilt returns over a sin already confessed, do not try to purify yourself again by self-punishment or promises; remember that he is seated, and nothing is left to add. If a sin is new, confess it, and the same blood that cleansed you once cleanses you still (1 John 1:7–9). Feeling usually follows faith, slowly. Let the fact lead.

Does Jesus really hold my life together, down to the small things? Yes: nothing in the universe he upholds is too small for him, the cells in your body, the timing of a phone call, the weather on the day of the funeral. And the one who holds it is not a force but the person who made purification for your sins. You can trust the details of your life to someone who has already given himself for the whole of it.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add by himself, which is why the King James Version reads when he had by himself purged our sins. The meaning is the same either way: the purification was his work alone.

verseByVerse.quote: having become as much superior to angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having become man and been exalted, the Son now stands as far above the angels as the name “Son” is above the name “servant”. The question behind it is not the ranks of heaven but which word, and which covenant, to live under.

Superior to angels. Why angels at all? In Jewish thought angels were the highest created beings and the mediators of the law (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2). To ask whether the Son outranks them is to ask whether the new word outranks the old one.

Having become. This does not mean the Son became a greater being; verse 3 has said what he eternally is. He gained a higher position. As the eternal Son he was always above the angels; in his incarnation he was made for a little while lower than the angels (2:9); and by his death, resurrection and ascension, as the God-man, he was exalted far above them (Ephesians 1:20–21; Philippians 2:9). “Superior” (kreittōn, better) is the keyword of Hebrews, used thirteen times: a better hope, covenant, sacrifice, country, resurrection. Everything that follows unfolds it.

The name he has inherited. Which name? The next verse answers: the one thing no angel is ever called in this unique sense, Son. It may also include Lord, the name above every name (Philippians 2:9–11). And it is inherited, which is family language again. A servant may be trusted with everything and inherit nothing; the name comes with the relationship.

A gap measured by a gap. A son is not a higher grade of servant; he is something different altogether. So the angels are not a little below Christ on the same ladder. They are on the other side of the line between Creator and creature. The writer proves it with seven Old Testament passages in a row, confident that his readers will take a text as settling the matter.

Lower, so that we could be raised. He laid aside the glory the angels had always watched him wear and went lower than they, so that we could be raised higher than we ever were; and he was given back the name above every name.

Why does it matter to me that Jesus is greater than the angels? Because whatever you are tempted to put alongside him ranks below him. Few Christians today are tempted to worship angels, but many are drawn to something that feels more impressive or more spiritual than plain trust in Christ: a powerful experience, a special teacher, a tradition, a technique for reaching God. The answer to every such pull is the one Hebrews gave: nothing God has made is on the level of the Son who made it. If you have him, you are not missing anything higher.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–14 — Seven Texts, and Not One of Them About an Angel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Scripture itself shows that the Son is not an angel but the Lord whom angels worship and serve. Seven quotations, all from Scriptures the readers already believed, make the case. God never called an angel his Son and King, but he commands the angels to worship his firstborn (vv. 5–6). Angels are servants, as passing as wind and fire; the Son is addressed as God, with an everlasting throne (vv. 7–9), and as the Lord who made the heavens and will outlast them (vv. 10–12). He alone sits at God’s right hand, and the chapter ends with a surprise: the angels are sent to serve his people (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology:
Texts About God, Applied to Jesus

Scriptures addressed to God, Psalm 45 and Psalm 102, are read as addressed to the Son (vv. 8, 10–12), and the angels are commanded to worship him (see the note on vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Readers who had lost property and standing were told that earth and sky are the temporary things; the Son remains.

Now: The angels, far from rivals, are sent to serve those who will inherit salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: For to which of the angels did God ever say, “You are my Son, today I have begotten you”? Or again, “I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son”? And again, when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says, “Let all God’s angels worship him.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
God never called any angel his Son and King, but he commands every angel to worship his Son, so the Son cannot be one of them.

To which of the angels. The argument is conducted entirely by quotation, and the question expects the answer none: search the Scriptures for the exception, and there is not one.

You are my Son. The first citation is Psalm 2:7, a coronation psalm in which God installs his King on Zion while the nations rage. “Today” is the day of enthronement: not the day the Son began to exist, but the day he was publicly installed as King. The New Testament applies it to Christ’s resurrection and exaltation, when he was declared the Son of God in power (Acts 13:33; Romans 1:4). The Father has one Son, and he loves to say so: at the coronation of David’s line, at the Jordan when the heavens opened, on the mountain when the face of Jesus shone, and by raising him from the dead.

I will be to him a father. The second is God’s promise to David about his offspring (2 Samuel 7:14). It first concerns Solomon, but the next line speaks of disciplining him for iniquity, and no sinful son of David could exhaust the promise of a throne established for ever (2 Samuel 7:13, 16). It points to the one who would.

The firstborn. “Firstborn” is a title of rank, not of chronology; it does not mean first created. God calls Israel his firstborn (Exodus 4:22), and David is made firstborn though he was the youngest of Jesse’s sons (Psalm 89:27). It means the heir, the one with pre-eminence (Colossians 1:15, 18). On when God brings him “into the world”, see the box at the end of this note.

Let all God’s angels worship him. The words match the Greek Old Testament of Deuteronomy 32:43 (compare Psalm 97:7), and they are decisive, because they command the angels to worship him. Angels refuse worship: when John fell at an angel’s feet he was told to worship God (Revelation 19:10; 22:8–9). Only God may be worshipped (Matthew 4:10). The one the angels are commanded to worship cannot be a creature at all.

But are angels not called sons of God? Yes, but always as a group: in Job the sons of God present themselves before the LORD and shout for joy at creation (Job 1:6; 38:7), the members of God’s heavenly court. What God never said to any angel is what he says here to one person: you are my Son, my heir, my king enthroned. Believers too are called sons of God, but by adoption, through the Son who is Son by nature (Galatians 4:4–7).

What does eternally begotten mean? That the Son shares the Father’s very nature, as a son does, without ever having had a beginning: the Father never existed without his Son, any more than the sun existed before its light (v. 3). A man makes a table, but he begets a son, someone of his own kind; so the Nicene Creed says the Son is begotten, not made, of one being with the Father. You need not picture it to believe it. It guards the truth that the one who died for you is not a creature God sent, but God himself who came.

How do I answer someone who says Jesus is a created being? Start where this chapter starts, with what Scripture says to him and about him. He made all things (v. 2; John 1:3), so he cannot be one of them. Angels are commanded to worship him (v. 6), and worship belongs to God alone. He is addressed as God (v. 8) and as the Lord who laid the foundations of the earth (v. 10). Read the chapter with your friend slowly, asking what each verse claims. Be gentle and patient; most who hold this view were taught it, and the Spirit uses the plain words of Scripture to open eyes.

Uncertain wording. In verse 6 the Greek word for “again” can go either with “says”, introducing one more quotation as in verse 5, or with “brings”, giving when he again brings the firstborn into the world. Both are possible Greek. If it goes with “brings”, the verse speaks of Christ’s return in glory; if not, the occasion may be his birth, when the angels praised God (Luke 2:13–14), or his exaltation. Either way, when the Father brings his Son into the world, the angels bow.

Textual note. The Dead Sea Scrolls contain a Hebrew text of Deuteronomy 32:43 that includes the line about the gods (or angels) bowing down, which supports the Greek translation used here as reflecting an ancient Hebrew form of the text. Most English Bibles translate the shorter Hebrew of Deuteronomy, so readers will not find this line there.
verseByVerse.note: The words of v. 6 match the Greek Old Testament of Deut 32:43, which is longer than the Hebrew.

verseByVerse.quote: Of the angels he says, “He makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flame of fire.” But of the Son he says, “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever, the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Angels are servants God makes and uses, but the Son is addressed as God himself, ruling for ever in perfect righteousness and joy.

He makes his angels winds. Psalm 104:4, in the Greek translation; the word for winds also means spirits. Wind and fire are powerful, but they pass and go where they are sent. The point is the word “makes”: however glorious, angels are creatures God uses as he wills.

Your throne, O God. Psalm 45 is a wedding song for an Israelite king, who is addressed as God (on the wording, see the box at the end of this note). Of a human king it was a breathtaking way to speak; its full meaning is realised only in the Messiah, who is truly God, and the writer builds his argument on it. The throne is for ever and ever (Daniel 7:14), against the changing winds and flames of the verse before. Every other throne in history has been a chair waiting for its next occupant; this one has never changed hands and never will.

Their own psalm. These believers confessed that the LORD our God is one. The writer is not smuggling divinity into the argument: a psalm they had sung all their lives addresses the Messiah as God. The Son does not deny that God is one; he fills out what it means.

The scepter of uprightness. Uprightness is straightness, justice (Isaiah 11:3–5). History has known many thrones and very few straight sceptres. This one has never bent.

You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness. Christ loved what is right and hated evil, perfectly, throughout his earthly life (4:15; 7:26), and that obedience, which none of us has matched, is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19). Loving right and hating wrong are one attitude seen from two sides: whoever loves people must hate what destroys them. Jesus could weep over Jerusalem and drive the traders from the temple in the same week, because the love and the hatred came from one heart.

God, your God. The Son is addressed as God, and he has a God: the Father and the Son are distinct persons, and the Son became man. As man he could say on resurrection morning, “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20:17). And “anointed” is the root of the word Christ: Messiah, Anointed One.

The oil of gladness. Oil was a sign of joy at festivals and coronations. His companions may be other kings or his people (the word is used of believers at 3:1 and 3:14); he is anointed with more joy than any of them. He endured the cross for the joy that was set before him (12:2), and now the joy is his.

Should a Christian hate anything? Yes: what Christ hates, which is wickedness, above all our own. But his hatred is never contempt for people; he hated sin and ate with sinners. So hate the lie, the cruelty, the abuse, the thing destroying someone you love, and hate it most fiercely in your own heart, where you can fight it. Then love the person enough to want him free of it.

Does following a righteous King mean I have to be grim? No. This King is anointed with the oil of gladness, and those who share his kingdom share his joy; in him holiness and gladness are one thing. A Christian who is serious about sin but has no joy has understood half the psalm. The sceptre is straight, and the throne is a wedding throne: Psalm 45 is a love song. Obey him gladly, because the one you serve is glad.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of Psalm 45:6 can be taken as “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever”, or, less naturally, as your throne is God’s throne or your divine throne, which some prefer so as not to call a human king God; the Greek of Hebrews could in theory mean God is your throne. But the writer plainly takes “O God” as spoken to the Son, the parallel “You, Lord” in verse 10 confirms it, and the ESV’s rendering is almost certainly right.

verseByVerse.quote: And, “You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the work of your hands; they will perish, but you remain; they will all wear out like a garment, like a robe you will roll them up, like a garment they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will have no end.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Words the psalm addresses to the LORD, the Creator, are here addressed to the Son: he made the heavens, they will wear out, and he will remain unchanged.

You, Lord, laid the foundation. The boldest of the seven quotations is Psalm 102:25–27, the lament of a man in deep affliction, whose days are like an evening shadow, turning from his own frailty to the permanence of God. The one he addresses is unmistakably the LORD, the God of Israel, the creator of heaven and earth. And Hebrews says: this is the Father speaking to the Son.

Texts about God are texts about him. Paul makes the same move: in Isaiah every knee will bow to the LORD; in Philippians, at the name of Jesus (Isaiah 45:23; Philippians 2:10). This is the strongest thing the New Testament says about Christ: not merely that he is like God, but that what the Old Testament says of the LORD is said of him.

The heavens are the work of your hands. Scripture now says what the writer said in his own voice (v. 2): the Son made the world. The hands that shaped the heavens were later held out to Thomas, with the marks still in them.

They will perish, but you remain. Earth and sky, the most permanent-seeming things there are, are the temporary items here. The Son will fold up the universe like an old coat (Isaiah 34:4), as you fold a jacket at the end of the day. Yet “changed” means transformed, not annihilated: new heavens and a new earth will take the old one’s place (Revelation 21:1; Romans 8:19–21), as a garment changed is replaced with something better, not with nothing.

You are the same. Unchangeableness here is no abstraction. Hebrews was written to people whose world was coming apart: property confiscated, some imprisoned (10:32–34). To them the writer says: the things you thought were solid are the garments, and the one you are being tempted to leave is the one who does not change. He will say it again in the plainest form: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever (13:8).

Everything grows old except him. The psalmist felt himself dying, and he lifted his eyes from his own fading to the God who does not fade. Hebrews tells us whose face he was seeing. It was the Son, who laid the foundations of the earth and will fold up the heavens like a cloak, and who in between took our fading flesh, let it wear out on a cross, and rose with it renewed. Everything grows old except him, and he has promised to make all things new.

If the world will be rolled up, does it matter how I care for it? Yes. The world is the work of Christ’s hands, and God will renew it, as he will raise our bodies, not discard them. So work done well, kindness and care for what God made are not wasted. What the passage forbids is putting your final trust in anything that can wear out. Enjoy the garment, look after it, and do not mistake it for the one who wears it.

How does an unchanging Christ help me when my life is falling apart? He is the one fixed point when everything else moves: your health, your work, your marriage, your feelings about God. The love he had for you before you were born is the love he has for you on the worst day of your life; his promises do not expire, and his intercession does not pause. When nothing feels solid, do not look for a solid circumstance. Look at him, and say to him the words of this psalm: you are the same.

verseByVerse.quote: And to which of the angels has he ever said, “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet”? Are they not all ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son sits enthroned at God’s right hand until every enemy is defeated, while the angels are sent out to serve those who will inherit salvation.

Sit at my right hand. The seventh quotation opens with the same question as the first (v. 5). It is Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse the New quotes most. Jesus used it to show that the Messiah is David’s Lord (Mark 12:35–37), and its fourth verse supplies the Melchizedek priesthood of chapters 5 to 7. Two things are given to the Son that are given to no creature: a place, at God’s right hand, and a promise, that his enemies will be subdued while he sits. Ancient conquerors put their feet on the necks of the defeated (Joshua 10:24). Christ reigns now, and his enemies are being subdued, the last enemy being death (1 Corinthians 15:25–26).

Until. This word tells the reader where he stands in the story: the subduing is under way and not finished, which is why the readers are suffering. The King is already enthroned; the victory is already certain; the last enemy is still in the field.

Ministering spirits. Now the writer says what angels are for. “Spirits” recalls the winds of verse 7, and “sent out” is present tense: continually being sent.

Those who are to inherit salvation. Here is the surprise at the end of the chapter: the ones angels are sent to serve are us, ordinary struggling Christians the world would not look at twice (Psalm 34:7; Acts 12:7–10). And “inherit” closes the circle begun in verse 2. The Son is heir of all things; those who are his inherit salvation. What is his by right becomes theirs by gift, and the angels, who inherit nothing, are sent out to look after the heirs.

In the flow. The first movement of the sermon ends here and leads straight into the first warning: therefore (2:1), if the message spoken through angels was binding, how much more the salvation announced by the Lord (2:2–3).

Running errands for his brothers. The King sits, the battle goes on, and the outcome is not in doubt. Every enemy of his people, sin and Satan and death itself, is on its way to becoming a footstool. And while he waits, the armies of heaven are sent out not to guard his throne, which needs no guard, but to look after his heirs. The one who for a little while was made lower than the angels now has them running errands for his brothers.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should pray to angels or seek contact with them (Colossians 2:18). They serve at God’s command, not ours.

What about Matthew 18:10 and Peter’s angel? Jesus says that in heaven the angels of his little ones always see his Father’s face (Matthew 18:10), and the disciples in Acts thought it was Peter’s angel at the door (Acts 12:15). God’s angels are concerned with his people, and the least of them are not overlooked in heaven. But these texts do not teach that each person has one angel assigned for life; the second is only what frightened disciples supposed. We can be sure that God sends his angels for his people; we are not told more, and should not invent it.

Why do I never see angels, if they are serving me? Because their service is usually hidden, by design, like most of what God does for his people: dangers turned aside that you never knew were coming, strength given in an hour you thought you could not survive. Elisha’s servant saw only the enemy army until God opened his eyes to the hills full of horses and chariots of fire (2 Kings 6:15–17). You need not see them, and should not try to contact them. Trust the God who sends them, and thank him for protection you will only fully know in glory.

In everyday life. Take the hint the angels give: find one heir of salvation this week, a weary believer or an elderly saint, and do for them something unseen and unthanked. It is the work of angels.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 110 is the Old Testament passage most often quoted in the New.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets,<sup>2</sup>but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the world.<sup>3</sup>He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power. After making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high,<sup>4</sup>having become as much superior to angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs.<sup>5</sup>For to which of the angels did God ever say, “You are my Son, today I have begotten you”? Or again, “I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son”?<sup>6</sup>And again, when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says, “Let all God’s angels worship him.”<sup>7</sup>Of the angels he says, “He makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flame of fire.”<sup>8</sup>But of the Son he says, “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever, the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom.<sup>9</sup>You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.”<sup>10</sup>And, “You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the work of your hands;<sup>11</sup>they will perish, but you remain; they will all wear out like a garment,<sup>12</sup>like a robe you will roll them up, like a garment they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will have no end.”<sup>13</sup>And to which of the angels has he ever said, “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet”?<sup>14</sup>Are they not all ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?

keyVerse.quote: Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the world.
keyVerse.note: This is the theme of the chapter and of the whole letter: God’s final word is his Son. Everything that follows, the seven statements of verse 3 and the seven texts about the angels, shows why this word cannot be bettered, and why turning from it means turning from God at the moment he has spoken most clearly.

1.reflection:
Verses 1–2 say that God spoke to the fathers “at many times and in many ways” but has now spoken to us by his Son. How should that shape the way you read the Old Testament, and the way you expect to hear God today?

Look at the seven statements about the Son in verses 2–3. Which of them most surprises or moves you? Why does it matter that the one who upholds the universe is the same one who made purification for sins?

The first readers were tempted to go back to something older, more visible and more respectable than Christ. What tempts believers today to set something beside Jesus or above him, and how does this chapter answer it?

Verse 14 says the angels are sent out to serve “those who are to inherit salvation”. How does it change the way you see yourself, and the weakest believers you know, to think of them as heirs whom heaven serves?

2.title: Lower Than the Angels: The Glory of the Humiliated Son
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 set the Son far above the angels. Chapter 2 draws the first warning from that (vv. 1–4), and then faces the obvious objection: if Jesus is so exalted, why did he suffer and die?

The message. Do not drift away from the great salvation the Lord himself has spoken, for his humiliation was not a defeat but the road by which he brings his brothers to glory. He became lower than the angels, a man of flesh and blood, to taste death for his people, break the devil’s grip on them through the fear of death, and become a merciful and faithful high priest who makes propitiation for their sins and helps them when they are tempted.

Why it was said. The first readers were tired, battered and quietly attending less (10:25), and a crucified Messiah was an embarrassment beside a faith with angels at Sinai and a priesthood in the temple (see the introduction). So the writer warns that the danger is quiet drift, and shows that the suffering they found shameful, in Jesus and in their own lives, is the road to glory.

How the chapter makes its case. The warning argues from the lesser to the greater: the law given through angels was binding, so how much more the salvation declared by the Lord and confirmed by God himself (vv. 1–4). Then Psalm 8: God meant human beings to rule his world; we do not see it yet, but we see Jesus, humbled to death and now crowned (vv. 5–9). It was fitting for God to perfect the founder of salvation through suffering, and he is not ashamed to call his people brothers (vv. 10–13). He shared their flesh and blood to break the devil’s power and the fear of death (vv. 14–16), and was made like them in every respect to be their high priest and help them in temptation (vv. 17–18).

Where it leads. The chapter’s great word is “brothers”. The one through whom all things exist took our flesh, called us his family in public, and went into death ahead of us. Here the letter first names him high priest (v. 17), the theme of its long central section (4:14–10:18): the one at God’s right hand knows from inside what it is to be tempted, afraid and dying.

For us. Drifting rarely feels dangerous; it feels like nothing. The remedy is not a burst of effort but attention to Jesus: “we see him” (v. 9). Whatever you are facing, temptation, shame, weakness or the fear of death, he has been there first, he is not ashamed of you, and he is able to help.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because the Son is so much greater than the angels, his word must not be neglected. The law given through angels carried real penalties (vv. 1–2); how much more serious, then, to drift away from the great salvation spoken by the Lord himself, passed on by those who heard him and confirmed by God with signs and gifts of the Spirit (vv. 3–4). The danger is not open rejection but quiet drift, and the cure is closer attention.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Danger Is Drift

The danger is not that someone dramatically renounces Christ but that he neglects him (see the notes on vv. 1–2 and 3–4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: If the law given through angels carried penalties, neglecting the salvation declared by the Lord is more serious still.

Now: The question is not whether you have renounced Christ but whether you are still paying attention.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard, lest we drift away from it. For since the message declared by angels proved to be reliable, and every transgression or disobedience received a just retribution,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God has now spoken through his Son, we must listen far more carefully than Israel had to listen at Sinai, or we will drift away. The danger in view is not open rebellion but a slow, unnoticed slipping from what we have heard.

Therefore. The word ties the first warning to the argument just made, and that is the pattern of the whole letter: teaching, then a pointed warning drawn from it, then more teaching. The Son is the radiance of God’s glory and the enthroned King; therefore his word cannot be treated casually.

We must pay much closer attention. Not you must, but we must: the preacher puts himself inside the warning, and he will do it again and again. These passages are not a man lecturing people he thinks less safe than himself.

Lest we drift away. To drift (pararyōmen) is to flow past or slip away, a word used of a ring slipping off a finger. It suits the picture of a boat that slips its moorings and is carried past the harbour mouth by a current the crew never noticed. Nobody decides to drift; drifting is what happens when nothing is decided at all. That was the readers’ danger: tired, battered and attending less (10:25), drawn by old ways that were warm and familiar, they need never have chosen to leave. The remedy is not to try harder to feel, but to attend to what you have heard.

The message declared by angels. The writer argues from the lesser to the greater. The message declared by angels is the law given at Sinai through angels (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19). It “proved to be reliable”, that is, legally binding: what it threatened, it carried out.

Transgression or disobedience. “Transgression” is stepping over the line; “disobedience” is literally mis-hearing, refusing to listen. Both were justly punished (Numbers 15:30–31). In God’s sight, refusing to listen is itself a sin.

Moored to a person. What holds a believer is not a rope of his own making. The letter will later call our hope a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, fastened behind the curtain where Jesus has gone ahead of us (6:19–20). To pay attention is to keep looking at the one who spoke. The fixed point is not our grip on the rope but the Saviour at the other end of it.

He did not have to warn us. The God who spoke at Sinai with fire and trumpet has spoken again, in his Son, and he did not have to warn us. A God who wanted to be rid of careless people would have let them drift without a word. Instead he shouts, like a man on the shore calling to a boat moving toward the rocks. Every warning in this letter is the Father calling his children back to the harbour, and the harbour is his Son.

How do I know if I am drifting? Drift is hard to see from inside, so look for small signs. Prayer has shrunk to emergencies. The Bible is opened less, and with less expectation. Missing church no longer bothers you. Sin that once grieved you merely irritates you. Your thoughts about God are mostly about what he has not done. None of these proves you are lost; each is a current. The remedy is not panic but attention: return to the word, prayer and the gathered church, and to the Son who is greater than all that pulls you away.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition held that the law was given through angels.

verseByVerse.quote: how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation? It was declared at first by the Lord, and it was attested to us by those who heard, while God also bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If disregarding the law brought judgment, there is no escape for those who neglect the far greater salvation spoken by the Lord himself and confirmed by God.

How shall we escape? The logic is uncomfortable because it is so simple. If the word that came through angels carried consequences, what of those who ignore the word that came through the Son? What there is no escaping is the judgment of God.

If we neglect. Not reject, deny or blaspheme, but be careless of: the word Jesus used of the wedding guests who paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business (Matthew 22:5). Nobody in this congregation was tearing up the gospel. They were letting it slide, and that is enough to be in danger.

Declared at first by the Lord. The message reached the readers through three witnesses. The first is the Lord Jesus himself, who came preaching that the time was fulfilled and the kingdom of God at hand (Mark 1:14–15). The salvation they were tempted to neglect was preached by its own author.

Attested to us by those who heard. “Attested” comes from the same Greek root as “reliable” in verse 2: the apostles, as eyewitnesses, confirmed the message as sure. The writer places himself in the second generation, one reason most think Paul did not write the letter (see the introduction).

God also bore witness. The third witness is God’s own, in the miracles of Jesus and the apostles (Acts 2:22, 43): signs point to a meaning, wonders astonish, miracles are works of power. And the gifts of the Spirit are distributed “according to his will”: God decides who receives what (1 Corinthians 12:11), which rules out treating any gift as an achievement or a right.

The order of the witnesses. The signs are spoken of in the past tense, as part of how the message was first confirmed. It has been confirmed and written, and the Spirit who once attested it with wonders now opens blind eyes to it through the word.

Such a great salvation. The warning is heavy because what is being neglected is enormous: a salvation planned before the foundation of the world, promised through a thousand years of prophets, preached by the Son with his own lips, sealed by his blood, confirmed by eyewitnesses who would not stop speaking even under the whip, and announced to people who did not ask for it and could not earn it. A man who loses a letter is careless; a man who loses a pardon from the king on the morning of his execution is something else.

Can a true Christian drift away and be lost? No, and the warning is still real. The writer includes himself, and the escape in view is escape from final judgment. But those who truly share in Christ hold fast to the end (3:14), and warnings like this are among the means God uses to keep them (compare 6:4–12): he keeps his children not in spite of the warnings but through them. The Christian who hears this and pays closer attention is doing exactly what it is for. The one who shrugs should be afraid, not because a true child of God can be lost, but because the shrug may show he never was one.

Is it not harsh to treat mere neglect so seriously? Only while we think of the gospel as advice. Ignore a friend’s tip and little is lost; ignore the pilot who warns that the current is carrying the ship onto the rocks, and it is no small thing, even if you never argue with him. Neglect is how the heart most often says no while still feeling respectable. So the warning is kind: it wakes the churchgoer and the careless together, and points both to a salvation so great that it is still offered to those who have neglected it.

Should I pray for healing, then? Yes, with confidence. Cessationism is not the belief that God has stopped healing, but that he no longer gives individuals the apostolic gift of healing at will. James tells the sick to call the elders to pray over them and anoint them (James 5:14–15), an instruction for the whole church age. So pray for the sick specifically and persistently, and leave the answer to God, who sometimes heals at once, sometimes through doctors and time, and sometimes gives grace to bear what he does not remove (2 Corinthians 12:7–10).

Where Christians differ: do miraculous sign gifts continue today? Pentecostal and charismatic Christians believe the miraculous gifts, such as healing, tongues and prophecy, continue in the same way throughout the church age. This commentary’s view: this verse describes the signs, wonders and miracles as God’s confirmation of the gospel through those who heard the Lord, that is, the apostolic generation (2 Corinthians 12:12). Their purpose was to authenticate the foundational revelation, and with that revelation complete, the sign gifts have ceased in that form. God still works powerfully, answers prayer, heals as he wills, and gives every believer gifts for service (Romans 12:6–8; 1 Peter 4:10–11). Many faithful believers, some in Reformed churches among them, think these gifts continue and often practise them with care and humility; their love for Christ is plain, and they are brothers. This cessationist view is held charitably toward them.
verseByVerse.note: The writer did not hear Jesus himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–18 — The Founder Made Perfect Through Suffering
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Son was made lower than the angels not in defeat but to bring his brothers to glory. Psalm 8 promised humanity rule over God’s world; we do not see that yet, but we see Jesus, humbled to death and now crowned (vv. 5–9). It was fitting that the founder of salvation be made perfect through suffering, and he is not ashamed to call his people brothers (vv. 10–13). He shared their flesh and blood to break the devil’s power and free them from the fear of death (vv. 14–16), and was made like them in every respect to become a merciful and faithful high priest, who makes propitiation for their sins and helps them when tempted (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology:
Fear of Death as Lifelong Slavery

We do not yet see everything subject to man, but we see Jesus: lowered, crowned, tasting death for everyone. He shared flesh and blood to break the devil’s hold through the fear of death, and to make propitiation as a merciful and faithful high priest.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A congregation that had lost property wondered why following a crowned Lord meant shame (see the note on v. 9).

Now: Because he suffered when tempted, he is able to help those being tempted, today.

verseByVerse.quote: For it was not to angels that God subjected the world to come, of which we are speaking. It has been testified somewhere, “What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you care for him? You made him for a little while lower than the angels; you have crowned him with glory and honor, putting everything in subjection under his feet.” Now in putting everything in subjection to him, he left nothing outside his control. At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God always meant human beings, not angels, to rule his world, and though we do not see that yet, the promise of Psalm 8 still stands.

The world to come. This is the new creation, begun by Christ and completed at his return. Some Jewish thought held that angels governed the nations in this age (Daniel 10:13, 20), but the coming world will be ruled by Christ and his people: not simply the Son, but humanity, in the Son.

Testified somewhere. A curious way to introduce Scripture (also 4:4), but not a vague one: the human author goes unnamed because the speaker who matters is God.

What is man, that you are mindful of him? The quotation is Psalm 8:4–6, following the Greek translation, a psalm about human dignity. David looks up at the night sky, overwhelmed by his smallness under the moon and stars, and the psalm’s answer is not that man is nothing, but that God remembers him, cares for him and has crowned him. “Son of man” in the psalm means a human being, but it became the title Jesus most often used of himself (Daniel 7:13), and the writer sees the psalm fulfilled in Jesus as the true representative man.

Everything in subjection. This is God’s first charge to humanity, to rule the earth (Genesis 1:26–28): man was made a gardener-king under the great King, with the rest of creation under his feet.

Not yet. Then the writer says the honest thing: the magnificent text is visibly not yet true. We do not rule. We are ruled: by decay, by circumstance, by disease and disaster, by the devil and by death. The fall disrupted God’s design (Romans 8:20–22).

A crown waiting for its head. The psalm was never only about humanity in general. Jesus took its second verse on his lips when children shouted hosanna (Matthew 21:16), and Paul reads its last line as fulfilled in the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 15:27; Ephesians 1:22). The crown Adam dropped was waiting for a head, and the dominion humanity lost is restored in one Man first and then, in him, to all who are his. That is why the writer can admit the not yet so honestly: he knows whose name comes next (v. 9).

If human beings were made to rule, why do I feel so small and powerless? Because you are living in the not yet, and the Bible does not pretend otherwise: one diagnosis or bereavement shows how little we control. But you were made for dignity, and the fall has damaged and delayed it, not cancelled it. In Christ it is being restored, and in the world to come the redeemed will reign with him (2 Timothy 2:12; Revelation 5:10). So feel your weakness honestly, without despising it: it is where Psalm 8 is waiting to be fulfilled in you.

Does this psalm say anything about how I treat other people? A great deal. If God is mindful of every human being, then no person is beneath your notice: not the unborn child, the elderly woman with dementia, the man sleeping in a doorway, the colleague you find tiresome. Each bears God’s image and was made for a crown, and contempt for any of them is contempt for something God has honoured.

In everyday life. Tonight, if the sky is clear, go outside for five minutes and look up, as David did. Let the size of it make you small. Then pray Psalm 8, and thank God that the Maker of all that is mindful of you.

Uncertain wording. The Greek brachy ti can mean “a little” in degree or “for a little while” in time. In the Hebrew of Psalm 8:5 it most naturally means a little lower in rank, and where the Greek translation has “angels” the Hebrew has God or heavenly beings. The ESV takes the writer to be using the time sense, as his argument in verse 9 suggests: a temporary humiliation followed by a crowning. Both are true of Jesus.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add, after the words about glory and honour, the line and set him over the works of your hands from Psalm 8:6, which is why the King James Version includes it. The meaning is not affected.

verseByVerse.quote: But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We do not yet see the world under humanity’s feet, but we do see Jesus: humbled to death and now crowned, because by God’s grace he tasted death for us.

But we see him. We do not see everything in subjection to man, but we see one man in whom the psalm has come true. This is seeing by faith: the readers had never laid eyes on Jesus, but they could see him in the gospel more clearly than their own circumstances.

Namely Jesus. At the point of humiliation the writer uses the human name for the first time in the letter: the carpenter’s son from Nazareth. He is the true man, the last Adam, in whom Psalm 8 is fulfilled (1 Corinthians 15:27, 45).

Because of the suffering of death. He was crowned and wears the crown still, and the order is everything: the crowning is because of the suffering, not in spite of it (Philippians 2:8–9). The cross is not an obstacle he overcame on the way to glory but the ground of it. That answers a congregation asking why following a crowned Lord has brought them poverty and shame: the pattern runs down first, then up.

Taste death for everyone. “Taste death” means to experience it fully (Mark 9:1). He did not sip and set the cup down; he drained it, so that those for whom he died would never taste it as judgment. “For everyone” means on behalf of each one; on who they are, see the box “Where Christians differ” at the end of this note.

Won on a hill outside the city. He tasted death, the bitterness and the God-forsakenness of it, for each of his own, and grace was the whole reason. The crown he wears now was not handed to him at a ceremony. It was won on a hill outside the city, on the day the crown on his head was made of thorns. Every believer who closes his eyes in death will find that death has already been tasted for him, and that the one who tasted it is waiting to share his glory and honour.

What grace is. Most of us hear “grace” as a soft word: God being nice, overlooking things, giving us another chance if we try harder. This verse will not let grace be vague or cheap. It is God’s free, undeserved favour, and here we see what it set in motion: “by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.” Grace is not God deciding the debt does not matter; it is God deciding to pay it himself. Timothy Keller often pointed out that real forgiveness is never free: when someone wrongs you, either they pay or you absorb the cost. At the cross God did the absorbing, in his Son. So grace is free to you only because it was so costly to him, and you cannot add to it, only receive it (for grace as fresh help in time of need, see on 4:16). When you catch yourself trying to make it up to God after a bad day before you dare to pray, stop, and thank him that the bill was paid before you began. See also Grace in the Theological Dictionary.

What it does not mean. “For everyone” does not mean all will be saved. Hebrews warns repeatedly that those who reject Christ face judgment (2:3; 10:26–31).

Can I tell an unbeliever that Christ died for him? You can tell him, truly and urgently, that Christ died for sinners, that his death is enough for anyone, and that whoever comes to him will never be cast out (John 6:37). The apostles did not begin by explaining whom God had chosen; they called everyone to repent and believe. Definite atonement does not narrow the offer; it guarantees that the offer is backed by a death that actually saves. You can say to anyone with full sincerity: come to Christ, and you will find that he died for you.

Where Christians differ: did Christ die for every individual equally? Many read “for everyone” as proof that Christ’s death was equally for every human being, making salvation possible for all. This commentary’s view: the surrounding verses define the everyone as the many sons brought to glory, the brothers he sanctifies, the children given to him by the Father (vv. 10–13). His death actually achieves their salvation: it brings them to glory, destroys the devil’s power over them, frees them, and makes propitiation for their sins (vv. 10, 14–17). This is definite atonement (sometimes called particular redemption): Christ tasted death for each one of those he came to save, and none of them will be lost. Jesus lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:15). Yet his death is of infinite value, sufficient for all, and the gospel is offered sincerely to every person. Many faithful Christians read “for everyone” as all people alike, and they preach the same cross as the only hope; this commentary differs from them as brothers.

Textual note. A few manuscripts and some early church writers read “apart from God” (chōris theou) instead of “by the grace of God” (chariti theou). The two look similar in Greek. “Apart from God” might refer to Jesus’ cry of abandonment on the cross, or to his dying for all apart from God himself. But the great majority of manuscripts read “by the grace of God,” and that is almost certainly original.

verseByVerse.quote: For it was fitting that he, for whom and by whom all things exist, in bringing many sons to glory, should make the founder of their salvation perfect through suffering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was worthy of God to bring his many children to glory through a Saviour who went ahead of them through suffering.

It was fitting. A startling word: the cross was what you would expect once you know who God is. To most people it looks like a stumbling block and folly (1 Corinthians 1:23); Hebrews says it suited him. Given his holiness and his love together, no other way would have done.

For whom and by whom. This is the Father: all things exist for him and come from him (Romans 11:36). He owed nothing to anybody, yet he chose this way of salvation, and it was worthy of him.

Many sons to glory. The sons are the redeemed, adopted as God’s children (Romans 8:14–17): God is not merely repairing damage but leading a great family home. And glory is not fame or a vague brightness; it is the splendour of what God is, which his sons will share as fully as creatures can: a raised body like Christ’s “glorious body” (Philippians 3:21), a character finally free of sin, for “we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2), and the rule over a renewed world that humanity lost (vv. 6–8). See Glory.

Perfect through suffering. “Founder” (archēgos) is a pioneer who goes first and opens a way, a champion who fights for his people (12:2; Acts 3:15). “Perfect” means to complete, to make fully fit for a purpose; in the Greek Old Testament it is used of consecrating a priest. Jesus was never morally imperfect (4:15; 7:26). What suffering completed was not his character but his qualification: through suffering and death he was made fully fit to be Saviour and High Priest (5:8–9).

Following tracks. He is out in front, on a road he has already walked. A suffering congregation was not lost in a wilderness; they were following tracks. We do not reach glory by climbing. We are brought, by a Son who went first, through suffering, so the hidden, unglamorous faithfulness of this week is not wasted: it is the road home.

Does this mean my suffering is part of the path too? Yes. Not that suffering earns glory, which Christ alone earned, but that God leads his sons to glory by the road their pioneer took. Your suffering is not a sign that you have taken a wrong turning or that God has forgotten you. It is country the founder of your salvation has already crossed, and he is leading you through it, not shouting directions from the far side. And it ends in glory: Paul could call the heaviest affliction light and momentary beside the eternal weight of glory it is preparing (2 Corinthians 4:17).

verseByVerse.quote: For he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified all have one source. That is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying, “I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise.” And again, “I will put my trust in him.” And again, “Behold, I and the children God has given me.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus and the people he makes holy belong to one family, so he gladly calls them his brothers and stands among them before God.

He who sanctifies. Jesus makes his people holy, setting them apart for God by his blood (10:10, 14; 13:12). One makes holy; the others are made holy; and yet the next phrase binds them together: they “all have one source”, most likely one Father, God (see the box at the end of this note). The one who makes holy and those he makes holy belong to the same household.

Not ashamed to call them brothers. To say he is “not ashamed” admits that he had every reason to be. These are the people described as drifting and enslaved by lifelong fear, and the radiance of the Father’s glory is not embarrassed to be publicly associated with them (Matthew 12:49–50). On the morning of his resurrection, his first message was to the men who had run away: go to my brothers (John 20:17). Much of human life is spent trying to become someone nobody would be ashamed to know. The gospel cuts that anxiety at the root: the one whose opinion matters most has already said, in public, that he is not ashamed of his people, and no one else’s approval can add to that or take it away.

I will tell of your name to my brothers. Three quotations follow. The first is Psalm 22:22, from the psalm of the crucifixion, at the point where it turns from anguish to triumph. The speaker has come through being forsaken by God, and the first thing he does is call his people brothers and sing among them in the congregation. When the people of God sing, the loudest voice in the room is his.

I will put my trust in him. The second is from Isaiah 8:17. Here is the Son, in his humanity, doing what most marks a creature: trusting God (12:2). Whatever faith is asked of us, he exercised it first, in the dark, on a cross.

I and the children God has given me. The third is Isaiah 8:18, where the prophet stands with his sons as signs to an unbelieving nation. Here Christ presents his own, given him by the Father, of whom he will lose none (John 6:37, 39). Between them the three texts make the family complete: a brother who sings with them, trusts alongside them, and presents them to God as his own.

What it does not mean. “One source” does not mean believers are divine as Jesus is. He is the eternal Son by nature; we are sons by adoption. He is the Sanctifier; we are the sanctified.

How can he not be ashamed of me, when I am ashamed of myself? Because his acceptance of you rests not on what you are in yourself but on what he has done for you. He calls you brother not because he overlooks your sin but because he has dealt with it: he is the one who sanctifies. Shame says you must hide; the gospel says you have been claimed. When shame rises, do not argue with it by listing your good points. Answer it with his words: here am I, and the children God has given me.

What does it mean that Jesus sings in the church? When the congregation praises God, Christ himself is present, leading the praise. Our worship is not a performance to win God over but joining the song of the risen Son, who declares the Father’s name to his brothers. You are not dragging your weary voice into a void on Sunday. You are standing next to the Son, and your weak praise is carried in his.

In everyday life. Picture the believer you are most inclined to be embarrassed by. Jesus calls him brother, and to sit with him, invite him home or speak well of him is simply to agree with Jesus.

Uncertain wording. “All have one source” is literally all of one, and the writer does not say one what. Most take it as one Father, God, who brings many sons to glory (v. 10); others suggest one ancestor, Adam or Abraham (v. 16), or one human nature. The context of sonship makes God likeliest; on any reading, the Sanctifier and the sanctified are one family.

verseByVerse.quote: Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son became fully human so that by dying he could break the devil’s power and set free those who were enslaved all their lives by the fear of death.

Flesh and blood. The Greek uses two different verbs. The children “share” flesh and blood as their settled condition; he “partook” of it by a single decisive act, taking up a nature that had not been his before. He did not merely appear human; he became fully human (John 1:14; 1 John 4:2).

Through death. He became mortal in order to die: not first to teach or set an example, but to have a life he could lay down. As God he could not die; as man he could. “Destroy” means not annihilate but render powerless, the word Paul uses when he says Christ abolished death (2 Timothy 1:10). The devil still exists; his weapon has been taken away.

The one who has the power of death. The devil held that power because he brought sin into the world, and sin brings death (Romans 5:12; John 8:44). He accuses sinners and holds them under death’s penalty. By dying for sin, Christ removed the ground of the accusation and broke his grip (Colossians 2:14–15; Revelation 12:10–11).

Lifelong slavery. The fear of death is a slavery that lasts a whole life. It makes a man grasp, hoard, protect himself, refuse risks and cling to comfort; much of what is called self-interest is fear of death in ordinary clothes.
