Leverage taken away. The devil holds people chiefly through fear. Take the fear away and the leverage is gone, which is why the early Christians were so hard for the empire to manage: you cannot finally threaten a man who no longer fears the worst you can do. Christians still die, and the parting still hurts. But the sting of death is sin, and its power is the law (1 Corinthians 15:56), and Christ has taken both. For the believer death is no longer going to be judged for his sins, but going to be with the one who bore them (Philippians 1:21–23).

The weapon broken on him. The Son put on mortality like armour that was meant to be pierced, walked into the enemy’s stronghold and let death take him, and the prisoners walked out. The devil drove the Son of God to the cross, and broke his own weapon on him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the devil now has no activity at all; he still prowls (1 Peter 5:8). His decisive power has been broken, and his final destruction is certain (Revelation 20:10).

Can we argue ourselves out of fearing death? Epicurus reasoned that death is nothing to us, since while we exist death is not here, and when death is here we are not. Modern versions are gentler: death is natural; live in the moment. Few survive a hospital corridor or a graveside. Hebrews takes the fear more seriously, as a signal telling the truth: death is bound up with sin, and after it comes judgment (9:27). Argument cannot cure that, any more than you can reason away a debt. A fear that tells the truth can only be answered by an event, and the event has happened: someone has gone into death for us, borne its full weight and come out holding the keys (Revelation 1:18).

I am a Christian, but I am still afraid of dying. Is something wrong with my faith? Not necessarily. The verse frees you from slavery to the fear, not from every feeling of it. Death is still an enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26); Jesus himself wept at a grave and was in anguish in the garden. But fear no longer has the last word or rules your choices. Bring it to him honestly, and ask him to show you what death now is for you: not the jaws of judgment but a door into his presence. Often it is the dying more than death itself we fear, and he has promised to be with you in the valley too (Psalm 23:4).

In everyday life. Fear of death rarely announces itself; it shows up as clinging to safety and refusing any risk for Christ. Freedom looks ordinary too: a generous gift given, a word for Christ spoken. And beside someone you love who is facing death, these two verses read aloud can say what is hard to say any other way.

verseByVerse.quote: For surely it is not angels that he helps, but he helps the offspring of Abraham.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son came to rescue human beings, not angels: he took hold of Abraham’s children, all who share Abraham’s faith.

It is not angels that he helps. To help here is to take hold of, the verb used of Jesus catching Peter as he sank (Matthew 14:31): not help from a distance, but a hand closing on someone who is going down. Fallen angels have no redeemer (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). The point is not that angels are neglected but that the incarnation was specific: he took hold of our nature, not theirs, because it was human beings he came to rescue.

The offspring of Abraham. Some Jewish Christians wondered whether following Jesus had cost them their place among Abraham’s people. Far from cutting them off from Abraham, the Son’s becoming man fulfils what was promised to him (Genesis 12:3; 22:18). And the phrase reaches beyond ancestry: Abraham’s true children are all who share his faith, Jew and Gentile (Galatians 3:7, 29; Romans 4:16).

He has taken hold of you. He passed by the angels, mighty and glorious, and stooped to the descendants of a nomad from Ur. He has taken hold of you, and he will not let go.

Why did God not save the fallen angels? Scripture does not tell us, and speculation is unprofitable. The verse says not that angels were refused but that the Son took hold of Abraham’s offspring, in sheer mercy toward people who had no more claim on him than anyone else. The right response is not to work out why, but to wonder that he took hold of us at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in the service of God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To be the priest his people needed, the Son had to become like them in every way, so that he could be merciful to them, faithful to God, and offer the sacrifice that turns God’s wrath away from their sins.

Like his brothers in every respect. Not in most respects, but body, soul, emotions, temptation, weakness, suffering and death: everything human except sin, the one exception the letter will add later (4:15). Hunger, exhaustion, grief and the fear in the garden were truly his. A high priest must be taken from among the people he represents (5:1); one who had not shared their condition could represent nobody.

A merciful and faithful high priest. Here the letter’s great theme, unfolded in chapters 5 to 10, is named for the first time: Jesus is the true high priest to whom Aaron pointed (Leviticus 16). The two adjectives face two ways: merciful toward us, because he knows from inside what it is like; faithful toward God, carrying out his task perfectly. Many human priests manage only one, severe men who are reliable or kind men who are lax. This one is both, standing on the human side of the gap and reaching across it.

To make propitiation. The word belongs to the Day of Atonement; the related noun names the mercy seat, the lid of the ark where the blood was sprinkled (9:5). Propitiation means satisfying God’s just wrath against sin by an offering, so that he is favourable toward sinners, and it includes expiation, the removal of sin itself. Christ is the propitiation for our sins (Romans 3:25; 1 John 2:2; 4:10), bearing as our substitute the penalty we deserved. “The people” are the brothers of verses 11 to 17, and there is no condemnation left for them, because there is no wrath left in the cup.

Not a bribe. Propitiation is sometimes said to sound pagan, like bribing an angry deity. But God’s wrath is no mood a gift could sweeten; it is his holy, unchanging hostility to evil. And the decisive difference is who provides the sacrifice. In paganism a man appeases a god. Here God in mercy supplies the offering and, in his Son, bears it himself: not bribery, but love paying the price out of its own heart.

If God is love, why does he need propitiation at all? Because his love is holy love. A God who shrugged at evil would not be loving but indifferent to its victims and its ruin; his wrath is perfect goodness responding to what destroys his world. The wonder of the gospel is that the God whose justice must judge sin is the God whose love provides the sacrifice. The cross is not love overcoming justice, or justice overcoming love, but both satisfied in one act, in one Person. So you can be completely sure of forgiveness: not because God has stopped caring about sin, but because he has dealt with it fully.

In everyday life. When you sin this week, notice which priest you go to in your mind. Some of us expect a rebuke from a severe one; some expect a shrug from a lax one. Go to the real one, merciful and faithful. Confess the specific thing, thank him that the wrath it deserved has already been borne, and, because he is faithful to God, ask him to help you turn from it.

Where Christians differ: did Christ’s death turn away God’s wrath? Some modern theologians reject propitiation, arguing that God’s love does not need appeasing, and translate the word only as expiation (removal of sin). This commentary’s view: Scripture teaches that God’s holy wrath is real (Romans 1:18; John 3:36), and that Christ’s death turned it away from his people by bearing it in their place (Isaiah 53:5–6, 10; Galatians 3:13). This is not an angry Father appeased by a loving Son against his will; the Father in love sent the Son to be the propitiation (1 John 4:10). Propitiation and expiation go together: Christ removed our sin and satisfied God’s justice. This is penal substitutionary atonement, the heart of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: For because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Jesus felt the full force of temptation and suffering, he knows how to help us in ours, and he comes when we call.

Suffered when tempted. The chapter ends not with a doctrine but with something Jesus is able to do. The word covers both temptation and testing, and he knew both: in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11), in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:36–46), and throughout his life (Luke 22:28).

Suffering in temptation. We tend to imagine that resisting temptation was easy for him because he was sinless. Hebrews says the opposite. Only the one who refuses all the way to the end knows the full force of the thing, because the one who gives in has stopped the pressure early. He felt the whole weight precisely because he never yielded, and that unbroken obedience, offered in our place, covers every time his people have yielded.

Able to help. “Help” (boēthēsai) was the ordinary word for answering a cry for help: not a sympathetic figure at a distance, but somebody arriving. Because he has been through it, he knows exactly what we face (4:15–16; 1 Corinthians 10:13). And “those who are being tempted” is present tense: the help is for the person in the middle of it this afternoon.

The swiftest helper in heaven. He is the radiance of God’s glory who carries the universe along, and he has been hungry in a desert, exhausted on a hillside, betrayed by a friend and pressed to the edge of his strength in a garden at night. The power to help and the heart to understand are in one person, so the cry of a tempted believer reaches a throne where the one who hears has been there and needs nothing explained. The letter will return to this at its turning point: let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace (4:16). The whole argument about priesthood exists so that frightened people will ask.

Could Jesus have sinned? Some Christians say he must have been able to, or his temptations would not have been real. The historic answer of the church is that he could not, because he is the eternal Son, and his human will was never set against the will of God; that is the more likely answer. But it does not make the temptation unreal. A bridge that cannot fall still bears the full weight of the train; a fortress that cannot be taken still feels the whole force of the siege (compare 4:15).

What does his help look like when I am tempted? Usually not a feeling that sweeps the temptation away, though sometimes the pull loosens when you pray. More often it is the way of escape God provides (1 Corinthians 10:13): a word of Scripture brought to mind, a door you can walk out of, a friend who calls, a strength to say no you did not have a moment before. So call to him at once, in a sentence, before you argue with the temptation, and take the way out, physically if you must. If you fall, run to him just as quickly: the one who helps the tempted also cleanses the fallen.

Does Jesus understand temptations he never faced in exactly my form? Yes. He was tempted in every way that matters: to doubt his Father’s goodness, to grasp for comfort, to take a shortcut to glory, to hate his enemies, to give up under pain and loneliness (Matthew 4:1–11). Every temptation you face is some version of these, and he knows the pull from inside, without the corruption that weakens our resistance. You will never be able to say to him, you do not understand.

It was declared at first by the Lord, and it was attested to us by those who heard,<sup>4</sup>while God also bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will.<sup>5</sup>For it was not to angels that God subjected the world to come, of which we are speaking.<sup>6</sup>It has been testified somewhere, “What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you care for him?<sup>7</sup>You made him for a little while lower than the angels; you have crowned him with glory and honor,<sup>8</sup>putting everything in subjection under his feet.” Now in putting everything in subjection to him, he left nothing outside his control. At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him.<sup>9</sup>But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.<sup>10</sup>For it was fitting that he, for whom and by whom all things exist, in bringing many sons to glory, should make the founder of their salvation perfect through suffering.<sup>11</sup>For he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified all have one source. That is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers,<sup>12</sup>saying, “I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise.”<sup>13</sup>And again, “I will put my trust in him.” And again, “Behold, I and the children God has given me.”<sup>14</sup>Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil,<sup>15</sup>and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery.<sup>16</sup>For surely it is not angels that he helps, but he helps the offspring of Abraham.<sup>17</sup>Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in the service of God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people.<sup>18</sup>For because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted.

keyVerse.quote: But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.
keyVerse.note: This verse is the hinge of the chapter. The glory Psalm 8 promised to humanity is not yet visible in the world, but it is visible in Jesus, and the order of his story, suffering first and then the crown, explains everything around it: why he became lower than the angels, why he calls us brothers, and why our own suffering is not a sign that we have taken a wrong turning.

2.reflection:
Verse 1 warns against drifting rather than rebelling. What currents tend to carry believers away from Christ without their noticing, and what helps you to “pay much closer attention” to what you have heard?

Verses 8–9 admit that “we do not yet see everything in subjection to him”, and yet “we see him”. Where do you feel the “not yet” most sharply, and how does looking at Jesus change the way you carry it?

Jesus “is not ashamed to call them brothers” (v. 11). How does that answer your own sense of shame, and how should it shape the way you treat believers you find awkward or hard to love?

Verses 14–18 say that Jesus shared our flesh and blood, went through death and suffered when tempted. Which of these means most to you at the moment, and what would it look like to go to him for help this week?

3.title: Greater Than Moses: Do Not Harden Your Hearts
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 1–2 showed the Son above the angels, made like his brothers so that he might be “a merciful and faithful high priest” (2:17). Chapter 3 opens the sermon’s second movement, which runs to 4:13: Jesus is greater than Moses, and he brings his people into the rest that Moses’ generation never reached.

The message. Fix your mind on Jesus, the faithful Son over God’s house, and do not let your heart grow hard towards him. Moses was faithful as a servant inside the house; Jesus is the Son over it and its builder, and we are that house if we hold on. The generation Moses led out of Egypt heard God’s voice and saw his works for forty years, and still died in the desert because they would not believe. God speaks the same “today” to us. The danger is not loud denial but slow hardening, which no one can see in himself, so believers must speak to one another every day.

Why it was said. To the first readers Moses was the greatest man who ever lived, the one through whom the law came, and the faith they were tempted to return to was the faith of Moses (see the introduction). They had begun boldly and were now weary, and some were drifting (10:25). The writer shows them that going back would not be loyalty to Moses, and that their real danger looked exactly like the danger of Moses’ own generation.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–6 compare Jesus and Moses, beginning with a compliment: both were faithful in God’s house (Numbers 12:7). But the builder has more glory than the house, and a son more standing than a servant; Moses testified to what was coming, and Christ is what he testified to. Verses 7–11 quote Psalm 95, where the Spirit says “today” and recalls Israel testing God in the wilderness. Verses 12–15 apply it: watch that no one among you has an unbelieving heart, and exhort one another daily, because sin deceives. Verses 16–19 cross-examine the psalm with three questions and land on one word: unbelief.

Where it leads. Moses could lead Israel out of Egypt but could not lead them in; he died looking at the land. Jesus is the apostle God sent to us and the high priest who goes to God for us (v. 1), the Son who builds his house out of forgiven sinners and will bring every member of it home. The voice Israel refused at Massah is the voice that has now spoken in him, and where Israel tested God in the wilderness, he trusted his Father in his own wilderness, in our place.

For us. Few people decide to harden their hearts; they are talked into it, one postponement at a time. The chapter’s answer is twofold: consider Jesus, on purpose and often, and do not try to keep yourself alone. Who speaks to you about Christ during the week, and to whom do you?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Jesus and Moses: Servant and Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus is worthy of more glory than Moses, because Moses served in God’s household and Jesus is the Son over it. The writer calls his readers to fix their minds on Jesus, the one God sent to them and the high priest who represents them (v. 1). He honours Moses as faithful (v. 2), then shows the difference: the builder outranks the house, and Christ, who builds it, stands with God, the builder of all things (vv. 3–4). Moses was a servant whose life testified in advance; Christ is the Son over the house, and that house is the church, whose members show they belong by holding on (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology:
Servant and Son

Moses is faithful in God’s house as a servant, while Christ is faithful over it as a son (see the notes on vv. 3–4 and 5–6).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jesus is both apostle, sent from God, and high priest, going to God for us.

Now: The letter’s constant remedy is to consider Jesus. Holding fast does not make us God’s house; it shows that we are.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, holy brothers, you who share in a heavenly calling, consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession, who was faithful to him who appointed him, just as Moses also was faithful in all God’s house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fix your mind on Jesus, whom God sent to you and who goes to God for you, and who was as faithful to his task as Moses was.

Therefore, holy brothers. “Therefore” (hothen, for this reason): because Jesus is the merciful and faithful high priest of 2:17–18. Naming his readers for the first time, the writer uses the warmest terms he has. Holy (hagioi, set apart): made holy by Christ (2:11). Brothers: what Jesus calls them (2:11). That shapes how the letter’s warnings are heard. The man about to say, “Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart” (3:12), begins by calling them holy brothers. He is warning people he believes are Christians.

You who share in a heavenly calling. “Share” (metochoi) means partners, partakers, the word used of the King’s companions in 1:9. The heavenly calling is a call from God in heaven to heaven and its glory (Philippians 3:14). Israel was called to an earthly inheritance in Canaan; these believers are called to a better country, a heavenly one (11:16). Losing property and standing could not touch what they really owned.

Consider Jesus. To consider (katanoēsate) is to fix the mind on something and think it through: attentive study, not a passing glance, the word Jesus used when he told his disciples to consider the ravens (Luke 12:24). It is the letter’s constant remedy: to a drifting, tired, frightened congregation the first instruction is not to try harder or to examine themselves, but to look at somebody (12:2).

The apostle and high priest of our confession. The two titles stand together nowhere else in Scripture, and this is the only place Jesus is called an apostle (apostolos, sent one): sent by the Father to bring God’s word to us (John 17:18). An apostle comes from God to men; a high priest goes from men to God. In the Old Testament every mediator held one office or the other: Moses was the sent one, Aaron the priest. Jesus is both, so this chapter compares him with Moses and the following chapters with Aaron. The Son came to us carrying the Father’s final word, and went back to the Father carrying us. He came down to speak and went up to intercede, and in both directions he was faithful.

Of our confession. “Confession” (homologia) is the faith they had professed aloud, probably at baptism, and were now under pressure to unsay. The word returns at 4:14 and 10:23, each time with the call to hold it fast.

Faithful in all God’s house. Jesus carried out perfectly the task the Father gave him (John 17:4). And the comparison with Moses begins with a compliment. The words come from Numbers 12:7, where God defends Moses against Aaron and Miriam: “He is faithful in all my house.” “House” (oikos) means God’s household, his people Israel. The writer does not begin by diminishing Moses but by agreeing with the highest thing Scripture says about him.

How do I actually consider Jesus? Think about him on purpose. Read a passage of the Gospels slowly and ask: what does he do here, what does he say, what does this show me of his heart? Turn the letter’s titles for him over in your mind: Son, Creator, radiance of God’s glory, apostle, high priest, pioneer, brother. Sing about him and pray to him. When you are anxious or tempted, deliberately turn your thoughts from the problem to the person. Considering Jesus is not a feeling you wait for; it is a direction you give your mind.

Textual note. The earliest manuscripts name him simply Jesus here; the KJV’s Christ Jesus follows later ones.

parallels.desc: He is faithful in all my house

verseByVerse.quote: For Jesus has been counted worthy of more glory than Moses—as much more glory as the builder of a house has more honor than the house itself. (For every house is built by someone, but the builder of all things is God.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus deserves more glory than Moses, as a builder deserves more honour than the house he builds, and the builder of all things is God.

More glory than Moses. To these readers Moses was the man who spoke with God face to face, through whom the law came, the founder of the nation’s whole religious life. His face shone with reflected glory when he came down from the mountain, so that he had to veil it (Exodus 34:29–35; 2 Corinthians 3:7–18). Jesus is the radiance of God’s glory itself (1:3). The moon is beautiful, but it shines because the sun does.

The builder and the house. The writer does not find fault with Moses. His argument is about position: however fine a house is, the honour goes to its builder. And God’s house is his people: Moses belongs to them, whereas Christ made them a people. Moses is a stone in the wall; Christ laid the foundation, chose the stones and set every one in place.

The builder of all things. This bracketed sentence is easy to skip. Every house has a builder; God is the builder of everything; Jesus is the builder of this house. The reader is left to draw the conclusion chapter 1 reached with Psalm 102: Jesus is identified with God, the Creator (1:2, 10).

A house made of forgiven sinners. The Son designed the household of God before the world began, chose its members in love (Ephesians 1:4), and paid for the building with his own blood (Acts 20:28). He is no landlord visiting now and then; he lives in what he built, among people who were rubble when he found them.

Is it wrong to admire great Christian leaders? No; Scripture itself honours Moses, and tells us to remember our leaders and imitate their faith (13:7). Admire them and thank God for them. The danger is when admiration slides into dependence, and a preacher, author or movement becomes the house rather than a part of it. When a favourite leader falls, a believer who trusted the builder grieves but stands; one who trusted the stone collapses with it. Give leaders the honour due to a faithful servant, and keep the glory for Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, to testify to the things that were to be spoken later, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son. And we are his house, if indeed we hold fast our confidence and our boasting in our hope.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses served faithfully inside God’s house, pointing ahead to Christ; Christ rules over it as the Son, and we are that house if we keep holding on to our hope.

As a servant. Both were faithful, and the writer says so twice. The difference is position: in the house or over it, servant or son (1:5). The word for servant is not the usual doulos but therapōn, a more dignified term for an honoured attendant, the very word the Greek Old Testament uses of Moses in Numbers 12:7. It is the most respectful word available, and still it is not son.

To testify. That is Moses’ function, and no small one. The tabernacle, the priesthood and the sacrifices were testimony given in advance about someone still to come. Jesus said so plainly: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me” (John 5:46; Luke 24:27).

Over God’s house as a son. “Over” (epi) means set over, in charge of, and “as a son” names a standing no servant has: heir and master of the household (1:2). The title Christ appears here for the first time in Hebrews (in the earliest manuscripts), at the very moment the writer sets him over the whole household of God.

And we are his house. Without warning the argument turns to the congregation. The house is them, sitting in somebody’s room hearing this read (1 Timothy 3:15; Ephesians 2:19–22). Moses served in a tent that was taken down; Christ rules over a house that will never be dismantled, made of people he has redeemed and the Spirit indwells.

If indeed we hold fast. Here is the first of the letter’s “if” clauses about belonging. “Hold fast” (kataschōmen) is keep a firm grip; “confidence” (parrēsia) is boldness, openness of speech; “boasting” is exultation. Membership in God’s house is shown by holding firm (3:14; 6:11; 10:23).

The grip and the hand. A Christian is not kept by his own grip: Christ is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him (7:25). God keeps his people by means of warnings like this one, so a genuine believer reads them and holds on tighter rather than despairing. A child on a cliff path holds his father’s hand, and the father holds the child’s wrist. The child’s grip is real; the father’s is the reason he is still on the path.

What does confidence and boasting in our hope look like? Confidence is freedom to speak openly about Christ and to come to God without cringing. Boasting is glad, unembarrassed pride in what God has promised, the way a bride speaks of her wedding day. These readers were tempted to go quiet so that the neighbours would leave them alone. Holding fast means refusing to be ashamed: still saying at work and at the family table that your hope is in Christ, and still praying as a child who expects to be heard. The opposite of boasting in hope is not humility. It is embarrassment.

Where Christians differ: does this conditional mean true believers can be lost? Arminians (Christians, many of them Methodist or Wesleyan, who hold that a true believer can finally fall away) read the if as meaning that a genuine member of God’s house may fall away and cease to be part of it. They hold it out of real seriousness about the warnings, and they are brothers in Christ. This commentary’s view: the verse says we are his house if we hold fast; it does not say we will cease to be his house if we do not. Holding fast is the evidence of genuine membership, not its cause. Verse 14 makes the logic clearer: we have come to share in Christ (perfect tense, already true), if we hold firm to the end. Perseverance proves that we have truly come to share in him; those who fall away show they never did (1 John 2:19). The warning is real, and God uses it as a means to keep his people persevering (Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5).

Textual note. The KJV adds firm unto the end here, following later manuscripts; the phrase is certainly original at verse 14.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–19 — Today, If You Hear His Voice
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God still says “today”, and the way to miss his rest is the way Israel missed it: by hearing his voice and refusing to trust him. The writer reads Psalm 95 as the Spirit speaking now, recalling the generation that saw God’s works for forty years and was shut out by his oath (vv. 7–11). He warns that one unbelieving heart in a congregation is one too many, and gives the remedy: daily exhortation against sin’s deceit (vv. 12–13). Holding our first confidence to the end shows that we truly share in Christ (vv. 14–15). Three questions then trace Israel’s failure to its root: unbelief (vv. 16–19).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Remedy Is Other People

Because sin deceives, the safeguard is outside the individual: exhort one another every day (see the note on v. 13).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Those who fell in the wilderness were the ones who had come out of Egypt.

Now: They stayed out through unbelief, so belief is the way in (see the note on v. 19).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion, on the day of testing in the wilderness, where your fathers put me to the test and saw my works for forty years. Therefore I was provoked with that generation, and said, ’They always go astray in their heart; they have not known my ways.’ As I swore in my wrath, ’They shall not enter my rest.’”
verseByVerse.commentary:
God still speaks the words of Psalm 95 to his people: today, while you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as Israel did in the wilderness, or you too will miss his rest. Verse 6 ended with a condition, if we hold fast; now the writer shows what failing to hold fast looks like, in an argument running to 4:13.

Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says. The tense is present. The writer quotes Psalm 95:7–11, a text roughly a thousand years old, which he will later say God spoke through David (4:7), and introduces it not as what the Spirit said but as what he says (10:15). When you open your Bible, the Spirit is not reminiscing; he is speaking to you.

The wilderness generation. Psalm 95 began as an invitation to sing joyfully to the rock of our salvation, then turned suddenly to this warning. Worship and warning belonged together: even God’s oath of judgment was sung, so that later generations would not harden.

Today. “Today” (sēmeron) is the key word of the warning, repeated in verses 13 and 15 and in 4:7. The psalm already used it to reapply an old event to its own generation; Hebrews reapplies the psalm. The offer is dated the present, and it will not last for ever.

Do not harden your hearts. “Harden” (sklērynēte) means make stiff, stubborn, and the command is addressed to them. The heart hardens through repeated refusal to listen, as Pharaoh hardened his heart when the frogs were taken away (Exodus 8:15); each refusal makes the next easier. Scripture also says that God hardened Pharaoh; here hardening is something people do to themselves, and the two truths stand side by side without cancelling each other.

Meribah and Massah. The psalm’s Hebrew place names, Meribah (quarrelling) and Massah (testing), become in the Greek rebellion (parapikrasmos) and testing (peirasmos): Exodus 17, where Israel demanded water and asked whether the LORD was among them or not (Exodus 17:1–7). They had walked through a parted sea weeks before.

They saw my works. The tragedy in one line: they demanded that God prove himself again, after the plagues, the Red Sea, the manna, the water from the rock, the cloud and the fire. The writer lets “forty years” go with what they saw (in the psalm, and in v. 17, it goes with God’s anger): forty years of visible miracle, and still no faith in that generation as a whole; only Caleb and Joshua stand out. Evidence alone does not produce trust.

Provoked … they have not known my ways. “Provoked” (prosōchthisa) is God’s holy anger at persistent unbelief: not the irritation of a bad-tempered deity but the grief of a Father whose children watched him feed them every morning for forty years and still called him a liar. His verdict locates the problem in the heart, not in the desert. They lacked no information; they knew his works, but they did not know him.

The oath. God bound himself by an oath (Numbers 14:21–23, 28–35): for that generation the offer was at last withdrawn. “Rest” (katapausis) was first the rest of the promised land, where God would give his people peace from their enemies (Deuteronomy 12:9). But, as Hebrews 4 goes on to show, the land was only a picture of the rest God himself entered on the seventh day, which he still offers to his people.

The voice at Massah. The voice Israel refused in the wilderness is the voice that has now spoken in the Son (1:2), and the letter will say so: “See that you do not refuse him who is speaking” (12:25). Paul goes further: the rock that gave them water was Christ, and they put Christ to the test (1 Corinthians 10:4, 9). Then the Son went into his own wilderness, hungry for forty days, and when Satan urged him to make God prove himself, he answered from the very chapter that remembers Massah: “You shall not put the Lord your God to the test” (Matthew 4:7; Deuteronomy 6:16). Where Israel tested God and hardened, Jesus trusted and obeyed, perfectly and in our place, and his people stand before God in his obedience, not in their own uneven record.

In everyday life. Hardening rarely feels like rebellion; it feels like postponement: the apology that can wait, the sin you will deal with after this busy month, the step of trust you will take when life is calmer. The psalm’s word for all of that is today. If something has been on your conscience while you read, answer it before you sleep. Tomorrow is the word hardening always uses.

Would I believe if God showed me a miracle? This psalm says otherwise: the wilderness generation saw all of it. Jesus said the same of the rich man’s brothers: if they will not listen to Moses and the Prophets, they will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead (Luke 16:31). The problem is rarely evidence; it is a heart that does not want God to be God over it. That does not make every honest question rebellion: Jesus gave Thomas the evidence he asked for (John 20:27), and the gospel invites examination. But it humbles both the sceptic, who may need to ask what he would lose if Christ were true, and the churchgoer, who has seen God at work and can still grow hard. Both need a new heart that hears his voice today.

What if I am afraid I have already hardened my heart? Then you are hearing his voice, and it is still today. A truly hardened heart does not worry about being hardened; that this warning troubles you is evidence that the Spirit is at work in you. Do not sit and analyse your condition. Do what the psalm asks: hear his voice and respond, now. Confess what you have been resisting, turn to Christ, and ask him to soften your heart. He has never yet turned away anyone who came to him (John 6:37).
verseByVerse.note: Meribah (“quarreling”) and Massah (“testing”) were where Israel tested God for water.

verseByVerse.quote: Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watch that no one among you, not even one, has a heart that refuses to trust God and so walks away from the living God.

Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you. “Take care” (blepete) means watch out, be on guard, and it is addressed to the whole community of professing believers. Not lest you all fall away, but lest it be in any one of you. A broadly sound congregation can contain one person quietly going the other way. A shepherd with ninety-nine sheep in the fold still counts, and misses the one.

An evil, unbelieving heart. Literally a heart evil of unbelief: the two words are welded together. We treat unbelief as a problem of the mind and evil as a problem of morals; Hebrews will not separate them. This unbelief is not honest doubt but a heart that refuses to trust God.

Fall away from the living God. The verb (apostēnai), to stand off from, to withdraw, is the one behind our word apostasy. And what is being left is not Christianity or the church but the living God. The readers imagined a change of religious arrangement, back to the temple, God’s own institution. The writer tells them what the move really is: a step away from a God who is alive, and who has spoken to them in a Son (1:2). To come to Christ is to come home to the living God, who has never yet refused a returning child.

Is it fair to call unbelief evil, when I cannot help what I find believable? Yes, because unbelief in Scripture is not first a matter of the head; no one is blamed here for finding a hard question hard. The heart this verse describes has heard God speak, seen what he has done, and decided not to trust him, which is to treat the living God as a liar (1 John 5:10). Doubting a stranger is not wrong; refusing to trust a friend who has never once let you down is an insult. God has given more than enough reason, above all in the Son he did not spare. Unbelief at its core is not a lack of light but a preference for the dark (John 3:19). Someone still honestly searching is not being called wicked here, but invited to keep looking at Christ.

How do I tell doubt from an unbelieving heart? Doubt struggles toward God; an unbelieving heart walks away from him. The father who cried, I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24), had a great deal of doubt and brought all of it to Jesus. Do I want to trust him, even when it is hard? Do I bring my questions to him, or use them as reasons to stay away? Am I still praying, reading and with God’s people, even haltingly? If so, you are a struggling believer, and Christ is gentle with such (Isaiah 42:3). If you have stopped wanting him and are glad to be free, that is the condition this verse warns against; turn back today, while it is still called today.

What should I do if someone in my church seems to be falling away? Notice, and do not look away. Go to him personally and gently, with love and a question rather than an accusation: how are you, really, with the Lord? Listen before you speak. Pray for him. Keep inviting him, keep in touch even if he stops coming, and tell the elders so that they can shepherd him too. The aim is always restoration (Galatians 6:1; James 5:19–20). You cannot change his heart, but God often uses one faithful friend to call a wanderer home.

verseByVerse.quote: But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called “today,” that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s remedy against hardening is other believers speaking to us every day, because sin deceives and a hardening heart cannot see itself. The prescription is not what we expect: not examine yourselves, or pray harder, but other people, talking to you, daily.

Exhort one another. To exhort is to call someone to your side (parakaleite), from the same root as the name Jesus gives the Holy Spirit, the Helper (John 14:16). It covers encouraging, urging, comforting and admonishing, and is neither nagging nor flattery. And it is one another: every believer to every other, not just pastors to people. The Spirit who is himself the one called alongside has put us alongside one another, so that sin’s whispering is answered every day by the voice of the gospel in the mouth of a brother.

The word of Christ between brothers. Daily encouragement carries not general cheerfulness but Christ: letting the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another (Colossians 3:16). Sin deceives by keeping a heart from looking at him; a brother answers by turning it back to him, to his cross, his promises and his return. Exhortation in Hebrews is always, in the end, another way of saying consider Jesus (3:1).

Every day, as long as it is called today. Not every week: every day, which cannot describe a congregation whose members are strangers from Sunday to Sunday. Isolated Christians are vulnerable, as a coal taken out of the fire goes grey on the hearth. And the stretch of time called today will not always be called that, both because life is short and because Christ will return.

The deceitfulness of sin. “Hardened” is passive: hardened by sin. “Deceitfulness” (apatē) is trickery, and that is sin’s method. It presents itself not as sin but as reasonable, deserved, temporary, or nobody’s business. Few people harden deliberately. They are talked into it, and the voice doing the talking is their own; a hardening heart cannot diagnose itself, because the condition feels normal from inside. So the answering voice has to be somebody else’s, and daily, because the deceiving is daily too.

A sheep to turn a sheep. God did not save us to be solitary. When a friend’s word stops you on the edge of sin, the Good Shepherd is using a sheep to turn a sheep. How kind of God, to keep us not only by his own hand but by each other’s.

What does daily exhortation look like in a busy life? Something smaller than it sounds. A text in the morning with a verse that helped you. A question over coffee: how are you doing with the Lord? Thanks to someone for their faithfulness. A gentle question when a friend says something that worries you. Praying aloud together before you part. It need not be long or eloquent, only regular and real. And it works both ways: let others into your life enough that they can say a hard thing to you. If no one ever does, ask someone to.

What if I have no Christian friends near me? Then begin by making one. Join a small group or a midweek meeting; ask an older believer if you can meet regularly; invite someone from church for a meal. If you are housebound or far from other believers, use a phone call or a message, and ask your pastor to help connect you. Isolation is not neutral for a Christian but dangerous, and God has given you his people so that you need not keep yourself alone.

verseByVerse.quote: For we have come to share in Christ, if indeed we hold our original confidence firm to the end. As it is said, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who hold their first confidence firm to the end show that they truly have come to share in Christ, so the psalm’s call still stands: do not harden your hearts.

For we have come to share in Christ. The Greek perfect tense: something that happened and stands. We have become partners (metochoi, as at 3:1 and 6:4), and remain so. What belongs to Christ is shared with you: his righteousness is credited to your account (2 Corinthians 5:21), his Father has become your Father (John 20:17), and you will share his inheritance as a fellow heir (Romans 8:17).

If indeed we hold firm. He does not say we shall share in Christ if we hold on, as though the future were in the balance, but that we have become partakers, if indeed we hold on. Holding on later proves that the sharing was real from the start.

Our original confidence. Literally the beginning of our assurance: the boldness they had when newly converted, before the property was confiscated and the neighbours turned (10:32–34). “To the end” (mechri telous) is what makes it costly: not firm while it was exciting, but to the end of life or to Christ’s return. And the one who made us his partners has promised never to dissolve the partnership: he holds the beginning of our confidence, and he will hold the end of it.

As it is said. He quoted it eight verses earlier (v. 7), and will again (4:7). A preacher who has found the sentence he needs will not let his congregation put it down.

In everyday life. Remember what first made Christ precious to you. The confidence may be quieter now, but it is probably still there. Holding firm rarely looks heroic; it looks like opening your Bible on a morning when you feel nothing, confessing the same sin again, going to church when you would rather not. Perseverance is made of ordinary days.

But do these warnings not imply that a true believer could be lost? Arminian Christians (those who believe a true Christian can finally fall away) read them so, pointing to 3:12, 6:4–6 and 10:26–29; the debate and the grammar are set out in the “Where Christians differ” box at the end of the note on vv. 5–6. The same letter says that Christ always lives to make intercession for those who draw near through him (7:25), and it ends its sternest warning by saying, we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls (10:39). Those who truly have the share are kept, and one way they are kept is by heeding warnings like this.

Can I be sure now that I will hold firm to the end? Yes, and the ground of that certainty is not your strength but Christ’s. He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6); you are guarded by God’s power through faith (1 Peter 1:5). Assurance looks first to Christ and his promises, then to the Spirit’s witness and the fruit of a changed life (2 Peter 1:10). If you are trusting Christ today and want to go on trusting him, you have every reason to expect that you will, because he is the one holding on. Your part is to keep looking to him one day at a time; his is to bring you to the end.

verseByVerse.quote: For who were those who heard and yet rebelled? Was it not all those who left Egypt led by Moses? And with whom was he provoked for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness? And to whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, but to those who were disobedient?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people God shut out were not outsiders but the very people he had rescued from Egypt, so hearing God and being rescued are not enough without trusting him. Three questions, each answered by another, close every gap between that generation and this congregation.

For who were those who heard and yet rebelled? The writer is cross-examining the psalm, and the answers come from Numbers 14. “Heard”: they heard God’s voice. “Rebelled” (parepikranan): provoked, embittered.

Was it not all those who left Egypt led by Moses? This question shuts an escape route. A reader might comfort himself that the wilderness generation were outsiders, never really in. These were the people who came out of Egypt: the redeemed ones, who kept the Passover, walked through the sea on dry ground and sang on the far shore. Caleb and Joshua did go in, but they were rare exceptions: the people who rebelled were the people who had been rescued. Privilege did not protect them, and the readers too had heard the gospel and seen God’s work.

And with whom was he provoked for forty years? God did not lose his temper at the first complaint: he bore with them, and they provoked him, for four decades.

Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness? The phrase is from Numbers 14:29, 32, and it is grim. “Bodies” (kōla) is limbs, corpses. They dropped in the desert, one funeral after another for forty years, until the whole generation was in the sand. Not at once, not dramatically: they simply never arrived.

And to whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, but to those who were disobedient? “Disobedient” (apeithēsasin) is literally unpersuadable, which shows how the letter understands unbelief. They heard, they saw, and they were not persuaded. Disobedience and unbelief are two sides of one coin (v. 19): unbelief shows itself in disobedience, and disobedience flows from unbelief. Hearing is not enough; being rescued is not enough. Paul agrees: these things happened as examples for us (1 Corinthians 10:1–11).

Led out by Moses. Moses led them out, and could not lead them in; he died on Mount Nebo looking at the land (Deuteronomy 34:4). Even Joshua did not give them the rest God meant (4:8). The letter’s answer is a leader of a different kind: the founder of salvation who has already gone through death into glory and is bringing many sons with him (2:10), and who will lose none the Father has given him (John 6:39). Israel’s journey ended in graves. The church’s road ends at home, because its leader is the Son.

Were all who died in the wilderness lost for ever? Not necessarily. Moses himself was kept out of the land, yet appears with Christ in glory (Matthew 17:3): shut out of Canaan is not shut out of heaven. But Paul says that with most of them God was not pleased (1 Corinthians 10:5), and the writer uses their fate as a picture of final loss: they heard God’s voice, saw his works and would not believe. We are not told the eternal state of each one; the warning to us is about eternity.

I grew up in church and have seen God do good things. Is that not enough? It is a great gift, but not enough on its own. The wilderness generation had one of the greatest religious upbringings in history. A Christian home, baptism, years of sermons and real answers to prayer are meant to lead you to trust Christ yourself, today; they are not the same thing. So do not lean on your background; lean on him. Ask yourself not, have I been near the things of God? but, do I believe God’s promise in Christ, and am I following him now?

verseByVerse.quote: So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel failed to enter for one reason: they would not believe God’s promise. The chapter ends on that single word, unbelief, and it is not the one we would have chosen.

That they were unable to enter. Not that they tried and were physically prevented. At Kadesh they refused to go in, and when they changed their minds and attacked in their own strength, they were routed (Numbers 14:39–45). The inability is moral. Unbelief makes entering impossible, because entering was always a matter of trusting the God who promised.

Because of unbelief. Not idolatry, though they made a calf; not grumbling, though the wilderness narratives are full of it. The writer traces both to one root: a failure to take God at his word. The calf and the complaining were symptoms. God asked Moses: “How long will they not believe in me, in spite of all the signs that I have done among them?” (Numbers 14:11). Unbelief is the sin behind all sins.

Impeccable credentials. What these readers were pressed to go back to would look like devotion: temple, sacrifices, ancestral faith. The wilderness generation also walked away from a promise with impeccable religious credentials, and died in the desert.

The mercy in where the chapter stops. Unbelief is the reason they did not enter, which means belief is the way in, and no one is too far gone to believe. Now God’s word has come in a Son. The one who says, come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28), is the Lord who led Israel through the wilderness, made flesh, and the door unbelief closed on that generation he holds open to anyone who trusts him.

Where does faith come from, if I cannot make myself believe? From God, through his word. Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (Romans 10:17), and it is the gift of God (Ephesians 2:8). You cannot squeeze it out of yourself, but you can put yourself where God gives it: under the preaching of the gospel, in the pages of Scripture, among believing people, and on your knees asking for it. Faith grows not by staring at your faith but by looking at Christ and his promises. And the smallest true faith, faith like a mustard seed, rests on the same strong Saviour as the greatest.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore, holy brothers, you who share in a heavenly calling, consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession,<sup>2</sup>who was faithful to him who appointed him, just as Moses also was faithful in all God’s house.<sup>3</sup>For Jesus has been counted worthy of more glory than Moses—as much more glory as the builder of a house has more honor than the house itself.<sup>4</sup>(For every house is built by someone, but the builder of all things is God.)<sup>5</sup>Now Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, to testify to the things that were to be spoken later,<sup>6</sup>but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son. And we are his house, if indeed we hold fast our confidence and our boasting in our hope.<sup>7</sup>Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says, “Today, if you hear his voice,<sup>8</sup>do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion, on the day of testing in the wilderness,<sup>9</sup>where your fathers put me to the test and saw my works for forty years.<sup>10</sup>Therefore I was provoked with that generation, and said, ’They always go astray in their heart; they have not known my ways.’<sup>11</sup>As I swore in my wrath, ’They shall not enter my rest.’”<sup>12</sup>Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God.<sup>13</sup>But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called “today,” that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.<sup>14</sup>For we have come to share in Christ, if indeed we hold our original confidence firm to the end.<sup>15</sup>As it is said, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion.”<sup>16</sup>For who were those who heard and yet rebelled? Was it not all those who left Egypt led by Moses?<sup>17</sup>And with whom was he provoked for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness?<sup>18</sup>And to whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, but to those who were disobedient?<sup>19</sup>So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief.

keyVerse.quote: Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God. But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called “today,” that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.
keyVerse.note: These two verses turn the whole chapter into action. The danger is a heart that slowly stops trusting the living God, and because sin deceives, the person in danger is usually the last to see it. So God’s remedy is other believers, turning one another’s eyes to Jesus (v. 1) every day, while it is still called today.

3.reflection:
The writer’s first remedy for tired believers is “consider Jesus” (v. 1). What would it look like for you to fix your mind on him on purpose this week? Which of his titles in verse 1 means most to you, and why?

Verses 2–6 honour Moses and yet set Jesus above him as builder over house and son over servant. Which good things, leaders or traditions are you tempted to lean on in a way that only Christ can bear?

The wilderness generation saw God’s works for forty years and still did not trust him (vv. 9, 16–19). Why does seeing not automatically produce believing? Where do you see that same danger in a churchgoing life?

Verse 13 says sin hardens us by deceiving us, and that the remedy is daily encouragement from one another. Who has permission to speak honestly into your life? How could your group make “exhort one another every day” a reality?

4.title: A Rest That Remains: The Throne of Grace
4.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 4 finishes the sermon on Psalm 95 that began at 3:7, and then, at verse 14, turns to the subject at the heart of the letter: Jesus our great high priest, who will fill chapters 5 to 10.

The message. God’s rest is still open, and it is his own rest: not a strip of land but a share in the Sabbath joy of the God who finished his work. We enter it by faith, ceasing from the effort to make ourselves acceptable and resting on what Christ has finished, and we will enter it fully at the end. So take the promise seriously, because God’s word sees through every pretence. But do not fear being seen through: the one at God’s right hand is a high priest who feels our weakness and has made God’s throne a throne of grace.

Why it was said. The readers were being pulled back to a religion of land, temple and ancestry (see the introduction), perhaps reasoning that Israel’s promises had been fulfilled long ago in Canaan. They were also tired and conscious of failure, half expecting a holy God to keep them at a distance. The chapter answers both: the real rest is still ahead, and the way to God is open.

How the chapter makes its case. The promise still stands, but good news does no good unless it is received by faith (vv. 1–2). Psalm 95:11 set beside Genesis 2:2 shows that the rest is God’s own, there since creation (vv. 3–5). David, long after Joshua, still says “today”, so Joshua’s rest was not the final one (vv. 6–8). A Sabbath rest therefore remains, entered by resting from our works, and we must be diligent to enter it (vv. 9–11). God’s word cuts to our motives, and every creature is laid bare before him (vv. 12–13). The answer to that exposure is the high priest: hold fast, he sympathises, draw near (vv. 14–16).

Where it leads. Joshua and Jesus share one name. The first brought Israel into a land that could not give final rest; the second has passed through death and through the heavens and leads his people into God’s own rest. He cried “It is finished” and sat down, so that we could rest too. And the eyes from which nothing is hidden are the eyes of the one who intercedes for us, who was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin.

For us. Where are you still working for God’s approval, or hiding from him what he already sees? The chapter does not say try harder. It says rest on Christ’s finished work, and come, boldly and often, to the throne where mercy and grace are given out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — There Remains a Sabbath Rest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s rest is still open, and it is his own Sabbath rest, which believers enter by faith now and fully at the end. The promise outlived the generation that refused it, and good news profits only those who receive it by faith (vv. 1–2). Genesis 2:2 shows that the rest is God’s own, there since creation (vv. 3–5), and Psalm 95, spoken through David long after Joshua, shows that Canaan was not its fulfilment (vv. 6–8). So a Sabbath rest remains, entered by resting from our works as God did from his, and we must be diligent to enter it (vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.theology:
A Rest That Remains

Psalm 95 still says today centuries after Joshua, so the land was never the rest itself. What remains is a Sabbath rest: ceasing from our own works as God did from his.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The wilderness generation heard good news, and it did not benefit them because it was not united with faith.

Now: Strive to enter that rest. Trusting God is harder work than being busy for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, while the promise of entering his rest still stands, let us fear lest any of you should seem to have failed to reach it. For good news came to us just as to them, but the message they heard did not benefit them, because they were not united by faith with those who listened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The promise of God’s rest is still open, so take care that none of you misses it: the wilderness generation heard good news too, but it did them no good because they did not receive it by faith.

The promise still stands. The foundation of the chapter is a mercy: the wilderness generation forfeited the promise, but it did not lapse with them. God went on offering rest through Moses, Joshua, David and the prophets, and at last he offered it in his Son. A God who keeps a door open that long, for people that faithless, is astonishingly patient.

Let us fear. “Fear” (phobēthōmen) is not dread of a God who might turn on us without warning; the same chapter ends by sending its readers boldly to a throne of grace. It is the fear of someone who stands near something enormous and knows he could walk past it (Philippians 2:12; 1 Peter 1:17). And again it is let us, not you must: the preacher stands inside his own warning.

Should seem to have failed. The phrasing is unexpectedly gentle: not lest any of you fail, but lest any should seem (dokē: appear, be found) to have failed. The writer will not pronounce on who is in and who is out, yet the warning keeps its full weight. “Failed to reach” means to fall short, to come too late, like a traveller who arrives after the city gates have closed for the night.

Good news came to us. That sentence should stop a reader: the wilderness generation had good news preached to them (euēngelismenoi, we have had the gospel preached). Not the same details, but the same substance: a promise of a rest they had not seen, to be received by trusting God. They heard the promise of the land; we have heard the greater good news of Christ. The God of the exodus and of the cross deals with people the same way: he promises, and calls them to believe. Timothy Keller often pointed out that the gospel is not good advice, telling us what to do to reach God, but good news, announcing what God has done; and news is not achieved, only believed or ignored.

Not united by faith. United means mixed together, blended (synkekerasmenous). The message was heard and not absorbed (see the textual note below). Food that is not eaten does not nourish, however good the meal.

Why the same sermon does different things. What makes preaching profitable is not the preacher’s eloquence or accuracy, both of which the wilderness generation had in Moses, but whether faith mixes with what is heard. The same sermon profits one person and does nothing to the man beside him. And faith takes hold of a person. The Westminster Shorter Catechism (question 86) says that faith in Jesus Christ receives and rests upon him alone for salvation, as he is offered to us in the gospel. Rest is this chapter’s very word: faith mixed with the word is a sinner leaning his whole weight on Christ, and that leaning is already the beginning of rest.

How do I mix the word with faith when I hear it? By taking it as God speaking to you, and answering him. Before the sermon or the reading, ask the Spirit to open your heart. While you listen, listen for a promise to trust, a command to obey, a warning to heed, or a glimpse of Christ to adore. Afterwards, do not just evaluate it; say to God, I believe this, tell him what you will do about it, and talk about it with someone over lunch. Faith is not a feeling during a good sermon; it is leaning your weight on what God has said.

Textual note. The manuscripts differ. In some, the message was not combined with faith in the hearers (so the KJV: “not being mixed with faith in them that heard it”). In others, the hearers were not united in faith with those who truly listened, Joshua and Caleb (so the ESV). Either way, the message was heard and not absorbed.

verseByVerse.quote: For we who have believed enter that rest, as he has said, “As I swore in my wrath, ’They shall not enter my rest,’” although his works were finished from the foundation of the world. For he has somewhere spoken of the seventh day in this way: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works.” And again in this passage he said, “They shall not enter my rest.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who believe are entering God’s own rest, the rest he took when he finished creating. The oath of Psalm 95 shut one generation out, not everyone: God did not swear that nobody would enter, but that those would not.

We who have believed enter. Present tense. These believers have joined faith to the word, and so they are entering now, in part: rest from the burden of earning salvation, peace with God, rest of conscience (Matthew 11:28–29; Romans 5:1). They will enter it fully in glory.

Finished from the foundation of the world. The point is timing. God speaks in the psalm of “my rest”, and his rest has existed since the seventh day: not something he began providing at Sinai or in Canaan, but his own rest, which he invites his people to share.

The seventh day. Genesis 2:2 supplies the definition. God rested (katepausen, ceased) not because he was tired, for he does not faint or grow weary (Isaiah 40:28), but because his work was complete: the settled satisfaction of a maker who has finished and found it very good.

The day with no evening. Every other day of creation ends with the refrain, and there was evening and there was morning. The seventh day has no such close. Many readers have seen in that silence a picture of what the writer argues: God’s rest has no end, and has been waiting for guests since the world began.

Two texts side by side. Put Genesis 2:2 and Psalm 95:11 together, and the rest Israel failed to enter turns out to be God’s own Sabbath rest, of which Canaan was only a picture. If it has existed since creation, and a whole generation missed it, then it is still there for someone else to enter, as verse 6 will say.

A second finished work. The rest believers enter now stands on another finished work. On the cross the Son cried, It is finished (John 19:30), and then sat down at the right hand of God because nothing remained to add to his sacrifice (1:3; 10:12). The rest of creation was God’s delight in a world made good; the rest of redemption is his delight in sinners made clean.

In everyday life. Watch for the places where you still work for God’s approval: the anxious overwork in ministry, the guilt after a poor quiet time, the feeling that he must be disappointed in you. Stop and say: I have believed, and I am entering his rest. Then do the thing in front of you as a child at home, not as a servant on probation.

What is this rest like now, if I have believed? It is the rest of a forgiven person who no longer has to prove himself to God. Your standing is settled, so you need not earn his favour each morning or fear losing it each evening. It is rest of conscience, guilt answered by the blood of Christ, and rest from the search for meaning, because you have found the one you were made for. It is not an easy life; these readers were suffering. But underneath the trouble there is a floor that does not move. Augustine put it in a prayer: you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.

verseByVerse.quote: Since therefore it remains for some to enter it, and those who formerly received the good news failed to enter because of disobedience, again he appoints a certain day, “Today,” saying through David so long afterward, in the words already quoted, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God was still offering his rest through David long after Joshua, the rest Joshua gave in Canaan cannot have been the rest God meant, and it is still open.

It remains for some to enter. The rest was not abolished when the wilderness generation forfeited it; their places were left open. They failed “because of disobedience”, the word from 3:18: refusing to be persuaded. To disbelieve God is to disobey him, because his word came as a promise to be trusted.

Saying through David so long afterward. The decisive argument is about dates. Psalm 95 is attributed to David in the Greek translation (the Hebrew gives it no title). Centuries after Joshua, God is still saying “today”, still holding a rest open. If the promise had been fully realised in Canaan, why would David still offer it?

If Joshua had given them rest. Joshua did give them rest, in the ordinary sense: the LORD gave them rest on every side (Joshua 21:44–45). Evidently that was not the rest God meant: a man farming his own field in Judah under David was already in the land, and God still tells him not to harden his heart today.

Joshua and Jesus. In Greek, Joshua and Jesus are the same name (Iēsous), meaning the LORD saves. The first readers would have heard it at once; the KJV, rendering the Greek directly, reads if Jesus had given them rest, though the man meant is Joshua. The first Joshua brought Israel into an earthly land, and they still needed a rest. The second Joshua, Jesus, crossed the river of death itself and came up on the far bank alive, and the land he leads his people into is God’s own rest. The land was a picture, and possessing it did not settle the question: exactly what these readers needed to hear, drawn back as they were to land, temple and ancestral religion, which had never given anyone final rest.

In everyday life. Ask what you are expecting to give you rest: the next holiday, retirement, a paid-off mortgage, a settled family, a better church. None is wrong; each is a Canaan, real and good, and not the thing itself. Enjoy them as gifts, but stop asking them to be your rest. Tell Jesus, the greater Joshua, that you are looking to him for what no land can give.

Is the promised rest the same as heaven? It includes heaven, but it is larger than a place you go when you die. It begins now, when you trust Christ and cease from trying to save yourself (v. 3). It continues as peace with God in the middle of trouble, and comes to its fullness when Christ returns and his people enter the new creation, the true promised land, where there is no more death or mourning or pain (Revelation 21:4). Canaan pictured it; heaven anticipates it; the new heavens and new earth complete it. Finally it is not a location but a share in God’s own joy.

verseByVerse.quote: So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, for whoever has entered God’s rest has also rested from his works as God did from his.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Sabbath rest still awaits God’s people, and to enter it is to stop working for God’s acceptance, as God stopped when his work was finished.

A Sabbath rest. Throughout, the writer has said katapausis, rest. Here, once, he reaches for sabbatismos, a Sabbath celebration, a word found nowhere else in the Greek Bible. What remains is not merely relief but festive rest. On the seventh day God looked at a finished world and enjoyed it, and the rest held out to us is a share in that enjoyment: to stand before God with nothing left to prove, like a guest at a feast he has prepared, not a worker waiting to be paid (Revelation 19:9).

Rested from his works. To enter this rest is to stop working, in the way God stopped: because the work was finished, and there was nothing left to add to it. For us, it means we stop trying to earn God’s acceptance and rest on what Christ has finished. To the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness (Romans 4:5). It may also refer to the final rest: blessed are the dead who die in the Lord, that they may rest from their labours (Revelation 14:13). Both are true.

Why going back was a refusal to rest. Going back to the sacrifices meant a system where the work was never finished and no priest ever sat down. It would have felt like devotion; in this chapter’s terms it was a refusal to rest.

A rest they did not earn. God finished his work and rested, and invited his people to rest with him. Then the Son did the work they could not do, cried that it was finished, lay in a tomb through the Sabbath, and rose on the first day of a new week. Ever since, his people have gathered on that day to celebrate a rest they did not earn.

What it does not mean. Resting from works does not mean doing no good works. We stop working in order to be saved, and that frees us to do good because we are saved (Ephesians 2:8–10).

How do I rest from my works when I am naturally a striver? Notice what you are trying to prove, and to whom. Strivers often quietly believe that God’s love is in proportion to their output. Answer it with the gospel every day: Christ has finished the work, and you are accepted in him, not on your performance. Keep the Lord’s Day as a gift: worship, rest, enjoy people, leave the unfinished work unfinished, and discover that the world, and God, carry on without you. Good works will still flow, from rest rather than toward it, and gladder for it.

Where Christians differ: is the weekly Sabbath still binding on Christians? Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists hold that the seventh-day Sabbath still binds. Many in the Reformed and Puritan tradition, following the Westminster Confession, hold that the Sabbath commandment continues as a creation ordinance (Genesis 2:3), transferred to Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, a day of holy rest from ordinary work. Others see the Sabbath as wholly fulfilled in Christ, with no special day required. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest (Matthew 11:28–12:8; Hebrews 4:9–10), and Christians are not bound to the Old Testament Sabbath regulations. A weekly rhythm of rest is a wise and kind gift, and the early church gathered on the first day of the week, the Lord’s Day, to celebrate Christ’s resurrection (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10). So Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy and wisdom, not as a binding law or a means of earning favour, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17). Many godly brothers, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the fourth commandment carries over to Sunday as the Christian Sabbath (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8), and their view deserves real respect.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us therefore strive to enter that rest, so that no one may fall by the same sort of disobedience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be diligent to keep trusting God’s promise, so that none of you falls short of his rest as Israel did. Here the sermon on Psalm 95 begun at 3:7 ends as it opened, with concern for every single hearer (3:12).

Strive to enter. Work hard at resting. The verb (spoudasōmen) means to be diligent, to hurry, and its object is the rest. The apparent contradiction is resolved by verse 10: the works we rest from are our efforts to make ourselves acceptable to God. The striving commanded is the effort of trusting: to keep believing, to resist hardening, to hold fast (3:6, 14), when everything in the circumstances argues against it. It is far easier to be busy for God than to believe him. Resting on a promise when the property has been confiscated and the neighbours have turned is not passive; it has to be fought for.

The same sort of disobedience. “Fall” echoes the bodies that fell in the wilderness (3:17), and “same sort” is literally the same example, the same shape of failure (1 Corinthians 10:6, 11). Note the singular once more, no one, as at 3:12 and 4:1.

A failure of nerve. At the border of a good land, the wilderness generation heard of giants and walled cities and judged it too dangerous. Their disobedience was not a wild plunge into sin but a failure of nerve at the edge of a promise, which is the danger many Christians are actually in.

The one who went in first. Israel stood at the border and would not go in; the letter’s answer is a forerunner who did. He set his face to go to Jerusalem, sweated in the garden, and fought through the darkness of the cross, so that the rest would be open to us. Jesus has passed through the heavens (4:14) and entered behind the curtain as a forerunner on our behalf (6:19–20). The striving commanded is not finding a way into God’s rest alone, but following someone who has already arrived and who always lives to intercede for those still on the road (7:25). Faith strives toward a rest that its Saviour already occupies.

If God keeps me, why must I strive? Because God keeps you by making you strive. Perseverance is God’s work in you and your work at the same time: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:12–13). Your effort is not in competition with his grace; it is the form his grace takes in you. A ship crossing the sea is carried by the wind, and the sailors still trim the sails all night. If you want to keep going with Christ, that desire is his gift, and the warning is his way of strengthening it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–16 — Laid Bare, and Invited In
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: We are laid bare before God, and invited in. God’s word cuts through every pretence to the motives underneath, and no creature is hidden from the one to whom we must give account (vv. 12–13). But the one at God’s right hand is our great high priest, the Son of God who has passed through the heavens, who was tempted as we are yet without sin and feels our weakness (vv. 14–15). So we hold fast, and draw near with confidence to a throne of grace (v. 16). These verses open the letter’s central teaching, the priesthood of Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why the Exposure Comes First

The word lays us bare, and only then does the writer say, “since then we have a great high priest” (see the note on v. 13).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Drawing near was once the privilege of priests alone.

Now: Come to the throne of grace with confidence: mercy for what lies behind, grace for what lies ahead, help that arrives when it is needed.

verseByVerse.quote: For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s word is alive and at work, and it cuts through every pretence to the real motives of the heart. That is why the call to enter God’s rest must be taken seriously (v. 11).

For the word of God. The writer has just spent eleven verses showing that a psalm of David still says today a thousand years later. “The word of God” here means especially the warnings of Psalm 95, and with them all Scripture.
