Is living and active. “Living” (zōn): it comes from the living God (3:12) and keeps speaking. “Active” (energēs, from which we get energetic) means effective, at work: it convicts, converts, comforts and sanctifies. It goes out from God’s mouth and does not return empty (Isaiah 55:10–11); it is like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces (Jeremiah 23:29).

Sharper than any two-edged sword. The sword (machaira) is not the great battle blade but the short one for close work, and the word Paul uses for the sword of the Spirit (Ephesians 6:17). “Two-edged” is literally two-mouthed, a fine touch in a passage about a word that speaks.

Soul and spirit, joints and marrow. The writer is not listing the parts of a person but piling up pairs of things that cannot ordinarily be got between. Where does soul end and spirit begin, or a joint stop and the marrow start? Nobody can find the seam; this word can.

Thoughts and intentions. Discerning means able to judge, to sift, to pass verdict (kritikos, our word critical), and the two objects are exact. Thoughts (enthymēseis): what passes through the mind. Intentions (ennoiai): the purposes underneath, what we are actually after. That is the sting. Thoughts can be reported honestly; motives are harder, because the mind is expert at supplying respectable reasons for what it wanted anyway. The word of God gets between the stated reason and the real one. We do not judge Scripture; it judges us.

The sword from his mouth. This congregation was presumably telling itself that returning to the old ways was a matter of conscience, family or prudence; here is a word that separates the reason given from the motive underneath. It is the word God has spoken in his Son (1:2), and the New Testament puts this sword in Christ’s own mouth: John saw the risen Lord with a sharp two-edged sword coming from his mouth (Revelation 1:16). In the Gospels he knew what was in man (John 2:25), and he still went looking for Peter after the denial (John 21:15–19). It lays us open as the priest’s knife laid the sacrifice bare (v. 13), not to destroy but to heal, and then carries us straight to a high priest who was already wounded for everything the blade has found (Isaiah 53:5).

Why we are the last to know ourselves. Our culture says look within and trust your gut; experience says otherwise. We see vanity in a colleague and miss it in ourselves; we know the real reason for a friend’s decision, and have only respectable reasons for our own. The seventeenth-century French writer La Rochefoucauld observed that we grow so used to disguising ourselves from others that in the end we are disguised from ourselves. Scripture said it first: “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?” (Jeremiah 17:9). So the word has to come from outside us, and we will only let it in if we know whose hand holds the blade. Someone who still has to win his case before God will fight every exposure as a threat. Someone already declared righteous in Christ can afford to be read to the bottom, because there is nothing left to defend. The gospel makes self-examination safe not by lowering the standard but by settling the verdict first.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Scripture works like magic apart from the Spirit, who uses the word.

Why does the Bible sometimes feel dead to me, if it is living? Usually the problem is at the receiving end: a dull heart, a hurried reading, a mind full of noise. Sometimes it is a season of dryness God uses to deepen trust that does not depend on feelings. Keep reading anyway, slowly, and pray before you start: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18). Read aloud, read a whole book through, read with others, memorise a verse. The word is still at work even when you do not feel it, as seed in the ground is alive before anything shows.

Where Christians differ: are soul and spirit two different parts of a person? Some teach a threefold view of human nature (body, soul and spirit as three distinct parts), using this verse and 1 Thessalonians 5:23. This commentary’s view: Scripture generally uses soul and spirit interchangeably for the immaterial part of a person (Luke 1:46–47; John 12:27 and 13:21; Matthew 10:28). The body-and-soul view (dichotomy) fits the overall biblical teaching best. This verse does not teach that soul and spirit are separate components; like joints and marrow, it pictures the word cutting to the very core of a person. Faithful Christians hold the threefold view too, and nothing in the gospel hangs on the difference.

verseByVerse.quote: And no creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing is hidden from God: every one of us stands uncovered before him, and to him we must give account. The subject shifts from the word to the one who speaks it: to be read by the word is to be seen by God, from whom nothing in all creation is hidden (Psalm 139:1–16).

Naked and exposed. “Naked” (gymna) is bare, uncovered, and it carries the whole biblical weight of the word. Sin’s first fruit was the impulse to cover up and hide among the trees of the garden, and every religious system since has been in some measure a rearrangement of fig leaves. “Exposed” is a rarer word from the word for neck, and every picture it suggests says the same thing: there is no averting the eyes (see the box below).

To whom we must give account. Literally “with whom is our word” (pros hon hēmin ho logos), a play on verse 12: God’s word judges us, and we must give our word, our account, to him. And the one before whom we stand is the Son: the Father has given all judgment to him (John 5:22; 2 Corinthians 5:10).

Stripped in order to be clothed. The chapter would be unbearable if it stopped here, with a word that divides motive from motive, a God from whom nothing is hidden, and an account to be rendered. Any honest reader should feel exposed, and is meant to. So the writer goes straight on: “Since then we have a great high priest” (4:14). He has stripped his readers in order to tell them who is standing at the throne. The one who will judge is the same one who intercedes. There is one pair of eyes from which nothing is hidden, and they are the eyes that wept over Jerusalem. The God before whom every throat is bared gave his own Son’s back to the whip and side to the spear. To be naked before him is the end of every pretence, and for those in Christ it is the beginning of being clothed in a righteousness that will never be stripped away.

Does God see the things I have done in secret, even the shameful ones? Yes, every one: terrifying if you are hiding from him, the deepest relief if you belong to Christ. You are not going to be found out; you have been fully known all along, and he loved you and sent his Son anyway (Romans 5:8). So stop spending your strength on concealment. Bring the secret to him by name in confession; he already knows it, and you need not soften it. Where it is wise, tell a mature believer too (James 5:16). What is brought into the light with God is covered by the blood of Christ (1 John 1:7–9).

Is a God who sees everything not just a cosmic surveillance camera? No. A camera records and does not care; the God of this verse sees in order to judge, and also to save. Our dread of being seen is really a dread of being rejected, which is why we work so hard managing what others know about us. The gospel offers what no camera can: to be completely known and still loved. Hagar, alone and runaway in the desert, called the LORD a God of seeing, and it was a comfort to her, not a threat (Genesis 16:13). For those who hide from him, his gaze is judgment; for those who come to Christ, it is the look of a Father who knew the worst and sent his Son anyway.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “exposed” (tetrachēlismena) is rare and hard. It comes from the word for neck, and its uses point several ways: a wrestler’s hold that seizes the throat and forces the opponent’s face upward so that he cannot look away; a sacrificial animal whose neck was drawn back to expose the throat for the knife; a criminal forced to lift his face to the judge. Which picture the writer had in mind cannot be settled, but the sense is clear: laid open, with no way to turn the face aside.

verseByVerse.quote: Since then we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God, let us hold fast our confession. For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because our high priest is the Son of God who has gone into God’s very presence, and because he feels our weakness, having been tempted in every way yet without sin, we can hold on to our confession.

A great high priest. Aaron was the high priest; Jesus is the great high priest. Straight after the letter’s most exposing sentences (v. 13), the writer returns to the title of 2:17 and 3:1 and opens the main theme of chapters 4 to 10. Almost the same words come back at 10:19–23, so these verses and those are the two bookends of the letter’s central teaching about Christ.

Passed through the heavens. “Passed through” (dielēlythota) is perfect tense: he has gone through, and the result stands. The picture is the Day of Atonement, when the high priest passed through the courts and the curtain into the Most Holy Place, once a year, with blood (Leviticus 16). At his ascension Jesus passed through the heavens themselves into the very presence of God (9:24). The tabernacle was a copy; Christ entered the reality.

Jesus, the Son of God. Both names are needed: Jesus, the man from Nazareth who was hungry and tired and wept; Son of God, whom angels worship. Truly human, he can represent us; truly God, he offers a sacrifice of infinite worth.

Hold fast. The confession is the one named at 3:1, which they are under pressure to unsay. The order matters: not hold fast, and then you will have a priest; but we have a great high priest, so hold fast.

Able to sympathize. The double negative (“not … unable”) is there because the writer knows what his readers fear. A priest who has passed through the heavens sounds magnificent and remote, too grand to understand a struggling person; the writer denies it before it can be said aloud. “Sympathise” (sympathēsai) is to suffer with, to feel together with: not pity from above, which a superior offers an inferior, but feeling with. “Weaknesses” (astheneiai) are frailties, infirmities, limitations: not only sins, but the whole fragility of being human.

Tempted in every respect. The Greek tense means he was tested and still knows it from experience. He faced every kind of temptation, to doubt God, take shortcuts, avoid suffering, seek glory, give up: not every circumstance, but every type, at full force.

Yet without sin. “Without sin” (chōris hamartias): the one exception the note on 2:17 pointed ahead to. He never sinned, in thought, word or deed (7:26; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:22; 1 John 3:5). Some think this limits his sympathy, as though the sinless could not understand sinners. The opposite is true. The man who yields to a temptation never discovers how strong it was, because he stopped the pressure early; only the one who holds out to the end feels its full weight. Far from being less qualified to sympathise, he is the only person who has ever felt the whole force of what we surrender to. And he held out for us: his unbroken obedience is the righteousness counted to those who fail (2 Corinthians 5:21).

In heaven there is a man. He has passed through the heavens, and he has not forgotten what it is to be weak. The eyes that see every heart once wept at a friend’s grave; the one who upholds the universe once sat down tired by a well (John 4:6). He took his human nature into glory and wears it still. In heaven there is a man who feels for us, and he is God.

Did Jesus face temptations like mine, sexual temptation, despair, addiction? Every kind, though not every circumstance: he was never married, never old, never addicted. He knew the pull of hunger, comfort and pride in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11), and loneliness, betrayal and the desire to escape suffering in Gethsemane. There was one difference. Our temptations often rise from desires already disordered within us (James 1:14); his came from outside, never from a sinful heart. He felt them in full; he never fed them. So bring whatever temptation you face to him without shame. He will not be shocked, and he knows the way through.

Does his sympathy mean he excuses my sin? No. He sympathises with your weakness, not your sin; he feels with you in the struggle and is on your side against it. A friend who excuses you leaves you where you are; a friend who understands and also hates what is destroying you will help you fight it. Jesus is both merciful and faithful (2:17). Come to him expecting tenderness, and expecting him to lead you out.

Where Christians differ: could Jesus have sinned? This commentary’s view: the Son of God could not sin, yet his temptations were real, because his human nature genuinely felt their pull; his inability to sin does not lessen his sympathy but makes his help sure.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So come to God freely and often, for his throne is now a throne of grace, where mercy for the past and help for the present are given out. Everything in the letter so far builds to this sentence, and everything after builds on it.

Draw near. “Draw near” (proserchōmetha) is present tense: keep coming. It is priestly language (Leviticus 9:7; 21:17), what priests did and nobody else might do. The ordinary Israelite stood at a distance; only the high priest approached God’s presence, once a year, with blood, and approaching wrongly meant death. That the whole congregation is now told to draw near, at any time, is a revolution stated in two words.

With confidence. “Confidence” (parrēsia) was originally the right of a free citizen to speak openly in the assembly, the opposite of the slave’s silence. We are to come and speak freely: not arrogance, but freedom to come without fear, because of our high priest (10:19–22).

Exposed, and invited closer. Three verses earlier everything was laid bare, and the natural response to exposure is to cover up and withdraw. The writer says: precisely because you are seen through, come closer. With nothing left to hide, exposure turns out to be liberty rather than terror.

To the throne of grace. It is a throne, not a bench or a counter: God’s royal seat, and a throne is the last place a guilty man would ordinarily approach. For sinners, God’s throne would be a throne of judgment. But because of our high priest, it is a throne of grace (tō thronō tēs charitos), where grace is given out: power that gives rather than takes, a combination the ancient world rarely imagined. Behind the phrase stands the mercy seat, the lid of the ark of the covenant, God’s throne in the Most Holy Place, where he said he would meet with his people (Exodus 25:22). It was a throne with blood on it.

Mercy and grace. The two are distinct, and both are wanted. Mercy (eleos) is not getting what we deserve, pity and forgiveness for our sins; it looks backward. Grace is getting what we do not deserve, strength for what comes next; it looks forward. We need pardon for what is behind and power for what is ahead, and both are on offer at the same seat. “In time of need” (eukairon) is one word, meaning well-timed, at the right moment. And “help” (boētheia) comes from the same root as the verb at 2:18, where he is able to help: aid brought to someone who calls for it. It is not stockpiled; it arrives when needed, so we keep coming.

The King opens his court to beggars. In the old tabernacle one man, once a year, went trembling through the curtain with blood. Now the high priest has gone through the heavens with his own blood, and the King of the universe has opened his court to beggars and tells them to come boldly. Mercy for everything behind us, grace for everything ahead, because Jesus the Son of God is there, and he is ours.

What it does not mean. We need no saints, priests or Mary to approach for us; Christ is our only and sufficient high priest (1 Timothy 2:5).

How can I come boldly when I have just sinned again? By remembering that your confidence was never in your record. You come not because you have done well this week but because your high priest has passed through the heavens with his own blood, and he is the reason the throne is a throne of grace. The moment after a sin is exactly the time of need this verse means. Do not wait until you feel worthy, or punish yourself first. Come at once, name the sin, receive the mercy, and ask for grace to do differently next time. The longer you stay away, the harder you will find it to come.

What if I do not know what to pray? Come anyway, and say so. Bring a groan, a sentence, a name. The Spirit helps us in our weakness and intercedes for us when we do not know what to pray for as we ought (Romans 8:26), and the high priest at the throne already knows your need better than you do. Use the Psalms when you have no words; pray the Lord’s Prayer slowly; tell God plainly you are tired and need help. Boldness is not eloquence. It is coming in.

keyVerse.quote: For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin. Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.
keyVerse.note: The chapter’s warnings about God’s rest and God’s searching word lead here. The one before whom we are laid bare is a high priest who knows our weakness from the inside, and because of him the throne of God has become a throne of grace. That is why weary and failing believers can keep coming, and need never go back.

4.reflection:
Verse 2 says the good news did the wilderness generation no good because it was not received by faith. What helps you hear God’s word with faith rather than as mere information, and what gets in the way?

Verses 9–10 describe God’s rest as ceasing from our own works, as God did from his. Where are you still trying to earn God’s approval, and what would resting in Christ’s finished work look like there this week?

Verses 12–13 say God’s word lays bare the thoughts and intentions of the heart. Why is it frightening to be fully known, and how do verses 14–16 change that fear?

Jesus was “tempted as we are, yet without sin” (v. 15). How does his sympathy help you in your own weakness? What keeps you from drawing near to the throne of grace with confidence, especially straight after you have failed?

5.title: The Qualifications of the Perfect Priest
5.overview:
Where we are. At 4:14–16 the writer named Jesus “a great high priest” and invited the weary to the throne of grace. Chapter 5 begins to show what that means, opening the letter’s central argument, Christ’s priesthood after the order of Melchizedek, which runs to 10:18; then it breaks off to shake the hearers awake (5:11–6:20).

The message. Jesus is the high priest you need, and God himself appointed him. Every high priest had to be one of the people, gentle with those who stumble, and called by God rather than self-made. Jesus is all of these, without the flaw of needing a sacrifice for his own sins. He did not take the honour; the Father gave it, in the words of Psalm 110, “You are a priest forever”. And he was fitted for the work in anguish: the eternal Son prayed with loud cries and tears and learned in suffering what obedience costs. But the hearers are not ready for all this, not because it is too deep but because they have grown dull, and the cure is not more information but a faith that is put to use.

Why it was said. The readers were being drawn back to a visible priesthood in a temple that was still standing (see the introduction). A priest they could see, from the proper family, felt safer than one in heaven they could not see. The writer shows that Aaron’s line was only ever a sketch of the priest God promised. And he faces the deeper problem honestly: people who have stopped listening are not won back by a better argument alone.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–4 set out what makes a high priest: he is taken from among men, acts for them before God with gifts and sacrifices, deals gently with the ignorant and wayward because he too is weak, and is called by God, as Aaron was. Verses 5–10 show Christ meeting each mark, in reverse order: called by God as Son and priest (vv. 5–6), sharing our weakness in prayer and tears (vv. 7–8), and made perfect as the source of eternal salvation (vv. 9–10). Verses 11–14 turn to the hearers: they ought to be teachers, yet need milk again, because maturity comes by practice, and they have stopped practising.

Where it leads. Every high priest of Aaron’s line went into the Most Holy Place with blood for his own sins first. Our high priest needed none for himself, yet no priest ever came closer to the weakness of those he served. He knelt in a garden and pleaded with tears, and he was heard, not by being spared death but by being brought through it. The gentleness of verse 2 has a face: the Son who sweated in Gethsemane while his friends slept a stone’s throw away, and then went to die for them.

For us. You do not need to be strong to come to this priest; his office exists for the ignorant and the wayward. But you do need to be listening. Has the word been washing over you lately? What was the last thing God plainly showed you, and have you done it?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus is a true high priest, called by God and fitted for the work by suffering. Verses 1–4 set out the marks of a high priest: one of the people, acting for them before God, gentle with the weak because weak himself, and appointed by God, not self-chosen. Verses 5–10 show that Christ has them, in reverse order: his call by God as Son and priest (vv. 5–6), his share in human weakness (vv. 7–8), and the eternal salvation he brings (vv. 9–10). Where Aaron’s weakness meant sins of his own, Christ’s meant tears, prayer and obedience.
verseByVerse.theology:
Appointed, Not Self-Chosen

Christ shares our weakness and was called by God, and is named a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In the days of his flesh he prayed with loud cries and tears, and was heard.

Now: An answer that does not come in the form we asked for is not proof that we were unheard (see the note on v. 7).

verseByVerse.quote: For every high priest chosen from among men is appointed to act on behalf of men in relation to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. He can deal gently with the ignorant and wayward, since he himself is beset with weakness. Because of this he is obligated to offer sacrifice for his own sins just as he does for those of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A high priest is one of the people, appointed to bring them to God with sacrifices, and gentle with sinners because he is weak himself. The same weakness means he must also offer for his own sins.

What a high priest is. In Israel the high priest was the descendant of Aaron who alone, once a year on the Day of Atonement, went behind the curtain into the Most Holy Place with blood. Everything the readers loved about the temple came to its point in that one man on that one day.

Chosen from among men. The first mark: he is taken from among human beings (ex anthrōpōn lambanomenos), one of the people he represents. Only one who shares the condition of those he represents can stand for them, which is why the Son had to be made like his brothers in every respect (2:14–17). Not an angel, nor God in his bare deity: the one who would stand for us had to have our flesh.

On behalf of men. The second: he acts for people in their dealings with God (ta pros ton theon, as at 2:17). A prophet faces the people with a word from God; a priest faces God on behalf of the people, and his work is to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. So the letter will soon ask what this priest offers (8:3; 9:14).

Deal gently. The third mark, and the one he dwells on. The rare word metriopathein means to moderate one’s feelings, taking the measured path between two failures, indifference to sin and rage at it. One shrugs and leaves the sinner in his sin; the other explodes and drives him away from the altar. Anyone who has confessed something shameful to a minister knows how much it matters that the man across the desk neither flinches nor pretends it does not matter.

The ignorant and the wayward. He deals gently with those who sin without knowing (agnoousin) and those who wander off (planōmenois), like sheep that drift. Not the defiant. The law made provision for sins of ignorance and weakness, but none for the high-handed sin of a man who despised the word of the LORD with his eyes open (Numbers 15:27–31). That boundary surfaces again at 6:4–6 and 10:26. A priest’s gentleness is for the stumbling, not the scornful.

Beset with weakness. The verb perikeitai means to have something lying round you; it is used of the chain round Paul (Acts 28:20). Here weakness is worn like a garment, and it makes the gentleness possible: a man who knows his own frailty from the inside cannot despise anyone else’s. Harshness toward people who fail usually grows from forgetting our own failures; the self-righteous heart needs others to look worse so that it can feel safe.

For his own sins. The weakness that makes him sympathetic also makes him a sinner, who needs a sacrifice himself. On the Day of Atonement Aaron had first to offer a bull for himself and his house, and only then for the people (Leviticus 16:6, 11). That is the gap Christ fills. He shares our weakness but not our sin (4:15), and needs no sacrifice for himself (7:27). Every Aaron who ever stood at the altar went in trembling for his own sins; our high priest went in clean.

In everyday life. Who do you find it hardest to be patient with when he fails? Measured feeling is a priestly quality, now asked of every believer (1 Peter 2:9): neither shrug nor explode. And when you are the one who has fallen, notice where you go: away from God until you feel better, or straight to the high priest whose office exists for people in exactly your state.

How can a sinless Christ really understand my weakness? Because weakness and sin are not the same thing. Weakness is hunger, tiredness, grief, fear, being tempted and misunderstood; Jesus knew every one, hungry in the desert, weary at the well, troubled in the garden. Sin is giving way. And the one who never gives way feels temptation’s full force, because he has not let it off by yielding: the man who resists a storm all night knows its strength better than the one who goes indoors after ten minutes. You are not explaining your weakness to a stranger, but bringing it to the one person who has carried it all the way to the end.

Where Christians differ: are Christian ministers priests? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches call their clergy priests, who offer the sacrifice of the Mass (the Catholic name for the Lord’s Supper; the Orthodox speak of the Divine Liturgy) on behalf of the people. Many there love Christ sincerely; the disagreement is about what his once-for-all sacrifice leaves to be done. This commentary’s view: The New Testament never calls Christian ministers priests (hiereis) in this sense. Jesus is the one and only high priest of the new covenant, whose sacrifice was offered once for all (7:27; 9:25–28; 10:10–14), and there is no further sacrifice for sin to offer. All believers together are a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices of praise and good works (1 Peter 2:5, 9; Hebrews 13:15–16). Ministers are elders and shepherds, not sacrificing priests, and the Lord’s Supper is a remembrance and spiritual feeding on Christ, not a re-offering of him.

verseByVerse.quote: And no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one may make himself high priest; God must call him, as he called Aaron. The office is an honour to be given, never grasped.

Called by God, as Aaron was. The high priesthood was an honour (timē), never to be applied for or earned. God chose Aaron and his sons (Exodus 28:1), and when the tribes challenged it, he settled the matter with a sign (Numbers 17). It was plainly not Aaron’s by merit: this was the man who made the golden calf. It rested on God’s choice, not the man’s worth.

Scripture keeps this boundary with severity. Korah and his company were swallowed by the ground (Numbers 16); Saul lost his kingdom for offering the sacrifice himself (1 Samuel 13:8–14); King Uzziah went into the temple to burn incense and came out a leper (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). The severity is not arbitrary. If a man could appoint himself to represent others before God, the sinner’s hope would be only as good as the priest’s opinion of himself.

The setting. By the first century the high priesthood had become notoriously political. Herod and then the Roman governors appointed and deposed high priests at will, and the office was traded around a few powerful families; Annas and Caiaphas, who handed Jesus over, belonged to one of them (John 18:13). Readers tempted back toward the temple were being tempted toward a priesthood that had plainly taken the honour for itself. The writer goes back past all of it to God’s calling.

The staff that budded overnight. Korah grasped and fell, Uzziah grasped and was struck; the Son, who of all beings had the right to grasp, waited to be given. Set beside him the sign that settled Aaron’s call. A cut, dead stick was laid before the LORD, and in the morning it had budded, blossomed and borne ripe almonds: life out of deadness was God’s own seal on the priest he had chosen (Numbers 17:8). Hebrews remembers that staff, kept in the ark (9:4), and rests Jesus’ priesthood on a far greater seal of the same kind. He is priest by the power of an indestructible life (7:16), declared to be the Son of God in power by his resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:4). The Father gave him the honour, and proved it by an empty tomb.

In everyday life. Notice where you push for recognition: the credit you quietly steer toward yourself, the resentment when someone else is asked. Let God do the exalting (1 Peter 5:6). The person who has to appoint himself is always anxious about his position; the person God has placed can afford to be content.

How does a man know whether God is calling him to be a pastor? Not usually by a voice or vision, and Scripture never asks for one. Look for three things together: a desire to serve Christ’s people rather than be seen (1 Timothy 3:1); the character Paul lists, mostly ordinary godliness that others can verify: faithful in marriage, self-controlled, hospitable, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money, managing his home well (1 Timothy 3:2–7; Titus 1:5–9); and the ability to teach, confirmed by the elders and congregation who know him, not merely asserted by himself. The call of God normally comes through the church’s judgment, which is the opposite of taking the honour for oneself.

verseByVerse.quote: So also Christ did not exalt himself to be made a high priest, but was appointed by him who said to him, “You are my Son, today I have begotten you”; as he says also in another place, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ did not make himself high priest: God appointed him, the one he calls his Son, a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek.

Christ did not exalt himself. The one person who could have claimed the office in his own right did not. The Son through whom the world was made (1:2) waited to be given it. He “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped” (Philippians 2:6), and he said, “It is my Father who glorifies me” (John 8:54).

You are my Son. Two quotations make the appointment. The first, Psalm 2:7 (already at 1:5), establishes the relationship. Before office, there is sonship: the one who brings us to God is himself at home with God.

A priest forever. The second is Psalm 110:4, on which the whole letter turns. The psalm’s first verse, where the LORD tells David’s Lord to sit at his right hand, was quoted at 1:13. In a psalm Jesus himself read as speaking of the Messiah (Mark 12:35–37), God swears that the coming king will be a priest. Under Israel’s law that was impossible: kings came from Judah and priests from Levi, and the two lines never crossed.

Unless the priesthood in question is not Levitical. No Levitical priest could be a priest “forever”, since they all died. So God names another order: “after the order of” means of the rank or kind of Melchizedek, a line older than Levi and independent of him.

Who was Melchizedek? He appears in three verses of Genesis and nowhere else in the Old Testament except this psalm: king of Salem (probably the old name for Jerusalem; compare Psalm 76:2) and priest of God Most High in Abraham’s day. When Abraham returned from rescuing Lot, Melchizedek met him with bread and wine, blessed him, and received a tenth of the spoils (Genesis 14:18–20). Levi and Aaron did not yet exist, and he was king and priest at once; chapter 7 explains why that matters. For now the point is simple: God promised a priest who would also be king, and who would never die.

The writer stops. He names Melchizedek here and does not return to him until 6:20 (on why, see v. 11).

Does “today I have begotten you” mean the Son had a beginning? No. The psalm was first spoken over David’s son on the day he was crowned, when God publicly owned the king as his son. Paul applied the “today” to the day God raised and enthroned Jesus (Acts 13:33): the day the eternal Son was publicly installed as the messianic king and priest. It is a coronation word, not a birth certificate. Hebrews has already said that the Son made the worlds and is the exact imprint of God’s nature (1:2–3); he had no beginning, and the church confessed it in the Nicene Creed: he is “begotten, not made”.

verseByVerse.quote: In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his earthly life Jesus prayed in anguish to the Father who could save him from death, and the Father heard him. Here the Son shares our weakness to the full, as a high priest must (v. 2).

In the days of his flesh. The years when the Son lived in a body that could tire and bleed and die. Those days are over, but what happened in them is the ground of everything this priest is for us.

Prayers and supplications. “Offered up” is the priestly word of verse 1. “Supplications” (hiketērias) was used of the suppliant who came holding an olive branch wrapped in wool, the sign of a man pleading for his life. He who upholds the universe (1:3) pleaded like that, for us.

With loud cries and tears. Strong crying (kraugēs ischyras), a shout rather than a murmur, and tears. Most likely the writer means Gethsemane, where Jesus said his soul was very sorrowful, even to death, where his sweat became like great drops of blood, and where he prayed three times for the cup to pass (Matthew 26:36–46; Luke 22:39–46); perhaps he includes the cries from the cross (Mark 15:34, 37). Luke 22:43–44, with the angel and the sweat like drops of blood, is missing from some early manuscripts, though many others include it, so most modern Bibles keep it with a note. No Gospel records tears in the garden; the writer either knows more about that night or draws out what the Gospels imply. Either way, the Son of God did not face the cup with serene detachment.

Why did he pray like that? Many brave men have died calmly, but the cup was not merely death. What Jesus faced was the wrath of God against sin, poured out on the one who would bear it for others (Isaiah 53:10; Mark 14:36). His holy human soul recoiled from it as no sinful soul ever could, because he knew the Father’s love perfectly and was about to be forsaken. The loud cries are the measure of what our salvation cost.

Able to save him from death. The Father could have rescued him from dying. The Greek can also be read as save him out of death (ek thanatou): bring him through death and out the other side, in resurrection.

He was heard. Every reader feels the difficulty: he was heard, and he died. The answer lies in the prayer itself, which was conditional: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). A prayer that ends that way is answered when the Father’s will is done, and it was. He was strengthened in the garden (Luke 22:43), carried through death and raised out of it on the third day: heard, not by escaping death, but by triumphing over it. And he was heard “because of his reverence” (eulabeia, godly fear), the attitude of a son who wants above everything not to displease his Father, not because of the volume of the crying.

In everyday life. The Son of God did not get what he asked in the form he asked it, and was heard. Unanswered prayer is not evidence of being unheard. Bring the request again, with tears if they come, and leave the form of the answer with him. A no that ends in resurrection is a better answer than a yes that ends anywhere else.

Why would the Son of God need to pray at all? Because he was truly man as well as truly God, and a true man depends on God. Jesus prayed through the night before choosing the twelve, rose early to pray, prayed at his baptism and on the mountain, not as an act for the disciples’ benefit. In his human nature he lived by faith in his Father, as we must, and in the garden that dependence was tested to the uttermost. His prayers are part of the obedience by which he saved us.

Is it wrong for me to cry out to God in anguish, or to ask him to take something away? No. The sinless Son did both. Loud cries and tears are faith speaking honestly to the only one who can help, and the Psalms are full of them. What made Jesus’ prayer holy was not calm but submission: he asked plainly, then put the Father’s will above his own. Ask God with all your heart to heal, rescue or spare; then learn to add his words: nevertheless, not my will, but yours.

Is this not a Father forcing his Son to suffer? No. Father and Son are one God with one saving purpose, and the Son came gladly to do his Father’s will (John 4:34); no one takes his life from him, he lays it down of his own accord (John 10:18). The cries show how terrible the cost was, not that he was coerced: “not my will, but yours” is the free choice of a Son who loves his Father and his people. The cross is not one person punishing another for his own satisfaction; it is the triune God himself bearing the cost of saving sinners, in the person of the Son.

Uncertain wording. “Because of his reverence” translates apo tēs eulabeias. The noun usually means reverence or godly fear, as in 12:28 (“with reverence and awe”), and the preposition most naturally gives the reason he was heard, as the ESV takes it. But the word can also mean fear or dread, and some have read the phrase as meaning that he was heard and set free from his fear, that is, from the terror he felt; the King James has “was heard in that he feared”. The ESV’s reading fits the word’s use elsewhere and is the likely meaning. Either way, the Father heard his Son.
verseByVerse.note: Most likely a reference to Jesus’ agony in Gethsemane.

verseByVerse.quote: Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered. And being made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him, being designated by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son learned in suffering what obedience costs, and, made perfect through it, he became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him. God has named him high priest after the order of Melchizedek.

Although he was a son. Sonship did not exempt him from suffering; in this letter suffering is the path by which he leads many sons to glory (2:10).

He learned obedience. The Greek plays on two words that sound alike: emathen, he learned, and epathen, he suffered, echoing a familiar Greek proverb that suffering teaches. It cannot mean he moved from disobedience to obedience, for he was never disobedient. He learned it by experience: the difference between a man who has always intended to be loyal and the same man after loyalty has cost him everything. In the garden and on the cross he came to know what obedience weighs, as he became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8). And it was obedience in our place. We never obey perfectly; he did, and by the one man’s obedience the many are made righteous (Romans 5:19).

Made perfect. Brought to completion, made fully fit for an office (as at 2:10): not moral improvement, since he had no flaw, but fully equipped as Saviour and High Priest.

The source of eternal salvation. Source means cause (aitios): he does not merely point the way to salvation, he brings it about. And it is eternal: an annually repeated sacrifice produced an annually repeated forgiveness; the salvation Christ causes lasts forever (9:12).

To all who obey him. Not those who believe, as we might expect, but those who obey (hypakouousin, literally those who listen and respond). In this letter the two are not alternatives. The wilderness generation’s failure was called disobedience in one verse and unbelief in the next (3:18–19; 4:6). Paul speaks of the obedience of faith (Romans 1:5; 16:26), and John sets believing in the Son against not obeying the Son (John 3:36). Faith that never moves the feet was never the thing Hebrews means by faith. And notice the symmetry: he learned obedience; he saves those who obey. The road the Son walked is the road his people walk, and his Spirit now walks it in us.

Designated by God. God publicly hailed him high priest in the words of Psalm 110:4. The writer is ready to explain it, but he has looked at his congregation and seen that they cannot yet take it in.

What it does not mean. “All who obey him” does not mean salvation is earned by obedience. The obedience in view is trusting and following Christ, the fruit and expression of faith.

Am I among those who obey him, when my obedience is so patchy? The verse describes the direction of a life, not a flawless record. Those who obey him have bowed to him as Lord, want to do his word, fight sin, confess it when they fall, and keep coming back. Your obedience will be imperfect all your life (1 John 1:8–9); what marks a believer is that he does not make peace with failing, and runs to Christ, not away from him. Grief over your disobedience and longing to please him are themselves his Spirit’s work in you. And remember whose obedience saves you: his, offered perfectly in your place.

Does suffering make me holier automatically? No. Suffering is a tool in a Father’s hand (12:5–11), but the same trial that softens one man hardens another; it trains those who keep trusting God in it. Jesus learned obedience through suffering because he kept obeying while he suffered. So in pain, keep doing the next right thing, keep praying, keep trusting, and the suffering will not be wasted.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer cannot yet go on to Melchizedek, because his hearers have stopped listening. The trouble is not the subject but their ears (v. 11). They have known the faith long enough to teach it, yet they need the ABC again, like grown children still on milk (vv. 12–13). Maturity is a trained sense, built by constant practice in telling good from evil (v. 14), so the cure is not more information but faith put to use.
verseByVerse.theology:
What Maturity Actually Is

Maturity is not a store of information but a trained sense (see the note on v. 14).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The readers had become dull of hearing; they had not always been so.

Now: When Scripture seems dry, ask whether the dullness is in the passage or in the hearer.

verseByVerse.quote: About this we have much to say, and it is hard to explain, since you have become dull of hearing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer has much more to say about Christ’s priesthood, but it is hard to get across, because his hearers have grown sluggish in listening. The difficulty lies in their ears, not in the subject.

About this we have much to say. At the door of his central argument the writer stops. There is much more to say about Melchizedek, and he will say it (7:1–28), but first he must deal with the ears that will hear it. From here to the end of chapter 6 he steps aside, and the step aside is part of the argument: rebuke (5:11–14), call to go on (6:1–3), warning (6:4–8), encouragement (6:9–12) and God’s oath (6:13–20). At 6:20 Melchizedek returns.

Hard to explain. Dysermēneutos means hard to put into words, and the reason is not that the subject is obscure but “since you have become dull of hearing”. It is a bold thing for a preacher to say, and he says it without malice. He has called these people holy brothers (3:1) and will call them beloved (6:9). He is not writing them off, only telling them why the sermon is stalling.

Dull of hearing. “Dull” is nōthroi: sluggish, slow, heavy, a word used of a numb limb or a lazy animal; it comes back at 6:12, translated “sluggish”. The decisive word is “become” (gegonate, a perfect tense: you have become, and you are now). They were not always like this. Once they took the word in eagerly and stood their ground publicly, losing property for it, as the writer will remind them (10:32–34). The dullness was acquired gradually, probably without their noticing: the drifting 2:1 warned of, showing first in how they listen. Few people decide to stop hearing. Often the truth begins to demand change or suffering, and the easiest way to avoid a demand is not to hear it clearly.

The ear that was never dull. Set these sluggish hearers beside their priest. The Greek word for obedience (hypakoē) is built on the verb to hear, and Jesus learned obedience (5:8): his whole life was hearing his Father and doing what he heard. Isaiah gives the Servant’s own testimony: morning by morning the Lord GOD wakens his ear to hear as one who is taught, and he is not rebellious; he gives his back to those who strike him (Isaiah 50:4–6). That is Gethsemane and the cross. Our ears grow dull; his never did, and our salvation rests on that perfect hearing. He is also the word these readers had stopped attending to, for God has spoken to us by his Son (1:2).

He stopped his greatest argument. How patient God is with slow hearers. Instead of closing the book on a congregation that had stopped listening, he stopped his greatest argument to win them back to it. Christ has far more to say to us than we have ever taken in, and he opens our ears, because he means us to hear every word.

In everyday life. Read on Saturday the passage that will be preached and pray over it for a few minutes; the sermon becomes a conversation already begun.

How can I tell whether I have become dull of hearing? Sermons wash over you, and by Sunday lunch you cannot say what the text was. You know the answers, but they no longer surprise or humble you. You read the Bible, if at all, to tick it off. You prefer teaching that entertains or confirms what you already think. And you have not acted on the last thing God clearly showed you. That last sign is usually the root: the ear grows dull when the will has stopped obeying. The remedy begins not with more information but with doing the last thing you heard, and then asking God, honestly, to open your ears again (Psalm 119:18).

verseByVerse.quote: For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to teach you again the basic principles of the oracles of God. You need milk, not solid food, for everyone who lives on milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, since he is a child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers who have known the faith long enough to teach it, yet still need its first lessons, are like grown children still living on milk. The rebuke is not that they know little but that they have not grown.

By this time you ought to be teachers. These were not new converts; they should have been instructing others, and instead need the alphabet again. Not that everyone should hold office (James 3:1), but the ordinary path of a believer runs from being taught to being able to explain: a parent explaining the gospel to a child, a friend opening a passage over coffee, an older woman training a younger (Titus 2:3–5).

The basic principles. Ta stoicheia tēs archēs, the elements of the beginning, the ABC of “the oracles of God”, his revealed word. Chapter 6 lists the first things (6:1–2).

Milk, not solid food. Paul uses the same image (1 Corinthians 3:1–2), and Peter tells new believers to long for pure spiritual milk (1 Peter 2:2). Milk is exactly right for an infant; the problem is a person still on it years later. “Unskilled” (apeiros) is literally without experience, never having handled the thing.

Knowledge that is never used. The complaint is not that they have not read enough, but that knowledge never exercised matures nobody. A man can sit under good teaching for decades and remain an infant, because hearing without doing produces nothing (James 1:22–25). And knowledge can become an idol of its own. Knowing the right answers can make a person feel safe with God while keeping him at arm’s length, which is a very religious way of not listening.

Milk and solid food are both Christ. The oracles of God, in this letter, have one climax: in these last days God has spoken to us by his Son (1:2). The ABC these readers keep relearning is the first word about Christ (6:1), and the solid food the writer longs to serve them is more of Christ: his priesthood after the order of Melchizedek. Growing up is never growing past him into something more advanced, but going deeper into the one in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). The infant and the mature are fed at the same table, and the food is the same person. God rebukes his children for staying small because he has prepared a banquet for them, and will not be content until they sit down to it.

Does this verse condemn me if I am not a natural teacher? It does not ask you to become a preacher. It asks whether you have grown enough to help someone else understand and follow Christ. Can you explain simply who Jesus is and why he died, or point a struggling friend to a promise? If not yet, that is a direction for growth, not a reason for shame. Learn one passage well enough to explain it, and then explain it to one person. Teaching in this sense is mostly the overflow of a believer who has been feeding well.

Uncertain wording. “The word of righteousness” is a compressed phrase, found only here, and its exact sense is uncertain. It may mean the message about righteousness, how God makes sinners right with himself; or the skill of using God’s word to tell right from wrong; or simply mature, right teaching as against the ABC. Verse 14, which speaks of distinguishing good from evil, makes the second the likely meaning, though the three overlap.

verseByVerse.quote: But solid food is for the mature, for those who have their powers of discernment trained by constant practice to distinguish good from evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Maturity is a trained sense, built up by habitual practice, that can tell good from evil. Solid food belongs to those whose faith has been put to use.

Solid food is for the mature. “Mature” (teleioi) is grown-up, related to the word for Christ being made perfect in verse 9.

Powers of discernment trained. Aisthētēria are literally the organs of perception, the physical senses. Moral and spiritual judgment is pictured as a sense that perceives directly, like a trained palate that knows good food from bad without consulting a chart. “Trained” is gegymnasmena, the gymnasium word, from which we get gymnastics: exercised as an athlete trains a body. The form of the verb means trained in the past and still fit now.

By constant practice. Hexis: habit, a condition produced by repetition. Not by a crisis or a conference.

To distinguish good from evil. Both moral good and evil and true and false teaching. The readers needed to discern that the old covenant, though good, had been surpassed, and that turning back would be turning away from Christ.

The measure of the mature. Maturity, the goal of the whole Christian life, is measured by the stature of the fullness of Christ (Ephesians 4:13). Tempted in the wilderness, he told good from evil at once and answered every lie with Scripture (Matthew 4:1–10). Christian maturity is the mind of Christ formed in his people (1 Corinthians 2:16), until his instincts become theirs. The Son who was made perfect through suffering is bringing many sons to that same maturity, and he is a patient trainer: he feeds, exercises and corrects us for a lifetime, until at last we see him and are like him, with every sense awake to his glory.

The comfort in it. Solid food is withheld from these readers not because they are unintelligent but because the sense has not been exercised. That is comfort as well as rebuke: if maturity came by intellect, most Christians would be excluded; it comes by practice, which is open to everybody. The grandmother who has never read a theology book but can smell false teaching at fifty paces is mature in exactly this sense. And the writer’s next words, at the head of chapter 6, call them to “go on to maturity” (6:1). He does not leave them where they are.

How do I actually train my discernment? The way an athlete trains: small, regular, real exercises. Read Scripture daily, asking what each passage shows you of God and asks of you. Before decisions, even small ones about words, money, time or entertainment, ask what God’s word says, act on it, and notice afterwards whether it was right. Test teaching with an open Bible (Acts 17:11). Watch how mature believers judge things. Confess quickly when you get it wrong. Over years, what began as slow, deliberate thinking becomes instinct.

Is discernment the same as being critical? No. Some mistake suspicion for discernment and spend their lives finding fault with sermons and other Christians. The discernment of this verse recognises and delights in the good as quickly as it detects the evil. A mature palate relishes what is good, not only spits out the bad. True discernment makes a person humbler, more thankful and more careful with his own heart, not sharper with everyone else’s.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>For every high priest chosen from among men is appointed to act on behalf of men in relation to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.<sup>2</sup>He can deal gently with the ignorant and wayward, since he himself is beset with weakness.<sup>3</sup>Because of this he is obligated to offer sacrifice for his own sins just as he does for those of the people.<sup>4</sup>And no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was.<sup>5</sup>So also Christ did not exalt himself to be made a high priest, but was appointed by him who said to him, “You are my Son, today I have begotten you”;<sup>6</sup>as he says also in another place, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”<sup>7</sup>In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence.<sup>8</sup>Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered.<sup>9</sup>And being made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him,<sup>10</sup>being designated by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek.<sup>11</sup>About this we have much to say, and it is hard to explain, since you have become dull of hearing.<sup>12</sup>For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to teach you again the basic principles of the oracles of God. You need milk, not solid food,<sup>13</sup>for everyone who lives on milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, since he is a child.<sup>14</sup>But solid food is for the mature, for those who have their powers of discernment trained by constant practice to distinguish good from evil.

keyVerse.quote: Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered. And being made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him,
keyVerse.note: These verses hold the chapter’s heart: the high priest God appointed was fitted for his work not by ceremony but by suffering. The Son never needed to be made obedient, yet he learned in Gethsemane and at the cross what obedience costs, and that finished obedience is now the cause of a salvation that never runs out. The same verses quietly show the shape of the Christian life: those he saves are those who listen to him and follow.

5.reflection:
Verses 1–3 say a high priest must deal gently with the ignorant and wayward, neither shrugging at sin nor exploding at it. Which way do you lean when someone fails, and how does Jesus’ gentleness with you change that?

Jesus prayed “with loud cries and tears” and “was heard” (v. 7), yet he still went to the cross. What does his prayer teach you about bringing anguish to God, and about prayers that seem to go unanswered?

The writer says his readers have “become dull of hearing” (v. 11). What are the signs that the word has stopped reaching us, and what helps you to hear it again?

According to verse 14, maturity comes by “constant practice” in telling good from evil. What is one ordinary, everyday decision where you could begin to practise this deliberately this week?

6.title: Press On to Maturity: The Anchor of the Soul
6.overview:
Where we are. At 5:11 the writer broke off his teaching on Christ’s priesthood to rouse his dull hearers. Chapter 6 completes that pause, the third and sharpest of the letter’s warnings, and ends by bringing him back to Melchizedek (v. 20), ready for chapter 7.

The message. There is no standing still with Christ: go on, or you will slide back. Some people come close enough to the gospel to taste its gifts and still turn away for good, and for them there is no other sacrifice to come back to. But the writer is sure of better things for his beloved readers, because he can see the fruit of salvation in them, and God will not forget it. And their hope does not finally rest on the strength of their grip. It rests on God’s promise, confirmed by his oath, and on Jesus, who has gone into God’s presence ahead of them and holds them there like an anchor.

Why it was said. Persecution and weariness were pulling the readers back toward the synagogue, whose beliefs overlapped with the first lessons of the Christian faith (see the introduction). Going back looked like a small step. The writer shows them how great a step it would be, and how secure is the hope they would be leaving.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–3 call them to build on the foundation instead of laying it again, and list its six stones in three pairs. Verses 4–8 give the reason standing still is dangerous: those who have been enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift and shared in the Spirit, and then fall away, cannot be restored to repentance; two fields drink the same rain, and the crop shows which is which. Verses 9–12 turn at once to confidence: the writer sees their love for God’s people and urges each of them to keep hope’s full assurance to the end. Verses 13–20 ground that hope in God himself, who swore by himself to Abraham, so that by two unchangeable things, his promise and his oath, frightened people may hold on to an anchor fixed behind the curtain.

Where it leads. The chapter’s two impossibilities face each other: it is impossible to restore those who finally reject Christ (v. 4), and it is impossible for God to lie (v. 18). Between them stands the only sacrifice there is. The Son of God was crucified once, and to turn from him is ruin, because there is nothing beside him; to flee to him is life, because there is nothing his blood cannot cover. The oath God swore on the mountain over Abraham’s spared son was kept at Calvary, where God did not spare his own. And the high priest who went behind the curtain did not come out again alone: he went in as our forerunner, and the rope is fastened to us.

For us. Warning and assurance belong to the same sermon. If these verses frighten you, the fear itself is a good sign; run to Christ, the city of refuge whose gates are never shut. If they do not move you at all, ask what is growing in your field.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Hardest Warning, and the Confidence After It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Standing still is not safe, so go on to maturity, and go on in hope. The writer calls his hearers to build on the foundation instead of laying it again (vv. 1–3). He warns that those who have tasted the blessings of the gospel and then turn away cannot be restored, like a field that drinks the rain and bears only thorns (vv. 4–8). At once he adds that he is sure of better things for them, because God has seen their love (vv. 9–10), and he urges each one to keep hope’s full assurance to the end, like those who inherit the promises through faith and patience (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Passage Set Out Honestly

Sincere Christians read verses 4–6 differently. The list describes what was received and seen, not what saves; and five verses later the writer calls his readers beloved and speaks of things that belong to salvation.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Two fields drink the same rain; the crop shows the soil.

Now: The warning is not addressed to the anxious. God is not unjust so as to overlook love shown in serving the saints.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us leave the elementary doctrine of Christ and go on to maturity, not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God, and of instruction about washings, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. And this we will do if God permits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not keep laying the foundation of the faith again; build on it, and go on to maturity in Christ. The writer includes himself, and knows that the progress depends on God.

Let us leave the elementary doctrine. “Leave” sounds alarming until you see the picture, a building: “not laying again a foundation”. You do not abandon a foundation by building on it, but by digging it up every few years to check it is still there. These readers kept returning to the basics and never got a wall up.

In the flow. The “therefore” is surprising: he has just said they need milk (5:12), and now he says, let us go on. Standing still is not safe (vv. 4–8), so he gives them solid food, Christ’s priesthood (chapter 7), and trusts God to make them able to take it in (v. 3).

Go on to maturity. Literally, let us be carried along (pherōmetha, passive), used of a ship running before the wind and of the prophets carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:21). God carries his people forward into the knowledge of Christ, which has no ceiling: growth is something we press into and something God does to us at once. And he says “let us”: the preacher is not standing on the finished storey calling down.

Not laying again a foundation. Six items follow, probably in three pairs. The first is conversion: repentance from dead works and faith toward God, the two sides of one turning, away from and toward. Dead works are deeds that lead to death or come from spiritual death: sinful deeds, and perhaps also religious works done to earn God’s favour (9:14).

Washings and the laying on of hands. The second pair concerns entry into the Christian life. The many washings of the old covenant gave way to one Christian washing, for those who have turned from dead works to faith (on the word, see the end of this note). The laying on of hands was used in the New Testament to bless, to heal and to commission for service (Acts 6:6; 13:3; 1 Timothy 4:14), and in the apostles’ ministry as the moment the Spirit was given (Acts 8:17; 19:6).

The resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. The third pair is the last things: the bodily resurrection of all people (John 5:28–29) and God’s everlasting judgment (9:27). These were among a convert’s first lessons.

Nothing that belongs to Christ alone. The striking thing about the list is that almost nothing in it is distinctively Christian. Every item could have been taught in a synagogue: repentance, faith in God, ceremonial washing, laying on of hands, resurrection, judgment. A devout Pharisee would have affirmed them all. The readers were stalled where Judaism and Christianity overlap, and had never moved on to what belongs to Christ alone, his priesthood, his sacrifice, his finished work, and that is exactly why going back looked so easy: if you have built nothing above the shared foundation, stepping off it costs nothing you can see. That is the quiet danger of respectable religion: a person can believe in God, repentance and judgment and still have no use for a priest, because the heart would rather manage its own standing with God than owe everything to someone else.

And this we will do if God permits. Progress in understanding is granted, not merely resolved. The phrase also prepares for verses 4–6, where God does not permit renewal.

In everyday life. Where do you keep digging up the foundation, re-examining your assurance every week without ever resting on it? Stand on what God has laid, and build: go deeper into Christ’s priesthood, his once-for-all sacrifice, his intercession for you now.

Does “washings” here teach anything about how to baptise? Not directly; the verse is about instruction, not method. But it fits the New Testament’s teaching that baptism belongs at the beginning of the Christian life, and the order of the first pair matters: those who have turned from dead works and trusted God are the ones who are washed. That is why this commentary, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, holds believer’s baptism, while gladly honouring paedobaptist brothers who read the covenant signs differently and love the same Saviour. Whichever view a Christian holds, the point of the verse stands: baptism is foundation, not a place to camp.

Does the laying on of hands still give the Spirit today? The Spirit is given to every believer at conversion, through faith in Christ, not through anyone’s hands (Romans 8:9; Galatians 3:2). In Acts the Spirit sometimes came at the laying on of apostolic hands, as the gospel crossed new boundaries and the church’s foundation was being laid (Acts 8:14–17; 19:6). Acts does not present those moments as a pattern for every believer. Many Pentecostal and charismatic brothers pray with laying on of hands for a fresh filling of the Spirit, meaning to honour him; this commentary differs from them as fellow believers. What continues is the laying on of hands with prayer to set apart elders and missionaries for their work (Acts 13:3; 1 Timothy 4:14), a sign of the church’s blessing and recognition, not a channel of power.

Uncertain wording. “Washings” (baptismōn) is plural, and it is the ordinary word for ceremonial cleansings (9:10; Mark 7:4), not the usual term for Christian baptism. So it is not certain exactly what this instruction covered. Most likely it taught Jewish converts how Christian baptism differed from the washings they had known all their lives, and from the baptism of John (Acts 19:1–5).

verseByVerse.quote: For it is impossible, in the case of those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, and have shared in the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the age to come,
verseByVerse.commentary:
People can know the blessings of the gospel from the inside, in the light, the gifts and the Spirit’s work in the church, and still turn away from Christ for good. For them, verse 6 will say, there is no way back to repentance.

For it is impossible. The most disputed sentence in the letter. “Impossible” (adynaton) stands first for emphasis: not difficult, but impossible, the word used of God’s inability to lie (v. 18) and of the blood of bulls taking away sins (10:4). What is impossible is not stated until verse 6: “to restore them again to repentance”. Everything between describes the people in view. The “for” explains verses 1–3: there is no safe standing still. This is the sharpest so far of the letter’s five warnings, and it is followed at once by the writer’s confidence (v. 9) and the anchor behind the curtain (vv. 19–20).

A word first to the anxious reader. If these verses frighten you, the fear itself is good news. The people described here are not worried about Christ; they have turned their backs on him and do not want him back. A believer who loves Christ and still falls into the same sin, who hates it, fights it and grieves over it, is not falling away: that struggle is the Spirit’s work in him, the Spirit at war with the flesh, his old sinful nature (Galatians 5:17; Romans 7:22–25). Depression, numbness and dark seasons of doubt are not apostasy either. Hold that as you read on, and remember how this chapter ends: with a hope anchored where Jesus has gone for you.

Once been enlightened. “Once” (hapax) is once for all. Light has fallen on them: they heard and understood the gospel (10:32). Some early Christian writers used “enlightened” as a name for baptism.

Tasted the heavenly gift. Not a sip: at 2:9 Jesus tasted death for everyone, and he did not sample it. The word means real experience of heaven’s blessing within the life of the church.

Shared in the Holy Spirit. The word is the one used at 3:1 and 3:14. They had taken part in the Spirit’s work in the community, his convicting power, his gifts and blessings, as Judas shared in the apostles’ ministry and was sent out to heal with the rest (Matthew 10:1–8).

The goodness of the word and the powers of the age to come. They found Scripture good, perhaps with joy, like the seed on rocky ground that springs up quickly and has no root (Matthew 13:20–21). And they have seen the miracles of 2:4, the foretaste of the age to come. These were not outsiders. They had been inside, near the fire, warmed by it.

The crowd that ate the bread and left. Such people stood around Jesus himself. In John 6 a crowd had eaten the bread he multiplied, seen his signs and followed him across the lake. He told them plainly that they were seeking him for the loaves, not for himself, and that he was the bread of life come down from heaven (John 6:26, 35). When his words grew hard, many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him (John 6:66). They tasted his gifts and refused him. Every gift of heaven comes in Christ, and the dividing line runs between those who have received his benefits and those who have received him.

Not only the taste but the feast. How rich the goodness of God is, that he pours light and tastes of heaven even on those who finally reject him. And how much richer his grace to his own, who are given not only the taste but the feast, not only the Spirit’s nearness but his indwelling for ever. We rest on Christ, who never lets go of anyone the Father has given him.

How can someone share in the Holy Spirit and not be saved? Because the Spirit works in more ways than regeneration: he convicts the world of sin (John 16:8), gives gifts in the church, and stirs, sobers and attracts people who hear the word. Balaam prophesied when the Spirit of God came upon him, and died among the enemies of God’s people (Numbers 24:2; 31:8). Saul had the Spirit come on him and ended consulting a medium (1 Samuel 10:10; 28:7). Judas preached and healed. Jesus warned of many who would say on the last day that they had prophesied and done mighty works in his name, to whom he would say, “I never knew you” (Matthew 7:22–23). Being near the Spirit’s work is not being born of him. Regeneration, the word used in the view below, is that new birth: the Spirit giving new life to a heart that was dead, so that the person truly turns to Christ and goes on trusting him (John 3:3–8; Ezekiel 36:26).

Then how can I know I am not one of these? Not by the size of your experiences, since these people had large ones, but by what the Spirit produces over time. Do you trust Christ himself, not your experiences, for acceptance with God? Do you want to please him? Do you hate your sin, fight it, and confess it when you fall? Do you love other Christians and serve them (v. 10; 1 John 3:14)? Do you keep coming back to his word, even when it is hard? These are the things that belong to salvation, usually clearer to others than to the anxious person himself. If you find even a weak longing for Christ in you, rest on his promise and not on your feelings: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

Where Christians differ: are these true believers? Four main views: (1) these are genuine believers who lose their salvation (the Arminian view, held by many earnest Christians, that a true believer can finally fall away); (2) these are genuine believers, but the warning is hypothetical, describing what would happen if they could fall away, which they cannot; (3) these are genuine believers who lose rewards, not salvation; (4) these are people who experienced the blessings of the gospel community without being regenerated, and whose falling away shows they were never truly saved. The first view meets a difficulty in the letter itself, which says Christ is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him (7:25); and on this reading the loss would be irreversible, which few who hold it actually teach. The second fits the theology but reads thinly against the urgency of the warning, and the third cannot do justice to burning (v. 8) or to 10:26–31. This commentary’s view: The fourth view best fits the passage and the whole of Scripture. Every phrase in verses 4–5 describes real experiences possible without regeneration: being enlightened (understanding the gospel), tasting (experiencing without fully receiving), sharing in the Spirit’s work (as Judas and Balaam did), tasting the word with joy (like the rocky soil). The passage does not use words like justified, born again, saved or sanctified of these people. In verse 9 the author distinguishes them from those who have “things that belong to salvation.” And in the land illustration (vv. 7–8) the same rain falls on two kinds of ground, but the fruit reveals the soil. Scripture elsewhere teaches that those whom God saves he keeps (John 10:28–29; Romans 8:29–30; Philippians 1:6). The warning is real: such people exist, and God uses this warning to stir true believers to persevere.

verseByVerse.quote: and then have fallen away, to restore them again to repentance, since they are crucifying once again the Son of God to their own harm and holding him up to contempt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who knowingly abandon Christ cannot be brought back to repentance, because they have rejected the only sacrifice there is and taken the side of those who crucified him.

Then have fallen away. To fall aside, to defect (parapesontas): not stumbling into sin but the deliberate abandonment warned of since 3:12, which for these readers meant renouncing Christ and returning to the old system to escape persecution, publicly and for good.

To restore them again to repentance. “Again” implies they had once shown repentance, outwardly at least. They have rejected Christ’s sacrifice, the only means of forgiveness (10:26). A drowning man who pushes away the one rope thrown to him has refused the only rescue there is.

Crucifying once again the Son of God. The verb (anastaurountas) means to crucify again, or to crucify up, on a cross. Rejecting Christ, they side with those who crucified him and declare that he deserved it. And it is “to their own harm” (heautois, for themselves, to their loss): Christ cannot be crucified again in fact, but they crucify him for themselves, and the ruin is theirs.

Holding him up to contempt. Making a public example of someone: they have said before witnesses that the crucified man was rightly crucified.

The only sacrifice there is. The Son of God was crucified once, outside the city, bearing the contempt of the world, and his blood does what no other offering could: it cleanses every sinner who comes to him, the denier, the adulterer, the persecutor, the backslider. To turn from it is ruin, because there is nothing beside it. To flee to it is life, because there is nothing it cannot cover.

The pastoral force. The warning is not addressed to the anxious (see the note on vv. 4–5). The people in view are not agonising; they have walked out (1 John 2:19).

What about the Christian who has really wandered? This verse does not describe him. A believer may fall into serious sin and stay away for a season, cold and defensive. Peter denied Christ three times with curses, and Jesus had prayed that his faith would not fail, and told him, “when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). David committed adultery and murder, and wrote Psalm 51. The warning is against final apostasy, not backsliding. Whoever wants to come back to Christ may come, and the church is to restore him in a spirit of gentleness (Galatians 6:1). The door is not shut on anyone who knocks.

If true believers cannot finally fall away, why warn them? Because the warnings are one of the means God uses to keep them. God preserves his people not by switching off their wills but by speaking to them, with promises that draw and warnings that alarm. A “Danger” sign at a cliff edge is not pointless because people heed it and stay safe; that is how it works. The elect do persevere (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6), and they persevere partly because passages like this one make them flee to Christ. The danger is real for those near the church but not in Christ, and for true believers the warning is a fence God has built on the path.

Is this the same as the unforgivable sin? They are closely related. Jesus spoke of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (Mark 3:28–30): deliberately calling the Spirit’s plain work in Christ the work of the devil, against the light. Hebrews 6 and 10 describe the same settled, knowing, public rejection of Christ. Neither is committed by accident or in weakness, nor by someone who wants forgiveness. Any sin that is repented of is forgiven, because the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7).

Should a church refuse to receive back someone who left the faith and now returns? No. The church cannot read hearts, and this verse describes from God’s side what happens to the hardened; it is not a policy for the elders. If someone who walked away returns professing repentance, receive him with joy, as the father received the prodigal (Luke 15:20–24), test the fruit patiently, and welcome him to the Lord’s Table when it is evident.
