That he has come back at all suggests he was not the person this verse describes.

Uncertain wording. Both verbs, crucifying and holding up to contempt, are present participles describing something still going on, and Greek leaves open how they relate to the main clause. Most translations, the ESV among them, take them as giving the reason: “since they are crucifying once again”. Some read “while”: as long as they go on publicly repudiating Christ, they cannot at the same time be repenting of it. The causal reading is more natural. Either way, the impossibility lies in their settled rejection of the only sacrifice there is.
verseByVerse.note: Christians have read this warning in different ways; all agree it is a real warning against turning away from Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: For land that has drunk the rain that often falls on it, and produces a crop useful to those for whose sake it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God. But if it bears thorns and thistles, it is worthless and near to being cursed, and its end is to be burned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two fields drink the same rain, and the crop shows which is which: fruitful ground receives God’s blessing, while ground that bears only thorns ends in burning. So people who receive the same gospel are known by what grows in them.

Land that has drunk the rain. The rain is the same on both fields, and the ground has genuinely absorbed it: “drunk” matches the tasting and sharing of verses 4–5. The rain is God’s repeated blessing: the gospel preached again and again, the Spirit’s work, the fellowship of believers.

A useful crop, and a blessing. Good land responds to the rain with fruit: by their fruits you will recognise them (Matthew 7:16–20). And fruitful land is blessed further, as the vinedresser prunes the fruitful branch so that it bears more (John 15:2).

Thorns and thistles. The exact phrase of the curse in Eden (Genesis 3:17–18; see thorns and thistles). The unfruitful ground is doing what cursed ground does.

Near to being cursed. Not cursed, but near to a curse (kataras engys). Near is not yet: while a field is only near, there is time for something else to come up, and the whole letter is written to make that happen.

Its end is to be burned. A picture of final judgment (10:27; John 15:6). The fruit shows the soil; the soil determines the end.

Fruit that comes from the Son. Jesus taught the same lesson: “Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). The harvest God blesses grows out of union with Christ, not the soil’s own strength.

Christ wore the thorns. God’s rain falls on fields that do not deserve a drop; on his own people he does more, making the soil itself new. The thorns and thistles were the curse of Eden, and Christ wore them on his head so that the ground of his people’s hearts could be blessed.

How do you tell the fields apart? By the crop: not by the intensity of the experience or how much was tasted, but by what is growing now, which is exactly what the writer points to next, their love shown in serving the saints (v. 10).

What fruit am I looking for, and what if mine looks small? Mostly ordinary fruit: trust in Christ that keeps returning to him, love for God’s people, hatred of sin and a fight against it, honesty, kindness, patience under trial, joy in God’s word, the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23). It grows slowly. A small crop is still a crop; thorns are not small wheat. And remember who makes good soil. The new heart is God’s gift (Ezekiel 36:26), and the vinedresser does not neglect his vineyard. If you see little, do not despair; ask him to work, stay under the rain of his word, and look again in a year.

verseByVerse.quote: Though we speak in this way, yet in your case, beloved, we feel sure of better things—things that belong to salvation. For God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name in serving the saints, as you still do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer is sure his readers are not the people he has just described, because God has seen the love they have shown to his people, and he will not forget it.

Beloved. After one of the hardest paragraphs in the letter comes its only “beloved” (agapētoi). The warning was not to tell these people he had given up on them. “Feel sure” (pepeismetha) means we have been persuaded, and remain convinced. He is not being polite: that is not you, he says, and I am confident of it.

Better things, because a better Christ. “Better things” (ta kreissona) is the letter’s key word, and it nearly always points to Christ and what he brings: a Son better than the angels (1:4), a better hope (7:19), a better covenant (7:22), better sacrifices (9:23), sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (12:24). So he is not praising his readers’ superior character, but saying that they belong to the better Priest, and that the things which accompany salvation in them overflow from their share in him (3:14).

Things that belong to salvation. Some things always go with genuine salvation, and they are missing from the list in verses 4–5. Those experiences can happen without salvation; the fruit of verse 10 accompanies it.

God is not unjust. The ground of his confidence is the crop: the parable asked how to tell the fields apart, and he points at what is growing in this one. Far from being unjust (adikos), God is faithful to his promises and will not forget the fruit of faith. Their service has not earned salvation; but a God who produced such fruit and then discarded the field would be unjust to his own work. He will acknowledge it, down to a cup of cold water (Matthew 10:42; 25:34–40). None of that service was flawless, and it did not need to be: through Jesus Christ the imperfect offerings of his children are acceptable to God (1 Peter 2:5), because his obedience was whole.

Serving the saints. “For his name” (eis to onoma autou) means for God’s sake: they loved his people because they were his. And the verb comes twice, past and present: having served (diakonēsantes) and still serving (diakonountes). They had cared for persecuted believers, visited prisoners and accepted the plundering of their property (10:32–34). Dull of hearing as they were, they were still looking after people. That is fruit, and he treats it as decisive: “We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers” (1 John 3:14).

He does not overlook it. There is comfort here for anyone whose service has gone unnoticed. The meals taken to a sick house, the years of unremarkable faithfulness to awkward people, the hospital visit nobody thanked you for, the prayers for a church that never knew who was praying: God is not unjust so as to overlook it. He may be the only one who has not.

In everyday life. Look for the fruit in someone else this week and tell them, as the writer did. And if some act of love has dropped away since a keener season, a visit, a meal, a regular prayer for a struggling believer, pick it up again for his name.

If he is so sure of them, why did he warn them? Because confidence about a congregation and warnings to it work together. He is sure of the body as a whole, yet any one person in it might be quietly slipping (v. 11); and true believers respond to warnings, so his warning is part of how God will keep them. A doctor sure of a patient’s recovery still tells him firmly to finish the medicine.

verseByVerse.quote: And we desire each one of you to show the same earnestness to have the full assurance of hope until the end, so that you may not be sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each believer should pursue the full assurance of hope with the same earnestness he already shows in love, and so follow those who inherit God’s promises through faith and patience.

Each one of you. “Each one” is the individual concern of 3:12 and 4:1. Confidence about the body must not become a blanket over someone quietly slipping. He asks them to apply to their hope the diligence (spoudē) they already apply to their neighbours.

Full assurance of hope. Full assurance (plērophoria) is a mind filled to the brim with confidence. It is something to pursue and grow into, not presumption but a fruit of faith (10:22; 2 Peter 1:10).

So that you may not be sluggish. Sluggish (nōthroi) is the word of 5:11. Sluggish ears and sluggish lives are one condition, with one remedy. What had run out was not information, nor the zeal of the start, but the long, unglamorous willingness to keep believing a promise that had not yet arrived.

Imitators. Against the dullness, examples of people who waited and received. “Imitators” (mimētai) is the word Paul uses when he says, “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1). Chapter 11 will complete the theme, as the long line of the faithful passes before us. “Faith and patience” run together to the letter’s end. Patience (makrothymia) is being long-tempered: the endurance that keeps going when the promise is slow. Faith takes God at his word; patience keeps taking him at it for years.

The last name on the list. The line of the faithful that begins with Abraham ends with Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross (12:2). And he is more than an example, because the promises the faithful inherit are inherited in him, the heir of all things (1:2).

Can a Christian really be sure he is saved, or is that arrogant? He can, and it is not arrogance, because the confidence rests on God. Hebrews wants every believer to have full assurance. It rests first on God’s promises in Christ, which cannot fail (vv. 17–18), and is confirmed by the Spirit’s witness that we are God’s children (Romans 8:16) and by the fruit he produces in us (v. 10). The Westminster Confession says that true believers may be infallibly assured, though they may wait long and struggle for it, and that it may be shaken and then revived (Westminster 18.3–4; 1689 18.3–4). Assurance is humble certainty: I am sure, not because I am strong, but because he is faithful.

How do I grow in assurance? Look mostly at Christ and his promises, not mostly at yourself. Read and trust the promises made to all who come to him (John 6:37; 10:28). Use the means of grace: the preached word, the Lord’s Supper, prayer, fellowship. Obey in the small things, because disobedience clouds assurance and obedience clears it, and deal quickly with known sin. Serve others, as these readers did. And when you are low, remember that assurance is not the ground of your salvation: a believer with weak assurance is as safe as one with strong assurance, because both are held by the same hand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — Two Unchangeable Things, and an Anchor Behind the Curtain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The believer’s hope is as certain as God himself. God swore by himself to Abraham, who waited patiently and received what was promised (vv. 13–15). Since an oath ends human disputes, God added one to his promise, giving two unchangeable things to those who have fled to him for refuge (vv. 16–18). That hope is an anchor fixed in God’s presence, where Jesus has gone ahead of us as a high priest for ever, which brings the writer back to Melchizedek (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology:
An Anchor That Goes Upward

God confirmed his promise with an oath so that we might have strong encouragement. Our hope is anchored behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone ahead of us as forerunner.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Abraham waited twenty-five years for Isaac, not always steadily, and obtained the promise.

Now: We are those who have fled for refuge. The storm is here; the anchor is fixed in heaven, where no storm reaches.

verseByVerse.quote: For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself, saying, “Surely I will bless you and multiply you.” And thus Abraham, having patiently waited, obtained the promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God bound himself by an oath to bless Abraham, and Abraham, after long and patient waiting, received what was promised. He is the example of faith and patience that verse 12 called for.

A promise to Abraham. The father of the nation is the pattern of waiting. God promised Abraham descendants, land and blessing for all nations (Genesis 12:1–3).

He swore by himself. The occasion is Genesis 22, just after Abraham had raised the knife over Isaac, when the promise looked most impossible and he had proved he would trust God with it anyway. It is the only place in Genesis where we hear God swear an oath to Abraham: “By myself I have sworn, declares the LORD” (Genesis 22:16). An oath calls on something greater than yourself as the guarantee, and God has nothing greater. So he swore (ōmosen) by himself: the guarantee of the promise is his own existence, and for it to fail he would have to cease to be God.

Surely I will bless you. From Genesis 22:17, shortened. Behind it lies a doubled Hebrew expression, literally blessing I will bless you, which underlines the certainty.

Having patiently waited. Everything hangs on this phrase (makrothymēsas, having been patient). Count the years. Abraham was seventy-five when the promise was first made and a hundred when Isaac was born (Genesis 12:4; 21:5). Twenty-five years, most of them with no evidence whatever, in which he twice passed off his wife as his sister to save his own skin, took Hagar to arrange the heir himself, and laughed when God repeated the promise (Genesis 12; 16; 17:17; 20). The waiting was long and patchy, and Hebrews still calls it patience.

Obtained, and not yet. At 11:13 the writer will say, “These all died in faith, not having received the things promised.” Abraham received Isaac, the first fulfilment, not the city or the blessing to all peoples: kept in part, not yet in full, which is exactly our position.

The oath sworn over a son. God swore the oath on the mountain where Abraham had received his son back from the knife and a ram had died in his place, and the oath itself names an offspring in whom all the nations of the earth will be blessed (Genesis 22:13–18). Paul says that offspring is finally one person, Christ (Galatians 3:16). And the New Testament reads the scene as a shadow of a greater giving: Abraham’s son was spared, but God did not spare his own Son, and gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32). The promise sworn over Isaac was kept at Calvary.

The comfort in a patchy patience. What the New Testament commends in Abraham is not that he never wobbled but that he was still there at the end, because God was still there. God kept his word to a wavering old man, and he will keep it to us.

How do I wait when God seems to be doing nothing? Abraham’s story answers in three ways. First, remember what God has said, not what you assumed he would do; Abraham held a promise, not a timetable. Second, keep obeying in the meantime, as Abraham kept building altars, moving when told and praying. Third, do not try to force the outcome; taking Hagar was the fruit of impatience, and it brought grief for generations. Waiting on God is steady trust that goes on doing the next right thing while the promise ripens.

verseByVerse.quote: For people swear by something greater than themselves, and in all their disputes an oath is final for confirmation. So when God desired to show more convincingly to the heirs of the promise the unchangeable character of his purpose, he guaranteed it with an oath, so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God added an oath to his promise, not because his word needed it but so that those who have fled to him for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold on to their hope.

Something greater than themselves. Because people are not reliably truthful, an oath calls something greater to witness, and the matter is closed.

To the heirs of the promise. God’s bare word is already utterly reliable; an oath cannot make him more truthful. It adds nothing to God and everything to our confidence, and he swore it for that reason alone. The oath sworn on a mountain to one old man was made for everyone who would ever inherit the promise, Abraham and all who share his faith (Galatians 3:29): the congregation hearing this letter, and anyone reading it now.

The unchangeable character of his purpose. “Unchangeable” was used in legal documents of a will that cannot be altered. God’s saving plan cannot change: the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (Romans 11:29).

He guaranteed it with an oath. Literally, he mediated, he stood in the middle as guarantor (emesiteusen). God put his own name up as the security, so that his promise is as safe as he is. And the pledge did not stay a matter of words. By another sworn word, “You are a priest forever” (Psalm 110:4), God made Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant (7:20–22), so that the guarantee given to Abraham now stands in a living person at his right hand.

Two unchangeable things. His promise and his oath, because God cannot lie (Titus 1:2). “Impossible” is the word that opened verse 4, and the two impossibilities face each other: it is impossible to restore someone who has finally turned his back on Christ, and it is impossible for God to lie. The second is the one to build on.

We who have fled for refuge. The picture (hoi kataphygontes) is drawn from the cities of refuge (Numbers 35; Joshua 20), where a man who had killed accidentally ran for his life to a walled town, pursued by the avenger of blood. Safe inside and dead outside, he ran, undignified and desperate. That is a Christian: not a seeker weighing options but a man running for his life to God in Christ, the only place that will hold him.

Strong encouragement. The hope set before us is eternal salvation in God’s presence, like the prize at the end of a race (12:1–2). God swore an oath so that frightened people would keep their grip.

The avenger has no claim left. The city of refuge is Christ himself, whose gates are never shut against a sinner who flees to him. In Israel the manslayer could go home only when the high priest died (Numbers 35:25, 28). Our High Priest has died, and the avenger has no claim left; and he lives for ever, so the freedom he won can never be revoked.

What does fleeing for refuge look like for me? It means coming to Christ as your only safety from God’s just judgment, and coming back whenever guilt or fear pursues you. The manslayer did not stop on the road to prove his innocence; he ran. So when your conscience accuses you, do not try to settle it by your own record. Go to Christ in prayer, plead his blood, and rest inside the walls. You do not flee once and then live outside. You live in the city.

But what if my grip on the hope is weak? God gave two unchangeable things for exactly such people. Your safety does not depend on the strength of your hold but on the strength of the city: the manslayer was safe because he was inside, not because he was brave. Hold fast as well as you can, and when you cannot, remember that the one who swore the oath holds you (John 10:29).

verseByVerse.quote: We have this as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, a hope that enters into the inner place behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf, having become a high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Christian’s hope is an anchor fixed in God’s own presence, where Jesus has gone ahead of us as our high priest for ever.

A sure and steadfast anchor. Early Christians carved the anchor in the catacombs as a symbol of hope. A bad anchor fails by breaking or by dragging; this one is sure and steadfast, and does neither.

Behind the curtain. An anchor goes down; this one goes up and in. The curtain is the veil of the Most Holy Place (Exodus 26:31–33; Leviticus 16:2, 12), where God’s presence dwelt, the barrier no one crossed but the high priest, once a year, with blood. The anchor is lodged there, not in circumstances, nor in the believer’s steadiness, nor even in the visible church. The cable runs out of this world altogether and is made fast inside the sanctuary of God, where nothing can move it.

The storm and the anchorage. A ship in heavy weather is held by ground it cannot see. For a congregation whose property had been seized, that is the entire point. His people will not drift away, because Christ will not let go.

A forerunner. “Forerunner” (prodromos) is one who runs ahead, used of scouts sent before an army. Preachers have often pictured a small boat carrying a ship’s anchor ahead into a harbour too shallow for the ship, though there is little ancient evidence for the practice. Either way, a forerunner goes first so that others follow. The high priest of old went behind the curtain alone and came out again, and nobody followed him. This one went in and stayed, and the rope is attached to us (10:19–20). And he went “on our behalf” (hyper hēmōn): as our representative, so that where he is, we shall be.

A high priest forever. Psalm 110:4 returns for the third time, bringing the writer back to 5:10. His congregation warned, reassured and anchored, chapter 7 resumes the argument he broke off.

In everyday life. When the bad news comes this week, what do you reach for: your plans, your savings, the approval of the people around you? All of those are in the sea. When you feel yourself drifting, pray one sentence that names where your anchor is: Lord Jesus, you are in heaven for me.

What if I feel no hope at all? Then this verse is for you more than for anyone. The anchor does not depend on the feeling of the sailor. In the worst storm nobody on board feels secure, and the ship holds, because the anchor is fixed somewhere the storm cannot reach. Your hope is not your feeling of hopefulness but Christ, alive in God’s presence for you. On days when you feel nothing, tell yourself where he is: he is your forerunner, and he always lives to intercede for you (7:25).
verseByVerse.note: The high priest passed behind the curtain into the Most Holy Place once a year, on the Day of Atonement.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore let us leave the elementary doctrine of Christ and go on to maturity, not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God,<sup>2</sup>and of instruction about washings, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment.<sup>3</sup>And this we will do if God permits.<sup>4</sup>For it is impossible, in the case of those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, and have shared in the Holy Spirit,<sup>5</sup>and have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the age to come,<sup>6</sup>and then have fallen away, to restore them again to repentance, since they are crucifying once again the Son of God to their own harm and holding him up to contempt.<sup>7</sup>For land that has drunk the rain that often falls on it, and produces a crop useful to those for whose sake it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God.<sup>8</sup>But if it bears thorns and thistles, it is worthless and near to being cursed, and its end is to be burned.<sup>9</sup>Though we speak in this way, yet in your case, beloved, we feel sure of better things—things that belong to salvation.<sup>10</sup>For God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name in serving the saints, as you still do.<sup>11</sup>And we desire each one of you to show the same earnestness to have the full assurance of hope until the end,<sup>12</sup>so that you may not be sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.<sup>13</sup>For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself,<sup>14</sup>saying, “Surely I will bless you and multiply you.”<sup>15</sup>And thus Abraham, having patiently waited, obtained the promise.<sup>16</sup>For people swear by something greater than themselves, and in all their disputes an oath is final for keyVerse.quote: We have this as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, a hope that enters into the inner place behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf, having become a high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.
keyVerse.note: After the letter’s sharpest warning, the chapter ends here, and so must the anxious reader. The believer’s hope is not fastened to his feelings or his steadiness but to a person in God’s presence: Jesus, who went behind the curtain for us and stayed. These verses also bring the writer back to Psalm 110:4 and open the way to his great argument about Christ’s priesthood.

6.reflection:
Verse 1 calls us to build on the foundation rather than keep laying it again. In what ways do Christians stay stuck at the beginning, and what would it look like for you to go on to maturity in Christ?

Verses 4–8 describe people who tasted real blessings and still turned away, and verses 9–10 point to the fruit that belongs to salvation. How do these verses help us to tell the difference, and how should we speak to someone who is frightened by them?

God “is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name in serving the saints” (v. 10). Whose quiet service could you notice and encourage this week?

Verses 16–20 picture hope as an anchor fixed where Jesus has gone. What do you tend to reach for when life becomes stormy, and how does knowing where Jesus is now steady you?

7.title: The Order of Melchizedek: A Priest Forever
7.overview:
Where we are. After the warning and encouragement of 5:11–6:20, the writer returns to the title with which chapter 6 ended: Jesus has become “a high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek” (6:20). This chapter, the centre of the letter’s teaching on his priesthood, explains it, and opens the way to chapters 8–10.

The message. Jesus is a priest of a different and better kind than Aaron’s sons. He holds his office not by ancestry but by God’s oath and a life death could not destroy, so he can do what no priest of Israel did: save completely and for ever everyone who comes to God through him. The old priesthood was not the original that Jesus copies; it was the arrangement that waited for him.

Why it was said. The readers were being drawn back to a priesthood they could see, with Scripture behind it and centuries of descent from Aaron (see the introduction). The obvious objection to their faith was this: how could a man from Judah, crucified and with no temple, be anyone’s priest? The writer answers from their own Scriptures, using one story in Genesis and one line of a psalm.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–3 draw Melchizedek from Genesis 14: king of righteousness and peace, priest of God Most High, without recorded genealogy or death, “resembling the Son of God”. Verses 4–10 show him greater than Abraham, who tithed to him and was blessed by him, and so greater than Levi. Verses 11–19 turn to Psalm 110:4: a promised priest of another order proves Levi’s priesthood could not perfect, and a priest from Judah, qualified “by the power of an indestructible life”, brings a change of law and a better hope by which we draw near. Verses 20–25 add the oath, making Jesus guarantor of a better covenant, and his endless life, in which he always intercedes. Verses 26–28 gather it up: a holy high priest who offered himself once for all.

Where it leads. Israel kept king and priest apart; in Jesus they are joined, as Melchizedek once pictured. And the chapter ends where every sacrifice was heading: a priest with nothing to bring but himself, who brought it, and now lives at God’s right hand to plead for those he died for. No other priest’s care outlived his funeral; this one’s never ends.

For us. No pedigree, ritual or human go-between can bring you nearer to God than Jesus already has. You do not need another priest, another sacrifice or a better week. Come to God through him, today, and let his endless intercession be your confidence when your own prayers run out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Melchizedek, and What Abraham Did
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Melchizedek was greater than Abraham, and therefore greater than every priest descended from him. The writer first draws the portrait from Genesis 14: a king of righteousness and of peace, priest of God Most High, with no recorded beginning or end, made to resemble the Son of God (vv. 1–3). Then he weighs two things that happened when they met: Abraham gave him a tithe and received his blessing, and the lesser is blessed by the greater (vv. 4–7). Levi’s priests die, while Scripture speaks of this priest as living, and Levi himself, still in Abraham’s body, paid the tithe too (vv. 8–10).
verseByVerse.theology:
Reading the Silence of Scripture

Genesis gives Melchizedek no genealogy, and the writer reads the silence as a portrait of a priesthood that does not rest on descent. Abraham tithed to him and was blessed by him: the lesser by the greater.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Levi, not yet born, paid tithes to Melchizedek through his ancestor Abraham.

Now: Righteousness comes first, then peace (see the note on vv. 1–2).

verseByVerse.quote: For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God, met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, and to him Abraham apportioned a tenth part of everything. He is first, by translation of his name, king of righteousness, and then he is also king of Salem, that is, king of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Long before Israel had any priests, a king of Salem served as priest of the true God, blessed Abraham and received a tenth from him. The writer starts from this short story in Genesis because the man, and even his names, were shaped to point ahead.

The argument resumes. The argument broken off at 5:11 resumes, and it turns on a man who appears in three verses of Genesis (14:18–20) and one line of one psalm (110:4). Chapter 6 ended with Jesus entering behind the curtain as a high priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek (6:20); chapter 7 explains the title.

King of Salem, priest of the Most High God. Salem was probably the early name of Jerusalem (Psalm 76:2), where David would reign and the temple would stand. “Priest of the Most High God” (El Elyon in Genesis) is the arresting phrase. Centuries before Sinai, before Levi was born, a king in Canaan, outside Abraham’s line, is already a priest of the true God, the creator of heaven and earth, and Abraham recognises him as such. Priest and king in one person, as Christ is.

Met Abraham. Abraham had just rescued Lot by defeating four kings (Genesis 14:1–17). On the way home a stranger comes out with bread and wine, blesses him in the name of God Most High, receives a tenth of the spoil, and vanishes from the narrative. That tenth will carry the argument of verses 4–10: the man to whom the promises were made handed over a tithe, and a tithe is what you give to a superior.

King of righteousness. The writer reads the names as the Bible’s own writers did, as carrying meaning. Malki-tsedeq is king of righteousness, and Christ is the righteous King the prophets promised, the branch of David who would be called “The LORD is our righteousness” (Jeremiah 23:5–6).

King of peace. Salem is shalem, related to shalom, peace. Christ is the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6), who makes peace between God and sinners and is himself our peace (Ephesians 2:14).

First righteousness, then peace. The writer presses the order: “first” king of righteousness, “and then” king of peace. That is the shape of the gospel, and it cannot be reversed: “righteousness and peace kiss each other” (Psalm 85:10), and “since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God” (Romans 5:1). That is why the cross was necessary. A holy Judge cannot make peace by pretending wrong was never done; the wrong had to be put right first: Christ bore its penalty and gives his own righteousness to all who trust him (2 Corinthians 5:21). Declared right with God on the ground of what Christ has done, we have peace as the fruit.

How did Melchizedek know the true God, outside Abraham’s family? Genesis does not say, and we should not invent an answer. The knowledge of God had not yet died out everywhere after the flood, and God makes himself known where he will; Melchizedek is one of a few such figures, like Jethro the priest of Midian later on. He is a quiet sign that the God of Abraham was never a tribal deity, but God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth, who always intended blessing for all nations.

Was the bread and wine a kind of Lord’s Supper? Not in the sense of a sacrifice. It was hospitality for a tired army returning from battle, and Hebrews, which makes so much of every detail, never mentions it. Christians have long seen in it a lovely foreshadowing of the table where Christ, our priest-king, feeds his people, but it gives no support to the idea that the Supper is an offering of Christ’s body by a priest. The whole point of this chapter is that Christ offered himself once for all (v. 27).

Where Christians differ: are believers required to tithe? Some teach that the tithe, a tenth of income, binds Christians, since Abraham tithed before the law of Moses, Jacob vowed a tenth (Genesis 28:22), and Jesus told the Pharisees not to neglect the tithe (Matthew 23:23). Others answer that Abraham’s tenth is recorded as a single gift from the spoils, not a rule; that the tithes the law commanded belonged to the Levitical system that this chapter says has changed (v. 12); and that Jesus was speaking to men still under that law. This commentary’s view: Abraham’s tithe was a voluntary act of honour on a single occasion. The New Testament does not command a fixed percentage. It teaches generous, regular, proportional, cheerful giving (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:1–15; 9:6–7). A tenth is a good starting guide for many, but Christians under grace should often give more, not less, and never under compulsion.

verseByVerse.quote: He is without father or mother or genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but resembling the Son of God he continues a priest forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Genesis presents Melchizedek with no family line, no birth and no death, and so makes him a likeness of the Son of God, the priest who truly never ends. The writer is reading the silence of Scripture, a way of arguing his readers would have followed easily.

Without father or mother. The three words are apatōr, without father, amētōr, without mother, and agenealogētos, without genealogy. They have been read as making Melchizedek a supernatural being. But Genesis is a book of genealogies, telling who fathered whom, how long they lived and when they died, and Melchizedek walks in with none of it. For a priest that is extraordinary, because the Levitical priesthood depended entirely on family records: after the exile, men who could not produce them were excluded (Ezra 2:61–63). Melchizedek has no papers whatever, and is a priest of the Most High God.

Neither beginning of days nor end of life. The writer takes the silence as deliberate: a portrait with the genealogy left out, sketching a priesthood that does not depend on descent and does not end with a funeral. God drew him with a few strokes, a priest-king who appears without origin and vanishes without a grave, and left the portrait waiting for the original.

Resembling the Son of God. “Resembling” (aphōmoiōmenos) is made to resemble, and the direction is easy to get backwards. The writer does not say Christ is like Melchizedek, but that Melchizedek was made like the Son of God. The eternal reality came first; the man in Genesis is the sketch. The Son truly has no beginning or end; Melchizedek only appears so in the record.

He continues a priest forever. True of Melchizedek only in that the text never records him stopping; true of Christ absolutely, and that is the point of the whole chapter. Verse 3 lays down the two threads the chapter will pull: no genealogy (vv. 11–17, a priesthood resting on who he is) and no end of life (vv. 16, 23–25, a priest who lives for ever and so can save for ever).

In everyday life. Your standing with God does not depend on your pedigree either. Some Christians feel second-class because they did not grow up in church; others quietly rely on their Christian background. Neither counts in the priesthood of Christ.

Is it fair to build an argument on what Scripture does not say? Yes, when the silence is part of the shape God gave the text. God, who inspired Genesis, chose to present Melchizedek without parents in a book where almost everyone else gets a genealogy, and then named him in a psalm about an eternal priest. And the case never rests on silence alone. Its foundation is the plain statement of Psalm 110:4, sworn by God; the silence of Genesis illustrates what the psalm declares.

Where Christians differ: was Melchizedek Christ himself? Some believe Melchizedek was a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ (a Christophany), or an angel. This commentary’s view: Melchizedek was most likely a real, historical human king and priest, whose recorded life God arranged to foreshadow Christ. The text says he was made like the Son of God, which would be odd if he were the Son: a thing does not resemble itself. He is a type, a living prophecy, not the reality itself. His lack of recorded genealogy is the point, not a claim that he literally had no parents.
verseByVerse.note: Genesis records no parents, birth or death for Melchizedek. The writer draws out the meaning of that silence, not a claim that Melchizedek had no parents.

verseByVerse.quote: See how great this man was to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the spoils! And those descendants of Levi who receive the priestly office have a commandment in the law to take tithes from the people, that is, from their brothers, though these also are descended from Abraham. But this man who does not have his descent from them received tithes from Abraham and blessed him who had the promises. It is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham gave Melchizedek a tenth and received his blessing, and both acts show that Melchizedek was the greater man. The argument rests on two customs the readers understood perfectly: who pays tithes to whom, and who blesses whom.

See how great this man was. “How great” asks for a measurement. The payer was not simply Abraham but “the patriarch”, the greatest name a Jewish reader possessed, and the spoils are literally the top of the heap, the choicest part.

The descendants of Levi. Under the law of Moses the Levites received tithes from their own relatives, the other tribes, by written command (Numbers 18:21–26). Melchizedek was no Levite and had no legal right to collect; Abraham’s tithe was freely given.

Blessed him who had the promises. The second and stronger argument. Abraham, the bearer of the blessing for all the families of the earth (Genesis 12:2–3), received a blessing from a stranger.

Beyond dispute. Literally without any contradiction (chōris pasēs antilogias): in that world it was a self-evident fact. A formal blessing runs downhill: father to son, as Isaac blessed Jacob and Jacob his sons (Genesis 27; 48–49); priest to people, as Aaron blessed Israel (Numbers 6:22–27); king to subject. So Abraham, the father of the nation, put himself in the lower place twice in one meeting, and Genesis records it without comment. The readers had read that chapter all their lives and may never have noticed what it implied. And Christ, the reality of whom Melchizedek was only a sketch, has come not to receive our tithes but to give himself.

Why does it matter to me who was greater than whom? Because the readers were tempted to go back to the Levitical priests as if they were the real thing, and their own Scriptures show that before Levi was born, Abraham bowed to a greater priest. If Abraham honoured the shadow, how much more should we honour the reality? Leaving Christ for anything else, however old and venerable, is trading the greater for the lesser. And the blessing you receive from Christ comes from above, from the greatest, with all of God’s authority behind it.

verseByVerse.quote: In the one case tithes are received by mortal men, but in the other case, by one of whom it is testified that he lives. One might even say that Levi himself, who receives tithes, paid tithes through Abraham, for he was still in the loins of his ancestor when Melchizedek met him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Melchizedek outranks Levi’s priests in two more ways: Scripture speaks of him as one who lives, and Levi himself, still unborn, paid him tithes in Abraham.

Mortal men. Literally dying men. The Levitical priesthood was a relay, designed around mortality (see vv. 23–25).

It is testified that he lives. Not “who lives”, but “of whom it is testified that he lives”: Genesis records no death, and Psalm 110 says, “You are a priest forever.” This points to Christ, who truly lives for ever (v. 16).

One might even say. The writer knows he is pressing hard, and offers this as a way of seeing the thing, not a knock-down proof.

In the loins of his ancestor. In the Hebrew way of reckoning, a descendant is present in his ancestor and acts in him. So the tribe that would one day collect Israel’s tithes had already, in Abraham, paid them to somebody else. The Levitical priesthood bowed to a greater priesthood before it existed, and Genesis 14 had been sitting in the Torah, the five books of Moses, all along saying so.

Representation is the logic of the Bible. It is why the sin of one man could involve a race, and why the obedience of one man can make many righteous (Romans 5:12–19). A modern reader who finds it strange that one person can stand for many will find most of the doctrine of salvation strange, since it all runs on the same principle.

In everyday life. The man who represented an Israelite before God would one day be carried out to his grave. Think about whom you lean on spiritually: a pastor, a parent, a gifted friend. Thank God for them, and let them point you past themselves to the one representative who will never be carried out.

Is it fair that I should be counted in someone else? It can feel unfair when the head is Adam, whose sin brought death to all. But the same principle is the only reason anyone is saved. Without a representative, Christ could not have stood in our place, and his death and righteousness could not count as ours; no one complains about being counted righteous in Christ. The question is not whether we are represented, because everyone is, but by whom: Adam or Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–28 — A Priest Forever, and the Change That Follows
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s oath in Psalm 110:4 has installed a new kind of priest, and he can do what the old priests never could: bring sinners all the way to God. A promise of another priest proves the old priesthood could not bring anyone to the goal, and a new priesthood means a changed law (vv. 11–12). This priest comes from Judah, qualified not by ancestry but by an indestructible life (vv. 13–17), so the weak former command gives way to a better hope by which we draw near (vv. 18–19). Sworn in by oath, he guarantees a better covenant (vv. 20–22); living for ever, he saves to the uttermost and always intercedes (vv. 23–25); holy and exalted, he offered himself once for all (vv. 26–28).
verseByVerse.theology:
Change the Priesthood and the Law Must Follow

The law rested on the Levitical priesthood, and God has replaced that priesthood by oath with a priest who holds office by the power of an indestructible life.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The former priests were many, because death stopped each one.

Now: He is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if perfection had been attainable through the Levitical priesthood (for under it the people received the law), what further need would there have been for another priest to arise after the order of Melchizedek, rather than one named after the order of Aaron? For when there is a change in the priesthood, there is necessarily a change in the law as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s promise of a different priest shows that Levi’s priesthood could never bring anyone to God’s goal, and a new priesthood brings a change of law with it. The argument now turns from Genesis to the psalm.

If perfection had been attainable. “Perfection” (teleiōsis) means bringing a thing to its intended goal: the root of “made perfect” in 2:10 and 5:9, and a keyword of the letter. Here it means bringing people fully into God’s presence, with sins dealt with completely and consciences cleansed (9:9; 10:1, 14). The question is not whether the Levitical priesthood was good, but whether it could finish anything. It could not.

Under it the people received the law. The law established the priesthood, and the priesthood administered the law. They stand or fall together.

What further need would there have been for another priest? Psalm 110 was written by David, centuries into the Levitical system, and in it God announces a priest of a different order. You do not announce a replacement for something that is working.

Rather than one named after the order of Aaron? God did not promise a better Aaron, a reformed Levitical priesthood with holier men in it. He promised a different order altogether.

A change in the law. “Change” is transfer, the word for moving something elsewhere. Since the law of Moses was tied to the Levitical priesthood, a new priesthood changes the whole Mosaic arrangement, with its sacrifices, priesthood and ceremonies. The first readers were drawn back to the temple, sacrifices, food laws and calendar as God’s own commands, and the writer agrees that they were. But the whole structure hung on a priesthood that God himself has changed. The law was not bad; its foundation has been replaced by the God who laid it, and a building does not outlive its foundation.

In everyday life. Old-covenant instincts survive in much of our religion: the feeling that a bad week puts you outside until you have made up for it. Keep God’s commandments gladly, as his child, and come to him through Christ alone, today, as you are.

Does this mean the Ten Commandments are abolished? No. The law that changes is the law bound up with the priesthood: the sacrifices, the temple, the purity rules and the calendar. Reformed Christians have long distinguished the ceremonial law, fulfilled in Christ and set aside; the civil law, given to Israel as a nation; and the moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, which still shows believers how to love God and neighbour (Matthew 5:17–19; Romans 13:8–10). Others say the whole law of Moses has given way to the law of Christ, but agree that its moral demands come to us again in the New Testament, written on the heart (8:10). What changes is not God’s standard but the way to him.

Should Christians keep the Old Testament food laws and festivals, then? Not as a duty before God. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), and Paul calls the festivals, new moons and food rules a shadow whose substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17). A Christian may eat or abstain, and may learn much from Passover or the Day of Atonement, which point so clearly to Christ. What he must not do is treat them as necessary for acceptance with God or as a mark of superior holiness. That was exactly the pull these readers felt: going back to a priesthood God has retired.

Uncertain wording. “Under it” is compressed in the Greek (ep’ autēs, literally “on it”). It may mean that the law was given on the basis of the priesthood, resting on it as a foundation, or more loosely that it was given in connection with it. The sense is clear either way: law and priesthood were bound together, so that changing one changes the other (v. 12).

verseByVerse.quote: For the one of whom these things are spoken belonged to another tribe, from which no one has ever served at the altar. For it is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah, and in connection with that tribe Moses said nothing about priests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus came from Judah, a tribe the law never allowed at the altar, so his priesthood cannot be Levi’s; it must be a new kind. What looked like an objection becomes evidence.

Another tribe. Under the law, priesthood was a matter of tribe, and the boundary was absolute. No man from Judah ever served at the altar, and when King Uzziah presumed to burn incense in the temple, he was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:16–21).

Descended from Judah. “Evident” (prodēlon) means obvious, common knowledge. The genealogies were public (Matthew 1:1–16; Luke 3:23–33), and the deliverer had always been expected from Judah and from David: the sceptre shall not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10), and he is the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Revelation 5:5). The word for “descended” (anatetalken) is lovely: it is used of the sun rising and of a shoot springing up, and the prophets used both pictures of the Messiah, the sunrise from on high (Luke 1:78) and the branch from Jesse’s stump (Isaiah 11:1).

The two requirements collide. The Messiah had to be from Judah, because the promise said so. A priest had to be from Levi, because the law said so. And Psalm 110 says the Messiah will be a priest. So his priesthood must be of another kind.

Moses said nothing. Again the argument runs on a silence: there was no provision, because the priesthood being announced was never going to run through the law. Anyone defending the old arrangement could say, correctly, that Jesus had no right to the Levitical priesthood. The writer concedes it: Jesus holds a different office, established by an oath the law knew nothing about.

Why did God arrange it so that the Messiah would come from the wrong tribe for priesthood? So that no one could mistake Christ’s priesthood for a continuation of the old one. Had Jesus been a Levite, his ministry could have been read as the best chapter of the old system. By bringing him from Judah, God made it plain that something new had come: a king who is also a priest, uniting the two offices Israel had always kept apart. The kings could rule but not atone; the priests could atone in shadow but not rule. Christ does both, perfectly and for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: This becomes even more evident when another priest arises in the likeness of Melchizedek, who has become a priest, not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent, but by the power of an indestructible life. For it is witnessed of him, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is a priest not because of his ancestry but because of who he is: his life is one that death could not destroy, so he is a priest for ever. The change of priesthood becomes clearer still in the kind of priest God promised.

Another priest. “Another” (heteros) means another of a different kind: not a successor but a different species of priest.

Not by bodily descent. Literally a law of a fleshly commandment: a rule about physical pedigree. Not character, devotion or gifts, but birth. A godly Israelite from the wrong tribe could not serve; an indifferent one from the right family could.

An indestructible life. Power (dynamis) is the word for the mighty works of 2:4. Akatalytos means undissolvable, related to the word for taking down a tent or pulling down a building (2 Corinthians 5:1): not a life that merely goes on, but one that cannot be ended. The resurrection is behind the phrase. Death did its worst and could not dissolve it, as Peter preached at Pentecost (Acts 2:24). One priesthood rests on records of ancestry that can be lost, as they were after the exile (Ezra 2:61–62); the other is guaranteed by an empty tomb.

It is witnessed of him. Everything hangs on “forever”: only someone with an indestructible life could be a priest for ever. He needs no successor and cannot be replaced by a better one.

From an empty tomb for ever. Men tried to destroy our High Priest’s life with nails and a spear and sealed it in a tomb, and on the third day it broke every bond. That same life is now spent, without pause, in priestly care for us. Every other priest’s ministry ended at a funeral; his goes on from an empty tomb for ever.

What difference does an indestructible life make to me? Your priest cannot be taken from you. Every human helper can be lost, by death, distance, illness, failure or their own limits. Christ cannot. His care does not depend on his health, his mood or his circumstances, and no crisis in your life or the world will interrupt it. His life is also the guarantee of yours: “Because I live, you also will live” (John 14:19).

What should this mean for how churches choose leaders? Not pedigree. The old priesthood ran on bloodline; the new people of God are to be led not on the basis of family, wealth, education or connections, but on character and gifts given by the Spirit (1 Timothy 3:1–7). A pastor’s son is not thereby fit to be a pastor, and a convert from a broken home is not thereby disqualified. A church that follows a priest qualified by an indestructible life should look for leaders marked by his life in them.

verseByVerse.quote: For on the one hand, a former commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness (for the law made nothing perfect); but on the other hand, a better hope is introduced, through which we draw near to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has set aside the old command about priesthood, which could not bring anyone to completion, and has given a better hope through which we draw near to him. These are strong words about God’s own law, and they must be read exactly: the writer is not saying the law was a mistake or evil.

A former commandment is set aside. “Set aside” (athetēsis) was a legal term for annulling a decree.

Because of its weakness and uselessness. “Weakness” (asthenes) is powerlessness; “uselessness” (anōpheles) is unprofitableness. They judge the law for one purpose only: it could not achieve full cleansing and access to God. At what it was given to do, exposing sin, regulating a nation and pointing forward, it was perfectly effective. It was useless for making anybody perfect, which it never claimed to do. A thermometer is useless for heating a room, and the fault is not in the thermometer. And the weakness lay in the flesh, the sinful human nature it had to work with: what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do, God did by sending his own Son (Romans 8:3).

The law made nothing perfect. Not “nobody” but “nothing”: the law brought nothing at all to its goal. It pointed to perfection but could not provide it (10:1); it was a guardian until Christ came (Galatians 3:24).

A better hope. “Better” is the letter’s signature word: a better priest, covenant, promises, sacrifices, country. The better hope is the new covenant hope in Christ, “introduced” to take the place of what was set aside.

We draw near. And then the purpose: “through which we draw near to God”. That is the point of the genealogies, tithes, tribes and oath: not to win an argument but to bring people into the presence of God. The old system existed to manage distance: curtains, courts, and a single man admitted once a year. The new one exists to remove it (4:16; 10:19–22). Where once one man could approach, once a year, trembling, with blood not his own, now the weakest believer may come at any hour, by the blood of the Son of God. “Draw near” (engizomen) is the letter’s word for what a Christian actually does, and everything else is scaffolding around it (James 4:8). That exposes a quiet idol of religious people: we can come to love the scaffolding, the routines and the sense of being in the right place, more than the God it was built to bring us to.

If the law made nothing perfect, why did God give it? It was never meant to make perfect. It was given to show sin for what it is (Romans 3:20; 7:7), to restrain evil, to set Israel apart, and above all to point forward: every sacrifice, washing, feast and priest was a picture of Christ. Like scaffolding, it was essential until the building stood, and then it came down. The law did not fail; it did its work, which was to lead us to Christ, so that we might be justified by faith (Galatians 3:24).

What does drawing near to God actually look like? It is the whole life of faith gathered into one act: coming to God, through Christ, with nothing in your hands. You draw near when you pray to God as Father in Jesus’ name, confess sin and receive his forgiveness, hear his word with faith, come to the Lord’s Table, and worship with his people. And you come without the old fear, because the way is open. You do not need a priest, a holy place, a special mood or a good week; you need Christ. Much of our praying is errands, and the throne invites them. But drawing near also means simply coming to be with God, with no performance and no promise to do better (Father, I come in Jesus’ name), and then staying a while. The curtain is open, and you are welcome.

verseByVerse.quote: And it was not without an oath. For those who formerly became priests were made such without an oath, but this one was made a priest with an oath by the one who said to him: “The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind, ’You are a priest forever.’” This makes Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God swore an oath when he made Jesus priest, so his priesthood can never be revoked, and Jesus himself stands as guarantor that the better covenant will be kept. The argument about God’s oath in chapter 6 now applies to the priesthood.

Not without an oath. God does not swear because his plain word could be doubted, but because we are slow to believe it; the oath is his kindness to weak faith (6:17). Aaron and his sons were appointed by command (Exodus 28–29); God never once swore to the Levitical priesthood.

With an oath. Psalm 110:4 again, now with the words left out before: “The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind”. An arrangement made by command can be amended by a later command; one established by the oath of God cannot. Christ’s priesthood is irrevocable.

The guarantor. A surety (engyos, a legal and commercial term used only here in the New Testament) stands behind an obligation with his own property and person: if the debtor fails, the guarantor pays. Judah offered himself to his father in exactly this way for Benjamin: I will be a pledge of his safety; from my hand you shall require him (Genesis 43:9), and when the moment came he offered to become a slave in the boy’s place (Genesis 44:32–33). Jesus personally guarantees that his people’s debts are paid and that God’s promises to them will be kept.

Why a guarantor matters. Covenants fail because one party does, which is exactly what happened to the first one: “they did not continue in my covenant” (8:9). Jesus is not the new covenant’s administrator or witness but its surety, so it cannot fail on our side, because our side has a guarantor who has already paid. Not a document but a person: one of the strongest securities a first-century reader knew. And “better covenant” (kreittonos diathēkēs) is the first mention of covenant in Hebrews; chapter 8 will develop it as the new covenant of Jeremiah 31.

Everything was required of him. Judah pledged himself for one brother and was never required to pay. The Son of God stood surety for a great multitude, everything was required of him, and he paid it with his own blood. There is no security in the universe stronger than that.

In everyday life. When your failures make you wonder whether God will finally give up on you, remember that the new covenant does not rest on your keeping it but on Christ’s guaranteeing it: Jesus is the guarantor. Then, because you are secure and his Spirit is in you, take up the obedience you have been avoiding. A child who knows his place in the family is safe obeys from love, not from fear of being sent away.

What is a covenant? A binding relationship God establishes with promises, sealed in a solemn way, and more than a contract. The new covenant, established in Christ’s blood (Luke 22:20), Christ both makes by his death and guarantees by his life.

Textual note. The KJV adds “after the order of Melchisedec” here, following later manuscripts; the earliest manuscripts end the quotation at “forever”.

verseByVerse.quote: The former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever. Consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Jesus never dies, his priesthood never passes to anyone else, and so he can save completely and for ever all who come to God through him. Everything in the chapter now comes down to a single sentence.

Many in number. Josephus, the first-century Jewish historian, counted eighty-three high priests from Aaron to AD 70: eighty-three funerals. Aaron died on Mount Hor, and his son was dressed in his garments (Numbers 20:23–29); every priest’s intercession ended at death.

Permanently. The word (aparabaton) can also mean non-transferable. He has no successor, because he never dies, and the robes will never come off him.

To the uttermost. “Able” (dynatai) means he has the power. He saves entirely, leaving nothing unfinished, and permanently, without expiry: no sinner too far gone, no sin too great, no time too long.

Those who draw near to God through him. The only qualification named. Not those who understand, or who have never failed, but those who come, and keep coming, through Christ alone (John 14:6).

He always lives to intercede. What is Christ doing now? Praying for his people, without stopping, and this is why he can save like that. “Make intercession” (entynchanein) is to plead or appeal on behalf of. It is not begging an unwilling Father, but his presence before the Father as the one whose sacrifice has been accepted, presenting his finished work for his people and asking for all they need (Romans 8:34; 1 John 2:1). It guarantees their perseverance: he prayed for Peter that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:32), and he prays for all his own (John 17:9, 15, 20, 24). God keeps those he has truly brought to himself trusting him to the end. They may stumble badly, as Peter did, but they will not finally fall away, because he who began a good work in them will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).

At three in the morning. When a Christian is too tired or too ashamed to pray for himself, someone at the right hand of God is praying for him and has not paused. The salvation reaches to the uttermost because the interceding does.

Everyone finds a priest. To many people today a priest is the least modern idea in the Bible, and Hebrews does retire the whole order of human priests. But the need has not gone away. People still want someone to stand between them and their failures, to hear the worst and tell them they are all right, and they look for it in a counsellor’s room, a partner’s reassurance, the approval of friends or the verdict of a crowd online. Some are real gifts, but every such priest grows tired, can be mistaken, cannot take anything away, and in the end dies, as Israel’s high priests did. Here is the one priest who needs no successor. He does not merely reassure us that our sins are not so bad; he has borne them. He never tires of hearing our name, and when every other voice falls silent, his is still speaking for us.

Do Christians, then, need human priests? No. If Christ holds his priesthood permanently and offered himself once for all (v. 27), no other mediator is needed and no sacrifice is to be repeated. There is one go-between for us before God, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5); every believer draws near through him (4:16; 10:19–22), and the whole church is a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9). Pastors are shepherds and teachers, not priests. We may and should ask one another to pray for us, but no believer needs anyone except Christ to stand between him and God.

If Jesus is praying for me, do I still need to pray? Yes, and his praying is why your prayers count. You pray in his name, so your prayers rise to the Father carried by his intercession, made acceptable by his blood, as a father’s love makes a child’s requests welcome, not unnecessary. On the days you cannot find words, both he and the Spirit pray for you (Romans 8:26–27, 34). You are never praying alone.

Can I be beyond his saving? Not if you come to God through him. The verse names no limit except coming. Whatever you have done, however long you have been away, however many times you have fallen in the same place, the word is uttermost. The only person beyond his saving is the one who will not come. If you are coming, or want to come, you are exactly the person this verse is about.

Uncertain wording. “To the uttermost” translates eis to panteles, which can mean completely, to the fullest extent, or for all time. The context supports either: the chapter speaks of a priest who lives for ever (vv. 23–24) and of the perfection the old priesthood could not reach (vv. 11, 19). The ESV’s “to the uttermost” keeps both in view, and both are certainly true of Christ’s saving.

verseByVerse.quote: For it was indeed fitting that we should have such a high priest, holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens. He has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people, since he did this once for all when he offered up himself. For the law appoints men in their weakness as high priests, but the word of the oath, which came later than the law, appoints a Son who has been made perfect forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is exactly the high priest sinners need: holy and exalted, he needed no sacrifice for himself, and he offered himself once for all.

Such a high priest. “Fitting” is the word of 2:10: it suited the character of God to provide him. Five descriptions follow, moving outward from his character to where he now is.

Holy, innocent, unstained. The first word (hosios) means devout, wholly given to God: his heart towards God. The second is literally without evil (akakos): guileless, with no malice towards people. The third is undefiled (amiantos). The high priest had to avoid ritual defilement and could not go near a dead body, even his own father’s (Leviticus 21:10–15). Jesus touched lepers and the dead, and instead of being defiled by them, he made them clean. He is holy towards God and harmless towards us, spotless in a world of stains.

Separated from sinners. This needs care. “Separated” (kechōrismenos) is a perfect tense: set apart, and remaining so. The friend of tax collectors and sinners, who ate with them (Luke 15:2), is not being described as aloof. The separation is one of character and, since the ascension, of place. He was among sinners without becoming one, and is now exalted beyond their reach to harm him.

Exalted above the heavens. Raised to the highest place (4:14; Ephesians 4:10). The old high priest went through a curtain; this one has passed through the heavens and sits above them.

No need to offer sacrifices daily. Priests offered morning and evening (Exodus 29:38–42), and the high priest yearly; the repetition proved their inadequacy (10:1–4, 11). And they offered “first for his own sins”, as in 5:3. Jesus had none.

Once for all. “Once for all” (ephapax) is once, finally, never to be repeated (9:12, 26, 28; 10:10), one of the letter’s great words. The last words, “he offered up himself”, are where the chapter has been heading, the first explicit statement in Hebrews that Christ’s sacrifice was his own self. Every other priest offered a bull, a goat, a lamb; this one brought himself: priest and sacrifice in one person, which no priest of Israel had ever been or could be.

A Son made perfect. The chapter closes on its two contrasts: weak men against a Son, and a temporary command against a later oath. Psalm 110 came centuries after the law of Moses, and God does not swear to things he means to revise. “Made perfect” is the word of 2:10 and 5:9, fully qualified for his office, and its form here means he remains so for ever. The whole chapter is gathered up, and the next three are opened: the sanctuary where he serves (chapter 8) and the once-for-all offering of himself (chapters 9 and 10). 8:1 will call this the main point.

In everyday life. We often try to offer something more for our sins: an extra effort at religion, a period of feeling bad, a promise to make up for it. Each is a small attempt at a daily sacrifice. Stop offering. Confess, thank him that the offering is finished, and go and serve him out of gratitude rather than debt. The Supper you take on Sunday is a remembrance of a finished work, not a top-up.

Why does a sinless Son need to be made perfect? Perfect here means not morally improved but completed for a task. Jesus was always without sin, but to be our high priest he had to become man, obey, suffer, die, rise and ascend; then he was fully and finally qualified, as a surgeon who has completed the operation has not become a better man but has done the work. Christ has done it, and his qualification will never lapse.

If he offered himself once for all, what does that mean when I fail again? There is no new sacrifice to be made for you, and none needed. When you confess sin, you are not asking Christ to be offered again but resting on the offering already made, which covers your past, present and future sins. Repentance is real and necessary, but it is not payment. The payment was once, and it was enough. Come back to the cross not to add to it but to receive from it again what it has already accomplished.

Where Christians differ: is Christ’s sacrifice re-presented in the Mass? Roman Catholic teaching holds that the Mass (the Catholic celebration of the Lord’s Supper) is the same sacrifice of Calvary made present again in an unbloody manner, offered for the living and the dead. Catholics mean by this to honour Christ’s one sacrifice, not to add to it, and the disagreement should be stated with care. This commentary’s view: Hebrews insists that Christ offered himself “once for all,” and that unlike the old priests he has no need to offer repeatedly (7:27; 9:25–28; 10:10–18). Where there is forgiveness, there is no longer any offering for sin (10:18). The Supper is a memorial of Christ’s one sacrifice and more than a memorial: by faith and through the Spirit believers truly feed on Christ, spiritually, not physically (1 Corinthians 10:16; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 30.7; the Westminster Confession 29.7). It is not a repeated sacrifice or a re-offering of it.

keyVerse.quote: Consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them.
keyVerse.note: Every step of the chapter, from Melchizedek to the oath to the indestructible life, leads to this sentence, and “consequently” says so. Because Jesus lives for ever, his saving is complete and has no end, and the only condition named is coming to God through him. It is the verse to hold when you feel too far gone, too often fallen or too weak to pray.

7.reflection:
Abraham, the man who carried God’s promises, honoured a greater priest and received his blessing (vv. 1–10). What old, respectable or familiar things are you tempted to lean on instead of Christ, and what does this chapter say to that?

Verse 19 says the whole point of priesthood is that “we draw near to God”. What does drawing near to God look like in an ordinary week for you, and what makes you hold back?

Jesus “always lives to make intercession” for those who come to God through him (v. 25). How might it change your prayers, your fears or your sense of failure to know that he is praying for you now?

Jesus offered himself “once for all” (v. 27). In what ways do Christians still try to add their own sacrifices for sin, and how can we help one another rest in a finished work?

8.title: A Better Covenant: Written on the Heart
8.overview:
Where we are. Having shown that Jesus is the better high priest (4:14–7:28), the writer states the “point” of it all and turns to where he serves and under which covenant. With chapters 9 and 10 this is the heart of the letter: a better sanctuary, covenant and sacrifice.

The message. We already have the high priest we needed, seated in the real presence of God, of which the tabernacle was only a God-given copy. He mediates the new covenant promised through Jeremiah, in which God himself undertakes to write his law on his people’s hearts, be their God, be known by each of them, and forgive their sins for ever. By calling it new, God marked the old as old: going back would be going back to a shadow.

Why it was said. The readers were being drawn back to a temple that still stood, its priests still offering (v. 4; see the introduction). Following Jesus felt like losing something solid: a holy place, a visible priest, an ancient covenant. The writer shows them they have lost nothing real.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–2 give the main point: our high priest is seated in heaven, serving in the true tent. Verses 3–5 explain why: earthly priests serve a copy and shadow, as God’s word to Moses about “the pattern” shown on the mountain proves (Exodus 25:40). Verse 6 is the hinge: his ministry is as much better as his covenant, which rests on better promises. Verses 7–12 prove it from Jeremiah 31:31–34: God found fault with a people who did not continue in his covenant, and promised one in which he does the decisive things himself, with forgiveness as the foundation. Verse 13 concludes that the word “new” makes the first covenant old.

Where it leads. The new covenant needed one man on the human side who would not break it, and God provided him: the Son who could say, “your law is within my heart” (Psalm 40:8), and who took the cup of the new covenant in his blood. Because his one offering paid for sin, God remembers his people’s sins no more, and the priest who made it sits at the Father’s right hand, his work finished.

For us. The old covenant spoke in “if”; the new speaks in God’s “I will”. Live this week on his promises rather than on your performance, and beware the habits that quietly take us back to the shadows: a priest between us and God, a holier building, a running tally of our record. Christ is our priest, and our sins are remembered no more.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — A Minister in the True Tent
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Our high priest serves in heaven itself, the real sanctuary, and so his ministry is better than any earthly priest’s. The writer sums up his argument: we have a priest seated at God’s right hand, serving in the tent the Lord himself set up (vv. 1–2). On earth he would have no place, for the priests there serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly sanctuary, as God’s instruction to Moses showed (vv. 3–5). Verse 6 ties his better ministry to the better covenant he mediates, resting on better promises, and opens the rest of the chapter.
verseByVerse.theology:
Copy, Shadow, and the Pattern on the Mountain

The earthly tent was a copy of what Moses was shown. Christ ministers in the true tent, and the covenant he mediates is better because it rests on better promises.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Readers grieving the loss of the temple had not been shut out of the sanctuary.

Now: They had been let into the one the sanctuary pictured (see the note on vv. 1–2).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the point in what we are saying is this: we have such a high priest, one who is seated at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, a minister in the holy places, in the true tent that the Lord set up, not man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sum of all that has been said is this: our high priest has sat down beside God’s throne and serves in the real sanctuary in heaven. And he is ours now.

The point. The word (kephalaion) means the chief thing, and also the sum of an account, the total at the bottom of the column. After seven chapters of argument, here is the bottom line.

We have such a high priest. “We have”: he belongs now to the frightened congregation hearing this read. Why would they return to the old priesthood, when they already have this one?

Seated at the right hand. The seated posture (ekathisen) has been in the letter since 1:3, and by now the reader knows what it signifies: his work is finished (10:12). The Levitical priests stood daily at a work that never ended (10:11). And the seat is at the right hand of the throne, the place of supreme authority (Psalm 110:1). This priest does not wait on the throne’s pleasure; he shares its authority. “The Majesty” is a reverent way of naming God himself, whose glory once filled the tent so that even Moses could not go in (Exodus 40:34–35). The man at his right hand is not tolerated in that light; he belongs there.

A minister in the holy places. A minister (leitourgos, from which we get liturgy) performs priestly service for others. He has sat down, because the work of atonement is finished; and he still ministers, because his love for his people is never finished.

The true tent. There is a real sanctuary, and it is not in Jerusalem. “True” (alēthinos) does not mean genuine as against fraudulent, for the tabernacle was no fake. It means the original as against a copy. Moses built a good copy; the Lord himself pitched this tent (9:11, 24).

The answer to their grief. For readers grieving the loss of the temple, perhaps shut out by their own families for following Jesus, this is a large answer. You have not been shut out of the sanctuary. You have been let into the one it pictured, and a man of your own flesh and blood is sitting in it.

If my high priest is in heaven, is he far away from me? He is far above, but not far off. Heaven is the place of all power and all access, not a distant room out of earshot. He sympathises with our weaknesses (4:15), always intercedes for us (7:25), and by his Spirit is with his people to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20). Our prayers reach the throne, because the one who presents them sits at the Father’s right hand. A high priest on earth could only get as close as a curtain. Ours is inside.

verseByVerse.quote: For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices; thus it is necessary for this priest also to have something to offer. Now if he were on earth, he would not be a priest at all, since there are priests who offer gifts according to the law. They serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things. For when Moses was about to erect the tent, he was instructed by God, saying, “See that you make everything according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
