Earthly priests serve in a sanctuary that was only a God-given copy of the heavenly one, so Christ’s priesthood belongs in heaven, not on earth. Moses’ own instructions prove it.

Something to offer. A priest must have an offering, so what does this priest offer? The answer was given at 7:27, “he offered up himself”, and chapters 9 and 10 will work it out: a single offering, made once (9:14).

If he were on earth. A startling admission: under the earthly arrangement Jesus has no standing whatever, since he was from Judah (7:13–14). His sacrifice was made on earth, at the cross, but he entered heaven with it and serves there. “There are priests who offer” is present tense: the temple was still standing, which suggests the letter was written before AD 70 (see the introduction).

A copy and shadow. Two careful words. A copy (hypodeigma) is a sketch, an outline, a model of something real. A shadow (skia) is cast by a body: it has the shape and none of the substance, and it proves the body exists (10:1; Colossians 2:17). Neither word means false. A shadow genuinely tells you something, but nobody prefers it once the man has walked into the room. What the tabernacle drew in outline, the cross and the empty tomb have filled in with flesh and blood.

The pattern on the mountain. Then the proof, from Moses himself. “Instructed” (kechrēmatistai) is a word for a message from God, and the message was Exodus 25:40. The “pattern” is typos, a model or design, from which we get “type”. God did not simply hand Moses measurements; he showed him something on Sinai and told him to reproduce it exactly. By God’s own founding instructions the tabernacle was a copy, and the original was not on earth. This is not a Greek philosopher’s idea of shadows read into Scripture, but the plainest reading of what God said when the tent was commissioned. And it turns the readers’ crisis round. They thought they were leaving the real thing for something less tangible, and they had it exactly backwards: the incense, the lampstand, the altar and the veil were the sketch, and Christ is the substance.

The shadows bowed and gave way. The God who showed Moses the pattern had his Son in mind all along. Every curtain and lampstand was his sketch of the coming one, and when the Son came, the shadows bowed and gave way. He is the tent where God dwells with men, the priest who enters, and the offering he brings.

How far should I look for Christ in the details of the tabernacle? Far enough to follow the New Testament, and carefully beyond it. Hebrews shows the main lines: the priest, the sacrifices, the altar, the curtain, the Most Holy Place, the blood, the ark (9:1–14). John sees Jesus as the one who tabernacled among us (John 1:14), and the curtain tore when he died (Matthew 27:51). Those lines are sure. But the writer himself declines to go into every detail (9:5), and hidden meanings in every peg and thread are usually invented. Hold the big picture: God dwells with his people only through a priest and a sacrifice, and Christ is both.

Is it wrong to have beautiful church buildings, or to call the worship room a sanctuary? No, provided we know what they are. A church building is not a temple where God is more present than elsewhere, and no place on earth is holy ground in the old covenant sense; the church is the people, not the bricks (1 Corinthians 3:16; 1 Peter 2:5). A beautiful building can serve worship, but if a building, a style of music or a ritual starts to feel necessary for meeting God, we have drifted back towards the shadows. The true sanctuary is in heaven, and we enter it by faith wherever we gather.

Where Christians differ: will the temple and its sacrifices be restored? Some dispensationalists (Christians who see a distinct future programme for national Israel, including a literal thousand-year reign of Christ on earth) expect a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem with renewed animal sacrifices during that millennium, often as memorials. They hold this out of a sincere wish to take prophecies such as Ezekiel 40–48 literally, and they too insist that nothing could add to Christ’s sacrifice. This commentary’s view: Hebrews teaches that the earthly sanctuary and its sacrifices were shadows, now fulfilled and made obsolete in Christ (v. 13; 10:1–18). To return to them would be to go back from the reality to the shadow, the very thing the letter warns against. The true temple now is Christ himself and his people (John 2:19–21; Ephesians 2:19–22), and the future hope is the new creation where God and the Lamb are the temple (Revelation 21:22).

verseByVerse.quote: But as it is, Christ has obtained a ministry that is as much more excellent than the old as the covenant he mediates is better, since it is enacted on better promises.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s ministry is better than the old priests’ by exactly as much as his covenant is better, because it rests on better promises. Verses 1–5 showed where Christ serves; verses 7–13 will prove from Jeremiah that his covenant is better.

But as it is. The phrase turns from what would be true on earth to what is actually the case. “More excellent” is the word used of his name in 1:4, and the writer measures it: his ministry is better by as much as his covenant is better. Covenant is the word that will carry chapters 8 to 10.

The covenant he mediates. A covenant (diathēkē) is a binding arrangement, initiated by God, in which he commits himself to his people and they to him. A mediator (mesitēs, go-between; 1 Timothy 2:5) stands between two parties who cannot deal directly. Moses mediated the first covenant (Galatians 3:19), standing on the mountain between a holy God and a terrified people who begged him to speak to them instead, lest they die (Exodus 20:19). Christ mediates the new (9:15; 12:24).

Two mediators. Moses pleaded for the people, even asking to be blotted out of God’s book for their sake (Exodus 32:32), but he could not pay for their sin, and the arrangement failed anyway. This mediator is also the guarantor (7:22) and the sacrifice (7:27). He did not merely deliver the covenant; he stood between God and us and held it together with his own blood.

Better promises. “Enacted” is legally established. The better promises are those of verses 10–12: an inward law, a personal relationship with God, knowledge of God among all his people, and complete forgiveness. The old covenant’s promises depended on Israel’s obedience, which failed; the new are guaranteed by Christ (7:22).

The verbs have changed hands. So the new covenant is better not because its rules are easier, but because of what God undertakes to do. The Sinai covenant said: if you keep my statutes, you shall live (Leviticus 18:5). The new one says: “I will put my laws into their minds”, “I will be merciful”, “I will remember their sins no more”. The doing has passed from the people to God.

In everyday life. Much Christian life runs on “if”: if I pray more, stop this habit, serve better, then God will accept me. That is how the old covenant spoke. Take one new covenant promise, “I will remember their sins no more”, and live this week on God’s “I will” instead of your own “if”. Obedience will follow, not as the price of acceptance but as its fruit.

Were Old Testament believers saved in a different way from us? No. Everyone who has ever been saved has been saved by grace through faith in the promised Saviour. Abraham believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6; Romans 4:3), and David rejoiced in the forgiveness of sins (Romans 4:6–8). The faithful of Israel looked forward through the sacrifices and promises to the Christ to come, as we look back to the Christ who has come. What differs is the administration: shadows then, substance now; promise then, fulfilment now (the Westminster Confession 7.5–6). Chapter 11 will parade the Old Testament believers as our examples of faith, not as people saved by a different route.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — The New Covenant Promised by Jeremiah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God himself promised a new covenant, and by doing so he declared the old one old. The writer frames Jeremiah 31:31–34 with two short comments. Before it: if the first covenant had been all that was needed, no second would have been promised, and the fault lay with the people who broke it (vv. 7–9). Then come the four promises: God’s law written on the heart, God as their God, every member knowing him, and sins remembered no more (vv. 10–12). After it: the word new marks the first covenant as old and ready to vanish (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Verbs Have Changed Hands

In Jeremiah's promise God says “I will”: the law written on the heart, knowledge of God for all, and sins remembered no more.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: God found fault with the people, not with the covenant.

Now: God does not forget; he has resolved never to act toward his people on the basis of their sins.

verseByVerse.quote: For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no occasion to look for a second. For he finds fault with them when he says: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt. For they did not continue in my covenant, and so I showed no concern for them, declares the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s own promise of a new covenant shows that the first was not final, because the people under it did not keep it.

If the first covenant had been faultless. The argument used of the priesthood at 7:11: God does not announce a new covenant while the old one is doing everything required.

He finds fault with them. “Finds fault” (memphomenos) means blames, and the blame falls on the people: “they did not continue in my covenant” (v. 9). The defect was not in the covenant’s standard but in those who were party to it. Paul agrees: the law is holy, righteous and good (Romans 7:12), but the flesh, our sinful human nature, made it powerless (Romans 8:3). A perfect law given to imperfect people cannot produce righteousness, and the old covenant had no power to change hearts.

The days are coming. The quotation runs from here to verse 12: Jeremiah 31:31–34, all four verses, usually reckoned the longest citation of the Old Testament anywhere in the New. The writer wants it all in front of his readers, because the Old Testament itself announced the passing of the old arrangement. Jeremiah spoke early in the sixth century BC, as judgment closed in and exile loomed because of Judah’s covenant-breaking. It is hope announced at the point of greatest ruin: as the city was about to fall, God did not say that all was over between him and his people.

A new covenant. “New” (kainē) is new in quality: not another edition of the old but a different kind, and entirely God’s initiative.

Israel and Judah. The whole of God’s people, divided after Solomon, gathered again under one covenant. Jesus took the cup and called it the new covenant in his blood (Luke 22:20), and Paul calls himself a minister of a new covenant (2 Corinthians 3:6).

By the hand. The image is tender: the exodus as leading a child by the hand. “When Israel was a child, I loved him,” God says through Hosea (Hosea 11:1–4).

They did not continue. Israel broke the covenant again and again, beginning with the golden calf at the foot of the very mountain where it was made (Exodus 32).

I showed no concern. This follows the ancient Greek translation of Jeremiah; the Hebrew reads “though I was their husband” (Jeremiah 31:32). Either way, the hand that had led them out of Egypt let them go into Babylon.

A partner who did continue. The new covenant needed a partner on the human side who would not break, and God provided him. Israel was called God’s son and failed in the wilderness (Hosea 11:1); Jesus, the true Son, went into the wilderness and did not fail (Matthew 2:15; 4:1–11). Of his Servant God says that he will give him as a covenant for the people (Isaiah 42:6). The new covenant will not fail as the old did, because at its centre stands one Israelite who kept faith all the way to the cross, and he is the guarantor of his people’s side of it (7:22).

In everyday life. If your life feels like a collapsing covenant, a broken marriage or a pattern of failure you cannot escape, notice when God spoke these words: at the point of ruin, to people who had brought the ruin on themselves. Do not wait until things improve to look for his promise.

Who is this covenant for? The promise is made to the house of Israel and of Judah, and dispensational Christians hold that it will be fulfilled to the nation of Israel in the future, the church sharing only some of its blessings. But Hebrews quotes it to explain what Christ has already done for its readers. He is the mediator of this better covenant now (v. 6; 9:15); the Holy Spirit bears witness to it now (10:15–17); believers have already come to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant (12:24). The more likely reading is that the new covenant is fulfilled in Christ and his people, Jew and Gentile together; its promises are already ours, though their fullness, when all shall know the Lord, waits for his return. Those who agree on this still differ over Paul’s hope that all Israel will be saved (Romans 11:26–27): some expect a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before the end; others read all Israel as all God’s elect, Jew and Gentile. On either view there is one covenant, one Mediator and one people, and every Jew who comes to Christ comes home to promises first made to his fathers.

Uncertain wording. The Greek behind “he finds fault with them” can be construed in two ways, and some manuscripts have a slightly different form (an ESV footnote mentions it). God may be finding fault with the people, or finding fault with the first covenant as he speaks to the people. The difference is small: verse 7 has said the first covenant was not “faultless”, meaning not final, and the quotation itself places the failure in the people (v. 9). The old covenant could not last because it could not change the hearts of those under it.
verseByVerse.note: The longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament runs from v. 8 to v. 12.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And they shall not teach, each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, ’Know the Lord,’ for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the new covenant God promises to write his law within his people, to be their God, and to be known personally by every one of them.

On their hearts. The first promise: inward transformation. Under the old covenant the law was written on tablets of stone (Exodus 31:18) and stood outside the people, telling them what to do. The content does not change; God does not promise a different or easier law. What changes is where it is written. The problem was never the standard but hearts that did not want it, and the remedy is not a lower demand but a new heart: I will give you a new heart, and I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes (Ezekiel 36:26–27; 2 Corinthians 3:3). This is regeneration, the new birth: the Spirit giving life to a heart that was dead towards God, so that it now loves what it once resisted (John 3:3–8). The law is not abolished but taken inside.

A different kind of obedience. So new covenant obedience is doing what the heart itself now wants, which is why the New Testament can say that his commandments are not burdensome (1 John 5:3) without lowering any of them. A child who loves music does not experience practice the way a child forced to the piano does, though the scales are the same. To a new heart God’s commands are not a cage but the shape of its freedom: I will walk in a wide place, for I have sought your precepts (Psalm 119:45).

Their God, my people. The second promise: relationship. It runs through the whole Bible to the new creation, where the voice from the throne says exactly this (Genesis 17:7; Revelation 21:3). It is the sentence God keeps saying, and everything else exists to make it true. He does not admit us to a building; he gives us himself.

What it means that he is our God. Everyone has a god in the sense that matters: something they look to for security, worth and joy. When the Lord says, “I will be their God”, he offers to be that himself, and binds himself to it by covenant. He takes responsibility for our guilt (v. 12), our needs and our future, and we belong to him, never ownerless or alone. It was made good at a cross: Thomas, seeing the wounds of the risen Jesus, could say, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28). When you are anxious this week, do not stop at telling yourself that God exists. Tell yourself he is your God, and bring him what you are carrying.

They shall not teach. The third promise. The New Testament plainly commands teaching (5:12), so the promise is not that instruction ceases. Under the old covenant, people were born into the community and then had to be urged to know the Lord, and many never did. In the new covenant no member needs that urging, because every member already knows him.

They shall all know me. “Know” is not just knowledge about God but personal, saving knowledge: this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3). There are no second-hand members. “From the least of them to the greatest” removes the ranks: no inner circle with access and an outer ring who take it on trust, no class of priests standing in between.

The first heart with the law written on it. Before God wrote his law on any of his people’s hearts, there was one heart where it was already written. The psalm Hebrews puts in the mouth of Christ as he comes into the world (10:5–7) goes on: “I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart” (Psalm 40:8). Jesus is the first man in whom the new covenant’s promise was simply true, and he writes it in his people by giving them his Spirit (2 Corinthians 3:3). The knowledge of God every member shares comes through him too: “no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matthew 11:27).

In everyday life. Choose one commandment you obey grudgingly, perhaps truthfulness at work or honouring a difficult parent, and pray the promise over it: Lord, write this one on my heart. Then obey, and watch for the change from duty to desire; meanwhile your halting obedience is accepted for the sake of the one in whose heart that law was always written.

Do the Ten Commandments still bind the Christian, then? Yes, as the moral law God writes on the heart, though not as terms by which we earn life. What becomes obsolete (v. 13) is the Mosaic administration: priesthood, sacrifices, temple and Israel’s civil law (see the note on 7:11–12).

The Sabbath. The fourth commandment is where views differ most. Many Reformed Christians, with the Westminster and 1689 Confessions, hold that the Sabbath continues as the Lord’s Day, moved to the first day of the week in honour of the resurrection (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8). Others hold that the Sabbath rest is fulfilled in the rest Christ gives (4:9–10; Colossians 2:16–17), while still gladly gathering on the Lord’s Day. This commentary holds that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ and the Lord’s Day is his gift, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest rather than kept as a law of rules; no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5), and those who hold the Westminster and 1689 view are to be honoured. Both agree that God’s people need worship and rest, and that Christ is the true rest.

How do I know God has written his law on my heart? Not by never sinning, but by what you love and what grieves you. Do you want to please God, even when you fail? Does sin that once felt natural now trouble you? Do you love God’s word, even when it rebukes you? Do you know God, not only facts about him, so that you speak to him as your Father? These are the marks of a new heart, which feels the law not as a weight outside but as a description of what it longs to be. If that longing is in you, God put it there.

Where Christians differ: who belongs to the new covenant? Paedobaptists (those, such as Presbyterians and Anglicans, who baptise the infants of believers) see the new covenant, like the old, as including believers and their children, and so baptise infants as covenant members. This commentary’s view: One of the key differences between the old and new covenants is that all members of the new covenant know the Lord personally, from the least to the greatest, and have the law written on their hearts. The old covenant community was mixed, including many who did not know God; the new covenant community, properly understood, consists of those who have been regenerated. This is why baptism, the sign of the new covenant, belongs to those who profess faith. This credobaptist conclusion is held charitably towards paedobaptist brothers, who agree that only the regenerate are truly saved but understand the visible covenant community differently.

verseByVerse.quote: For I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Underneath every other promise lies this one: God will forgive his people’s sins completely and never hold them against them again. The little word “For” at the front makes it the reason the others are possible.

I will be merciful. Law written on hearts, God as their God, everyone knowing him: none of it can happen while the sin question is open. “Merciful” (hileōs) means favourable, gracious, and it is related to the word for propitiation (2:17). A propitiation is an offering that removes God’s just anger against sin by taking it in the sinner’s place, and Christ is that offering (Romans 3:25; 1 John 2:2). Mercy here is not God deciding that sin does not matter, but God satisfied that sin has been paid for. The “iniquities” (adikiai) are their wrongs, their unrighteous deeds.

Remember no more. The Greek uses a strong double negative: I will certainly never again remember. It does not mean God is forgetful; a God who could lose track of the past would be a smaller God, not a kinder one.

What remembering means. To remember, in Hebrew usage, is not chiefly to call something to mind but to act on it. When God remembered Noah, he acted for him and the waters subsided (Genesis 8:1); when the thief asked Jesus to remember him, he was asking to be acted for (Luke 23:42). So not to remember sins is a settled determination never to act on them: never to hold them against his people, raise them again or punish them. He removes our transgressions as far as the east is from the west and casts our sins into the depths of the sea (Psalm 103:12; Isaiah 43:25; Micah 7:19). That is stronger than forgetting. A God who had forgotten might be reminded. This God knows exactly what was done and has decided, on grounds outside the sinner altogether, never to bring it up.

The reversal. This reverses the old arrangement at its most painful point. The yearly Day of Atonement was a reminder of sins year by year (10:3), saying in effect: here we are again. The new covenant promises sins completely and permanently forgiven (10:17–18). For a congregation drawn back to that calendar, this is the most personal argument of all: they were thinking of leaving a covenant in which God never raises their sins for a system whose centrepiece brought them to mind every year.

Sins forgotten, a Saviour remembered. On the night Jesus inaugurated this covenant, he took the cup, poured out for the forgiveness of sins (Matthew 26:28), and said, “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19–20). God remembers their sins no more, and his people remember Christ. The record of debt is not lost but nailed to the cross and cancelled (Colossians 2:14). Where once a priest went in every year with blood that reminded God and the people of their sins, now a high priest sits at the right hand of the Majesty, and the subject is closed. Who is a God like this, pardoning iniquity and delighting in steadfast love (Micah 7:18)?

What it does not mean. Not that believers never face the consequences of sin or God’s discipline (12:5–11). The guilt and condemnation are gone for ever.

If God remembers my sins no more, why can I not stop remembering them? Because memory and conscience are not God’s verdict. You may remember a sin all your life, and Satan, the accuser, will gladly remind you. The question is whether God holds it against you, and he has said he will not. When an old sin rises, do not argue with the memory or try to make up for it. Answer it with the promise: God will remember it no more, because Christ has paid for it. Let the memory become an occasion for thanks rather than shame (1 John 1:9; Romans 8:1).

Does this mean I must forgive and forget when others sin against me? Forgive, yes, freely and from the heart, as God in Christ forgave you (Ephesians 4:32). Forgetting in the sense of losing the memory is not possible, and God does not ask it. He asks what he does: that you decide not to hold the wrong against the person, not to keep bringing it up, not to take revenge. That does not mean pretending nothing happened, trusting someone who has not changed, or staying exposed to abuse; forgiveness and safety are different questions, and a victim of abuse should seek protection and help. But in your heart, release the debt to God, as he has released yours.

verseByVerse.quote: In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete. And what is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to vanish away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By calling the covenant new, God himself declared the old one old, and what is old is on its way out.

He makes the first one obsolete. You cannot call something new without implying that something else is old. When God spoke of a new covenant through Jeremiah, six centuries before Christ, he already marked the old one as passing.

Growing old. The words are used of clothing worn thin and of a person ageing: a garment fraying at the seams, a body bending with age.

Ready to vanish away. When this was written the sacrifices were still being offered daily. In AD 70 the Romans destroyed the temple, and the sacrificial system stopped and has never resumed. The writer is arguing from a text, not a newspaper, but any reader who lived another decade watched the argument confirmed in the most literal way. Notice the tense: the old covenant is growing old, near to disappearing. The temple was busy, the smoke went up every morning, and it looked permanent, but the writer tells them what they are looking at: an institution in its last days, kept going by habit, with the reality it pictured already seated at the right hand of God. Going back to it would be stepping onto a floor about to give way.

A covenant that will never age. Verse 13 closes the case and opens chapter 9, which walks through the old tent piece by piece. There is nothing to go back to but a covenant God has called old. In its place stands his Son, mediator of a covenant that will never age, priest of a sanctuary that will never be destroyed, offering of a sacrifice that will never be repeated.

What it does not mean. The Old Testament Scriptures are not obsolete; they testify to Christ. What is obsolete is the old covenant as a system.

Does this chapter give any ground for contempt towards Jewish people? None at all. The writer was almost certainly Jewish, writing to Jewish believers. The new covenant was promised in Israel’s own Scriptures, to Israel, by Israel’s God, and its mediator is a son of David from the tribe of Judah. Saying that the old covenant has given way to the new is not saying that Jews are worse than Gentiles; the fault Jeremiah found was in human hearts, and every Gentile heart has the same disease. Paul, who taught the same truth, had great sorrow and unceasing anguish for his people (Romans 9:1–3). The right response is not pride but love and prayer, and a glad offer of the Messiah to the people from whom he came.

Are there old-covenant habits that Christians fall into? Yes, often without noticing: treating the minister as a priest who must stand between us and God; treating a building as holier than a kitchen table; measuring ourselves by external rules while our hearts stay cold; feeling that God keeps a running tally, restarted each Sunday; believing that our standing depends on our performance this week. Each is a kind of going back to the temple. The new covenant answer is the same each time: Christ is our priest, the law is written on our hearts by the Spirit, our sins are remembered no more, and we know God ourselves.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the point in what we are saying is this: we have such a high priest, one who is seated at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven,<sup>2</sup>a minister in the holy places, in the true tent that the Lord set up, not man.<sup>3</sup>For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices; thus it is necessary for this priest also to have something to offer.<sup>4</sup>Now if he were on earth, he would not be a priest at all, since there are priests who offer gifts according to the law.<sup>5</sup>They serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things. For when Moses was about to erect the tent, he was instructed by God, saying, “See that you make everything according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain.”<sup>6</sup>But as it is, Christ has obtained a ministry that is as much more excellent than the old as the covenant he mediates is better, since it is enacted on better promises.<sup>7</sup>For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no occasion to look for a second.<sup>8</sup>For he finds fault with them when he says: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah,<sup>9</sup>not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt. For they did not continue in my covenant, and so I showed no concern for them, declares the Lord.<sup>10</sup>For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.<sup>11</sup>And they shall not teach, each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, ’Know the Lord,’ for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest.<sup>12</sup>For I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.”<sup>13</sup>In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete. And what is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to vanish away.

keyVerse.quote: For I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.
keyVerse.note: This last promise of Jeremiah’s new covenant is the foundation of the others: until sin is dealt with, no heart can be renewed and no one can know God as his own. It reverses the old covenant at its most painful point, for the yearly sacrifices brought sins to mind again (10:3). And it is made good by the priest of verses 1–2, whose one offering means God will never bring those sins up again.

8.reflection:
The writer’s main point is that “we have such a high priest” seated in heaven (v. 1). Why do you think he puts it that way, and how could it steady a believer who feels shut out, alone or far from God?

The tabernacle was a God-given copy and shadow of something greater (v. 5). How does this help you read the Old Testament? Where are Christians tempted to prefer shadows, such as buildings, rituals or routines, to Christ himself?

In verses 10–12 God says “I will” again and again. Where does your Christian life tend to run on “if” instead? Which of these promises do you most need to live on this week?

God says, “I will remember their sins no more” (v. 12). How should that shape the way you treat a past sin that still haunts you, and the way you forgive those who have wronged you?

9.title: The Blood of Christ: Once for All Into the Holy Place
9.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 8 showed Jesus serving in the true tent as mediator of the new covenant, and ended with the first covenant “ready to vanish away” (8:13). Chapter 9 sets Christ against that covenant’s sanctuary and sacrifices, at the heart of the letter’s teaching on the atonement.

The message. The way into God’s presence, closed for fourteen centuries, has been opened by the blood of Christ, once for all. By the old tent’s curtains and its one day a year, the Holy Spirit was saying “not yet”. Christ has entered heaven itself with his own blood, won a redemption that never expires, and cleansed what no animal could reach, the conscience. He will come again, not to deal with sin, but to save.

Why it was said. The readers were being drawn back to a temple still standing (see the introduction), whose worship was beautiful, ancient and plainly given by God. Could one death outside Jerusalem be worth leaving all that for? The writer answers from the old system itself: by its own design it confessed that it could not do what Christ has done.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–10 walk through the tent and its services and draw the lesson: the way in was not yet open, and the sacrifices could not perfect the conscience. Verses 11–14 set Christ against every line: a greater tent, his own blood, once for all, a cleansed conscience. Verses 15–22 explain why it had to be a death: a covenant, like a will, takes effect through death, and “without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins” (v. 22). Verses 23–28 show why it happens only once, and that he will appear a second time.

Where it leads. Every Day of Atonement the people waited outside until the high priest came out alive, the sign that the offering had been accepted, and the chapter ends with the church waiting like that. Christ appeared once to put away sin (v. 26), appears now before God for us (v. 24), and will appear a second time, bringing nothing but salvation (v. 28). The door he opened has never been shut again.

For us. No religious effort can reach your conscience, and you need no other offering. Bring the guilt you carry to his blood, serve the living God not to pay but because you are paid for, and wait for him eagerly, not fearfully.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Closed Door, and the Blood That Opened It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The old sanctuary was built to say “not yet”; the blood of Christ has opened the way. The writer tours the tent, its furniture and its ark (vv. 1–5), then its services, where only the high priest entered the inner room, once a year and never without blood (vv. 6–7). By this the Spirit showed that the way into God’s presence was not yet open and that the sacrifices could not cleanse the conscience (vv. 8–10). Then he sets Christ against it point by point: a greater tent, his own blood, once for all, an eternal redemption (vv. 11–12), and a conscience made clean to serve the living God (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology:
Architecture That Preached

By the tabernacle's design the Holy Spirit was saying not yet (see vv. 6–10). Its sacrifices could not perfect the conscience; the blood of Christ does (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The ark held manna, Aaron's staff and the tablets, with the mercy seat over them.

Now: A cleansed conscience is set free from dead works to serve the living God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now even the first covenant had regulations for worship and an earthly place of holiness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the first covenant had God-given worship and a holy place, but it was a holy place belonging to this world. The writer begins his comparison by honouring the old order before showing its limit.

A tour of the building. Chapter 8 ended by calling the first covenant obsolete (8:13), and chapter 9 opens with the same words, “the first covenant”, then takes the readers round its sanctuary. Many in his congregation were tempted to go back to the old worship precisely because it was so beautiful, so ancient and so plainly given by God. So he does not sneer at it. He walks them through it, room by room, until they can see what it was for: it was always a picture, and the one it pictured has come.

Regulations for worship. Both terms are respectful. “Regulations” (dikaiōmata) are requirements God himself laid down; nobody invented this worship. “Worship” (latreia) is priestly service, the work of approaching God. Only the adjective “earthly” (kosmikon, belonging to this world) hints at a limit, and it does all the work. The sanctuary was holy, but it was made of the same materials as the world it stood in, acacia wood, goat hair, linen and gold, a copy and shadow of the heavenly one (8:5).

Why does a Christian need to know about a tent that no longer exists? Because God built it to teach the gospel before the gospel arrived, and the New Testament explains Christ in its terms. Mercy seat, veil, atonement, sprinkled blood and access make sense only against this building, and the curtain torn at Jesus’ death (Mark 15:38) only if you know what it was for. Reading Exodus 25–40 and Leviticus 16 with this chapter open beside them is one of the surest ways to grow in understanding the cross. The tabernacle is not a puzzle for specialists; it is a picture book God drew for his children.

verseByVerse.quote: For a tent was prepared, the first section, in which were the lampstand and the table and the bread of the Presence. It is called the Holy Place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first room of the tent, the Holy Place, held the lampstand and the table with its bread, and it was as near to God as an ordinary priest ever came.

A tent was prepared. The writer always speaks of the tent (skēnē), the portable sanctuary built in the wilderness (Exodus 25–40), never of Herod’s temple standing in Jerusalem as he wrote: the meaning lies in the pattern God showed Moses on the mountain, not in what later kings added. The Holy Place (Hagia) was about thirty feet long and fifteen wide.

The lampstand and the table. The lampstand (lychnia) was the golden menorah with its seven lamps, beaten from a single piece of gold, its cups shaped like almond blossoms (Exodus 25:31–40). It burned continually, because the tent had no windows: the only light in the house of God was the light God commanded. The table carried the bread of the Presence, twelve loaves set out fresh every Sabbath, one for each tribe (Leviticus 24:5–9), as if the whole nation sat before the face of God as his guests.

The furniture was preaching him. Jesus said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), and “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). For centuries the lamp and the loaves in that windowless room had been saying the same thing.

verseByVerse.quote: Behind the second curtain was a second section called the Most Holy Place, having the golden altar of incense and the ark of the covenant covered on all sides with gold, in which was a golden urn holding the manna, and Aaron’s staff that budded, and the tablets of the covenant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behind a second curtain lay the Most Holy Place, where the ark of the covenant kept memorials of Israel’s history with God.

Behind the second curtain. One curtain hung at the entrance of the tent and another between the two rooms (Exodus 26:31–33). They were the point of the architecture: barriers, in a building designed to teach people how far away they were. The inner room, the Holy of Holies (Hagia Hagiōn), was a perfect cube, about fifteen feet each way, dark, silent and empty except for the ark, and there the glory of God was pleased to dwell. When John describes the new Jerusalem, the city is a cube too (Revelation 21:16): the whole redeemed world becomes the Most Holy Place.

The ark of the covenant. The ark (kibōtos, a chest) was a wooden box about four feet long, overlaid inside and out with gold (Exodus 25:10–22): the most sacred object in Israel, and quite simply a box with things in it.

Manna, staff and tablets. The three objects are a small sermon. The manna was bread from heaven, given to people who grumbled about the food (Exodus 16:32–34). Aaron’s staff was a dead stick that flowered overnight, to settle a rebellion against the priesthood God had chosen (Numbers 17:1–11). The tablets were the law, which Israel had broken before Moses got down the mountain (Exodus 32:19; Deuteronomy 10:1–5). So the holiest box in the world held memorials of complaint, rebellion and disobedience, kept in gold in the presence of God. And each points to Christ: the true bread from heaven (John 6:32–33), the chosen priest who came back from death to life, and the one man who kept that law from his heart.

But 1 Kings says there was nothing in the ark except the tablets. It does, in Solomon’s day (1 Kings 8:9). But the writer is describing the tabernacle of Moses’ day, when the urn of manna and Aaron’s staff were laid up before the testimony (Exodus 16:34; Numbers 17:10). Centuries later, after the ark had been captured by the Philistines and moved from place to place, only the tablets remained. The two passages describe different moments.

Uncertain wording. Exodus places the golden altar of incense in the Holy Place, just before the curtain (Exodus 30:1–6), yet the writer says the Most Holy Place had it. He says “having”, not that it stood inside: in use it belonged to the inner room, for on the Day of Atonement the high priest carried its coals and incense in, so that the cloud covered the mercy seat (Leviticus 16:12–13), and 1 Kings 6:22 likewise speaks of the altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary. Some take the word (thymiatērion, a place or vessel for incense) to mean the golden censer, as the KJV does. The altar is the likelier sense, and nothing turns on it.

verseByVerse.quote: Above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat. Of these things we cannot now speak in detail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Above the ark, under the wings of the cherubim, lay the mercy seat, where blood was sprinkled and God met his people. It was the centre of the whole building.

The cherubim of glory. Two golden cherubim stood on the lid of the ark, facing each other, their wings spread over it (Exodus 25:18–22): cherubim of glory, because the glory of God dwelt between them, and from there God promised to meet and speak with Moses (Exodus 25:22; Numbers 7:89).

The mercy seat. The lid itself was the mercy seat (hilastērion), the place of atonement, where the high priest sprinkled blood once a year (Leviticus 16:14–15). Paul uses exactly this word of Christ, whom God “put forward as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25).

Of these things we cannot now speak in detail. The preacher pulls himself up. His argument is not about furniture but about the one day in the year when the high priest went behind the curtain.

The picture on the lid. Inside the box lay the record of the people’s rebellion. Above it hovered the glory of a holy God. And exactly between them lay the lid where blood was sprinkled. God did not look down on the broken law directly; he looked at it through the blood. That is the gospel in gold and wood: the record of sin is real and is not thrown away, the holiness of God is real and is not lowered, and between them is the blood of a sacrifice. Christ is that mercy seat, the place where the wrath of God is turned away and God meets sinners in peace. This God wanted to live among the people who had just made a golden calf, and at the heart of the house he gave them he put not a throne of judgment but a seat of mercy.

In everyday life. Most of us carry a private record of our failures, and take it out when we are tired or ashamed. The tabernacle does not tell you to pretend the record is not there; it tells you where to put it: under the mercy seat, under the blood. When a remembered sin accuses you, do not argue that it was not so bad or bury it under a better week; name it to God, and remember that he looks at it through the blood of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: These preparations having thus been made, the priests go regularly into the first section, performing their ritual duties, but into the second only the high priest goes, and he but once a year, and not without taking blood, which he offers for himself and for the unintentional sins of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Priests served in the outer room every day, but only the high priest entered the inner room, once a year, never without blood, and first for his own sins. Every detail said how hard it was to come near to God.

The priests go regularly. The writer moves from the architecture to what happened in it, and uses the present tense, most likely because the temple services were still going on as he wrote (see the introduction). “Regularly” (dia pantos) means continually: every morning and evening to tend the lamps and burn incense, every Sabbath to change the bread (Exodus 27:20–21; 30:7–8).

Performing their ritual duties. Literally, completing their services (tas latreias epitelountes), and next day the duties were all waiting again: always being completed and never complete. No seat for the priest appears among the tent’s furnishings; he stood at his service day after day (10:11).

Only the high priest, once a year. One man out of a nation. Only once a year, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29–34), going in more than once that day, but only on that day. Never without blood: no man walked into the presence of God on his own merits, not even the holiest man in Israel. And first for himself, a bull (Leviticus 16:11), because the man doing the representing was himself part of the problem; then for the people, a goat (16:15). Together they add up to this: for some fourteen centuries, access to God amounted to one man, on one day, with a basin of blood, having first dealt with his own sin. God did not do this because he was content with the distance. He did it so that when his Son came, his people would know exactly what he had done.

The sins it did not reach. “Unintentional sins” (agnoēmata) are sins of ignorance and error, the sins for which the law’s sacrifices were given (5:2; Numbers 15:22–29). For the high-handed sin, done in defiance of God, the law named no offering (Numbers 15:30–31), though it did provide for some wilful wrongs that were confessed and repaid (Leviticus 6:1–7). The Day of Atonement did cleanse the people from all their sins before the LORD (Leviticus 16:21, 30), but that cleansing was ceremonial, and no animal’s blood could truly take a sin away (10:4). The sins a man chose with his eyes open still lay on his conscience when he went home. David knew it. After Bathsheba and Uriah he wrote: “you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it” (Psalm 51:16). There was no animal for what he had done; he could only throw himself on the mercy of God.

A high priest with no bull of his own. The writer lets his readers feel the shape of a closed door before setting Christ against it. Aaron had to bring a bull for himself first; Christ is holy, innocent and unstained, and has no need to offer for his own sins (7:26–27). Aaron represented the people while sharing their guilt; Christ represents them while bearing it. Aaron went in once a year and came out to die like his fathers; Christ went in once for all and lives for ever to intercede (7:24–25). The one man, the one day and the basin of blood were a portrait drawn in outline, and Jesus is the face that fills it.

In everyday life. A faithful Israelite lived and died without ever coming nearer to God than a curtain. Tonight you may pray, perhaps briefly and tiredly, and come straight into the presence of God through Christ, with no bull, no goat and no priest between you. Remember the curtain, and thank him that you may come in.

Is there forgiveness for a sin I committed knowing it was wrong? Yes. This is exactly the sin the old sacrifices could not reach, and exactly the sin Christ came to deal with. Peter denied Jesus with full knowledge, three times, with curses, and was restored on the shore (John 21:15–19). Do not reclassify a sin committed with your eyes open as a weakness so that it will feel forgivable. Call it what it was, confess it, and trust the blood shed for precisely that. That it grieves you is a sign that the Spirit is at work in you, not that you are beyond reach.

verseByVerse.quote: By this the Holy Spirit indicates that the way into the holy places is not yet opened as long as the first section is still standing (which is symbolic for the present age). According to this arrangement, gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the conscience of the worshiper, but deal only with food and drink and various washings, regulations for the body imposed until the time of reformation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through the tent’s design the Holy Spirit was teaching that the way into God’s presence was not yet open, and that its sacrifices could not cleanse the conscience. The whole arrangement was temporary, waiting for the time when God would set things right.

By this the Holy Spirit indicates. “Indicates” (dēlountos) means makes clear. The Spirit who gave Moses the pattern was speaking through the architecture, a sermon in cloth and gold preached silently for centuries, and its message was two words: not yet. The road (hodos) into the true presence of God was not open, and every priest who stopped at the second curtain was preaching it. The first tent was “symbolic” (parabolē, a parable), its meaning hidden in plain sight until the one it pictured came.

Cannot perfect the conscience. Then the verdict, the heart of the chapter. “Perfect” (teleiōsai) means bring to completion, to the goal. “Conscience” (syneidēsis) is the inner awareness of guilt, the knowledge we carry about ourselves. The sacrifices did what they were given to do, but they could not reach the conscience. A man could bring his goat, watch it die, see the blood applied, walk home ceremonially clean, and still know perfectly well what he had done (10:1–4).

Until the time of reformation. Food laws (Leviticus 11), drink offerings and rules about drink (Numbers 6:3), ritual washings (Leviticus 15; Numbers 19) were “regulations for the body” (dikaiōmata sarkos), “imposed” (epikeimena) like a load; Peter called the law a yoke “that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear” (Acts 15:10). The “reformation” (diorthōsis) is the setting straight of things, a word medical writers used of setting a broken limb. The old arrangement had an expiry date written into it from the beginning.

Torn from the top. That time arrived in a person. When Jesus died, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51; Mark 15:38): from the top, so God did it, not men. Soon the letter will say that we now have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way he opened for us through the curtain (10:19–20).

A description you can check from the inside. You can attend, give, sing and serve and still lie awake with the thing you did; the old system was designed so that the ache would remain until something could answer it. The modern versions seldom involve goats. The churchgoer who trusts his attendance and the unbeliever who trusts that he is at least a decent person are both offering something that cannot reach the conscience, and the same blood is offered to both.

What it does not mean. Not that believers under the old covenant had no forgiveness. They were truly forgiven through faith in God’s promise, looking forward to what the sacrifices pointed to (11:39–40; Romans 3:25; 4:6–8; on the ground of it, see v. 15). But the sacrifices themselves could not give the settled conscience that Christ’s finished work now gives. The saints of old were forgiven, and longed for what we have been shown.

Do the food laws and washings apply to Christians today? No. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), and Peter was told not to call common what God has made clean (Acts 10:15). The moral law, summarised in the Ten Commandments, still shows us how to love God and our neighbour; but the ceremonial laws were shadows, and the substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, 19.3). No food and no washing brings a Christian nearer to God.

Why do I still feel guilty after I have prayed and gone to church? Sometimes because we are leaning on the activity, and religious activity cannot do what only Christ’s blood does. Ask what you are trusting: the fact that you prayed, or the one you prayed to. Sometimes guilt lingers because a particular sin has not been confessed, or a wrong done to someone has not been put right; then the remedy is to do that. And sometimes the conscience is oversensitive and needs to be taught by Scripture, often with the help of a wise pastor or biblical counsellor. In each case, bring it to Christ, and believe what God says about his blood.

Uncertain wording. “The first section” (prōtē skēnē, first tent) meant the outer room in verses 2 and 6, and may do so here, a barrier before the inner room; or it may mean the whole first tabernacle, set against the “greater and more perfect tent” of verse 11. And “the present age” could mean the time of the old order or the writer’s own day. The likeliest sense is that the whole first arrangement, while it stood, was a parable that the way was still shut; either way the point is the same.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Christ appeared as a high priest of the good things that have come, then through the greater and more perfect tent (not made with hands, that is, not of this creation) he entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ has entered the true presence of God once for all, not with animal blood but with his own, and so has won a redemption that never expires. After ten verses of curtains and restrictions, the sentence breaks like a door opening.

The good things that have come. The blessings of the new covenant (tōn genomenōn agathōn) are already present: real forgiveness, access to God, a clean conscience. The one who brings them is already here.

The greater and more perfect tent. The sanctuary Christ passed through is the heavenly reality the tabernacle copied: greater (meizonos) because it is God’s own dwelling, and more perfect (teleioteras) because it does what the earthly one could only picture, bringing a man into the presence of God. “Not made with hands” sets human shrines against God’s reality (Acts 7:48; Mark 14:58), and “not of this creation” puts it outside the whole order of made things. It is heaven, the presence of God himself (v. 24).

Once for all. There is the word again, ephapax, as in 7:27, and set against verse 7 it is the whole argument. The high priest went in every year and came out again, and next year had to go back. This one went in once in all history, at his ascension, and sat down (1:3; 10:12).

An eternal redemption. “Redemption” (lytrōsis) is release by ransom, as of captives and slaves. “Eternal” is the letter’s contrast with the annual: not a release renewed each autumn, but one that never expires, and “securing” (having obtained) means it is already achieved.

By means of his own blood. Every high priest walked behind that curtain carrying blood that was not his, handling somebody else’s death. This priest brought his own: he had already been the sacrifice before he entered as the priest. He was the priest and the lamb, and needed no animal to stand in for him, because he was standing in for us. Blood signifies life given up in death (Leviticus 17:11), and this was the blood of the sinless Son of God (Acts 20:28).

A redemption actually secured. Christ obtained not a possible redemption, offered to all and secured for none, but an actual redemption for those for whom he died. When a ransom is paid, the captive goes free; a redeemed slave does not go back to the market to see whether he is still free. His death did not make salvation merely possible; it accomplished it, and the Spirit will apply it to every one of those for whom it was paid (John 6:37–39; 10:11, 27–29). Reformed Christians call this definite or particular redemption (see also v. 28), and the same Christ is freely held out to everyone.

What it does not mean. “By means of his own blood” does not mean that Christ carried a vessel of blood into heaven; he entered by virtue of a death already accomplished. Nor does his work in heaven complete an unfinished sacrifice. The sacrifice was finished on the cross: “It is finished” (John 19:30). In heaven he appears for us on the ground of what was done, and intercedes for us (7:25), but he never offers again.

Does eternal redemption mean I can never be lost? Yes, if you belong to Christ. A redemption that could be lost would last only as long as the redeemed held on. But the ransom was paid by Christ and accepted by the Father, and the one who redeemed you keeps you (John 10:28–29; Romans 8:33–39). That does not make sin unimportant. The redeemed are given a new heart and will persevere in faith and holiness, though with falls along the way, and Hebrews warns sharply against drifting, because warnings are one of the means God uses to keep his people. But your security rests on what he secured, not on how firmly you hold him.

Textual note. Many manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “good things to come” (mellontōn), as in 10:1. The difference is small: the good things have arrived in Christ and will be fully enjoyed when he returns.

verseByVerse.quote: For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the sprinkling of defiled persons with the ashes of a heifer, sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If animal blood and a heifer’s ashes could make the body ceremonially clean, the blood of Christ, who offered himself to God, will far more surely cleanse the conscience and set us free to serve the living God. The argument runs from the lesser to the greater, and begins by granting that the old rites worked.

Goats, bulls and a heifer. The blood of goats and bulls was shed on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). The ashes of a spotless red heifer, burned outside the camp with cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet yarn, were mixed with water and sprinkled on anyone who had touched a dead body (Numbers 19). In a world full of death, everyone needed the water sooner or later.

The purification of the flesh. And it worked. “Sanctify” (hagiazei) is to make holy: the rite really restored ritual purity, so that a man could worship again. But it was purification of the flesh (tēs sarkos katharotēta): it made a man fit to come back into the camp, and did not reach the man inside.

How much more. If the shadow worked outwardly, how much more (posō mallon) will the substance work inwardly. Three things are said about this offering. First, it was offered “through the eternal Spirit”, most likely the Holy Spirit, who anointed and empowered Christ throughout his ministry (Luke 4:18; Acts 10:38) and in his self-offering (on the wording, see below). The whole Trinity is in the sentence: the Son offers himself, through the Spirit, to the Father. Calvary was not the Father doing something to an unwilling Son, nor the Son persuading a reluctant Father, but the one God acting together to save.

Offered himself. Second, “himself” is the difference between this and every sacrifice before it. No animal ever volunteered. This victim walked to it (John 10:17–18), after praying with loud cries and tears (5:7). He was both priest and sacrifice.

Without blemish to God. Third, “without blemish” (amōmos), the requirement for every sacrificial animal (Leviticus 22:20–22), here applied to a moral life. Every lamb was inspected for defects. This one was inspected by enemies who wanted a charge and could not find one; by Pilate, who found no guilt in him; by a dying thief, who said “this man has done nothing wrong”; and by the Father, who was well pleased (1 Peter 1:19; 2:22; Luke 23:4, 41).

Purify our conscience from dead works. Here is the answer to verse 9: not the flesh but the conscience, which goes on accusing after the ritual is complete. “Dead works” (nekra erga), as in 6:1, are works that lead to death: our sins, and perhaps also religious works done to earn God’s favour. As touching a corpse defiled a man, so dead works defile the conscience. We have all been handling death, and the blood of Christ is the water that cleanses from it.

To serve the living God. Dead works, living God: the contrast is exact. “Serve” (latreuein) is to worship, to serve as a priest. An uncleansed conscience produces only religious effort, performed to settle a debt it never settles; a cleansed conscience is released into service.

Working not for our pardon but from it. The ashes of a heifer could make a man clean enough to come back into the camp. The blood of Christ makes a sinner clean enough to come into the presence of the living God. The whole Godhead bent down to wash the conscience of people who had been handling death all their lives, and having washed us, he does not send us away. He takes us into his service, priests of the living God, working not for our pardon but from it.

How do I know my conscience has been cleansed, when I still remember what I did? Cleansing is not forgetting. Paul never forgot that he had persecuted the church (1 Timothy 1:13–15), but he remembered it as a forgiven man, and it made him wonder at grace rather than sink under guilt. A cleansed conscience no longer accuses you before God, because it has accepted God’s verdict on the blood of Christ. The memory may still bring sorrow and make you gentle with others; but when it says you are condemned, answer it with this verse.

What is the difference between serving to pay and serving because you are free? The work may look the same; the difference is in the heart. The man who serves to pay is anxious, keeps score, and is crushed when he fails, because his standing depends on it. The man who serves because he is free works hard too, but gladly: he can rest without guilt, fail without despair, and rejoice when someone else gets the credit. If your service feels like an unpaid debt, you have probably slipped back into dead works. Go back to the blood, and begin again from there.

Uncertain wording. “Through the eternal Spirit” (dia pneumatos aiōniou) has no article in Greek, so it is not certain whether the writer means the Holy Spirit or Christ’s own eternal divine nature, in which he offered himself. Most, with the ESV’s capital letter, take it of the Holy Spirit, the likeliest meaning; either way the offering had eternal worth because of who offered it.
verseByVerse.note: The ashes of a red heifer were mixed with water to cleanse anyone defiled by touching a corpse.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–28 — A Death That Reaches Backward, and a Return Without Sin
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: It had to be a death, and it had to happen only once. Christ’s death puts the new covenant into force and redeems even those who sinned under the old one (v. 15), as a will takes effect only when its maker dies (vv. 16–17). The first covenant itself was sealed with blood, for without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness (vv. 18–22). And because Christ’s sacrifice is the real one, offered in heaven itself, it never needs repeating (vv. 23–26): as each of us dies once and then faces judgment, Christ was offered once to bear sins, and will appear a second time to save those who wait for him (vv. 27–28).
verseByVerse.theology:
How the Old Testament Saints Were Saved

Christ's death redeems from transgressions committed under the first covenant (see the note on v. 15).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: At Sinai the book and the people were sprinkled with the blood of the covenant.

Now: Christ will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to save those eagerly waiting for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, since a death has occurred that redeems them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because his blood cleanses the conscience, Christ is the mediator of the new covenant, and his death redeems even those who sinned under the old one, so that all whom God calls receive the eternal inheritance.

The mediator of a new covenant. “Therefore”: because his blood cleanses the conscience (v. 14). A “mediator” (mesitēs) stands between two parties to bring them together, and the new covenant is the one God promised through Jeremiah, in which he writes his law on the heart and remembers sins no more (Jeremiah 31:31–34; 8:8–12). The covenant is made in his blood.

Those who are called. The Greek form (hoi keklēmenoi) means those who have been called and remain called: not those who volunteered, but those whom God has effectually called, by a call that does what it says (3:1; Romans 8:28–30). The gospel invitation goes out to all, but in his own people the Spirit makes it a summons that wakes the dead, as the voice of Jesus brought Lazarus out of the tomb (John 11:43–44).

The promised eternal inheritance. Family language (klēronomia): the Son was appointed heir of all things (1:2), and what is his by right becomes theirs by gift. Not the land of Canaan, which Israel lost, but eternal life, the new creation, God himself: an inheritance “imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven” (1 Peter 1:4).

A death has occurred. The death is Christ’s, and it redeems (apolytrōsis, release by ransom). The heirs inherit only because a death has taken place. And the death reaches backward, to the transgressions of people who lived and died under the old arrangement. That answers an old question: if the blood of bulls and goats could not take away sins (10:4), on what basis were Abraham, Moses and David forgiven? On exactly the same basis as we are; the payment was made afterwards.

Credit against a payment God intended to make. Paul says the same: in his divine forbearance God had passed over former sins, and showed his righteousness at the cross, “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:25–26). Scripture has not two ways of salvation, an older by law and a newer by grace, but one: everyone ever saved was saved by the same death, some looking forward to it, some looking back. Abel’s lamb, Abraham’s ram, the blood on the doorposts in Egypt, the goat of every Day of Atonement, all drew on an account that would be paid in full on a hill outside Jerusalem. God has only ever had one way of saving sinners, and it has always been his Son.

How do I know if I am one of the called? Not by trying to look into God’s secret decrees, but by looking at Christ. Those whom God calls, he brings to faith in his Son (John 6:37, 44). If you are trusting Christ, however weakly, you were called; nobody comes unless the Father draws him. If you are not sure you are trusting him, do not wait for a sign: come to him now, for he has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out. The call of God is heard in the invitation of the gospel.

Were Old Testament believers saved by keeping the law? No. They were saved by grace through faith, exactly as we are (Romans 4:1–8; Galatians 3:6–9). Their sacrifices expressed faith and repentance and pointed to the coming sacrifice, but they were not the ground of forgiveness; the ground was the death this verse describes. Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness, the righteousness of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: For where a will is involved, the death of the one who made it must be established. For a will takes effect only at death, since it is not in force as long as the one who made it is alive. Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A will takes effect only when the one who made it dies, and so the new covenant came into force through Christ’s death, just as the first covenant was inaugurated with blood.

For where a will is involved. The writer is playing on a word. The Greek diathēkē means both covenant and testament, and in everyday Greek it usually meant a last will. He has used it in the first sense for two chapters, and here turns it to the second: an inheritance (v. 15) comes through a will, and a will requires a death.

The death must be established. A will “takes effect” (bebaia, valid, in force) only at death. It is a real document the day it is signed, and does nothing whatever until that one event. Christ is the mediator, and there is a promised inheritance, but the testator had to die before anybody could receive anything.

Not even the first covenant. “Inaugurated” (enkekainistai) means dedicated, put into effect. The writer swings back to the other sense of the word: the Sinai covenant was ratified with blood (v. 19; Exodus 24:3–8), and in ancient covenant-making a sacrificial death often sealed the agreement (Genesis 15:9–18; Jeremiah 34:18–20). Whichever way you read diathēkē, somebody has to die before it operates.

The cross as the reading of a will. The cross was a sacrifice and a penalty borne, and also the death that made a will operative, when an estate long promised became available to the heirs. In every other case the testator is dead when the will is read, and has no further say. This testator rose on the third day, and is himself the executor of his own will: he sees to it personally that every heir receives what was left to him.

All of it, and himself with it. The Son is the heir of all things, and he wrote into his will people who had nothing to bring and every reason to be left out: rebels, debtors and strangers to the covenant. He did what no rich man ever does for a beggar: he died, so that what was his by right could become theirs by gift, and the estate he left is not a portion of his goods but all of them, and himself with them.

If a will can be changed, can God change his mind about me? No. A human will can be altered while the testator lives, but this one came into force by his death, and the testator who rose does not revoke it. Its terms are fixed in his blood, and he lives to see them carried out (7:25); God’s promises in Christ are yes and amen (2 Corinthians 1:20). The will names its heirs as those who are called and who trust the Son, and if you are trusting him, you are named.

Uncertain wording. Some translators keep “covenant” throughout verses 16–17, reading them of a covenant ratified by a representative death, the slain animal standing for the covenant-maker. The ESV reads “will”, and verse 17 favours it, because a document “not in force as long as the one who made it is alive” fits a will exactly. Both readings land in the same place: the covenant could not come into force without the death of Christ.
verseByVerse.note: The Greek word for “covenant” can also mean a “will,” and the writer uses both senses.

verseByVerse.quote: For when every commandment of the law had been declared by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying, “This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you.” And in the same way he sprinkled with the blood both the tent and all the vessels used in worship. Indeed, under the law almost everything is purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses sealed the first covenant by sprinkling blood on the book, the people and the tent, because under the law cleansing and forgiveness come only through a death. The writer wants the blood in his readers’ eyes.

Declared to all the people. The scene is Exodus 24, the ratification of the covenant at Sinai. Moses first read the Book of the Covenant to the people, and they promised to obey (Exodus 24:3–7). Nobody was bound to something they had not heard.

Scarlet wool and hyssop. Hyssop was a small bushy plant used as a brush. It painted the blood on the doorposts at the Passover (Exodus 12:22) and was used in the cleansing of lepers (Leviticus 14:4–7); David prayed, “Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean” (Psalm 51:7); and at the cross a sponge of sour wine was lifted to Jesus on a hyssop branch (John 19:29).

The book, the people, the tent and the vessels. Exodus mentions blood on the altar and the people (Exodus 24:6–8), and oil on the tent and its furnishings, with blood on the altar (Exodus 40:9–11; Leviticus 8:15, 19). The writer adds the book, the water, scarlet wool and hyssop, and blood on the tent, drawing on the law’s other cleansing rites (Leviticus 14:4–7; Numbers 19:6, 18) and perhaps on a tradition his readers knew. Nothing he adds contradicts Exodus. Picture a nation standing in the open, and blood flicked over them and over the scroll, binding document and people together. Nothing used in the worship of a holy God by sinful people could be used without being cleansed first.

Almost everything. The “almost” (schedon) is careful. Some things were purified by water or fire (Numbers 31:22–24), and the very poor could bring flour for a sin offering (Leviticus 5:11–13). But blood was the main means, and the exceptions prove the rule by their rarity.

Without the shedding of blood. “Shedding of blood” (haimatekchysia), blood-pouring, may be a word the writer coined himself. “Forgiveness” (aphesis) is release, cancellation. Sin deserves death (Romans 6:23), and forgiveness comes only when a substitute dies in the sinner’s place, life given for life (Leviticus 17:11). This is penal substitution, which the whole sacrificial system taught: Christ bearing the penalty of our sin in our place. He was pierced for our transgressions (Isaiah 53:5), and God made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21).

The blood of the covenant. Moses’ words from Exodus 24:8 were heard again in an upper room, from a man holding a cup: “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many” (Mark 14:24), “the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20). Jesus was quoting Sinai deliberately. At Sinai the people stood under the blood of calves and goats and promised to keep a law they would break within weeks. In the upper room Jesus said the same words, then went out and shed his own blood for people who would break their promises that same night. The blood of the old covenant bound the people to obey; the blood of the new secured forgiveness for those who had not.

In everyday life. When someone wrongs you, forgiveness turns out to cost something. You cannot simply say it did not matter; it did. To forgive is to absorb the cost yourself rather than make the other person pay it: the lost money, the hurt reputation, the pain you carry and refuse to repay. That is a small picture of what God did. When you find it hard to forgive, look at the cross, where your own debt was absorbed, and ask the Spirit who has poured God’s love into your heart (Romans 5:5) to make you able.

Is this not a primitive idea of a God who needs blood? The point is not that God is appeased by suffering, the pagan idea of an angry deity bribed with blood. It is that sin is not a debt that can simply be written off, as though the wrong had never mattered. A God who overlooked evil would not be kind; he would be indifferent to the people it destroyed. A judge who lets the man who abused a child walk free because he is a forgiving sort of person is not merciful but corrupt. Forgiveness is free to the one forgiven and costly to the one who forgives, and the cross is what it costs when the wrong is against God. And God in love provided the death himself, in his Son (Romans 5:8; 1 John 4:10): the one who demanded the blood is the one who gave it.

Why does the Lord’s Supper use wine for blood? Because Jesus applied the covenant words of Sinai to his own death, and gave the cup as the sign of it. The wine does not become blood; it is a sign and pledge of the blood once shed, and by faith those who drink it truly feed on Christ and the benefits of his death, spiritually and not physically (1 Corinthians 10:16; 11:25–26; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 30.7; the Westminster Confession 29.7). It is not a repeated sacrifice, since this chapter insists there is only one, but a meal of remembrance and communion. Come to it as a forgiven sinner, examining yourself, not as someone trying to make yourself worthy.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these rites, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. For Christ has entered, not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf. Nor was it to offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest enters the holy places every year with blood not his own, for then he would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. But as it is, he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s one sacrifice opened the true, heavenly sanctuary, where he now appears before God for us, and it never needs repeating, because it actually put sin away.

The copies and the heavenly things themselves. “Copies” (hypodeigmata), as in 8:5, are sketches or patterns, and the copy was cleansed with animal blood. The heavenly reality needed “better sacrifices”, plural to match the old rites, but meaning Christ’s single sacrifice, offered once (vv. 25–26). On why heavenly things should need cleansing, see below.

Into heaven itself. Earthly shrines are only copies (antitypa, corresponding figures) of the real. Christ entered not a heavenly building but heaven itself, the very presence of God.

Not repeatedly. If Christ’s offering worked the way the old ones did, it would need renewing, and since sin has been in the world from the beginning, he would have been dying over and over since Eden. A sacrifice that has to be repeated is a sacrifice that did not work.

At the end of the ages. “The end of the ages” (synteleia tōn aiōnōn), their completion, is where the New Testament places the cross (1:2): not in the middle of history but at its climax. Everything before ran toward it; everything since runs from it.
