To put away sin. “Put away” (athetēsis) is a strong word: to abolish, annul, the word used of setting aside the former commandment (7:18). Sin was not merely covered, as the old rites covered it, but abolished, its guilt cancelled and its power broken, “by the sacrifice of himself”.

On our behalf. “Now”: at this very moment. “Appear” (emphanisthēnai) is to show oneself before someone’s face. The high priest went behind the curtain with the names of the tribes cut into stones on his shoulders and on the breastpiece over his heart (Exodus 28:9–12, 29). This one went into the presence of God carrying us, and he is there now (7:25; Romans 8:34; 1 John 2:1).

What it does not mean. Christ’s appearing for us does not mean that the Father is reluctant and must be talked round. It was the Father who sent him (John 3:16), and Christ appears before a Father who loves us as he loves the Son (John 16:26–27; 17:23).

What is Christ doing in heaven now? He is appearing for you. Not repeating his finished sacrifice, but presenting himself, whose sacrifice was accepted, as the ground on which you are received. He intercedes for his people, as he prayed for Peter (Luke 22:32; Romans 8:34). He rules all things for the church (Ephesians 1:20–22), and he is preparing a place (John 14:2–3). When you pray, you come to a Father before whom your Saviour is already standing, with your name on his heart.

Does the Roman Catholic Mass repeat Christ’s sacrifice? Roman Catholic teaching calls the Mass a true and propitiatory sacrifice, the same sacrifice as Calvary offered in an unbloody manner, and denies that it is a new one. But this passage rules out any continuing offering of Christ for sin: he does not offer himself repeatedly; he appeared once for all to put away sin. The Lord’s Supper is a remembrance of that one sacrifice and a communion in it, not a re-presentation of the victim to God for propitiation (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 30.2; the Westminster Confession 29.2). Hebrews returns to this again and again (7:27; 10:10–14, 18): where there is forgiveness, there is no longer any offering for sin.

Uncertain wording. Why would “the heavenly things themselves” need purifying? Not because heaven is defiled. The likeliest sense is that the way for sinners into the heavenly sanctuary had to be opened by blood, as the tabernacle had to be dedicated before it could be used. Some add that God’s people are themselves his true house (3:6), and they needed cleansing. Either way, the real sanctuary required a real sacrifice.

verseByVerse.quote: And just as it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment, so Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As every person dies once and then faces judgment, Christ died once to bear the sins of many, and he will come again, not to deal with sin, but to bring full salvation to those who wait for him.

Appointed to die once. “Appointed” (apokeitai) means laid up, reserved. Death is not an accident of biology but an appointment kept, God’s appointment because of sin (Genesis 3:19; Romans 5:12). And “once” (hapax) rules out any scheme of repeated lives (those Jesus raised, like Lazarus, were brought back to this life and died again, which is not reincarnation), and sets the pattern the next verse needs: one death, then the reckoning.

After that comes judgment. Every person faces the judgment (krisis) of God. At death the soul goes at once into conscious existence, the believer to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8), the unbeliever to punishment (Luke 16:22–26); at Christ’s return all will be raised and judged (John 5:28–29; Revelation 20:11–15).

To bear the sins of many. “So Christ” follows the human pattern exactly: offered once (hapax prosenechtheis), matching the one death of every person, and then something follows. But his death was for others. “To bear the sins” (anenenkein hamartias, to carry up sins) is Isaiah’s verb: “he bore the sin of many” (Isaiah 53:12). Not to sympathise with sinners but to shoulder what they owed, bearing their penalty in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24).

Will appear a second time. Here the parallel turns: what follows his death is not judgment for him, for he has been judged already, in our place. “Appear” (ophthēsetai) means will be seen: his coming will be visible. The picture is from the Day of Atonement. No one was allowed in the tent while the high priest made atonement, and the people waited outside (Leviticus 16:17). He went in under a warning that he could die there (Leviticus 16:2, 13), and when he came out alive, the offering had been accepted, and the waiting turned to joy. So Christ will come out from heaven, to the joy of his people.

Not to deal with sin. Literally “without sin” (chōris hamartias): not to bear sin again. For anyone afraid of the second coming, the sin business is finished. He is not returning to reopen the file or to see whether his first coming worked.

Eagerly waiting. “To save” (eis sōtērian) means the final and full salvation of his people, including the resurrection of their bodies (Romans 8:23; Philippians 3:20–21). “Eagerly waiting” (apekdechomenois) is a mark of true believers (Titus 2:13; 2 Timothy 4:8). After all the blood and curtains and ashes, this is the Christian: someone at the window, looking down the road, waiting for a man who has already dealt with everything that could have made the waiting frightening.

Three appearings. Three times in a few lines the writer says Christ appears: once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin (v. 26), now in the presence of God for us (v. 24), and a second time to save (v. 28). Past, present and future are all held by the one sacrifice.

Not the judgment but the Judge. Every one of us has an appointment we cannot cancel: death, and then the judgment. Christ kept that appointment for us. He died once, and the judgment that should have followed our death fell on him, as he bore the sins of many. So for his people the order of the verse is changed: after death comes not the judgment but the Judge, the one who was judged in their place. He who came the first time carrying their sins will come the second time without them, bringing nothing but salvation.

What it does not mean. “Appear a second time” does not mean a secret coming before his visible return. Scripture speaks of one future return, visible and glorious, at which he gathers his people and judges the world (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). Many sincere Christians expect a secret rapture before a time of tribulation; this commentary reads the gathering of believers and the visible return as one event, because the same passages place them together. Either way, he is coming for his own.

Does “many” mean that Christ bore the sins of only some? The word comes from Isaiah 53:12, where it sets the one servant against the great number he saves, and Jesus used it of his own death, a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). Many Christians take it simply to mean the multitude. Reformed Christians take it to mean that he actually bore the sins of a definite people, all who will be saved, the many sons he brings to glory (2:10). The second is the more likely, since to bear sin is to carry it away, and those whose sins he carried will never have to bear them (compare 2:9). Faithful Christians differ over this without doubting each other’s love for the cross. Either way, many is not few, and the invitation is to all: no one who comes to him will find that he was not included.

Wouldn’t another life be kinder? Many in the modern West say they believe in reincarnation, and the appeal is plain: another life sounds like a second chance, more time, no final verdict. Yet where the idea was born, rebirth is not good news but a wheel to be escaped, in which each life pays the debts of the last and the accounts are never closed; and in a world of endless retakes nothing would quite count. Hebrews is more sobering and more hopeful. You have one life, and it matters; it is written in ink. But Christ also had one death, and his “once” answers ours: he did not need to come back and try again, because he did not fail the first time. The second chance people long for is not found in another life. It is offered in this one, today, by the one who will come a second time not to deal with sin but to save.

Will Christians be judged at the last day? Yes, but not to decide whether they are saved. Believers too will stand before God, and their lives will be opened (2 Corinthians 5:10; Romans 14:10–12). But their guilt was settled at the cross, and “there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). What remains is a Father’s public acknowledgement of his children, and the reward of what was done in his name, even a cup of cold water (Matthew 10:42). That should make us serious about how we live, and not afraid of the day.

What happens to my believing loved ones who have died? They are with Christ, consciously, now. To be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8), and Paul calls it far better (Philippians 1:23). They are not unconscious, nor in purgatory, nor wandering, but at rest and in joy, waiting with us for the resurrection of the body. When Christ appears the second time, God will bring them with him (1 Thessalonians 4:14), and their bodies will be raised and made like his. You may grieve, and you should; but you grieve as one who has hope.

Where Christians differ: is there a second chance after death, or a purgatory? Some teach that those who never heard the gospel will have an opportunity to believe after death. Roman Catholic teaching holds that many believers must pass through purgatory to be purified before heaven. Others teach soul sleep, unconsciousness until the resurrection, or the annihilation of the wicked. Such views are often held out of real compassion, or a sincere reading of hard texts. This commentary’s view: this verse is clear: death, then judgment, not a further opportunity; our destiny is fixed at death (Luke 16:26). Believers enter conscious joy with Christ immediately (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23). There is no purgatory, because by a single offering Christ has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (10:14), and that leaves nothing to be paid afterward. For believers the verdict was given at the cross; what remains is a review for reward (2 Corinthians 5:10), not a sentence to be served. Unbelievers face conscious punishment, eternal and real (Matthew 25:46; Revelation 14:11). The time to respond to the gospel is now (3:13; 2 Corinthians 6:2).

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

who made it is alive.<sup>18</sup>Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.<sup>19</sup>For when every commandment of the law had been declared by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people,<sup>20</sup>saying, “This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you.”<sup>21</sup>And in the same way he sprinkled with the blood both the tent and all the vessels used in worship.<sup>22</sup>Indeed, under the law almost everything is purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins.<sup>23</sup>Thus it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these rites, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these.<sup>24</sup>For Christ has entered, not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf.<sup>25</sup>Nor was it to offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest enters the holy places every year with blood not his own,<sup>26</sup>for then he would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. But as it is, he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.<sup>27</sup>And just as it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment,<sup>28</sup>so Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him.

keyVerse.quote: How much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on what the old sacrifices could do, cleanse the body, and what they could not, cleanse the conscience (v. 9). Here the answer arrives: the Son, offering himself through the Spirit to the Father, cleanses the inner guilt no ritual reached. And the cleansing has a purpose: not relief only, but free and glad service of the living God.

9.reflection:
The tabernacle was built so that its curtains, restrictions and single day of entry said “not yet” (vv. 6–8). What does it mean to you that you may now come straight into God’s presence through Christ? How might it change the way you begin to pray?

Verse 9 says the old sacrifices could not “perfect the conscience”. What do people, including churchgoers, rely on today to quiet a guilty conscience, and why can none of it reach the guilt itself?

Christ cleanses our conscience “from dead works to serve the living God” (v. 14). What is the difference between serving God to pay a debt and serving him because the debt is paid? Where do you see each in your own life?

Verses 27–28 set our one death and judgment beside Christ’s one offering and second appearing. How does this passage help a Christian face death, and how can it make us eager rather than afraid for his return?

10.title: Once for All: The New and Living Way
10.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 10 completes the letter’s central argument on priesthood, covenant and sacrifice, begun at 7:1, and then turns it into appeal. From verse 19 the teaching becomes the exhortation that runs to the end of the letter.

The message. Christ’s one offering has done what the endless sacrifices never could: it has perfected for all time those God sets apart, so that he remembers their sins no more and no other offering remains. Therefore come in. Draw near to God with confidence, hold fast your hope, keep meeting and stirring one another up, and do not throw away your confidence, because the one sacrifice cannot be replaced and the coming one will come.

Why it was said. The readers were being drawn back to a temple where priests still stood and offered every day (v. 11; see the introduction). They had once suffered gladly for Christ (vv. 32–34), but now some had stopped meeting (v. 25) and all were weary. Going back looked like a return to something solid; the writer shows it would be leaving the only sacrifice there is.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–4: the yearly sacrifices, by being repeated, confessed that they had not removed sin; they only brought it to mind. Verses 5–10: Psalm 40 shows what God wanted instead, a willing Son in a prepared body, by whose will we are sanctified once for all. Verses 11–14: the priests stand daily, but Christ offered once and sat down. Verses 15–18: Jeremiah’s promise settles it, for where sins are remembered no more, no offering remains. Verses 19–25 draw the “therefore”: draw near, hold fast, consider one another. Verses 26–31 warn that for one who knowingly tramples the Son there is no other sacrifice, only judgment. Verses 32–39 recall the readers’ former courage, call them to endure, and end in confidence: we are not of those who shrink back.

Where it leads. The chapter turns on a posture. Every priest stood, because his work was never done; Christ “sat down at the right hand of God” (v. 12). The Son who said, “I have come to do your will”, did it to the end in the body prepared for him, let that body be torn to open the way, and now sits waiting until his enemies are made his footstool. The way into God’s presence is no longer a ritual but a person, and he is ours.

For us. Guilt that comes back every year, and religion that keeps on offering, are the old system again. Rest on the finished sacrifice, come to God by it boldly, keep gathering with his people, and if you are weary, remember that the righteous live by faith and the coming one will not delay.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — One Sacrifice, and a Priest Who Sat Down
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christ’s single offering has done what the law’s sacrifices never could, so no other offering for sin remains. The yearly sacrifices, by being repeated, confessed that they had not removed sin (vv. 1–4). Psalm 40 shows what God wanted instead: a willing Son in a prepared body, by whose will we are sanctified once for all (vv. 5–10). The priests stood daily; Christ offered once and sat down, having perfected his people for all time (vv. 11–14). And Jeremiah’s promise settles it: where God remembers sins no more, there is no longer any offering for sin (vv. 15–18).
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Tenses in One Sentence

By a single offering Christ has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (see the note on vv. 11–14). Where sins are forgiven, there is no longer any offering for sin (see vv. 15–18).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The yearly sacrifices were a reminder of sins (see vv. 3–4).

Now: Standing before God does not wait on our progress (see the note on vv. 11–14).

verseByVerse.quote: For since the law has but a shadow of the good things to come instead of the true form of these realities, it can never, by the same sacrifices that are continually offered every year, make perfect those who draw near. Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, since the worshipers, having once been cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law’s sacrifices could point towards forgiveness but never finish it, and the fact that they had to be repeated proves it.

A shadow of the good things. The writer gathers up threads laid since 7:1: the shadow (8:5), the sacrifice repeated year after year (9:7, 25), and the conscience the old rites could not reach (9:9, 14). A shadow (skia) tells you a body is there, and roughly what shape, but it does not show you the face. “The good things to come” are the blessings of the new covenant in Christ (9:11): real forgiveness, open access, a cleansed conscience.

The true form. “True form” (eikōn) is the image, the actual likeness, the very substance. The contrast is between a shadow and the thing that casts it: the law had the shadow; Christ is the body (Colossians 2:17). For fourteen centuries Israel lived with the shadow of the cross falling backward across its history, and those who saw it most clearly knew that something was coming toward them.

It can never make perfect. “Never” (oudepote): not a system that worked imperfectly, but one that could not, in principle, finish the job. “Continually” (eis to diēnekes) means perpetually; “every year” is the Day of Atonement; and “make perfect” (teleiōsai), as in 7:19 and 9:9, means to bring to the goal, full cleansing and access to God.

Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered? Plain reasoning any worshipper could have done: the repetition is the evidence. A medicine that cures is not taken for ever. Had the Day of Atonement settled the matter, there would have been no need for another the following autumn; the calendar coming round again confessed that nothing had been concluded.

No longer any consciousness of sins. “Having once been cleansed” (hapax kekatharismenous) means cleansed once for all; “consciousness of sins” (syneidēsis hamartiōn) is a conscience of sins, the sense of guilt. A sacrifice that truly worked would leave no nagging guilt before God, not because the worshipper had grown forgetful or hardened, but because the thing was settled. There is no next year for the sins of God’s people, because the Son of God dealt with them once.

The same accusation, year after year. Put that test to any religious system, including those people build for themselves inside Christianity. If you are still trying to quiet this year the accusation you were quieting last year, the method is not working. Penance done again, a vow renewed every January, a frantic burst of devotion after every fall: the Day of Atonement come round again.

A secular Day of Atonement. A culture that stops believing in sin is not thereby free of guilt. The historian Wilfred McClay, in an essay titled “The Strange Persistence of Guilt” (2017), argued that modern people have lost the old religious ways of dealing with guilt but not guilt itself, and that one of the few exits left is to claim a victim’s standing, since victims cannot be guilty. We still accuse, demand confession and cast out the offender; we have lost only the part where the debt is declared paid. That is the Day of Atonement without the goat: the moralist quiets the accusation with effort, the secularist with denial or blame, and both are back at the altar next year. Hebrews offers neither a better technique nor a softer standard, but a finished sacrifice and a conscience allowed to rest.

Should a Christian ever feel guilty? Yes, when he sins; that is the conscience working as God made it, and the Spirit uses it to bring us back (2 Corinthians 7:10). What this verse rules out is guilt that stays after a sin has been confessed and forgiven, as if the matter were still open before God. That is not humility but unbelief about the sacrifice, and its answer is not to do more but to believe God: the sin is cleansed, once for all. Feel sorrow for sin, confess it, turn from it, and then let it go, because God has.

verseByVerse.quote: But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year. For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Far from removing sins, the yearly sacrifices brought them to mind again, because the blood of animals could never take sin away.

A reminder of sins. We think of the Day of Atonement as the day sins were dealt with; the writer says its actual effect was to bring them to mind (anamnēsis, remembrance). The high priest laid both hands on the head of the live goat and confessed over it all the iniquities of the people, and the goat was led away into the wilderness (Leviticus 16:21). Not an annual clearing of the books but an annual reading of them aloud, and a devout Israelite grew old hearing it. The new covenant promises instead that God will remember sins no more (8:12; 10:17).

It is impossible. “Impossible” (adynaton) is the same absolute word as 6:4 and 6:18. Not inadequate, not partial: it cannot be done, and it never could. “Take away” (aphairein) means remove, lift off.

Why an animal cannot do it. Sin is a moral matter between a person and his Maker. An animal cannot choose right or wrong, has consented to nothing, does not share the sinner’s nature and is not of infinite worth. Only the sacrifice of a sinless man who is also God could take away sin: a man, to stand in the place of men; sinless, to have no debt of his own; God, to give the offering infinite value.

So what were the sacrifices for? They taught a nation over many centuries that sin costs life, that God provides the victim, and that the innocent dies in the place of the guilty: a language, so that when the reality came there would be words for it. When John the Baptist pointed at Jesus and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29), no one in earshot could miss the echo: God had spent centuries teaching them the word “lamb”.

Something better to remember. Year after year the goat went into the wilderness, and would have to go again. Then the Lamb of God went out of the city carrying their sins to a cross, and they did not come back. Jesus used the same word, anamnēsis, of the Lord’s Supper: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:24–25). The old ritual remembered sins; the new remembers the Saviour who removed them. He has not asked us to forget what we were. He has given us something better to remember.

What it does not mean. Not that Old Testament believers were not truly forgiven. They were, by grace through faith, on the credit of the sacrifice Christ would offer (9:15; Romans 3:25), not by the animals.

How should I remember my sins at the Lord’s Supper? Truly, but as forgiven. Examine yourself before you eat (1 Corinthians 11:28), with honest confession and a turning from what is wrong. But the Supper is not the Day of Atonement, where sins are read out and left hanging; it remembers Christ, who bore them. Look at your sins only long enough to see them laid on him, then look at him. Come not because you are worthy, but because you need him and he has invited you.

verseByVerse.quote: Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said, “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me; in burnt offerings and sin offerings you have taken no pleasure. Then I said, ’Behold, I have come to do your will, O God, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book.’”
verseByVerse.commentary:
What God wanted was never the animals but a heart and will wholly given to him, and the Son came into the world, in a body God prepared, to give exactly that.

When Christ came into the world. The writer puts Psalm 40 on the lips of the incarnate Son at the moment of his coming. David wrote the words, but the writer hears them as the Son’s own words to the Father about why he came.

Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired. “Sacrifices” (thysia) are animal sacrifices and “offerings” (prosphora) grain offerings; “burnt offerings” (holokautōmata, wholly burnt) and “sin offerings” (peri hamartias) complete the main kinds. God commanded them all; he is not renouncing his own institution. The prophets speak the same way: “to obey is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22); “I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6; Psalm 51:16–17; Micah 6:6–8). It is a comparison: God took no pleasure in these for their own sake, but in what they pointed toward, obedience from the heart.

A body prepared. The Greek translation the writer uses reads “a body have you prepared for me” (on the Hebrew, see below), and he uses it because it points precisely to the incarnation. God did not want a body brought to the altar. He prepared one, and it walked there (v. 10).

I have come to do your will. The sentence the writer builds on: no bargaining, no conditions, just arrival and willingness (idou hēkō, behold, I have come). His whole life was given to it, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34; 6:38), and it ended in a garden where the same will was spoken in agony: “not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39, 42). Luke adds that his sweat became like great drops of blood (Luke 22:44), though some early manuscripts lack that verse.

The scroll of the book. The “scroll of the book” (kephalis bibliou) is the roll of Scripture, which testifies of Christ (Luke 24:27, 44; John 5:39). The incarnation was no rescue plan improvised after things went wrong; it was in the book.

A will saying yes. If bulls and goats cannot take away sins, what can? Not a better animal, but a human will, in a prepared body, saying yes. God had always wanted a human being who would give himself wholly to him, and there had never been one. So God prepared one. All he had ever wanted from the human race, a heart that loved him and a will that obeyed, he found at last in this man, and found it for us.

In everyday life. Religion easily becomes offerings instead of obedience: the hymn sung while nursing a grudge, the money given while refusing to forgive. God does not want the offering instead of you; he wants you. Before any religious duty today, say the psalm’s words to God about one specific thing: here I am, I have come to do your will. You will not do it perfectly; only Christ has. He did, and by his obedience you are counted righteous (Romans 5:19), so your halting yes is accepted for his sake, and the Spirit who wrote his law on your heart (v. 16) makes it real.

Did Jesus know from the beginning that he had come to die? Yes. The psalm puts these words in his mouth as he came into the world, and the Gospels show him foretelling his death (Mark 8:31; 10:45; John 10:17–18). As a true man he grew in wisdom (Luke 2:52), his understanding of his mission deepening through Scripture and prayer, but he did not stumble onto the cross. It was at the centre of the Father’s will from the start, which is why his death was an offering and not an accident.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of Psalm 40:6 says, literally, ears you have dug for me (the ESV: “you have given me an open ear”). The expression is unique and its exact sense uncertain: most take it as ears opened to hear and obey (compare Isaiah 50:5); some connect it with the servant’s ear pierced at the doorpost for lifelong service (Exodus 21:6), though the verb differs. The Greek translation reads “a body have you prepared for me”, probably taking the ear, the organ of obedience, as the part for the whole: a whole person prepared to obey. The two agree, and the writer uses the wording that names what the Hebrew implied.
verseByVerse.note: “A body have you prepared for me” follows the Greek Old Testament; the Hebrew of Ps 40:6 reads “you have given me an open ear.”

verseByVerse.quote: When he said above, “You have neither desired nor taken pleasure in sacrifices and offerings and burnt offerings and sin offerings” (these are offered according to the law), then he added, “Behold, I have come to do your will.” He does away with the first in order to establish the second. And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalm itself announces that the Son’s doing of God’s will replaces the sacrifices, and by that will, through the one offering of Jesus’ body, we have been made holy once for all.

When he said above. The writer takes his quotation apart into two statements, in order: first the negative, God did not desire sacrifices; then the positive, “Behold, I have come to do your will.”

Offered according to the law. The four kinds of sacrifice stand for the whole system, and then comes a remarkable aside: “these are offered according to the law”. The psalm’s rejection applies to the very offerings the law required: in the middle of the old covenant God signalled, through David, that they were not his final desire.

He does away with the first. The second replaces the first. “Does away with” (anairei) is a strong verb, to take up and remove, to abolish; “establish” (stēsē) is its opposite, to make stand. The first is the sacrificial system; the second is Christ’s obedience to God’s will.

By that will. The summit of the chapter. “By that will” (en hō thelēmati) is the will of God, his saving purpose, which the Son came to do. We are holy to the Lord not because we were willing but because Jesus was. And “we have been sanctified” (hēgiasmenoi) should stop any reader anxious for years about his progress: the Greek form means something completed whose result still stands. Here it means being set apart, consecrated to God and made fit for his presence, a once-for-all act (as in 1 Corinthians 6:11), not the ongoing process of growth in holiness.

The offering of the body. The “offering” (prosphora) is of the “body” (sōma) prepared for him (v. 5), made “once for all” (ephapax), the word the whole letter has been driving toward. The body God prepared in the womb of Mary was given on the cross, and the one who said “I have come” could say at the end, “It is finished” (John 19:30).

Two kinds of holiness, in the right order. This once-for-all setting apart is not confused with the daily business of becoming holy: verse 14 names both in one breath, and how they belong together, and in which order, is treated in the note on vv. 11–14.

If I am already sanctified, why do I still struggle with sin? You have been set apart for God, but not yet made completely like him, as a bride is fully married on her wedding day and spends a lifetime learning what that means. Your struggle is often evidence that you are his, since the unconverted do not fight sin as an enemy (Galatians 5:17). Fight on from the position Christ has given you, not toward it.

verseByVerse.quote: And every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God, waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool for his feet. For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests stood every day because their work was never done; Christ offered one sacrifice and sat down, because by it he has finished, for all time, the work that makes his people right with God.

Every priest stands. One word, prepared since 1:3: “stands” (hestēken). Exodus lists the tabernacle’s furniture in detail, and there is no seat for the priests, as if a priest whose work was finished were a contradiction in terms. They stood every day for some fourteen centuries, from Aaron to the writer’s own day.

The same sacrifices. “Repeatedly” (pollakis, many times) and “the same”: endless repetition of identical sacrifices. “Take away” (perielein) means strip off, remove entirely.

He sat down. One sacrifice (mian), effective for ever. The contrast is made entirely with a posture. They stand, he sits; they offer repeatedly, he offered once. And he sits at the right hand of God, the place of honour and rule, which no Levitical priest ever approached.

Waiting. Psalm 110:1 once more (1:13). Seated and waiting: that tells you where we are in the story. The atonement is finished; the subduing of enemies is not, and the readers felt the difference. His waiting (ekdechomenos) is a king’s calm, and not idle: he reigns while the Father subdues his enemies, through the advance of the gospel now and finally at his return (1 Corinthians 15:24–28).

Perfected for all time. Two tenses in one sentence, and holding them together is the Christian life. “Perfected” (teteleiōken) is a perfect tense, done and remaining done, and “for all time” rules out expiry. “Being sanctified” (tous hagiazomenous) is present and continuous: unfinished, still in progress this morning. On the basis of one offering his people are already complete in God’s sight; in their own experience they are halfway through and struggling. Our standing is perfect, our daily life improving, and the one guarantees the other. Get them the wrong way round and the Christian life becomes unbearable, for a person who thinks his standing depends on his progress will never rest.

In everyday life. Picture where Christ is as you go about your day: seated, not pacing, not still working to make up for your failures. Much Christian activity is done standing, as if acceptance were never finished. Do your duties today seated, so to speak: from rest, not toward it. When you fail, remember that the one who perfected you sits at the right hand of God, and his work does not wobble when yours does.

How can I be perfect and still be such a mess? The perfection is in Christ’s offering, not your performance. God sees you through the single sacrifice as complete, as a man whose debt is cleared is fully paid even if his house is untidy, while the Spirit cleans up the mess, slowly and really. You are being sanctified because you have been perfected, not in order to be. When you see the mess, do not doubt your standing; thank God for it, and ask him to make you what he has declared you to be.

Where Christians differ: can a believer lose what Christ’s sacrifice achieved? Some teach that a believer’s perfected standing can be forfeited, through serious sin or ceasing to believe: the Arminian view (that saving grace can in the end be resisted and lost), held by many earnest Christians who want the letter’s warnings taken seriously. This commentary’s view: this verse says Christ has perfected his people for all time by a single offering, and what is perfect for all time cannot be undone. Christ’s death did not merely make salvation possible; it actually and permanently perfected those for whom it was made, guaranteeing their final glory (Romans 8:30). This is the ground of both definite atonement (that Christ died to save a particular people and surely saves them) and the perseverance of the saints (that all who truly believe will be kept to the end).

verseByVerse.quote: And the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us; for after saying, “This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws on their hearts, and write them on their minds,” then he adds, “I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more.” Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scripture itself confirms the argument: under the new covenant God forgives sins so completely that no further offering for sin remains.

The Holy Spirit also bears witness. Present tense again, as at 3:7: the Jeremiah passage of chapter 8 returns, shortened, as testimony the Spirit gives now, to us, today.

This is the covenant. The writer quotes only two clauses of Jeremiah 31:33–34, leaving out the promises that all shall know the Lord and that he will be their God. He takes the law written on hearts, and the sins remembered no more, and his purpose arrives in verse 18.

Laws on their hearts. The new covenant does not abolish God’s law; it writes it inside. What was on stone, outside a man and accusing him, is now in the heart, changing him. The Christian still needs the Bible, but now wants what it commands, because God has given him a new heart and put his Spirit within him (Ezekiel 36:26–27). It is what the psalm says of Christ: “I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart” (Psalm 40:8).

Remember no more. The climax of the new covenant (8:12): complete, permanent forgiveness. He writes his law on our hearts so that we love what he loves, and closes the file on all we have done against it. Now the writer draws an inference he did not draw in chapter 8.

No longer any offering. If God will never bring a person’s sins up again, there is nothing left for a sacrifice to do. An offering deals with an outstanding matter; where the matter is closed, it makes no sense. This concludes the whole argument from 7:1: since sins are fully forgiven, no further sacrifice is needed or possible.

Why going back made no sense. Here is the decisive argument against what the readers were contemplating. Going back to the temple would be no harmless supplement or ancestral loyalty, but to keep offering for sins God has said he will not remember, which implies that his promise is not true.

No offering for sin in the church. The verse also settles a question that has divided Christians: whatever the church does when it gathers, it is not offering a sacrifice for sin. The New Testament knows sacrifices of praise and doing good (13:15–16) and the body as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1), but no repeatable offering for sin, and this verse is why. The Lord’s Supper is a remembrance of the one sacrifice and a communion in it, not a further offering of it (see 9:25–26). With that the letter’s great doctrinal argument is complete, and from verse 19 it turns to what the readers must do about it.

How can an all-knowing God forget my sins? He does not lapse in memory; he knows what you did. To remember sins no more is covenant language: he will never again bring them up against you or act on them, like a judge who will not retry an acquitted man. When your heart or the accuser brings up a forgiven sin, answer that God himself has promised not to. If he will not hold it against you, you need not hold it against yourself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–39 — Let Us Draw Near, Hold Fast, and Consider One Another
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because the way into God’s presence is open and the great priest is ours, draw near, hold fast and keep one another going, for the only alternative is to walk away from the one sacrifice there is. The “therefore” of verse 19 turns teaching into three appeals, faith, hope and love: draw near, hold fast, stir one another up, and do not stop meeting (vv. 19–25). Then the solemn warning: for one who knowingly tramples the Son, no other sacrifice remains, only judgment (vv. 26–31). But the writer recalls the courage his readers once showed (vv. 32–34), calls them to endure, for the coming one will come (vv. 35–38), and ends sure that they are not of those who shrink back (v. 39).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Curtain Is His Flesh

The way into the holy places has been opened through the curtain, his flesh. So draw near, hold fast because he who promised is faithful, and stir one another up.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: These believers had once joyfully accepted the plundering of their property (see vv. 32–34).

Now: The warning of verses 26–31 is aimed at deliberate repudiation of Christ, not at a struggling believer (see the note on vv. 26–27); and it ends in assurance (v. 39).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh, and since we have a great priest over the house of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Jesus’ blood has opened the way into God’s very presence, and because he is our great priest there, every believer may now come to God boldly.

Therefore, brothers. Teaching turns to application. Everything from 4:14 to 10:18, the priest, the covenant, the sanctuary and the sacrifice, now becomes the ground of three exhortations. And he calls them brothers: the warnings that follow are spoken inside a family.

Confidence to enter. Boldness (parrēsia, as at 4:16) is the free citizen’s right to speak openly in the assembly. The place is the one the letter has been circling, the room behind the curtain. What only the high priest could do once a year, every believer may now do at any time.

By the blood of Jesus. The only ground offered: not sincerity, improvement or a life that has earned an audience, but his sacrifice. And note the name: Jesus, the human name, the name of the man who bled.

The new and living way. “New” (prosphatos) means fresh, recent: the way into God’s presence was opened by a recent death, and it never grows old. “Living” (zōsa): not a dead ritual path but a way that is alive, because it is a person. “I am the way,” Jesus said (John 14:6). He opened the road (enekainisen, inaugurated, as at 9:18) and walked it first.

Through his flesh. The curtain (katapetasma) was the barrier that kept people out, and the writer says the curtain is his flesh: the way in was opened by the tearing of it. When his body was broken on the cross, the temple curtain was torn from top to bottom (Mark 15:38), torn from above, because God did it, not men.

A beautiful barrier. The curtain was beautiful: blue and purple and scarlet, of fine twined linen, worked with cherubim (Exodus 26:31). The barrier was magnificent, and it had to be destroyed; so the most beautiful human life ever lived had to be torn so that we could come in.

A great priest. The second ground: not only an open way but a man at the end of it who belongs to us. “Great priest” (hierea megan) is a Hebrew way of saying high priest. “Over the house” recalls 3:6, where Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son, and we are that house.

He is the road. For centuries one man passed the curtain once a year and came out again. Now a whole family walks through every day, because the Son of God let his flesh be torn to make the way. He did not show us the road and leave us to find it; he is the road, and he stands at the end of it, waiting for his brothers and sisters to come in.

What it does not mean. Not that we approach God casually. We come with confidence because of Christ, but still with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire (12:28–29). Boldness is not swagger; it is the freedom of a child who knows he will be received.

What does confidence before God actually feel like? Not a feeling of being good enough, but the settled knowledge that you will be welcomed because of Jesus’ blood. You may come to prayer dull, ashamed or tongue-tied and still come with confidence, for it rests not on your state but on the way Christ opened. A child who has broken something still runs to his father, not proud of himself, but knowing his father.

Uncertain wording. The Greek of verse 20 is compressed, and it is not certain how “that is, through his flesh” connects to the rest. Most read it, as the ESV does, as explaining the curtain: his body, torn in death, is the curtain through which the way was opened. Others attach it to “the way”: the way he opened is his flesh, his whole incarnate life and death. Either way the point stands: we enter God’s presence only through the body Christ gave up for us.

verseByVerse.quote: let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since Christ has made us clean inside and out, come right into God’s presence with an honest heart and full confidence in him.

Let us draw near. The first of three exhortations: draw near, hold fast, consider one another (vv. 22, 23, 24); faith, hope and love, in that order. “Draw near” (proserchōmetha), as in 4:16, is the priestly word, now commanded of everybody. Four qualifications follow: two about the person coming, two about what has been done to him.

With a true heart. A genuine one (alēthinos), without pretence, not hypocritical or divided (Isaiah 29:13). God is not interested in a performance at the throne.

In full assurance of faith. The same phrase as 6:11 (plērophoria), complete conviction: not certainty about oneself, which nobody has, but about the ground just described, the blood, the way, the priest.

Sprinkled clean. The second pair describe things done to us that remain done. “Sprinkled” (rerantismenoi) recalls the blood that consecrated priests at their ordination (Exodus 29:21; Leviticus 8:30), and the people at the covenant’s ratification (9:19). The target is the conscience, the thing 9:9 said the old sacrifices could not reach. What accused him inside has been dealt with, so he can come with a true heart instead of one that hides.

Washed with pure water. Priests were also washed at their ordination (Exodus 29:4; 30:19–21), and God promised through Ezekiel: “I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean” (Ezekiel 36:25). Most see here Christian baptism, the outward sign of the inward cleansing just named (Acts 22:16; 1 Corinthians 6:11; Titus 3:5; 1 Peter 3:21). Some read it as purely figurative, but the pairing of inward cleansing and outward sign looks deliberate. Every priest of Israel was washed and sprinkled, and could go no further than the curtain; every believer has been sprinkled with better blood, washed with the water of the new covenant, and called all the way in.

No requirement of worthiness. Among the four there is no requirement of worthiness, preparation or progress; each is honesty or something Christ has done. A throne you must qualify for is not a throne of grace.

What it does not mean. Not that baptism cleanses the conscience. The heart is sprinkled clean by Christ’s blood, received by faith; baptism is the public sign of that cleansing, given to those who have drawn near in faith. That is one reason this commentary, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, holds to the baptism of believers, while honouring paedobaptist brothers (those who baptise the infants of believers, seeing baptism as the covenant sign that replaced circumcision) who read the covenant signs differently and love the same Saviour. A reader baptised as a baby should hear this as a family difference, not a slight on his faith.

What if I do not feel full assurance? Then come anyway, and honestly. Full assurance of faith is assurance about Christ, not a constant feeling about yourself, and doubts are common in true believers (Psalm 42; Mark 9:24). Do not stay away until you feel sure; draw near and look at the ground, the blood, the way, the priest. Assurance grows as faith looks at Christ, often while you pray rather than before. Bring your doubts to the throne of grace; they are safer there than anywhere.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep holding, without wavering, to the hope you have confessed, because the God who promised it will never fail you.

Hold fast the confession. The second exhortation, aimed most directly at these readers. “Hold fast” (katechōmen) means grip, retain, do not let go, as in 3:6, 14 and 4:14. “The confession” (homologia, as in 3:1 and 4:14) is what they had said publicly, probably at baptism, and were under pressure to unsay. In a hostile city a confession is no private opinion; it had cost them their property. And “of our hope” is our confident expectation of glory.

Without wavering. A single word (aklinē): not leaning, not tilting, something that stays upright under pressure rather than swaying between two positions.

He who promised is faithful. One short clause carries the weight, and not with the logic we would supply: not hold on because you are strong, or have held on so far, or because giving up would be shameful. The ground of our holding is his faithfulness (pistos; 6:13–18; 11:11; 1 Corinthians 1:9; 1 Thessalonians 5:24). His people’s history records it: Abraham waiting for a son, Israel for a land, the prophets for a Messiah, and all of them receiving what was promised in God’s time. Our grip may be weak, but his is not.

Perseverance, not mere determination. A man gritting his teeth relies on his grip, and grips fail; a man holding fast because the promiser is faithful relies on someone outside himself, and what he holds is not his feelings but what God has promised. A congregation slipping away (2:1) is not usually losing an argument; it is losing its grip in the dark. So the writer gives them no new argument; he points at the character of the one who made the promise.

The good confession before Pilate. Their confession is older than their baptism. Paul reminds Timothy of Christ Jesus, “who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession” (1 Timothy 6:13), using the same word. Alone and bound before the power of Rome, Jesus did not waver: he said he was a king and had come to bear witness to the truth (John 18:37), and it cost him his life. Every Christian who holds fast under pressure is holding to what Jesus held to first, and is held by the one who did not let go.

How do I hold fast when my faith feels weak? By looking away from your faith to the one who promised. Weak faith holding a strong Saviour is safe; strong faith in a weak saviour is not. In practice, keep to the ordinary means: God’s word, prayer even when it feels empty, his people, the Lord’s Supper, and saying again what you believe. You are not asked to feel strong, only to keep your grip on a promise made by someone who has never broken one.

verseByVerse.quote: And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give careful thought to how you can spur one another on to love and good works, and do not give up meeting together, for the nearer the Day comes, the more we need each other.

Consider how to stir up. The third exhortation turns outward, to each other. “Consider” (katanoōmen) is the verb of 3:1, used there of Jesus: helping a particular person forward needs the same attention as contemplating Christ.

Provoke one another. “Stir up” is startling. The noun is paroxysmos, from which we get paroxysm: a sharp provoking, an irritation. Luke uses it of the bitter quarrel between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:39). So we are to provoke one another, and what makes it good is what we provoke one another to.

To love and good works. Love that shows itself in deeds. Some friction between Christians is good: the friend who will not let you settle, whose example makes your comfort uncomfortable, whose generosity shames your caution, and who asks the question you hoped nobody would ask.

Not neglecting to meet together. The letter’s first concrete symptom: the drift of 2:1 showed in people who had stopped coming. “Neglecting” (enkataleipontes) is forsaking, deserting; “meet together” (episynagōgē) is assembling. And it is a habit (ethos): not a decision or repudiation but a pattern, which is how drifting works. The verse names no day, but from the beginning the church met on the first day of the week, the Lord’s Day (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10). Christians differ over whether it is a Sabbath kept by rule; this commentary believes the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), and that no one may bind another’s conscience about the day (Romans 14:5).

The reasons would have been good ones. Meeting was dangerous, marking you out in a city that had already plundered their property. Some may have been drifting, or quietly returning to the synagogue. The writer names it anyway: you cannot stir or be stirred from a distance. Today the reasons are usually softer: tiredness, sport, a busy week, or the wish to believe without being known. But a heart that wants Christ without his people wants a Saviour on its own terms, and the one who calls them his brothers (2:11) does not offer himself on those terms.

But encouraging one another. “Encouraging” (parakalountes) means exhorting, urging, coming alongside, as in 3:13, where the writer told them to exhort one another every day, as long as it is called today. Not flattery, but putting courage into someone.

The Day drawing near. “The Day” is the day of Christ’s return and judgment (1 Corinthians 3:13; 1 Thessalonians 5:2, 4), and every passing day brings it closer (engizousan, drawing near). It may also include the approaching destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, a foretaste of the final judgment that some of the first readers would live to see. Under pressure we withdraw and go quiet; the letter says the nearer the Day and the harder the times, the more of this, not less.

The Son who sings in the assembly. The letter has already put Psalm 22 on Jesus’ lips: “I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise” (2:12). The risen Son stands among his gathered brothers, leading their praise. And the word for meeting together is the one Paul uses of the last great gathering, “our being gathered together to him” at his coming (2 Thessalonians 2:1). Every gathering of his people is a small, early form of the one he will call when he comes.

People he died for. The Son of God did not save a scattered crowd of individuals; he loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). The awkward brother in the next row and the weary sister by the door are people he died for, given to us to provoke to love, to encourage and to carry, and not one of them will be missing when he calls them home.

In everyday life. Choose one person in your church and one way to spur them on this week: a message telling them what you saw God doing in them, an invitation to serve alongside you, a question about how they are really doing.

Does watching a service online fulfil this command? The word means gathering in one place, and stirring up needs people present to each other. For the sick, the housebound and the persecuted a livestream is a real mercy, and no one should feel guilty for what they cannot help. But for those who can come, watching is not meeting, and a settled habit of staying away is exactly the drift this verse warns against.

What if my church is difficult, or I have been hurt there? Take the hurt seriously, but do not take it out on Christ’s body by leaving it altogether. Some churches are unsafe, and if you or your children have been abused or controlled, you must get away and get help; God never asks anyone to stay under abuse. But usually the difficulty is ordinary: awkward people, dull sermons, a slight that still stings. Talk to someone you trust, go to the person who hurt you if you can (Matthew 18:15), and if you must move, move to another faithful church, not to no church. Every church is full of sinners; that is who it is for.

verseByVerse.quote: For if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a fearful expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For anyone who knowingly and persistently turns away from Christ, no other sacrifice remains, only the terrifying prospect of God’s judgment.

Sinning deliberately. The “for” explains the urgency of verses 23–25: neglecting to meet was the first step of a drift, and here is where that road ends. Read this fourth warning with the care given to chapter 6, and note that the preacher includes himself in the “we”. “Deliberately” (hekousiōs, wilfully) stands first in the Greek sentence, for emphasis, and the idea is a technical one. The law distinguished sins committed unintentionally, for which sacrifice was provided (Leviticus 4), from sin done with a high hand, in open defiance, for which the law named no offering and the sinner was cut off (Numbers 15:27–31). “Go on sinning” (hamartanontōn) is continuous: not a fall but a settled course.

The knowledge of the truth. Full knowledge (epignōsis): not the sin of the ignorant or deceived, but of those who had understood and confessed the gospel, which is more serious.

The sin in view. So the sin is specific: the informed, deliberate, persistent repudiation of Christ by someone who knows what he is walking away from. It is apostasy (abandoning the faith once confessed), the opposite of holding fast (v. 23), which verse 29 calls trampling the Son of God underfoot. It is not the sins of weakness all believers commit (1 John 1:8–10), nor the besetting sin a believer hates and keeps falling into and keeps fighting: a sin can be loved and hated at once, and the fight itself is the Spirit’s work (Romans 7:15–25; Galatians 5:17), nor a season of depression, grief or dryness in which faith feels faint. The person in view has stopped fighting and walked away.

No longer remains a sacrifice. The logic of verse 18 runs the other way: there, sins forgiven meant no further offering was needed; here, the one offering refused means no other is to be had. He has not exhausted a supply but refused the only sacrifice there is.

A fury of fire. “Fury of fire” (pyros zēlos) is literally a zeal of fire, a fiery jealousy, in the language of Isaiah (Isaiah 26:11): God’s holy zeal against those who oppose him. The word for adversaries (hypenantioi, opponents) makes the point: this is what awaits enemies, not stumbling sons. Apostates join the enemies of God (Philippians 3:18).

Only one way back. The severity of the warning measures the sacrifice’s worth. If there were many ways back to God, rejecting one would not matter much; there is only one, and it cost the blood of the Son of God. And that same sacrifice still stands today, sufficient for every sinner who comes to it, however deliberately he has sinned. The door that is shut to the one who tramples it is wide open to the one who knocks.

What it does not mean. Not that a believer who falls into serious sin is lost for ever. David committed adultery and murder, and was restored (Psalm 51); Peter denied Christ, and was restored. The warning is against a deliberate, persistent rejection of Christ. Nor does “consume” mean annihilation; Scripture describes the punishment of the wicked as conscious and eternal (Matthew 25:46; Mark 9:48; Revelation 14:11). Fire that consumes describes the ruinous character of judgment, not the end of the person who suffers it.

Am I lost if I have sinned deliberately since becoming a Christian? No, not if you still want Christ. Every believer sins knowingly at times; that is why David and Peter are such comfort. This verse means not a deliberate act of sin but a deliberate abandonment of the Saviour and contempt for his sacrifice. That you are troubled and want forgiveness shows you have not done that, for the apostate does not grieve over his rejection of Christ. Come back to the sacrifice that still remains for you, confess your sin, and believe the promise of 1 John 1:9.

Why does the warning say “we” if true believers cannot fall away? Because the writer addresses the church as it appears, true believers and some who only profess, and he cannot see hearts. And because warnings are one of God’s means of keeping his people: a true believer hears and is driven closer to Christ, which is how perseverance works. A guardrail on a mountain road does not mean cars regularly go over; it is why they do not. God has promised to keep his own (v. 39; John 10:28), and he keeps them partly by warnings like this one.

verseByVerse.quote: Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and has outraged the Spirit of grace? For we know him who said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.” And again, “The Lord will judge his people.” It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If rejecting Moses’ law brought death, then trampling on the Son, his blood and his Spirit deserves far worse, for the living God himself will judge.

Set aside the law of Moses. The argument runs from lesser to greater, as at 2:2–3. The law is Deuteronomy 17:2–7, and the offence there is idolatry, going and serving other gods. “Set aside” (athetēsas) means rejected, nullified. Deliberate rejection of the covenant brought death, with witnesses as the safeguard.

How much worse. A question: let the readers do the arithmetic. If rejecting the shadow was so serious, how much more the substance?

Trampled underfoot. Three descriptions escalate. “Trampled underfoot” (katapatēsas) is to treat with contempt. The Son God exalted, with his enemies under his feet (1:13), the apostate treats as dirt beneath his own.

By which he was sanctified. “Profaned” (koinon hēgēsamenos) is to reckon the holy as ordinary, as if Christ’s blood were a common criminal’s. “By which he was sanctified” (en hō hēgiasthē) is the hardest phrase in the passage, since it seems to call the apostate sanctified. The views are set out below; the best reading is that he was outwardly set apart as part of the covenant community without being born again inwardly, as all Israel was sprinkled with covenant blood at Sinai (9:19–20) though many were unbelievers. He is like the field in 6:7–8 that drank the same rain as the fruitful one and bore thorns.

The Spirit of grace. “Outraged” (enybrisas) is to treat with insolent contempt. “The Spirit of grace” is the Holy Spirit, who brings God’s grace and had worked among them (6:4). There is an echo of the unforgivable sin of blasphemy against the Spirit (Mark 3:28–29): to insult the one whose whole work is grace is to cut oneself off from grace.

Vengeance is mine. Two quotations from the Song of Moses: God himself will repay (Deuteronomy 32:35; Romans 12:19), and, sharper, he will judge his people (32:36). Belonging to the covenant community is no shelter from judgment; it is why judgment begins there (1 Peter 4:17).

The hands of the living God. To fall into his hands is to fall under his direct judgment, with no mediator. “Living” is the key word: an idol cannot see, act or judge; this God does all three, and he is not an idea to be managed but a consuming fire (12:29). Yet the phrase cuts both ways. To fall away from the living God (3:12) is to fall nowhere but into his hands; David once chose to fall into the hands of the LORD, for his mercy is great (2 Samuel 24:14). The same hands are the only refuge and the only danger, depending on how a man comes. For those who come through Christ, they are a Father’s hands.

In everyday life. Treat the blood of Christ as holy today. It becomes common in careless jokes about the cross, a Lord’s Supper taken absent-mindedly, an assumption that grace means God does not mind. Repent of that, and let the fear of God drive you not away from him but into his hands as a child.

A word to the frightened. These verses are meant to stop someone walking away, not to torment someone coming home. If you tremble because you love Christ and fear you have failed him, that is a sign of life: the person described treats the Son’s blood as common, and you are treating it as precious (on what the warning does not describe, see the note on vv. 26–27). The hands of the living God are fearful only to those who refuse his Son; to all who run to Christ they are open, and he has promised never to cast out anyone who comes (John 6:37).

How can a God of love speak like this? Love is not indifference. A father never angry at what destroys his children cares less, not more. God’s anger is his holiness set against everything that ruins the people he made, never an outburst. And the warning targets not sinners who come for mercy, but those who have known it and trampled it. The God who speaks these words gave his Son to bear that wrath for all who come to him (Romans 5:9; 1 Thessalonians 1:10). The cross proves that he does not delight in judgment, and is the only safe place to stand when you think of it.

How can I tell the difference between a true believer and someone only outwardly sanctified? About someone else you often cannot tell with certainty, and you are not asked to: both may be baptised, attend and know the truth. The difference shows over time: true faith goes on trusting and loving Christ and comes back after falling, while a merely outward profession at last treats him as common and walks away. For yourself, the question is not your baptism or attendance but whether you are trusting Christ now and want him. If you do, you are not the person of this verse. Look to him, not to your record.

Can someone who has walked away from Christ ever come back? Yes, if they come back. Many who drifted, even for years, have returned, showing they were his all along, like the prodigal, a son even in the far country. Only God knows who has finally hardened himself; the warning describes the end of that road, not everyone who has wandered on it. So pray for those you love who have walked away, and keep the door open. If you are the one who walked away and you want to return, the wanting is God drawing you. Come.

Where Christians differ: does this verse show that the sanctified can be lost? Christians answer in three main ways. Arminians (who hold that saving grace can be resisted) believe a real believer can turn away and be lost; they are brothers who take the warning with deep seriousness, pointing to the strong words: he was sanctified by the blood. Some take the warning as hypothetical: what would happen if a believer fell away, though God will not let it. Others hold that it describes someone who belonged to the covenant community, knew the truth and shared its privileges, but never truly trusted Christ, and at last walked away (6:4–8). This commentary’s view: sanctified in Hebrews can refer to the outward consecration of covenant membership, as when the whole people of Israel was sprinkled with covenant blood. The apostate had been outwardly identified with the new covenant community, baptised and sharing its life, and so outwardly set apart by the covenant blood, without inward renewal. Those whom Christ has perfected for all time by his single offering (v. 14) cannot be lost. Verse 39 draws the line between those who shrink back and are destroyed and those who have faith. The letter rests its readers’ perseverance on Christ, who is able to save to the uttermost (7:25). God keeps his own, and warnings like this one are among the means he uses to do it.

verseByVerse.quote: But recall the former days when, after you were enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings, sometimes being publicly exposed to reproach and affliction, and sometimes being partners with those so treated. For you had compassion on those in prison, and you joyfully accepted the plundering of your property, since you knew that you yourselves had a better possession and an abiding one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember how bravely you once suffered for Christ, gladly losing your goods because you knew you had something better that lasts.

Recall the former days. The tone changes completely. Having brought them to the edge, the writer reminds them who they are, as in 6:9–12, and tells us what had happened to them.

After you were enlightened. “Enlightened” (phōtisthentes), as in 6:4: when they first came to faith and the light of the gospel broke on them. The suffering came after the light: becoming Christians is what brought it on them.

A hard struggle. A great contest, fought in public: the word for struggle (athlēsis) gives us athlete. If the readers lived in Rome, as 13:24 may suggest, it was possibly the trouble under the emperor Claudius, who expelled Jews from Rome around AD 49, partly because of disturbances over one Chrestus (probably Christ), according to the Roman historian Suetonius (Acts 18:2).

Publicly exposed. Made a spectacle of, put on a stage: a theatre word (theatrizomenoi). Mocked in public, where honour and shame were the currency of a life. Paul used the same picture of the apostles: “we have become a spectacle to the world” (1 Corinthians 4:9).

Partners. “Partners” (koinōnoi) are sharers, and that took its own courage: to walk over and stand beside somebody who had been dragged out, sharing their shame, when you could have stayed indoors.

Compassion on those in prison. “Had compassion” (synepathēsate) is to suffer with, the word used of Christ in 4:15, who is able to sympathise with our weaknesses. Roman prisoners depended on friends for food and care, and to visit was to identify yourself with the prisoner’s crime (13:3; Matthew 25:36). These people went.

Joyfully accepted. Not merely endured: joyfully accepted, as their houses were emptied, perhaps by neighbours or a mob, with little hope of redress. It is what Jesus said would happen, “Blessed are you when others revile you and persecute you … Rejoice and be glad” (Matthew 5:11–12), and what the apostles did, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (Acts 5:41).

A better possession. Not by stoicism or pretending the loss was small, but by knowing they owned what the mob could not reach. “Abiding” (menousan) is the letter’s word for what lasts, set against everything that wears out like a garment (1:11). Their real treasure was in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and thieves do not break in and steal (Matthew 6:19–21; 1 Peter 1:4). Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add “in heaven”; the earliest do not, and the meaning is the same.

The reproach was his before it was theirs. Reproach (oneidismos) is a word this letter keeps for Christ. Moses counted the reproach of Christ greater wealth than Egypt’s treasures (11:26), and at the end the readers are told to go to Jesus outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured (13:12–13). The mockery in the streets was the shame he carried first, mocked, spat on and crucified in public, now falling on those who bore his name: to be shamed for Christ is to stand where he stood. And their better possession is Christ himself. He was stripped at the cross while soldiers gambled for his clothes, so that we might have riches that last; those who own him have more than the world can take away.

Be what you already were. They had once made that calculation under real pressure and come out singing. The writer asks them not to become something new, but to be what they already were. Memory is one of God’s gifts for perseverance: the grace that carried you once will carry you again.

In everyday life. Christians are still in prison for their faith. This week visit, write to or pray by name for one of them, as if you were in the cell beside them (13:3), and give something you own towards their help, since Christ is your better and abiding possession.

How can anyone be joyful when they are being robbed? Not by being glad of the loss, which is still a wrong, but by being gladder about something else. A man who has just inherited a fortune can lose his wallet with a smile. It is not natural cheerfulness and does not deny grief; it is the fruit of a heart whose treasure is in heaven, and it grows by setting your mind on what you have in Christ long before the loss comes.

Should Christians resist injustice, or just accept it joyfully? Both have their place. Paul appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen when that served the gospel (Acts 16:37; 22:25; 25:11), and Christians may rightly use lawful means to protect themselves, their families and the weak. But when the only way to keep your goods is to deny Christ, or there is no remedy, you let them go, and can do it with joy. The question is whether your heart is free to lose everything and still have Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Possibly the persecution under the emperor Claudius, who expelled Jews from Rome about AD 49.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward. For you have need of endurance, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not throw away your bold confidence in Christ; what you need now is endurance, to keep doing God’s will until you receive what he has promised.

Do not throw away. Not lose, as though it might slip out of a pocket: to throw away (apobalēte) is done on purpose, as a soldier might throw away his shield to run faster. And “confidence” (parrēsia) is the word of verse 19, 3:6 and 4:16: the boldness to speak, the freedom to come. They are in danger of discarding not a mood but their access. A quietness that no longer prays boldly or owns Christ openly can look like humility and really be the shield thrown away.

A great reward. The writer is not embarrassed by the motive; reward runs through this letter (11:6, 26) and is never treated as a lower motive. God rewards persevering faith and wants us to want the reward.

Need of endurance. Not better arguments or a fresh experience, but endurance (hypomonē): remaining under a weight without buckling (12:1–3; James 1:3–4). That is the diagnosis after ten chapters of theology, and it humbles anyone who assumes people leave the faith because they ran out of reasons. These readers had the reasons. What they were short of was staying power.

Done the will of God. Doing comes first and receiving after, not because the promise is earned, but because it lies at the end of a road that must be walked. What is promised is the eternal inheritance (9:15). Endurance is not waiting; it is continuing to obey while nothing visible changes.

The will he did first. The phrase has already been on the lips of the Son: “Behold, I have come to do your will, O God” (v. 7), and “by that will we have been sanctified” (v. 10). The will these weary believers must keep doing Christ has already done for them, to the cross and through it. They are not asked to win by endurance what he won by his, but to walk the road his obedience made safe, behind the one who endured the cross and is now seated at the right hand of the throne (12:2). He gives endurance to those tired of enduring, and a reward greater than all they have lost.

Is it wrong to serve God for a reward? No, if the reward is God himself and what he gives, not a lever for getting something else from him. Moses looked to the reward (11:26), and Jesus endured the cross for the joy set before him (12:2). God made us to want joy, and he is the greatest joy. It would be wrong to serve him only for earthly payment, or to think the reward wages earned; it is a Father’s gift, out of all proportion to anything we did, to strengthen us to keep going.

What if I am worn out and do not think I can keep going? Then this verse was written for you; these readers were tired too. Endurance is not the absence of weariness but continuing under it, a day at a time, and God gives it as you look to Christ (12:2–3). Do the next faithful thing, not the rest of your life. Rest if you need to, ask for help, and tell God honestly that you are weak. He gives power to the faint (Isaiah 40:29–31), and he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).

verseByVerse.quote: For, “Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay; but my righteous one shall live by faith, and if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ will come soon and will not be late; until then God’s righteous people live by faith, and he takes no pleasure in anyone who turns back.

Yet a little while. The writer quotes Habakkuk, the prophet of waiting, whose book opens with the complaint: “O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear?” (Habakkuk 1:2). He was told that the vision awaits its appointed time; if it seems slow, wait for it (Habakkuk 2:3). The words blend Isaiah 26:20 and Habakkuk 2:3–4 in the Greek translation, whose “a little while” (mikron hoson hoson) doubles itself to stress how short the wait is.

The coming one. Where Habakkuk’s Hebrew speaks of the vision coming, the Greek text the writer follows speaks of a person, “the coming one” (ho erchomenos), a title for the Messiah (Matthew 11:3), and the writer applies it to Christ’s return. The promise has a face. What Habakkuk waited for in the watchtower was finally not an event but a person, and he is coming. He came once in the fullness of time, not a day late. “Will not delay” (ou chronisei): it may seem slow, but it will come at the right time (2 Peter 3:8–9).

Shall live by faith. The sentence that changed Luther’s life, which Paul quotes at key points in two letters (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11). Hebrews uses it differently. Paul uses it to answer how a man is justified, counted righteous before God: by faith, not works. Hebrews uses it to answer how he keeps going: by faith, not sight. The emphasis falls on “live”: the righteous man does not merely begin by faith; he lives by it (on chapter 11 as the illustration, see v. 39).

If he shrinks back. To shrink back (hyposteilētai; compare Acts 20:27) is the verb used of furling a sail and of a soldier shrinking from danger.
