Faith goes forward when it cannot see; shrinking back is faith failing, as the wilderness generation shrank back at the border of a good land. “My soul has no pleasure in him” (ouk eudokei) says something severe with restraint: not rage but the withdrawal of delight, which from God is worse. But God delights in those who trust him in the dark, and he will not keep them waiting one moment longer than his love requires.

What it does not mean. Not that the writer expected Christ within a few years and was mistaken. “A little while” is God’s perspective: from his view the whole age between the comings is brief, and a thousand years are as one day (2 Peter 3:8). Every generation lives in the last hour, and every believer’s waiting is short compared with the eternity that follows.

Why does it feel as if Christ is taking so long? We measure time by our lifetimes; God measures it by his purpose. Peter answers directly: the Lord is not slow as some count slowness, but patient, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:9). Every day of delay gathers more of his people in. Meanwhile the righteous live by faith, trusting and obeying in the gap as Habakkuk did. And for each of us the waiting ends at death, when we go to be with him, never more than a little while away.

Textual note. The writer reverses the order of Habakkuk’s two clauses in the Greek translation, so that it is “my righteous one” of whom “if he shrinks back” is said. This makes clear that the warning is addressed to those who profess to be God’s people. The KJV’s “if any man draw back” adds words not in the Greek, which says simply “if he shrinks back”.

verseByVerse.quote: But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer is confident that he and his readers belong with those who trust Christ and are kept safe, not with those who turn back to ruin.

Not of those who shrink back. The chapter of the most frightening warning ends with the writer putting himself and his readers firmly on the right side of it. “Are not of those” is a statement of category, not of achievement: not “we have performed better”, but “we belong to a different kind”.

Preserve their souls. “Destroyed” (eis apōleian) is perdition, eternal ruin (Philippians 1:28; 3:19; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). Set against it is “preserve their souls” (eis peripoiēsin psychēs): literally the gaining, keeping or possessing of the soul, an idiom for coming through alive.

How the warnings work. The danger is described in the strongest terms, and then the readers are told it does not apply to them, the pattern of chapter 6, where the severest warning in the letter is followed at once by “we feel sure of better things” (6:9). Warning and assurance are not alternatives (on warnings as one of the means God uses to keep his people, see the note on vv. 26–27).

Defined by faith. The two categories are defined by one thing only: faith. Not endurance, though he demanded it; not good works, though he commended theirs. That is why Hebrews 11 follows: forty verses of people who had faith, so that a struggling congregation could see what it looks like worn by real men and women over a lifetime. And the crowd ends not with one of them but with Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith (12:1–2). Faith preserves the soul because of where it looks: away from itself, to the one who ran the race first and finished it.

Our souls are held. Faith is the whole difference between the lost and the saved, and faith is God’s gift. The God who has just shown us the fire stoops to say of trembling believers, you are not of those. Our souls are preserved because they are held, and the one who holds them laid down his life for them (John 6:39).

How can I be sure I am one of those who have faith? Look first at Christ, then at the evidence. Are you trusting him alone for your acceptance with God? That is faith, however weak it feels. Then look for signs of life: you come back to him after you fall, you want to be holy even when you are not, you love his people, and you cannot let him go. They are not the ground of your salvation but its fruit. If you find them, take this verse as spoken to you: you are not of those who shrink back.

10.text: <sup>1</sup>For since the law has but a shadow of the good things to come instead of the true form of these realities, it can never, by the same sacrifices that are continually offered every year, make perfect those who draw near.<sup>2</sup>Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, since the worshipers, having once been cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins?<sup>3</sup>But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year.<sup>4</sup>For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.<sup>5</sup>Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said, “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me;<sup>6</sup>in burnt offerings and sin offerings you have taken no pleasure.<sup>7</sup>Then I said, ’Behold, I have come to do your will, O God, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book.’”<sup>8</sup>When he said above, “You have neither desired nor taken pleasure in sacrifices and offerings and burnt offerings and sin offerings” (these are offered according to the law),<sup>9</sup>then he added, “Behold, I have come to do your will.” He does away with the first in order to establish the second.<sup>10</sup>And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.<sup>11</sup>And every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins.<sup>12</sup>But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God,<sup>13</sup>waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool for his feet.<sup>14</sup>For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.<sup>15</sup>And the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us; for after saying,<sup>16</sup>“This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws on their hearts, and write them on their minds,”<sup>17</sup>then he adds, “I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more.”<sup>18</sup>Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.<sup>19</sup>Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus,<sup>20</sup>by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh,<sup>21</sup>and since we have a great priest over the house of God,<sup>22</sup>let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.<sup>23</sup>Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful.<sup>24</sup>And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works,<sup>25</sup>not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near.<sup>26</sup>For if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins,<sup>27</sup>but a fearful expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries.<sup>28</sup>Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses.<sup>29</sup>How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and has outraged the Spirit of grace?<sup>30</sup>For we know him who said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.” And again, “The Lord will judge his people.”<sup>31</sup>It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.<sup>32</sup>But recall the former days when, after you were enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings,<sup>33</sup>sometimes being publicly exposed to reproach and affliction, and sometimes being partners with those so treated.<sup>34</sup>For you had compassion on those in prison, and you joyfully accepted the plundering of your property, since you knew that you yourselves had a better possession and an abiding one.<sup>35</sup>Therefore do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward.<sup>36</sup>For you have need of endurance, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised.<sup>37</sup>For, “Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay;<sup>38</sup>but my righteous one shall live by faith, and if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.”<sup>39</sup>But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.

keyVerse.quote: For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.
keyVerse.note: This verse gathers the argument of chapters 7–10 into one sentence: one offering, a work finished for ever, and a people still being made holy. Its two tenses hold the whole Christian life together, a standing before God that is already complete and a growth that is still under way, and the first guarantees the second. It is why no other sacrifice remains (v. 18), and why the weakest believer may draw near with confidence (v. 19).

10.reflection:
Verse 3 says the yearly sacrifices were “a reminder of sins every year”. Where do you see people, inside or outside the church, trying again and again to quiet the same guilt? How does Christ’s single offering (vv. 10, 14) answer it?

The priests stood daily, but Christ “sat down at the right hand of God” (vv. 11–12). What difference would it make this week to pray, work and serve from that finished work rather than towards it?

Verses 22–25 make three appeals: draw near, hold fast, and consider how to stir up one another. Which do you most need to hear, and whom could you encourage, or provoke to love and good works, this week?

The severe warning of verses 26–31 is followed at once by encouragement (vv. 32–39). How should a believer hear such warnings, and what would you say to a friend afraid that he has gone too far to come back?

11.title: By Faith: The Great Cloud of Witnesses
11.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 11 answers the words that close chapter 10, “my righteous one shall live by faith” (10:38). Ten chapters have shown that Jesus is better; now the writer shows what it looks like to live on that, before chapter 12 calls the readers to run their own race looking to Jesus.

The message. Faith takes God at his word about what cannot yet be seen, and acts on it, and this is what God has always commended in his people. It is not measured by results. The same faith shut the mouths of lions and was sawn in two, received the dead back alive and died hoping for resurrection. Every one of these believers died without receiving what was promised, because God was keeping something better, so that they and we would be made perfect together.

Why it was said. The readers had lost property and standing for Christ, and nothing they could see had improved; some were drifting back towards the visible, respected faith of the synagogue (see the introduction). They needed to know that living by an unseen promise was not a strange new burden but the way all God’s people had always lived, and that suffering for it was no sign that God had failed them.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–3 say what faith is: the title deed to what is hoped for, the evidence of what is not seen, the way we know even that the world was made. Verses 4–7 show faith before the flood: Abel accepted, Enoch taken, the principle that without faith no one can please God (v. 6), and Noah building in public. Verses 8–22 dwell on Abraham and his family, strangers in the land of promise, and pause (vv. 13–16) to say that they all died still waiting for a heavenly country, and God was not ashamed of them. Verses 23–31 follow Moses, the exodus, Jericho and Rahab. Verses 32–38 speed up: some were rescued by faith, and others, with the same faith, were tortured and killed. Verses 39–40 say why none of them received the promise: they were waiting for us.

Where it leads. The gallery is honest. Sarah laughed, Jacob deceived, Samson was a disgrace, and all are commended, because the roll measures not their record but the God they trusted. And every portrait faces forward to someone not yet named. Abraham received Isaac back “figuratively” from the dead; Moses chose “the reproach of Christ”; a lamb’s blood sheltered Israel from the Destroyer; martyrs refused release to rise to a better life. The next sentence of the letter names him: Jesus, “the founder and perfecter of our faith” (12:2), who endured the cross and sat down at God’s right hand. He is the something better they all died waiting for. The promise they greeted from afar has a face.

For us. Faith is not a feeling of certainty or a technique for good outcomes. It is trusting the God who promised and doing what he says, whether he brings you out of the fire or through it. And you are not alone in it: the stands are full of people who lived and died on the same promises with far less than you have been given. Look where they looked.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — By Faith: Title Deeds and Tents
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faith takes hold of what God has promised and not yet given, and without it no one can please God. Verses 1–3 say what faith is and show it at work in believing that God made the world. Abel, Enoch and Noah (vv. 4–7) show that faith pleases God whatever it brings. Then Abraham and his family fill the gallery (vv. 8–22): strangers in the land of promise, looking for a city God is building, offering up the son of promise, and dying still trusting, with God unashamed to be called their God (vv. 13–16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith as a Title Deed

Faith treats what God has promised as already ours, because it rests on the reliability of the one who promised (see the note on vv. 1–2). What everyone in this gallery is commended for is set out at v. 7.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob lived in tents in the land of promise (see vv. 8–10) and died without receiving it (see v. 13).

Now: God is not ashamed to be called the God of people who are visibly waiting for a better country (see the note on vv. 13–16).

verseByVerse.quote: Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen. For by it the people of old received their commendation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faith takes hold now of what God has promised but not yet given, and it is what God has always commended in his people. It met these readers’ exact difficulty: they could see the hostile neighbours and the plundered houses (10:32–34), but not what they had been promised.

The assurance of things hoped for. “Assurance” (hypostasis) is literally “that which stands under”, a foundation; at 1:3 it describes the very being of God. In some papyri it is used in property documents for something like a title deed, the paper that establishes a claim to something you do not yet hold. A man with the title deed to a house he has never seen owns it, and behaves accordingly. Faith is the title deed to what God has promised: the city, the inheritance, the resurrection, the return of Christ.

The conviction of things not seen. “Conviction” (elenchos) is a law-court word: proof, the evidence that settles a case. Faith functions as evidence of what cannot be seen: God himself, Christ at his right hand, and the events still to come (2 Corinthians 4:18; 5:7). Both words guard against the idea that faith is believing without reasons. Its reason is not how strongly we believe, but how reliable the one who promised is (10:23).

Received their commendation. Literally, they “were witnessed to” (emartyrēthēsan), a word that recurs through the chapter (vv. 4, 5, 39): God himself bears witness, in Scripture, that they pleased him.

The unseen one at the centre. What, above all, does faith see that the eye cannot? We do not yet see everything in subjection to man, the letter says, but we see Jesus, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death (2:8–9). He is the hidden centre of every hope here: the offspring promised to Abraham, the reproach Moses chose (v. 26), the something better the whole gallery died waiting for (v. 40). And the chapter runs straight on into the call to run “looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith” (12:2). Every portrait in this gallery is painted with its face turned towards him.

Nobody lives without faith. Many assume that faith is what religious people do instead of thinking, while everyone else goes by evidence. But no one lives by proof alone. You trust your memory, other minds, and scientists whose papers you have never read. The chemist and philosopher Michael Polanyi argued that all real knowing, even in science, rests on personal commitments and a trust that can never be fully spelled out. Even the rule “believe only what can be proved” cannot itself be proved. The question is never whether to trust, but whom. So the Bible does not ask for a leap away from evidence. It asks us to rest our weight on a Person who stepped into the visible world, was seen, heard and touched (1 John 1:1), and rose. Faith is not the opposite of reason; it is what reason does when it meets someone trustworthy.

How is faith different from positive thinking? Positive thinking trusts that things will turn out well because you expect them to; faith trusts that God will do what he has said because he has said it. It rests on his promise, not on the outcome, so it can be just as confident when the outcome looks bad. Abraham, as this chapter will show, expected his son to die and still trusted God. Positive thinking would have been useless on Mount Moriah.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faith understands that the universe exists because God spoke it into being out of nothing. The first example is not a person but something every reader already believed.

By faith we understand. “By faith” will open each example like a drumbeat. And faith is paired with understanding (nooumen, to perceive with the mind): it does not replace knowing; it is the way we come to know this.

By the word of God. “Universe” (tous aiōnas) is literally “the ages”: all of space and time, as in 1:2. God made it by speaking: God said, and it was (Genesis 1:3; Psalm 33:6, 9).

Not made out of things that are visible. Trace the visible world back and you arrive not at earlier stuff but at a word. Read with the rest of Scripture, the verse means that God created from nothing, ex nihilo, for he calls into existence the things that do not exist (Romans 4:17; Colossians 1:16). This was a radical claim against Greek philosophy, which generally held that matter was eternal and that a god at best shaped it.

Why start with creation? Because creation is the first and largest instance of what cannot be seen: nobody watched it, and everyone who believes it believes on testimony. The readers already ordered their whole view of reality around an event none of them saw; the writer will ask them to order their lives around a promise they cannot see either. The God who made everything from nothing can be trusted to keep every promise.

Through whom he made the ages. Hebrews has already named the Word by which the ages were framed: the Son, through whom God created the world and who upholds it by the word of his power (1:2–3). Faith in creation is faith not in an impersonal command but in a Person, the Saviour who made purification for sins and sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. The God who made the universe out of nothing makes new creatures out of sinners the same way: he speaks.

In everyday life. Look at something made today: the sky, a tree, your own hand. It was not there, and then God spoke, and it was. Set the worry you are carrying next to that fact, and tell him in a sentence that the God who made something out of nothing is not short of resources for it.

Does science contradict this verse? No honest science does, because science studies the visible world, and this verse is about where the visible world came from. It cannot see behind the beginning or tell you why there is something rather than nothing. Christians should welcome the study of creation, much of it pioneered by believers who wanted to think God’s thoughts after him. Where particular theories conflict with what God has plainly said, the theories are human and changeable, and God’s word stands.

Where Christians differ: how long did God take? This verse says God made the world by speaking, not how long he took; that question belongs to Genesis. Christians who hold to the full authority of Scripture read the days there as six ordinary days, as long ages, as a literary framework, or as analogical days, the last three often because they weigh the evidence for an old earth or the literary pattern of the chapter. Reformed Christians have differed on this without dividing, and such questions can be held with patience and humility. This commentary’s view: the days are six ordinary days. Genesis numbers them and marks each with evening and morning, and the fourth commandment builds our week on them: “in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them” (Exodus 20:11). With the genealogies of Genesis, those days point to a young creation. In any reading, the point of this verse stands: the world exists because God spoke.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain, through which he was commended as righteous, God commending him by accepting his gifts. And through his faith, though he died, he still speaks. By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death, and he was not found, because God had taken him. Now before he was taken he was commended as having pleased God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abel was accepted and Enoch taken to God for the same reason: both trusted God, and faith is what pleases him.

A more acceptable sacrifice. Genesis records that Abel’s offering was accepted and Cain’s refused without saying why (Genesis 4:3–5). Hebrews supplies the reason: faith. It was not merely that Abel’s was an animal and Cain’s grain, for the law later commanded both. Abel brought the firstborn of his flock and their fat portions, the best (Genesis 4:4), from a heart right with God; Cain’s heart was wrong, as his murder of Abel showed (1 John 3:12).

The same act is not the same act. Two people may sing the same hymn and give the same amount, and God may accept one and not the other, because he sees the heart. Cain shows religion used as a bargain: when his offering was refused, he was not humbled but angry, and the anger turned on the brother God had accepted (Genesis 4:5–8). Religion that tries to earn God’s favour always resents grace shown to someone else.

Commended as righteous. God himself bore witness to him by accepting his gifts. Abel is the first person in the Bible’s story to be called righteous, as Jesus called him (Matthew 23:35), and God declared him so on the ground of faith. To be declared righteous is to be counted in the right before God the Judge; the New Testament calls it justification, and from Abel on it has come by faith (Romans 4:5).

He still speaks. In Genesis it is Abel’s blood that cries out from the ground (Genesis 4:10); here it is his faith that goes on speaking. Nearly everyone in this chapter is dead, and still speaking.

Enoch was taken up. The shortest biography in Genesis: “Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him” (Genesis 5:24). Genesis 5 ends each life with the refrain “and he died”, but one man has no death recorded. God took him directly to himself, as he later took Elijah (2 Kings 2:11). “He was not found”, as the Greek of Genesis 5:24 puts it, as if people looked for him and he had gone on ahead.

Having pleased God. The Greek Old Testament renders “walked with God” as “pleased God” (euarestēkenai tō theō), which is where the writer gets the phrase. To walk with God is to please him, and to please him requires faith, which leads straight into verse 6.

Opposite outcomes, both commended. Abel died young and violently; Enoch did not die at all. Anyone reading this chapter as a list of what faith gets you has been warned in its first two entries.

A better word than Abel’s. Believers have come to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (12:24). Abel’s blood cried out against the one who shed it. Jesus, the Righteous One, was handed over by the leaders of his own people, and his blood pleads not for vengeance but for pardon. Luke records the prayer: “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34), a verse missing from some early manuscripts but widely received as genuine. Abel’s faith still speaks of a God who accepts sinners by faith; Christ’s blood is the reason he can.

What does it mean to walk with God? Living each day in his company, as two people walk a road together, talking as they go. In practice it is ordinary: speaking to him through the day, listening to his word, keeping in step with what he wants, turning back quickly when you wander off. Enoch did it for three hundred years while raising sons and daughters (Genesis 5:22), so it is not a life withdrawn from the world. The question is not whether you have had dramatic experiences, but whether you are keeping him company.

verseByVerse.quote: And without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can please God without faith, because coming to God means trusting that he is there and that he is good to those who seek him. This is the principle under the whole gallery: it explains why Enoch pleased God (v. 5), and answers 10:38, where God has no pleasure in one who shrinks back.

Impossible to please him. “Impossible” (adynaton) is the word the letter uses when it allows no exceptions (6:4, 18; 10:4). A person may live decently and give generously, and none of it pleases God if it is not done in faith, for whatever does not proceed from faith is sin (Romans 14:23). To do good without trusting God is to treat him as someone to be managed rather than believed. A husband who brings flowers every week but never believes a word his wife says has not pleased her.

Whoever would draw near. “Draw near” is the letter’s key verb for approaching God (4:16; 7:25; 10:22), and the two things the one drawing near must believe are strikingly modest. First, that he exists: the living God, not an idea or a force. Even demons believe that, and shudder (James 2:19); saving faith goes further.

He rewards those who seek him. Second, that he is worth approaching: those who seek him do not walk into an empty room. God is not indifferent, distant or stingy; he responds to those who seek him and gives them himself and his blessings (Jeremiah 29:13; Matthew 7:7–8). This is the harder of the two. Many believe God exists and live as though seeking him were pointless; faith is the confidence that it is not.

Reward without apology. The reward language runs through the chapter: Moses looked to the reward (v. 26), the patriarchs to a city (v. 10). Seeking God for his reward would be selfish only if the reward were something other than God himself. It is not: “Fear not, Abram, I am your shield; your reward shall be very great” (Genesis 15:1).

Drawing near through a priest. Who may draw near to a God this holy? Under the old covenant only the high priest, once a year and never without blood (9:7). The letter answers with a person: Jesus is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him (7:25), and has opened a new and living way through his own flesh (10:19–22). And God is not hiding: he has come looking for us in his Son, and draws us to seek him by his Spirit. No one has ever sought the living God in vain.

What about those who have never heard? This verse does not say that a vague belief in God is enough: the faith that pleases God draws near through Christ (7:25), and the God who rewards seekers sends them the message, as he sent Peter to Cornelius (Acts 10). The answer is not to speculate about them but to go to them.

Can my good deeds before I believed please God? Not in the sense this verse means. They may do others good, and God uses them. But they are not done in faith, from love for God and for his glory, and so they cannot make a person acceptable to him (the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, 16.7). That is humbling, and it is freeing. You do not have to bring a record to God. You come with empty hands, trusting Christ, and from then on even your small and imperfect works please him, because they are offered through his Son (13:21; 1 Peter 2:5).

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Noah, being warned by God concerning events as yet unseen, in reverent fear constructed an ark for the saving of his household. By this he condemned the world and became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Noah believed God’s warning of a judgment no one could yet see, and acted on it in public: his household was saved, the unbelieving world condemned, and he was counted righteous by faith.

Events as yet unseen. A flood of judgment such as had never happened (Genesis 6:13–17). Noah was told about something for which there was no evidence whatever, perhaps about a kind of rain he had never watched fall.

In reverent fear. One word (eulabētheis), holy fear, the attitude seen in Christ at 5:7. Noah took God seriously, which is the whole of his commendation.

Constructed an ark. Here faith becomes visible: a very large wooden object, probably built over years in full view of neighbours who had every reason to think him mad. No one in this gallery is commended for holding an opinion; every one is commended for something they did that made no sense apart from a word from God.

He condemned the world. Not by preaching at it, though Peter calls him a herald of righteousness (2 Peter 2:5), but by building. A man taking God at his word in public passes a verdict on everyone who has heard the same word and done nothing, simply by acting as though it were true.

An heir of the righteousness that comes by faith. The phrase is Paul’s (Romans 4; Philippians 3:9), placed on a man who lived before Abraham, the law and circumcision. Noah found favour in the eyes of the LORD (Genesis 6:8): grace came first, and God declared him righteous (Genesis 7:1). An heir does not earn his inheritance; he receives it because of whose he is. Noah’s right standing with God was not wages for building the ark but a gift received by trusting God’s word, the same gift every believer receives in Christ (Romans 4:4–5).

For the saving of his household. The shape of Noah’s story is the shape of the gospel: one man, moved by reverent fear, did what God said, and those who belonged to him, seven others, were carried through the judgment with him (Genesis 7:1; 1 Peter 3:20). Hebrews uses the same word of Jesus, heard because of his reverence (5:7–9), and calls the church his house (3:6). Noah’s obedience saved his family from drowning; Christ’s obedience to the point of death carries his whole household through the judgment of God itself (Romans 5:19).

Shut in by God’s own hand. God warned the world through a man with a hammer, year after year, while his patience waited. When the flood came, he shut the door himself (Genesis 7:16), and the ark rode on the very waters of judgment that drowned the world. So it is with all who are in Christ: the judgment broke over him, and those inside are carried through it, shut in by God’s own hand.

In everyday life. Is God calling you to obey him in something that looks foolish to others: giving when money is tight, setting Sunday apart for worship, refusing to cut a corner at work, staying faithful in a hard marriage? Do it by faith, as Noah did. Your obedience will be patchy, as Noah’s was after the flood (Genesis 9:20–21); Christ’s was not, and his is counted as yours.

What it does not mean. Not that Noah was saved by building the ark. He was saved by faith in God’s word, which showed itself in the building. Faith and obedience always go together, but they are not the same thing: his obedience showed his faith; it was not the reason God accepted him.

What if my family thinks my faith is foolish? Noah’s neighbours certainly did, and God did not ask him to win the argument; he asked him to keep building. Live faithfully, kindly and consistently, without preaching at people who are not listening and without hiding what you believe. God often uses steady obedience over years. Pray for each member of your family: God has often been pleased to bring families to himself through one member who believed first.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going. By faith he went to live in the land of promise, as in a foreign land, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, heirs with him of the same promise. For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham obeyed God’s call without knowing where it led, and lived as a stranger in the land promised to him, because he was looking for a lasting city that God himself is building.

Abraham obeyed when he was called. Abraham receives more attention than anyone else in the chapter (vv. 8–19), and his first act is obedience. “Called” (kaloumenos) is in a form that means “while he was being called”: he began to obey as soon as the call came (Genesis 12:1–4). The place was Canaan, promised to him and his descendants (Genesis 12:7; 15:18–21).

Not knowing where he was going. He obeyed first and found out afterwards. A man of seventy-five, having already left Ur, left his father’s household for an unnamed destination, with no map and no way of verifying what he had been told. Security then was land and kin, and he left both.

As in a foreign land, living in tents. He arrived, and was still a stranger, a resident alien (parōkēsen). He lived in a tent for a hundred years in the country God had given him (Genesis 12:8; 26:25; 33:18–19), and the only part of it he ever owned was a grave: a field with a cave, bought to bury his wife (Genesis 23:17–20). Son and grandson inherited the promise and the tent together, and none of the three saw the promise kept.

The city that has foundations. How could he be content with that? A tent is pegs and cloth, moved every season; a city has foundations, the part of a building that does not move. The city is the heavenly Jerusalem (12:22; 13:14), which John saw with twelve foundations (Revelation 21:2, 10–14). Abraham could live in the temporary because he was expecting the permanent. For readers whose houses had been plundered, here was a man who never had a house and did not mind.

Whose designer and builder is God. “Designer” (technitēs) and “builder” (dēmiourgos) are an architect’s and a craftsman’s words. Abraham never saw the city; he did know who was building it. God has drawn its plans, laid its cornerstone in Christ, and is building it still, out of living stones gathered from every nation.

Outside the camp, towards the city. Hebrews makes Abraham’s tent-life the shape of every Christian life. Jesus suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through his own blood, so let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured, for here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come (13:12–14). Abraham left Ur for a city he never saw; believers leave the comfort of the camp to follow a Saviour who went out ahead of them, and the road leads to the same city.

In everyday life. Jesus has gone ahead of you as a forerunner (6:20), so hold your earthly home and plans loosely. Let that shape one decision this week, such as what you spend on the house compared with what you give. And if you are unsettled, moving or without a home, take heart from Abraham: living in a tent is no sign that God has forgotten you.

How do I know if God is calling me to go somewhere? God does not usually name a journey to us as he did to Abraham. He guides us through his written word, wisdom, prayer, the counsel of mature Christians, and the circumstances he opens and closes. So the question is less what God has secretly decided than what faithfulness requires: what would serve Christ, love my family and use my gifts well. Then act, even without seeing the whole road. Abraham’s faith rested not on knowing where he was going, but on knowing who was leading him.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive, even when she was past the age, since she considered him faithful who had promised. Therefore from one man, and him as good as dead, were born descendants as many as the stars of heaven and as many as the innumerable grains of sand by the seashore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gave a son to a barren old couple because Sarah, for all her wavering, judged that the one who promised was faithful.

Sarah herself. Even Sarah. She laughed when she overheard the promise and then denied laughing (Genesis 18:12–15), and she had earlier arranged a substitute in Hagar rather than wait (Genesis 16:1–2): the old temptation, when God seems slow, to take control and make the promise happen yourself. Hebrews still says: by faith. God commends a faith not perfect, but real. And he turned her laughter of disbelief into the laughter of joy, and gave her a son named Laughter (Genesis 21:6).

She considered him faithful who had promised. Sarah was ninety and had always been barren (Genesis 11:30; 17:17), and faith looked past that to the one who had spoken. It is the phrase of 10:23: he who promised is faithful (pistos). Faith in this chapter is repeatedly a judgment about the character of the promiser rather than a feeling about the promise.

As good as dead. Nenekrōmenou is literally “deadened”, and Paul uses the word too (Romans 4:19). A hundred-year-old body and a ninety-year-old womb, and the writer softens neither. This is not optimism: humanly speaking, there was no way left. God chose to build his people out of a couple who could not have children, so that no one could say the nation came from human strength. He let the situation become hopeless first, and then he kept his word.

As many as the stars of heaven. The images are God’s own (Genesis 15:5; 22:17; 32:12), given to a childless man taken outside one night and told to look up. From one man as good as dead came a nation, and through Christ, children of Abraham from every nation: “if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring” (Galatians 3:7, 29).

From a body as good as dead to an empty tomb. Paul reads this moment as a picture of saving faith: Abraham did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, as good as dead, and the words counted to him as righteousness were written for us also, who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord (Romans 4:19–24). The God who brought Isaac out of a deadened body brought Jesus out of a sealed grave; faith trusts the God who gives life to the dead (Romans 4:17).

In everyday life. What seems dead in your life: a marriage gone cold, a child far from God, a sin you cannot seem to break? Do not pretend it is not dead. Bring it to God as it is, and tell him that you consider him faithful who has promised. If your sorrow is childlessness, remember that God made Sarah a particular promise; he does not promise every couple a child, and a long grief is no sign of weak faith. What he does promise is himself.

Is my faith real if it is mixed with doubt and failure? Very often, yes. Sarah’s was, and Hebrews commends it. The question is not whether your faith is pure, but whether it is resting on God. A trembling hand holding a rope is as safe as a steady one, because the rope does the holding. Bring your doubts to God honestly, as the father did who said, “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24), and keep looking at God’s faithfulness rather than your feelings. God is patient with faith that is still growing.

Uncertain wording. “Power to conceive” is literally “power for the laying down of seed” (dynamin eis katabolēn spermatos), an expression that usually describes the father’s part. So some take Abraham as the subject, with Sarah alongside him: by faith Abraham, together with Sarah, received power to become a father. The Greek allows either reading. Either way, both shared in the miracle by faith.

verseByVerse.quote: These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar, and having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth. For people who speak thus make it clear that they are seeking a homeland. If they had been thinking of that land from which they had gone out, they would have had opportunity to return. But as it is, they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The patriarchs died still trusting God’s promises without having received them, and because they longed for a heavenly homeland, God is not ashamed to be called their God.

These all died in faith. The writer interrupts the roll-call to state the chapter’s theme plainly: faith lives and dies on promises not yet received (vv. 39–40). “These all” most naturally means the patriarchs and their families (v. 9), since Enoch, for one, did not die.

Not having received the things promised. This rules out measuring faith by results. Every one of them died without the land, the nation, the Messiah or the heavenly city. Abraham got Isaac and a burial cave. Yet they did not die without salvation. They were saved as we are, by faith in God’s promise of the Christ who was to come, and his death covers their sins too (9:15).

Greeted them from afar. They were like travellers waving from a ship at a shore they will not reach on this voyage. Jesus said, “Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day. He saw it and was glad” (John 8:56).

Strangers and exiles on the earth. “Exiles” (parepidēmoi) are temporary residents. It is Abraham’s own description of himself when he came to buy the burial cave: “I am a sojourner and foreigner among you” (Genesis 23:4). Believers are pilgrims in this world (1 Peter 1:1; 2:11). And people who speak this way are seeking a homeland (patris, fatherland): a man who calls himself a stranger here has told you he belongs somewhere else.

Opportunity to return. Verse 15 closes the obvious escape. Ur was still there, and the road ran both ways. They did not go back, because their homesickness was not for anywhere they had left.

A better country. “Desire” (oregontai) is to stretch out for. They longed for heaven, God’s country, the new creation: “our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).

God is not ashamed. As Jesus is not ashamed to call us brothers (2:11). God calls himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Exodus 3:6), three men who lived in tents and died holding nothing, and Jesus used that title to prove the resurrection: he is not God of the dead, but of the living (Matthew 22:32). People visibly waiting for another country do not embarrass him. It is those who have settled down here, as though this world were home, who fit that title badly.

He has prepared for them a city. God has already made it ready (John 14:2–3; Revelation 21:2). Their hope is no fantasy. And he has given us a better name to call him by: the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who came from that city to bring us there.

Why are we homesick even at home? We are among the most mobile and loneliest people in history. The French philosopher Simone Weil, writing in 1943, argued that to be rooted is perhaps the most important and least recognised need of the human soul. Some respond by making one place, nation or tribe the home that will finally hold them, and grow fierce in defending it; others give up on belonging and call it freedom. Hebrews refuses both. These believers were strangers here because they were rooted somewhere else, so they were neither rootless nor tribal: they could love the land without worshipping it. And their root was not an idea. The Son of Man, who had nowhere to lay his head, went out homeless so that we might be welcomed into his Father’s house, where he has prepared a place for us (John 14:2).

Is it wrong to enjoy life here and want things to go well? No. God richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17), and a pilgrim may delight in a good meal, a happy marriage, a beautiful place and work well done. What this passage warns against is settling: treating this world as home, so that we would not really mind if Christ never came. The test is what you long for most. Enjoy the inns on the road with thanks; just do not mistake them for the destination.

Does God feel ashamed of me when I fail? Not if you belong to him. He is not ashamed to be the God of Jacob, a schemer and a liar for much of his life, because what counted was not Jacob’s performance but his faith in the promise. The shame of your sin was borne by Christ at the cross, where he despised the shame (12:2). You may feel ashamed of yourself; God, in Christ, is not ashamed of you.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac, and he who had received the promises was in the act of offering up his only son, of whom it was said, “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.” He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham’s greatest act of faith was to obey God’s command to offer Isaac while still holding God’s promise through Isaac, reasoning that God could raise the dead.

When he was tested. Genesis 22 is the summit of Abraham’s faith. God tested him (Genesis 22:1), not to tempt him to sin but to prove his faith. “Offered up” (prosenēnochen) speaks of a completed act: in intention and obedience the sacrifice was complete, though God stopped his hand.

His only son. “Only son” (monogenēs) means unique. Abraham had Ishmael too, but Isaac was the unique son of promise: “Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love” (Genesis 22:2).

Through Isaac shall your offspring be named. From Genesis 21:12. Everything God had promised depended on this boy. He was the promise in a body, and God told Abraham to kill him. The test was not merely whether Abraham loved God more than his son. He had to obey God’s command while still holding God’s promise, when the two seemed to cancel each other out, and leave it to God to make them fit. Timothy Keller, in Counterfeit Gods, noted that after so long a wait Abraham could easily have rested his whole hope on Isaac rather than on the God who gave him; the test brought the gift back under the Giver. Abraham came down the mountain still holding his son, but now in an open hand.

He considered that God was able even to raise him. “Considered” (logisamenos) is a reckoning word: he worked it out. The promise runs through Isaac; God does not lie; God has commanded Isaac’s death; therefore if Isaac dies, God will raise him. No one had ever been raised from the dead; Abraham inferred it from the character of God alone. Genesis records the conclusion in his words to the servants: “I and the boy will go over there and worship and come again to you” (Genesis 22:5).

Figuratively speaking. In a figure (parabolē), Isaac was as good as dead and came back down the mountain alive. The whole episode is a picture: a father, an only son carrying the wood up a hill, and a substitute provided by God. Abraham named the place “The LORD will provide”, and some two thousand years later, on a hill in the same region (if Moriah is the temple hill, as 2 Chronicles 3:1 suggests), he did. The greater Father did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32; John 3:16), and received him back from the dead, not figuratively but in reality.

The Son was the Lamb. Isaac asked on the way up: where is the lamb? His father answered better than he knew: God will provide for himself the lamb (Genesis 22:7–8). On Moriah the son was spared and a ram died in his place. At Golgotha there was no ram caught in a thicket, because the Son was the Lamb, and the Father who stopped Abraham’s hand did not stop his own. The LORD has provided.

What should I do when God seems to contradict his own promises? Do what Abraham did: reason from who God is. When circumstances seem to say that God has forgotten you, hold on to the fixed points: God does not lie, God is good, and God can raise the dead. Then obey what you know, even when you cannot see how it will work out. Abraham did not know about the ram when he climbed the mountain. He knew God. Often the provision comes only on the mountain.

How could God command a father to sacrifice his son? He never intended it to be carried out. It was a test (Genesis 22:1), and God stopped Abraham’s hand: “Do not lay your hand on the boy” (Genesis 22:12). The same God forbade child sacrifice in the plainest terms (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31; Jeremiah 7:31). The story is unique, and it points beyond itself: God spared Abraham’s son and did not spare his own. It gives no one warrant to harm anyone in God’s name. And if you have lost a child, this chapter does not ask you to see that loss as a test you passed or failed; the God of Moriah is the Father who gave up his own Son, and he is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18).

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Isaac invoked future blessings on Jacob and Esau. By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, bowing in worship over the head of his staff. By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave directions concerning his bones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaac, Jacob and Joseph, each near death, spoke and acted in faith about a future they would not live to see, because God had promised it.

Isaac invoked future blessings. Isaac was blind, deceived by his wife and younger son, and meant the blessing for Esau (Genesis 27:27–40). When he discovered the deception he trembled very violently, and then said of Jacob: yes, and he shall be blessed (Genesis 27:33). Hebrews commends that moment: Isaac saw that God had carried out his purpose even through the deception, and did not try to undo it.

Jacob, when dying. Another blind old man, another blessing against the expected order: Jacob blessed Ephraim and Manasseh, and deliberately gave the greater blessing to the younger, over Joseph’s objection (Genesis 48:14–19). The man who had stolen a blessing by deceit now gives one openly, trusting God’s choice of the younger instead of forcing it. Too weak to stand unsupported, he worships leaning on his staff; a staff was all he had when he first crossed the Jordan (Genesis 32:10).

Joseph made mention of the exodus. Joseph was the second man in Egypt, with a palace, a title and a family settled in the best land of the country. The exodus was centuries away. Yet he spoke of God bringing Israel out: God will surely visit you (Genesis 50:24).

Concerning his bones. He made Israel swear to carry his bones to Canaan (Genesis 50:25). His faith took the form of a funeral instruction: bones in a box, sitting in Egypt for centuries as a standing statement that this was not home. And they kept the promise. Moses took the bones (Exodus 13:19), they travelled forty years in the wilderness, and they were buried at Shechem after the conquest (Joshua 24:32), over four hundred years later.

The future the blessings were about. Not merely more children and land. Isaac gave Jacob lordship over his brothers and nations bowing down to him (Genesis 27:29), and from Jacob’s deathbed came the promise that the sceptre would not depart from Judah, and to him would be the obedience of the peoples (Genesis 49:10). This letter names the one it meant: our Lord was descended from Judah (7:14), the offspring in whom all nations would be blessed (Genesis 22:18; Galatians 3:16).

The grave that could not hold him. God kept his promises across centuries, through blind fathers, scheming sons and a coffin in Egypt. And the greatest grave in the story is the one outside Jerusalem, which held the Son of Judah for three days and then could not hold him. Because that tomb is empty, the graves of his people are like Joseph’s coffin: a standing statement that this is not home, waiting for the morning when he calls them out.

How should a Christian face death? As these men did: still trusting, still worshipping, still thinking about the future of God’s people. Death is an enemy, and it is right to grieve and even to fear the dying. But for a believer it is the doorway to being with Christ, and the body will be raised. Practically, put your affairs in order, speak blessing and the gospel to your family, forgive and ask forgiveness, and tell those you leave where your hope is. A deathbed can be one of the most powerful pulpits there is.

Textual note. “Staff” follows the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 47:31, where our Hebrew text reads “bed”. In Hebrew, bed (mittah) and staff (matteh) have the same consonants, and the vowel marks were added much later; the Greek translators read the word as staff. Both readings picture a dying old man bowing in worship, and neither changes the point.
verseByVerse.note: “Staff” follows the Greek Old Testament of Gen 47:31; the Hebrew text as later pointed reads “bed”; the consonants are the same.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–40 — The Turn: Some Were Tortured
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faith chooses God’s people and God’s promise over the world’s treasures, and holds on whether God rescues or lets his people suffer. Moses chooses the reproach of Christ over Egypt and shelters under the Passover blood (vv. 23–28); Israel crosses the sea, Jericho falls and Rahab is spared (vv. 29–31). Then the names come too fast to tell: some conquered by faith (vv. 32–35a), and others were tortured and killed by faith (vv. 35b–38). None received the promise in full, because God had provided something better that includes us (vv. 39–40).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Chapter Turns Over Mid-Verse

In verse 35 faith that raised the dead becomes faith that was tortured to death (see the note on vv. 35–38). Of such people the world was not worthy.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David and Samuel were far from consistent, and they are in the roll (see the note on vv. 32–34).

Now: All these died waiting for what the church now has (see vv. 39–40).

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king’s edict. By faith Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking to the reward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faith made Moses’ parents defy Pharaoh to save him, and made Moses himself leave the palace for the mistreated people of God, because he counted disgrace for Christ worth more than Egypt’s treasures.

Hidden by his parents. The first act of faith in the Moses section belongs to his parents, Amram and Jochebed (Exodus 6:20). Pharaoh had ordered every Hebrew baby boy thrown into the Nile (Exodus 1:22), and they hid Moses at great risk (Exodus 2:1–3). “Beautiful” (asteios) is the word of Exodus 2:2 and Acts 7:20, where Stephen says he was beautiful in God’s sight; perhaps they sensed that God had a purpose for this child. Like the Hebrew midwives, they feared God more than the king (Exodus 1:17).

When he was grown up. At about forty (Acts 7:23), Moses gave up his place at court. Raised in the royal household of the greatest power on earth, with its education, wealth and prospects, he walked away to identify with despised slaves (Exodus 2:11–12).

The fleeting pleasures of sin. The pleasures were real; the writer does not pretend Egypt was miserable. But they were fleeting (proskairos), lasting a season. On the other side was mistreatment, also real and also passing, and a lasting place among the people of God. He reckoned how long each would last. For Moses, staying in the palace would have been sin, because it meant denying God’s people and God’s call.

The reproach of Christ. A startling phrase, since Moses lived some fourteen centuries earlier. Reproach is disgrace: being sneered at and pushed to the edge for belonging to someone. It most likely means the disgrace God’s chosen people bear, which is the disgrace of their Messiah too (“Christ” means the Anointed One): one reproach, borne in different centuries (Psalm 89:50–51). Moses identified with the people through whom the Messiah would come, and looked ahead to him (John 5:46). “Greater wealth” is the language of business, and the readers were facing that reproach themselves (10:33; 13:13).

Looking to the reward. “Looking” (apeblepen) is fixing the eyes on, and it is verse 6 again. He was not being noble; he was counting in a reward the Egyptians could not see, weighing the eternal against the temporary (2 Corinthians 4:17–18). Moses left a palace for a brickyard and counted it riches. A greater than Moses left the glory of heaven, chose to be mistreated with the people of God, and bore their reproach to the end, becoming poor so that his people might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9).

In everyday life. Watch this week for the places where you are embarrassed to be identified with God’s people: the unimpressive church, the awkward believer. Christ was not ashamed to stand with you; stand with them.

What it does not mean. Not that wealth or high position is sinful in itself. Joseph and Daniel served faithfully in pagan courts. For Moses, remaining meant disobeying God’s call. The question is always what faithfulness requires of me here.

Is it right to disobey the government? Christians are to submit to governing authorities and honour them, because God has appointed them (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17). But when the state commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, we must obey God rather than men, as Moses’ parents, the midwives, Daniel and the apostles did. Such disobedience should be open, peaceful, limited to the point of conflict, and ready to bear the consequences. It is not a licence to rebel whenever we dislike a law.

Why are the pleasures of sin called pleasures? Because they are. Sin rarely tempts us with misery; it offers something sweet. The problem is that its enjoyment is short, its cost is long, and it takes what belongs to God. The way to resist is not to pretend sin is dull, but to set against it a greater pleasure: “at your right hand are pleasures forevermore” (Psalm 16:11). Moses gave up the palace because he had seen something better.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith he left Egypt, not being afraid of the anger of the king, for he endured as seeing him who is invisible. By faith he kept the Passover and sprinkled the blood, so that the Destroyer of the firstborn might not touch them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses stood up to Pharaoh because he feared the invisible God more than the visible king, and he kept the Passover trusting God’s word that the lamb’s blood would shelter Israel from judgment.

As seeing him who is invisible. A deliberate paradox (ton aoraton hōs horōn): God is invisible (1 Timothy 1:17), yet Moses lived as though he saw him. If the visible was made out of what cannot be seen (v. 3), the invisible is the more solid, and a man who reckons with it is being realistic. Moses stood before the most visible power on earth, unimpressed, because he was looking at somebody else in the room: he feared God more than Pharaoh, so he did not fear Pharaoh. “Endured” (ekarterēsen) is held out under weight (10:36). That is what the seeing produced: not a mystical experience, but forty years of keeping on.

He kept the Passover. The Passover (Exodus 12) was a new ritual, never done before. A lamb was killed and its blood painted on the doorposts of each Israelite house, and whether the firstborn son inside lived or died that night depended on it. Moses had only God’s word that blood on a doorframe would protect anyone.

The Destroyer of the firstborn. Ho olothreuōn is the one who destroys: the angel of death, or the Lord himself acting in judgment (Exodus 12:23). The Israelites were not exempt by nationality. The Destroyer passed over houses with blood on them, and only those: the letter’s whole argument in a single night’s history. What matters is not who you are descended from, but whether the blood has been applied.

The Firstborn not passed over. The lamb pointed to Christ, our Passover lamb, who has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7; John 1:29). That night every house in Egypt lost its firstborn except the houses marked with blood. At the cross the order was reversed. God’s own Firstborn (1:6) was not passed over: judgment fell on him so that it could pass over us, and every firstborn sheltered by that blood is enrolled in heaven for ever (12:23).

How can I see someone who is invisible? Not with the eyes, but by trusting what God has shown of himself in his word and in his Son. Jesus is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15); whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9). So you see the invisible God by looking at Christ in the Scriptures, until his reality weighs more with you than what you can see. Practically: time in the Gospels, and prayer that speaks to him as present. The more real he is to you, the smaller everything else becomes.

Was it not cruel of God to strike the firstborn of Egypt? It was judgment, not cruelty, and it came with warning. Egypt had thrown Israel’s baby boys into the Nile (Exodus 1:22), and God had told Pharaoh beforehand that Israel was his firstborn son, and that if Pharaoh would not let him go, Pharaoh’s own firstborn would die (Exodus 4:22–23). Nine plagues came first, each a call to repent. The holy Judge owes no sinner a long life; what is astonishing is that on the same night he provided a shelter from his own judgment. The real question is not why God judges, but why he spares anyone at all, and the answer is the blood. It remains one of Scripture’s hardest pages; the little ones who died that night were in the hands of the Judge of all the earth, who will do what is right (Genesis 18:25).

Uncertain wording. Which leaving does “he left Egypt” mean? Exodus says that Moses fled to Midian because he was afraid (Exodus 2:14–15). The likeliest reading is that this verse refers to the exodus itself (Exodus 12:31–42), when he led Israel out in defiance of Pharaoh, and that the writer then steps back to the Passover that opened the way. Others take it as the flight to Midian, read as a decision of faith rather than mere panic. Either way, Hebrews is not rewriting history; it is showing what kind of man Moses was.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith the people crossed the Red Sea as on dry land, but the Egyptians, when they attempted to do the same, were drowned. By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days. By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel passed through the sea, Jericho fell, and a Canaanite prostitute was spared, because each trusted God’s word where others with the same evidence did not.

The Red Sea. “The people” is Israel collectively, hemmed in between the sea and Pharaoh’s army, going forward at God’s command (Exodus 14:13–22). Their faith was weak: hours before, they had complained that Moses had brought them out to die in the wilderness (Exodus 14:10–12). Yet they obeyed, and walked through.

When the Egyptians attempted to do the same. The same water, the same seabed, the same walls on either hand, and two entirely different outcomes (Exodus 14:23–28). What saved Israel was not the act of walking into the sea, which the Egyptians did too, but God, whom Israel trusted, exactly as with Abel’s sacrifice in verse 4.

The walls of Jericho. Joshua 6: no siege engines, only marching, trumpets and a shout, as God commanded. Faith here looks absurd for a week: an army walking in silence round a fortified city, watched from the battlements. Nothing happened on days one to six. Faith often looks foolish for a while before it looks like anything at all.

Rahab the prostitute. The placing is deliberate: immediately after Moses stands a Canaanite woman of that trade, commended on the same terms. “Disobedient” (apeithēsasin) describes the people of Jericho, who had heard of the Red Sea and were melting with fear, but did not believe (Joshua 2:9–11).

A friendly welcome to the spies. Literally “with peace” (met’ eirēnēs). Rahab hid the spies and drew the conclusion her city refused: “the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath” (Joshua 2:11). She had less evidence than anyone in Israel and believed more than most of them, and James commends her faith shown in action (James 2:25). When the city fell around her, her house was spared, because the scarlet cord was in her window.

Written into the line of the Saviour. Matthew names her in the genealogy of Jesus: Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab (Matthew 1:5). The woman spared when her city fell became part of Israel, by Matthew’s list the great-great-grandmother of David, and an ancestor of the Messiah. Jesus told the religious leaders that tax collectors and prostitutes were going into the kingdom of God before them, because they believed (Matthew 21:31–32). The family tree of Jesus is full of people like Rahab, and that is no accident.

Can God really use someone with my past? Look at the names here: a people who had grumbled their way to the shore of the Red Sea, and a Canaanite prostitute. God did not choose them because they were respectable, and he does not wait for us to be. If you trust Christ, the wrong you have done is forgiven, and the wrong done to you is not yours to carry in shame, and God delights to show his grace by using people the world would have written off. The consequences of sin do not always vanish, and you should make amends where you can. But your history is not the end of your story; Rahab’s certainly was not.

Where Christians differ: did God approve Rahab’s lie? Rahab lied to the king’s men to protect the spies (Joshua 2:4–6). Some hold that deceiving those bent on murder is not the false witness the ninth commandment forbids, and point to the Hebrew midwives, with whom God dealt well (Exodus 1:19–20). Others, with Augustine and Calvin, hold that the lie was a sin, forgiven like the rest of her past, and that God honoured her faith in spite of it. This commentary’s view: Scripture commends Rahab for her faith, shown in her welcome of the spies and her protection of God’s people, and Hebrews and James hold up that faith as the pattern. Her deception was not a sin needing pardon, for deceiving those bent on murder is not the lie the ninth commandment forbids: she owed no truth to men coming to kill God’s servants, and those who hid Jews from the Gestapo stood where she stood. That narrow case is no licence for ordinary lying, which remains sin (Colossians 3:9).

verseByVerse.quote: And what more shall I say? For time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, of David and Samuel and the prophets— who through faith conquered kingdoms, enforced justice, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were made strong out of weakness, became mighty in war, put foreign armies to flight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is no time to tell of all the flawed judges, kings and prophets who trusted God, won victories and were made strong out of weakness. What puts them in the roll is not their consistency but the God they trusted.

And what more shall I say? “Time would fail me”: the preacher looks at his material and stops trying to cover it all. A common device in ancient speeches, and a skilful one: the sense of an endless supply says more than twenty further examples. Then he speeds up.

Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah. Not the names we would have chosen (Judges 4–16). Gideon defeated the Midianites with three hundred men (Judges 7), but demanded two signs with a fleece first, and later made an ephod that became an idol (Judges 8:27). Barak defeated Sisera (Judges 4), but would not go unless Deborah came with him. Samson’s life was a catalogue of appetite and folly, yet at the end he called on God and brought down the Philistine temple (Judges 16:28–30). Jephthah defeated the Ammonites (Judges 11) and made a rash vow that, as Judges 11 tells it, cost his daughter her life; the narrator grieves it and does not excuse it, and Hebrews names Jephthah for his trust in the LORD against the Ammonites, not for the vow.

David and Samuel and the prophets. David, the king after God’s own heart, who also committed adultery and murder. Samuel, the last judge and first great prophet, whose sons took bribes. The prophets: Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel and others.

What the roll is measuring. Not one is a model of consistency, and the readers knew those stories well. That tells you what the roll measures: not achievement or character, but the bare fact of having taken God at his word, in the middle of lives that were often a mess. God chose the fearful, the flawed and the foolish, so that no one could boast before him.

Conquered kingdoms. The achievements, rattled off at speed. Joshua, the judges and David conquered kingdoms (2 Samuel 8). “Enforced justice” is literally “worked righteousness” (eirgasanto dikaiosynēn): judges and kings like Samuel and David who ruled justly (1 Samuel 12:3–5; 2 Samuel 8:15). And they saw specific promises kept: not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made had failed (Joshua 21:45).

Lions, fire and sword. Daniel in the lions’ den (Daniel 6:22), and perhaps Samson and David, who killed lions (Judges 14:6; 1 Samuel 17:34–37); Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the furnace (Daniel 3:23–27), where a fourth figure walked with them in the flames; David escaping Saul (1 Samuel 19–27), Elijah fleeing Jezebel (1 Kings 19), Jeremiah protected from those who sought his life (Jeremiah 26:24).

Made strong out of weakness. The pattern of nearly every name: not strong men who stayed strong, but weak men made strong. The verb is passive: the strength was given to them, not found in them. Gideon, the least in his father’s house (Judges 6:15); Samson, blind and shackled (Judges 16:28); Hezekiah, raised from his sickbed (Isaiah 38). As the Lord told Paul, “my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).

Mighty in war. Jonathan and his armour-bearer (1 Samuel 14), David, Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 20). The list ends at its most triumphant, just before the turn in verse 35.

The Son these deliverers waited for. Every judge, king and prophet on this list was a partial sketch of the Son (1:1–2). They worked righteousness unevenly and briefly; of the Son God says that the sceptre of uprightness is the sceptre of his kingdom, for he has loved righteousness and hated wickedness (1:8–9). Gideon, Samson and David saved Israel for a generation, and died. The Son conquered by dying, and sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, a Deliverer who never needs replacing (1:3; 7:24–25).

In everyday life. Name your weakness to God today, specifically: fear, lack of ability, a past failure, a body that no longer works as it did. Then take one step in the thing he has given you to do, asking his Spirit, who raised Jesus from the dead (Romans 8:11), to make you strong out of weakness. And if what he has given you seems to achieve nothing, a prayer unanswered or a class that will not listen, you may be on the fourth day of seven at Jericho. Keep walking.

Why does God put such flawed people in the hall of faith? Because faith is trust in God, not confidence in oneself. God includes Samson and Jephthah to show that he works through the faith of sinners, and to give hope to everyone who knows his own failures. But Scripture’s honesty cuts both ways: their sins brought real harm, to themselves and others. God’s grace in using them is not permission to imitate their folly; it is an invitation to trust the same God.

Does “obtained promises” contradict verse 39? No. These men received particular promises in their lifetimes: victories, deliverances, sons. What none of them received was what was promised in the full sense, the coming of Christ and the city God has prepared. God kept his smaller promises along the way, and every one was a pledge of the great one.
verseByVerse.note: Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah are from Judges; the lions’ mouths recall Daniel, and the fire recalls his three friends.

verseByVerse.quote: Women received back their dead by resurrection. Some were tortured, refusing to accept release, so that they might rise again to a better life. Others suffered mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment. They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were killed with the sword. They went about in skins of sheep and goats, destitute, afflicted, mistreated— of whom the world was not worthy—wandering about in deserts and mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same faith that received the dead back alive also endured torture, poverty and death rather than deny God, and the world was not worthy of such people. In the middle of verse 35 the chapter turns: faith does not always bring deliverance.

Women received back their dead. A dead child handed back alive: the widow of Zarephath, whose son Elijah raised (1 Kings 17:17–24), and the Shunammite woman, whose son Elisha raised (2 Kings 4:18–37).

Refusing to accept release. The word for tortured (etympanisthēsan) probably refers to being beaten to death on a frame shaped like a drum. They were offered a way out by renouncing their faith, and would not take it. This probably refers to the martyrs under the Syrian king Antiochus IV Epiphanes around 167 BC, recorded in 2 Maccabees 6–7, which the readers probably knew: the old scribe Eleazar, and a mother and her seven sons, tortured to death rather than eat pork and deny the law of God.

A better life. Literally “a better resurrection” (kreittonos anastaseōs), the word of the first half of the verse. Some received their dead back by resurrection; others died in hope of one. The same faith produced both. The martyrs’ is the better: the widows’ sons would one day die again, but the martyrs looked to the final resurrection to eternal life.

Mocking and flogging. Jeremiah was beaten, put in the stocks, imprisoned and lowered into a muddy cistern (Jeremiah 20:2; 37:15; 38:6); Micaiah was imprisoned and fed on bread and water (1 Kings 22:27).

Sawn in two. Zechariah the son of Jehoiada was stoned in the court of the house of the LORD (2 Chronicles 24:20–22; Matthew 23:35). Jewish tradition, recorded in a later writing called the Ascension of Isaiah, says the prophet Isaiah was sawn in two under King Manasseh. Prophets were killed by Jezebel and Ahab (1 Kings 19:10), and Uriah the prophet was struck down by King Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 26:23).

Skins of sheep and goats. The prophet’s uniform, Elijah’s garment of hair (2 Kings 1:8): the men God sent to Israel living like vagrants in the country they were sent to. “Mistreated” (kakouchoumenoi) is the word of verse 25: they chose the lot Moses chose.

Of whom the world was not worthy. The great reversal of the chapter: the world looked at these people in goatskins, sleeping in caves, and reckoned them not fit to live. God’s verdict is that the world was not good enough for them.

Dens and caves. Elijah in the wilderness (1 Kings 19); the prophets whom Obadiah hid by fifties in a cave (1 Kings 18:4, 13); the faithful of the Maccabean period hiding in caves (1 Maccabees 2:29–38; 2 Maccabees 6:11).

The paragraph they most needed. A plundered congregation could read the first half of the list and wonder why their faith had produced no such deliverance. The second half says: it produced these people too, and God is not ashamed of them either.

The last name in the line. The list of sufferers does not stop at the caves. A few sentences later the writer names one more: Jesus, who endured the cross, despising the shame, and endured from sinners such hostility against himself (12:2–3). Matthew records that he could have asked for more than twelve legions of angels and did not (Matthew 26:53): he refused release. He suffered outside the gate (13:12). And because the God of peace brought him again from the dead (13:20), the better resurrection these martyrs died for is not a hope in the dark. They will follow him out.

The verdict over an empty tomb. The world’s verdict on such people was overturned on the third day: the world found God’s Son fit only for a cross, and God raised him and seated him in glory. The verdict of the world is temporary. The verdict of God, spoken over an empty tomb, is final.

Why does God deliver some believers and not others? Scripture does not give us his reasons in each case, and this chapter refuses to rank the delivered above the martyrs. James was killed with the sword and Peter freed from prison in the same chapter of Acts (Acts 12:1–11). What we are told is that God is wise and good in both, that he is with his people in the fire whether he takes them out of it or through it, and that every one of them will rise. If you prayed for healing and it did not come, it was not because your faith was too small. Some of God’s strongest saints are in the second half of this list.

Where Christians differ: does this make the Maccabean books Scripture? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches include 1 and 2 Maccabees in their Old Testament, and Protestants too have long valued them as history. This commentary’s view: the author refers to events of the Maccabean period, as he refers to the tradition about Isaiah, as true history, without quoting those books as Scripture. Referring to historical events recorded in a book does not make that book inspired. The Old Testament canon received by Jesus and the apostles is the Hebrew Scriptures (Luke 24:44), which do not include the Apocrypha. The canon is closed.

Textual note. After “they were sawn in two”, some manuscripts add “they were tempted”, which is why the King James Version has it. The extra word does not change the meaning of the passage.
