verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition says the prophet Isaiah was sawn in two under King Manasseh.

verseByVerse.quote: And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised, since God had provided something better for us, that apart from us they should not be made perfect.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All these were approved by God for their faith and still died without the great promise, because God was saving it for a day that includes us, so that they and we reach the goal together.

Commended through their faith. The chapter ends where verse 13 stood, with everybody still waiting, and with the word it began with: “commended” (v. 2). The conquerors and the sawn in two, the ones who shut lions’ mouths and the ones the lions ate: all approved by God.

Did not receive what was promised. “What was promised” (tēn epangelian) is the great promise: the coming of the Messiah, the new covenant, and its fulfilment in the eternal inheritance. They received many smaller promises (v. 33), but not the ultimate one.

Something better for us. “Something better” (kreitton ti) is everything the letter has been arguing: the better covenant, sacrifice and priest, the coming of Christ, the full revelation and accomplishment of salvation. They saw the shadow and greeted it from afar; we have the substance.

Apart from us they should not be made perfect. God will not bring Abraham to the goal without the congregation that first heard this letter read. “Made perfect” (teleiōthōsin) is being brought to the goal God intended: sins fully dealt with, a clean conscience before God (9:14), and at last the raised body in the city God has prepared. By a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (10:14). Abraham and Moses were waiting for that offering, and their perfection will be completed with ours at his return, one family brought to glory (12:23; Revelation 7:9). One day the great cloud of the faithful and the last believer to come to Christ will rise together, and see together the one they all believed in.

A congregation that did not know what it had. These readers were drifting back towards the old covenant order, the very era in which these giants longed for something better. The whole gallery had died waiting for what this discouraged little congregation already possessed. There is one people of God, not two: everyone in this chapter and everyone reading it arrives by the same faith, through the same sacrifice. For tired people, that means they are not running alone: the stands are full (12:1).

If they had such faith with so little, what does that say about me? It should humble you and encourage you. Humble, because Abraham trusted God with a promise and a tent, and you have the whole Bible, the cross, the empty tomb and the Spirit. Encourage, because the God who sustained their faith with less will sustain yours with more. You are not asked to be a hero, only to trust the God they trusted, now that he has kept the promise they died waiting for.

Where were the Old Testament saints in the meantime? Some traditions teach that they waited in a holding place below until Christ descended to set them free. Scripture gives little ground for that. Jesus told the dying thief, “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43), and this letter speaks of the spirits of the righteous made perfect, already in God’s presence (12:23). Believers who died before Christ were with God in conscious blessing. What they wait for, with us, is the resurrection of the body, the perfection that will come to the whole church together.

And through his faith, though he died, he still speaks.<sup>5</sup>By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death, and he was not found, because God had taken him. Now before he was taken he was commended as having pleased God.<sup>6</sup>And without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.<sup>7</sup>By faith Noah, being warned by God concerning events as yet unseen, in reverent fear constructed an ark for the saving of his household. By this he condemned the world and became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.<sup>8</sup>By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going.<sup>9</sup>By faith he went to live in the land of promise, as in a foreign land, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, heirs with him of the same promise.<sup>10</sup>For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God.<sup>11</sup>By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive, even when she was past the age, since she considered him faithful who had promised.<sup>12</sup>Therefore from one man, and him as good as dead, were born descendants as many as the stars of heaven and as many as the innumerable grains of sand by the seashore.<sup>13</sup>These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar, and having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth.<sup>14</sup>For people who speak thus make it clear that they are seeking a homeland.<sup>15</sup>If they had been thinking of that land from which they had gone out, they would have had opportunity to return.<sup>16</sup>But as it is, they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city.<sup>17</sup>By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac, and he who had received the promises was in the act of offering up his only son,<sup>18</sup>of whom it was said, “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.”<sup>19</sup>He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.<sup>20</sup>By faith Isaac invoked future blessings on Jacob and Esau.<sup>21</sup>By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, bowing in worship over the head of his staff.<sup>22</sup>By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave directions concerning his bones.<sup>23</sup>By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king’s edict.<sup>24</sup>By faith Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter,<sup>25</sup>choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin.<sup>26</sup>He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking to the reward.<sup>27</sup>By faith he left Egypt, not being afraid of the anger of the king, for he endured as seeing him who is invisible.<sup>28</sup>By faith he kept the Passover and sprinkled the blood, so that the Destroyer of the firstborn might not touch them.<sup>29</sup>By faith the people crossed the Red Sea as on dry land, but the Egyptians, when they attempted to do the same, were drowned.<sup>30</sup>By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days.<sup>31</sup>By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies.<sup>32</sup>And what more shall I say? For time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, of David and Samuel and the prophets—<sup>33</sup>who through faith conquered kingdoms, enforced justice, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions,<sup>34</sup>quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were made strong out of weakness, became mighty in war, put foreign armies to flight.<sup>35</sup>Women received back their dead by resurrection. Some were tortured, refusing to accept release, so that they might rise again to a better life.<sup>36</sup>Others suffered mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment.<sup>37</sup>They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were killed with the sword. They went about in skins of sheep and goats, destitute, afflicted, mistreated—<sup>38</sup>of whom the world was not worthy—wandering about in deserts and mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.<sup>39</sup>And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised,<sup>40</sup>since God had provided something better for us, that apart from us they should not be made perfect.

keyVerse.quote: Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen.
keyVerse.note: This sentence is the theme of the chapter, and every portrait that follows illustrates it. Faith treats what God has promised as solid enough to build a life on, and what cannot be seen as real enough to stake a life on, because its confidence rests not on the believer but on the faithfulness of the one who promised (10:23).

11.reflection:
Verse 1 calls faith “the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen”. How does this differ from the way faith is usually spoken of around you? Which of God’s unseen promises do you find hardest to treat as solid?

The chapter puts opposite outcomes side by side, Abel murdered and Enoch taken, some rescued from the sword and others killed by it, and commends them all (vv. 4–5, 33–37). Why does it matter that faith is not measured by results? How might it change the way you pray about a hardship?

The patriarchs acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth (v. 13). Where are you most tempted to settle down as if this world were home, and what would living as a pilgrim look like there this week?

Moses counted the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt (v. 26), and the whole gallery died waiting for what we now have in Christ (vv. 39–40). What does this chapter show you about Jesus, and how should it strengthen you when following him is costly?

12.title: Fix Your Eyes on Jesus: The Discipline of the Father
12.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 11 filled the stadium; chapter 12 says: run. It turns the roll call of faith into a race and brings the letter’s argument to its summit at Mount Zion. Chapter 13 then shows the life of those who belong to the kingdom that cannot be shaken.

The message. Your hardships do not mean that God has left you; they mean he is raising you as his children. So keep running with your eyes on Jesus, who endured the cross for the joy ahead and sat down at the finish. Do not trade your inheritance for relief, as Esau did. And do not refuse the God who speaks to you from heaven, because through Jesus’ blood you have already come to a mountain far better than Sinai.

Why it was said. The readers were weary rather than wicked: drooping hands and weak knees (v. 12). They had suffered shame and loss, though not yet blood (v. 4; see the introduction), and the old faith offered relief from the shame. They were reading their troubles as signs that God had abandoned them, and the writer reads the same troubles the other way.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–3: the witnesses of chapter 11 prove the course can be finished, and Jesus, the founder and perfecter of faith, shows how it is run, through the cross to the throne. Verses 4–11: Proverbs 3 shows their suffering to be a Father’s training, painful now and fruitful later, and the proof of sonship rather than its absence. Verses 12–17: so get up, mend the road for the limping, pursue peace and holiness, and watch over one another, so that no one becomes an Esau, who sold his birthright for one meal. Verses 18–24 set two mountains side by side: Sinai, untouchable, all fire and darkness and a voice the people begged to stop; and Zion, the heavenly city, with its festival of angels, the assembly of the firstborn, God the judge, and Jesus with his blood. Verses 25–29 sound the letter’s last warning: do not refuse the one who speaks; everything made will be shaken, but we are receiving a kingdom that cannot be, so worship with gratitude and awe, for our God is a consuming fire.

Where it leads. Jesus holds the whole chapter together. He is the runner who finished (v. 2), the Son who walked the road of discipline without needing correction, the true Firstborn who shares his inheritance with people who sold theirs, the mediator who is not afraid of God, whose blood speaks a better word than Abel’s (v. 24), and the King whose kingdom cannot be shaken. The readers thought they were being told to hold on; they are shown that they are being held, and that they have already arrived where Abraham was still travelling.

For us. When following Christ grows costly and tiring, read your hardships as a Father’s hand, not his absence, and look away to Jesus. And remember where you stand each time the church gathers: not at the foot of a terrifying mountain, but in a festival crowd before a holy God, with blood that speaks for you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Run the Race, and Read the Discipline
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Run to the end, looking to Jesus, and read your hardships as the training of a Father who loves you. The witnesses of chapter 11 prove the course can be finished (v. 1), and Jesus shows how it is run: through the cross to the throne (vv. 2–3). The readers’ sufferings, which have not yet cost them blood (v. 4), are the discipline Proverbs promised to God’s sons (vv. 5–6): proof that they are true children, not strangers (vv. 7–8), given by a Father who never errs, for their good, that they may share his holiness and bear peaceful fruit later (vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Timescales

Run looking to Jesus (see the note on v. 2). The Father's discipline is painful for the moment, but later yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained by it (see vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Suffering believers wondered whether God had abandoned them.

Now: Hardship received from God's hand is a mark of sonship, not of rejection (see vv. 7–8). Do not make light of it, and do not faint under it (see vv. 5–6).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight, and sin which clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since so many have finished the course by faith, throw off whatever slows you and keep running to the end. The race is the whole Christian life, and what it asks is not speed but endurance.

A cloud of witnesses. “Therefore”: all of chapter 11 is now put to work. These are not spectators judging how we do. The word for witness is martys, from which we get “martyr”, and chapter 11 uses its verb (“commended”) for people to whom God bore witness (11:2, 4, 5, 39). The stands are full of people who have already run: Abel and Abraham and Moses and Rahab and the martyrs in the caves finished the course because God carried each of them to the end. The crowd testifies not to their strength, but to his faithfulness.

Every weight. “Lay aside” means strip off, like clothing. A “weight” is not a sin but anything bulky that slows a runner, as ancient runners stripped off clothing that was perfectly respectable. Some things are not wrong and must still go, simply because they are heavy: distractions, entanglements, good things that crowd out the best.

Sin which clings so closely. Not merely something heavy but sin itself, wrapping round the runner’s legs like a long robe and tripping him (on the word, see below). In context it may be especially the sin of unbelief and turning back (3:12–13), which would stop the race altogether.

Run with endurance. “Run” is present tense: keep running. The race (agōn, from which we get “agony”) needs endurance, bearing up under a load, as in 10:36. And “set before us” is a quiet comfort: someone else marked out the course, and a runner is not responsible for its length or its gradients, only for staying on it.

The one runner who was never tripped. Every witness in the stands ran with a robe catching at his legs: Abraham’s lie about Sarah, Moses’ anger at the rock, David’s adultery. Only one has run the whole course unentangled: our high priest “in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (4:15). The crowd proves the race can be run; he is the reason it can be won. None of us runs a lap without stumbling, but his perfect obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), so a fall does not undo our standing. That is why the writer at once turns every eye to Jesus (v. 2).

What it does not mean. We do not run to earn salvation. The race is not a test to get in; it is the life of those whom Christ has already brought in.

How do I know what my weights are? Ask what regularly crowds out prayer, Scripture, worship or love for others, and what you reach for when you should be reaching for God: your phone, a hobby, an ambition, a crowded diary, even church work done at the expense of your family. Each runner decides his own, and other believers may carry things that you cannot. But if something keeps tripping your heart, lay it down, and see how much lighter the running becomes.

In everyday life. Name the sin that most often entangles you. You do not fight it on willpower: the Spirit who raised Jesus lives in you (Romans 8:11), and a friend is one of his ordinary means, so tell a trusted Christian and ask them to ask you about it.

Where Christians differ: are the departed saints watching us? Some read “surrounded by … witnesses” as teaching that departed believers watch and cheer us from heaven, and some traditions draw from it the practice of praying to the saints. This commentary’s view: the main sense of witnesses is those who testify by their faith, as chapter 11 has just shown (11:2, 4, 5, 39 use the related verb, “commended”). Whether the departed are aware of events on earth is not clearly taught, and Scripture gives no warrant for praying to them, for “there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). The departed saints are consciously with the Lord (Philippians 1:23; Hebrews 12:23), but our eyes are to be fixed on Jesus, not on them (v. 2).

Uncertain wording. “Clings so closely” translates a word (euperistatos) found nowhere before this verse in surviving Greek, so its meaning must be worked out from its parts. Most take it as “easily entangling” or “readily surrounding”; older suggestions include “much admired” and “easily avoided”. The ESV’s sense is the likely one.

verseByVerse.quote: looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep your eyes on Jesus: he began your faith and will finish it, and he ran the hardest course of all, through the cross to the throne.

Looking to Jesus. The word means looking away from everything else to one thing. The writer has just filled the stadium with heroes, and now turns every eye from them to him.

The founder and perfecter of our faith. “Founder” (archēgos) is the pioneer of 2:10, the man at the head of the column who opens the way; “perfecter” (teleiōtēs) is the finisher, who brings faith to its goal. So he stands at both ends of the course. (The Greek says simply “the faith”.) He is the supreme example of trusting God to the end, but more: the one who begins and completes faith itself in us (Philippians 1:6).

For the joy set before him. The same phrase as the race “set before us” in verse 1: he ran a marked course too, with something at the end he wanted (on the word “for”, see below). He did not go to the cross grimly. There was a joy he was after: the Father’s will done, his people redeemed, his exaltation (Isaiah 53:11; John 17:5; Philippians 2:9), or, as the letter has put it, “bringing many sons to glory” (2:10). His people were part of the joy set before him.

Despising the shame. The writer names not the pain but the shame, to a first-century reader the worse half. Crucifixion was designed as public humiliation: the victim usually stripped naked, mocked and cursed, for “a hanged man is cursed by God” (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). To despise the shame is to count it as nothing: he weighed the disgrace against the joy and judged it not worth considering. The readers were facing shame themselves (10:33; 13:13), and he shows them how to bear it.

Seated at the right hand. He has sat down and remains seated (1:3; 8:1; 10:12). He ran, he endured, he sat down: proof to every runner still on the course that the course ends. He is the finish line in person, and every runner who looks to him will cross it, because the one who started the race in us is waiting at the end of it.

How do I actually look to Jesus? By deliberately turning your attention to him as Scripture shows him: what he did, what he endured, where he is now, what he has promised. Read the Gospels, so that his face becomes familiar; dwell on the cross when you are tempted or ashamed; pray to him as someone present; and when trouble fills your horizon, ask what it looks like from his throne. It is not a feeling you wait for but a habit of the mind, which grows stronger with use.

Uncertain wording. “For the joy” translates a preposition (anti) that often means “in place of” but can also mean “for the sake of”. If the first, Jesus took the cross instead of the joy he might have kept (compare Philippians 2:6–8); if the second, he endured it to gain the joy ahead. Most take the second, because “set before him” matches “the race that is set before us” (v. 1): a prize waiting at the end of a course.

verseByVerse.quote: Consider him who endured from sinners such hostility against himself, so that you may not grow weary or fainthearted. In your struggle against sin you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you grow tired, measure your trouble against what Jesus endured; none of you has yet resisted to the point of blood. The comparison is meant not to shame the weary but to give their pain its true size, and company.

Consider him. “Consider” is an accounting word: reckon up what Jesus bore, do not merely feel something. He endured mockery, slander, betrayal, rejection, beatings and crucifixion from sinners, the very people he came to save.

Weary or fainthearted. Two words for exhaustion, like a runner whose strength fails. The remedy offered is not rest or a change of circumstances, but a comparison: measure yourself against him.

Your struggle against sin. They thought they were enduring hostility from neighbours; they are in a fight with sin itself: the sin of their persecutors, and the temptation to sin by giving up.

Not yet to the point of blood. Then he does the measuring for them. They had genuinely suffered humiliation, imprisonment and plundered houses (10:32–34), and he has praised them for it. Yet none of them has died. Jesus resisted to the point of blood, his own, shed so that ours would never have to be shed for our guilt.

Restoring the scale. A hard word, and a fair one. Exhaustion makes your own trouble fill the whole horizon, a normal part of being tired rather than a moral failure. The writer does not say their pain is not real, only that it is not the biggest thing in the room. And when we grow weary, Christ does not shame us; he shows us his wounds and gives us strength.

Is it wrong to feel that my suffering is too much? No. The Psalms are full of such feelings, and Jesus himself said, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death” (Matthew 26:38). This verse is not a rebuke to your feelings but a help for them: look at his pain, and let it give you perspective and company. Tell him honestly how hard it is, and ask for strength for the next step. You are not asked to pretend, but invited to consider him.

In everyday life. When you are weary, read a passion narrative slowly, perhaps Mark 14–15, noticing each kind of hostility he faced. Then look at your own hardest situation in that light. It may not shrink, but it may become the right size.

Textual note. Some manuscripts, including several of the earliest, read “against themselves”, meaning that sinners who opposed him were really harming themselves; but “against himself” makes far better sense of the sentence, and most translations follow it.

verseByVerse.quote: And have you forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons? “My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when reproved by him. For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your hardships are not a sign that God has turned against you, but the training a loving Father gives his children. Scripture had already told them so, if they had remembered it.

Have you forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons? A gentle, slightly reproachful question. Having shown them what Jesus suffered (vv. 1–3), the writer teaches them to read their own suffering as a Father’s training (2:10–11). Notice the present tense, “addresses”, as at 3:7 and 10:15: a passage from Proverbs arriving in the room this morning. And “exhortation” also means encouragement: hard as it sounds, what follows is comfort.

My son. The quotation is Proverbs 3:11–12, and “my son” comes first and governs all that follows: this is said inside a family. The voice that said to the eternal Son, “You are my Son, today I have begotten you” (1:5), now turns to us in the same family words, because that Son has made us his brothers. “Discipline” (paideia) is training, the whole raising of a child to maturity, of which correction is one part. The first error is to “regard lightly”: to shrug it off, or treat a hardship God has sent as mere bad luck.

Nor be weary. The second error is the opposite: to lose heart and collapse, as in verse 3. Some harden and refuse to ask what God might be doing; others are flattened and conclude he has turned against them. The verse forbids both.

The one he loves. The passage turns on this sentence. Discipline is evidence of love, not of rejection (Revelation 3:19; Deuteronomy 8:5).

Every son whom he receives. “Chastises” is stronger: to scourge, to whip. The writer does not soften it, and “every” leaves no exemptions. Proverbs 3:12 itself reads “as a father the son in whom he delights”; the writer quotes the Greek translation of the Old Testament, which reads the Hebrew slightly differently, with the same sense.

Discipline without wrath. How can a believer hear “scourges” and still call it love? Because the punishment his sins deserve has already fallen elsewhere: “upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5), and Christ was “offered once to bear the sins of many” (9:28). So a Christian’s discipline is never God settling accounts with him; Christ settled them. What remains is a Father training a son. The hardship that would be judgment for someone outside Christ is, for one inside him, the work of a Father who has received him and will never cast him off.

What it does not mean. Not that every affliction is punishment for a particular sin. The letter has just spent a chapter on people who suffered because they were faithful, and the readers’ suffering also came from faithfulness, yet God used it to train them.

How can I tell whether a hardship is God’s correction for a sin? Sometimes it is plain: you sinned, the consequences followed, and your conscience tells you so. Then repent, and receive the correction as a Father’s love. But often it is not plain, and you should not invent a sin to explain every trouble, as Job’s friends did. Ask God honestly whether there is anything he wants to show you, and listen to Scripture and wise friends. If nothing comes to light, treat the hardship as training: God is using it to make you more like Christ. The question is not mainly “Why?” but “How do I respond as his child?”

Is calling suffering discipline not just a way of excusing God? It would be if the verse called evil good, but it does not. The persecutors are still wrong, and the pain is still pain (v. 11). What it denies is that suffering is meaningless. A world without God leaves pain with no purpose at all; for God’s children, nothing is wasted. And this Father is not a distant official who never suffers. He “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32), and the Son endured the cross (v. 2). The one who trains us through hardship has walked into the worst of it himself.

verseByVerse.quote: It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? If you are left without discipline, in which all have participated, then you are illegitimate children and not sons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Discipline is what sons receive, so its presence proves you belong to the family; to be left without it would be the frightening thing.

For discipline. Their suffering has a purpose, training, and proves that God has not abandoned them. That does not make the persecutors right or injustice just. God is using it, and a Christian may read his hardest circumstances as a Father’s work without excusing those who cause them.

For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? An appeal to ordinary experience, which in that world needed no argument (Proverbs 13:24; 19:18). A father who took no trouble over a boy’s upbringing was not being kind but neglectful. A father who loved his son trained him.

In which all have participated. Every true child of God shares it, Jesus included, who “learned obedience through what he suffered” (5:8): not because he needed correcting, but because he was a true Son walking the road of sons.

Illegitimate children. A man does not train somebody else’s children. In that society an illegitimate son might be housed and fed but not raised, and usually had no right to inherit. So the absence of discipline is the frightening thing. The readers looked at their troubles and wondered whether they were still his; the writer says: this is what having a Father looks like.

God does not raise strangers. He has appointed his Son “heir of all things” (1:2) and made us “fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17), so every correction is a sign that the inheritance is real and our names are on it.

A grandfather in heaven. Our culture tends to equate love with affirmation, and on that view a God who disciplines cannot be loving. C. S. Lewis, in The Problem of Pain, observed that what many of us really want is not so much a Father in heaven as a grandfather in heaven, a kindly old man who likes to see young people enjoying themselves and asks nothing more. But we know better about children: the parent who never says no is not the most loving but the most indifferent, or the most afraid of being disliked. Real love wants the beloved to become good, and will be resented for a while to get there. God’s love is both tougher and softer than we imagined: tough enough to refuse to leave us as we are, and soft enough to have borne our punishment himself, so that what reaches us now is training and never wrath.

Should I worry if my life is fairly easy at the moment? No. Seasons of rest are God’s gift, to be received with thanks, not suspicion. Discipline is not always dramatic: it includes the daily correction of conscience by Scripture, frustrated plans, the small humblings that keep us dependent. What would be alarming is a life in which sin never troubles you and God never seems to interfere. Use the easy season to grow, to give, and to prepare for harder days.

In everyday life. If you are a parent, discipline as this passage describes: in love, for your child’s good, to form character, never in anger for your own relief. You have a Father who raises you that way.

parallels.desc: as a man disciplines his son, the LORD your God disciplines you

verseByVerse.quote: Besides this, we have had earthly fathers who disciplined us and we respected them. Shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live? For they disciplined us for a short time as it seemed best to them, but he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness. For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we respected the imperfect discipline of our earthly fathers, how much more should we yield to our heavenly Father’s, which is always for our good and aims at nothing less than his holiness in us. It hurts now, but it bears fruit later.

Earthly fathers. Again from the lesser to the greater. Children generally end up respecting the parent who took the trouble, and thinking little of the one who did not.

Shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live? Our earthly fathers gave us our bodies; God is the creator of our spirits, “the God of the spirits of all flesh” (Numbers 16:22; 27:16; Zechariah 12:1). And the promise attached is not comfort but life: submission to God’s discipline leads to life, rebellion against it to death (Deuteronomy 21:18–21).

As it seemed best to them. An honest comparison: human discipline lasts a few years and is a matter of judgment, often wrong, sometimes angry or inconsistent. God’s is “for our good”: never mistaken, never excessive, never selfish (Romans 8:28).

Share his holiness. A startlingly high aim: not merely better behaviour, but a share in his holiness. No creature will ever become God, but his children are made like him in character: “You shall be holy, for I am holy” (1 Peter 1:16).

The holiness he bought, the holiness he trains. “We have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (10:10); Jesus “suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (13:12). Discipline does not add to that holiness; it brings it out in daily life, until what is already true of his children in Christ becomes true in their character, and they grow like the one who sanctifies them and “is not ashamed to call them brothers” (2:11).

Painful rather than pleasant. An honest and kind sentence: discipline is not supposed to feel good, and “all” means no one is expected to enjoy it. “Later” is the word to watch: now, pain; later, fruit, a harvest of righteous character and of peace with God (James 3:18).

Trained by it. The word for an athlete’s training, as in 5:14. The same trouble can leave one person bitter and another gentle, depending on whether it was received as training or merely endured and resented. If you find bitterness in yourself, confess it, and ask God to turn the pain into training.

How can I think of God as a Father if my own father was harsh or absent? Slowly, honestly and with help. This passage admits that earthly fathers fail; God is not a larger version of your father, but the true Father of whom every good human father is a faint copy. Look at the Father revealed in Jesus: the Father who runs to the prodigal (Luke 15:20), who knows what you need before you ask, who gave his Son for you. Let Scripture redefine the word for you, and if the wounds are deep, talk with your pastor and seek out a biblical counsellor. If your father abused you, that was wrong, and God hates it; it was never his discipline.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not give up your inheritance, because you have already come to Mount Zion, and the God who speaks from there is not to be refused. So get up, mend the road for the limping, pursue peace and holiness, and watch that no one falls short of grace or trades the birthright away like Esau (vv. 12–17). You have not come to Sinai, with its fire, darkness and terror (vv. 18–21), but to the heavenly city, with its festival of angels, the assembly of the firstborn, God the judge, and Jesus with his speaking blood (vv. 22–24). So hear him who warns from heaven: everything made will be shaken, but the kingdom you are receiving cannot be, so worship him with grateful awe (vv. 25–29).
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Mountains

Believers have not come to the terrors of Sinai but to Mount Zion, to Jesus and his sprinkled blood (see vv. 22–24). And our God is still a consuming fire (see the note on vv. 28–29).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Esau sold his birthright for a single meal (see vv. 16–17).

Now: Watch for anyone falling short of grace (see v. 15), and ask what you could not bear to lose (see the note on v. 27).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So get up and keep going, and make the road smooth for the weak, so that the struggling are healed and not lost.

Drooping hands and weak knees. “Therefore”: since hardship is God’s loving training, get up. The words are Isaiah’s (Isaiah 35:3), spoken to a weary people waiting for God to act. The picture is a runner whose arms drop and knees buckle near the end: the writer sees his readers not as rebels, but as tired.

Straight paths. From Proverbs 4:26 in the Greek. The image shifts to the road: smooth the way, and live without crooked compromises.

That what is lame may be healed. The road is mended for others. A rough path that a healthy Christian crosses without noticing can turn a struggling one off the road altogether, so the church must consider its limping member when deciding how it walks (10:24). And the note to end on is hope: the lame are not written off but expected to recover.

Because your God will come. Isaiah goes on: the anxious are to be strong, for their God will come and save them, and the lame man shall leap like a deer (Isaiah 35:4–6). When John the Baptist asked from prison whether Jesus was the one to come, Jesus answered from this very chapter: “the lame walk” (Matthew 11:4–5). The one who came is a high priest who sympathises with our weaknesses (4:15), so the limping member is not pushed along by the strong alone. Christ walks the path with him, and has made his church a people who carry one another, so that no limping child of his is left on the way.

What does making straight paths look like in a church? Arranging our common life so that the weakest can keep walking: not flaunting a freedom that will stumble a weaker brother (Romans 14:13–21); living consistently, so that young believers are not confused by the gap between what we say and do; welcoming strugglers instead of making them pretend to be strong; teaching clearly; and helping in concrete ways, a meal, a lift to church, a listening ear. It also means removing obstacles we ourselves put there: gossip, cliques, harshness.

In everyday life. If you are the one limping, do the one small thing this verse asks: lift your hands, in prayer, and take the next step. “He gives power to the faint” (Isaiah 40:29).

verseByVerse.quote: Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pursue peace with everyone and holiness together, for no one will see the Lord without being made holy. Both are chased, never one without the other.

Peace with everyone. “Strive” is the pursuing word: chase it down (Psalm 34:14; Romans 14:19). And “with everyone” is as wide as it sounds, including the neighbours who had plundered their houses, with Paul’s necessary qualification: “If possible, so far as it depends on you” (Romans 12:18).

And for the holiness. Holiness is God’s gift and work in us (v. 10; 10:10, 14), and it too is pursued. Peace pursued alone becomes appeasement, agreeing with anything for the sake of quiet. Holiness pursued alone becomes a withdrawal that treats other people as a source of infection. Much wisdom in church life lies in keeping the two together.

Without which no one will see the Lord. To see the Lord is to enter his presence and enjoy him for ever: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8; 1 John 3:2–3; Revelation 22:4). Read alone, the clause could terrify a believer into thinking his sight of God depends on his own achieved purity.

Status and pursuit. The whole letter forbids that reading. “By a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (10:14): Christ has settled our standing. Nobody will see the Lord who has not been made holy by Christ, and nobody made holy by Christ will fail to pursue holiness; the pursuit is the evidence (3:6, 14). Holiness is the fruit, not the root, of salvation, and at death believers are made perfect in it (12:23).

How holy do I have to be to see the Lord? As holy as Christ, and in him you already are: your right to see God rests on his righteousness counted to you and his blood that cleanses you. The proof that you belong to him is not that you have arrived but that you are pursuing. Do I want to be holy? Do I hate my sin and fight it? Am I, over the years, being changed? Then you are on the road, however slowly, and on the last day you will see him and be like him.

How do I pursue holiness? Begin where the letter begins: you chase holiness because it is already yours in Christ (10:14), not to win his acceptance, and that frees you to be honest about how far you still have to go. Then a few ordinary steps. Name it. Holiness is never pursued in general; ask which sin you have quietly made peace with, and call it what God calls it. Cut the supply lines. “Make no provision for the flesh” (Romans 13:14): the website, the route home, the late-evening habit that feeds it. Feed on Christ. Sin loses its pull as something better fills the heart, so keep looking to Jesus (12:2) in his word, in prayer and at his Table. Do not run alone. “Exhort one another every day” (3:13): tell one trusted believer the truth and let them ask you about it. Get up quickly. When you fall, go straight back to the throne of grace (4:16) without first serving a sentence. The Father disciplines us “that we may share his holiness” (12:10), and he will finish what he has begun.

Must I make peace with someone who keeps hurting me? You must be willing for peace and do what is in your power: forgive in your heart, refuse revenge, speak the truth kindly, and seek reconciliation where it is safe and possible (Matthew 5:23–24; Romans 12:17–21). But peace with everyone does not mean pretending wrong is right, or putting yourself or others in danger. Reconciliation needs repentance, and where someone is abusive or unrepentant, you may and sometimes must keep your distance while still wishing them good and praying for them. Neither holiness nor peace requires you to stay under abuse.

In everyday life. Peace and holiness are usually lost in small places: the message left unanswered because silence was easier, the habit you stopped fighting because it seemed too small to matter. The verb is chase, and nobody catches anything standing still. If a sin you have made terms with still troubles you, that trouble is the Spirit keeping you in the race.

verseByVerse.quote: See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God; that no “root of bitterness” springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watch over one another, so that no one drifts back from God’s grace and no bitter, turned-away heart takes root and poisons the church.

See to it. The verb “to oversee”, addressed to the whole congregation, not only its leaders. “Fails to obtain” is to lag behind and miss it, as in 4:1. God’s grace is not insufficient; the danger is falling back before reaching it.

A root of bitterness. The phrase is from Deuteronomy 29:18, where Moses warns against anyone whose heart turns from the LORD to other gods: “Beware lest there be among you a root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit.” So it is first about what one turned-away heart does to a community, and only then, fairly, about private resentment.

Many become defiled. A root is established underground before anything shows. Then it sprouts and causes trouble, and many are defiled, because the damage never stays with one person. A bitter grievance that seems reasonable gathers sympathisers, and people who never went looking for a quarrel catch it. That is why the whole congregation watches early.

The grace that tasted death. Grace in this letter has a cross in it. By the grace of God Jesus tasted death for everyone (2:9), and because of him believers may draw near to the throne of grace to receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need (4:16). To fall short of the grace of God is to drift back from Christ himself and from the open throne he secured.

How do I know if bitterness is taking root in me? You replay the hurt; you rehearse speeches you will never give; you tell others about it to gather sympathy; you cannot hear the person’s name without a tightening inside; you begin to resent God for allowing it. Those are roots surfacing. Bring the hurt to God honestly; forgive as you have been forgiven (Ephesians 4:31–32), releasing the debt to God even when feelings lag behind; and where possible speak to the person rather than about them. Bitterness grows in the dark; take it into the light.

How should I watch over others without becoming a busybody? By caring, not policing: noticing who is missing, asking how someone really is, praying for them, and speaking gently when you see someone drifting or bitter (Galatians 6:1). Not gossip, suspicion or checking up on private lives. If you are concerned about someone, go to them, not to others about them. And let others watch over you: the person who receives loving correction gratefully is the one best placed to give it.

verseByVerse.quote: that no one is sexually immoral or unholy like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal. For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be like Esau, who traded what God had promised for a single meal; some losses cannot be undone, however bitterly they are regretted.

Sexually immoral or unholy like Esau. Two dangers: sexual immorality, and the godlessness of a man like Esau (on whether the first word also describes him, see below). Esau is not a monster but a man who was hungry. “Unholy” is profane, godless: someone for whom nothing is sacred, not because he sets out to be wicked, but because he cannot see why anything should be.

A single meal. The birthright was the rights of the firstborn: a double inheritance, leadership of the family, and in this family a share in the promise made to Abraham (Genesis 25:29–34). Esau traded it for a bowl of stew. “He ate and drank and rose and went his way. Thus Esau despised his birthright” (Genesis 25:34). He was hungry now, and a birthright was a thing you could not eat.

Drift with a price tag on it. Nobody was asking these readers to renounce Christ in a formal ceremony. They were being offered relief, property restored, neighbours placated, an end to the shame, in exchange for something that could not be seen or eaten. That is Esau’s trade: the unseen inheritance sold for relief now.

He was rejected. Later Esau wanted the blessing back but could not have it (Genesis 27:30–40). “He found no chance to repent” is a distressing sentence, to be read exactly. It does not say Esau repented and was refused forgiveness, which would contradict everything Scripture says about God. He wept for the inheritance he had thrown away, but there is no record that he ever regretted the contempt for God’s promise that made him throw it away. Some decisions cannot be unmade, and grief afterwards does not restore what was sold. That is the warning, and it is a mercy that it comes while there is still time. Esau found no place for repentance; at the throne of grace, no sinner who comes in the Son’s name is ever turned away.

One meal, or the joy set before him. The Greek sets Esau beside someone else in this chapter. Esau sold his birthright for (anti) a single meal; Jesus, for (anti) the joy that was set before him, endured the cross (v. 2). Esau gave up the future for the present because he was hungry now; Jesus gave up the present, its comfort, honour and life, for the joy ahead. Every temptation to trade the inheritance for relief is a choice between Esau’s bowl and Christ’s cross, and he “always lives to make intercession” for those tempted to sell (7:25).

Restored at a cross. Esau held the birthright cheap. God’s own Firstborn (1:6), the heir of all things (1:2), went to the cross to share his inheritance with people who had sold theirs for less than a meal. Now the church is “the assembly of the firstborn” (12:23), and what was thrown away at a cooking pot is restored at a cross.

Is it too late for me, as it was for Esau, if I have made choices I deeply regret? If you are grieving over your sin and turning to Christ, no. That you are sorry for the sin itself, and not only for its consequences, shows that you are not where Esau was. Some consequences may remain, a marriage ended, health damaged, years lost, but God’s forgiveness is never closed to the one who comes through Christ, and he is skilled at bringing good out of ruined things (Joel 2:25). Do not let Esau’s story frighten you away from God; let it send you to him now, while it is called today.

Why does Scripture put sexual sin next to Esau’s godlessness? Because both trade something holy for a momentary appetite. Sexual immorality treats as common a gift God made sacred, the union of husband and wife: Esau’s contempt for holy things again. And it is often how drift happens: not by argument, but by appetite. If you are struggling here, do not hide it. Confess it to God, tell a trusted believer, put practical barriers in place, and remember that Christ’s blood cleanses sexual sin as fully as any other (1 Corinthians 6:9–11).

Uncertain wording. Two things are uncertain. First, whether “sexually immoral” describes Esau. Genesis does not say so, though his marriages to two Hittite women grieved his parents (Genesis 26:34–35), and some later Jewish writings did describe him that way. More likely only “unholy” describes Esau, and the sentence names two separate dangers. Second, “no chance to repent” is literally “no place for repentance” (metanoias topon ouch heuren). It may mean that Esau could not change his father Isaac’s mind, because the blessing once given could not be taken back (Genesis 27:33), or that Esau himself could not find genuine repentance, because his tears were for the lost blessing, not for his sin. The “it” he sought with tears is probably the blessing (Genesis 27:34, 38). Either way, what he had despised could not be recovered.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have not come to what may be touched, a blazing fire and darkness and gloom and a tempest and the sound of a trumpet and a voice whose words made the hearers beg that no further messages be spoken to them. For they could not endure the order that was given, “If even a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.” Indeed, so terrifying was the sight that Moses said, “I tremble with fear.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have not come to Sinai, where God’s holiness kept terrified sinners at a distance. The writer recalls its terror so that the welcome of Zion can be seen for what it is.

What may be touched. The “For” ties this to the warning about Esau: do not sell your birthright, because of where you now stand. Verses 18–24 turn chapters 8–10 into two pictures, Sinai and Zion. “Come” is the letter’s verb for drawing near to God (4:16; 7:25; 10:22), and the first word about Sinai is the one thing nobody was allowed to do: touch it. The boundary was set, and the penalty was death.

Fire and darkness. Sinai at the giving of the law (Exodus 19:16–19; 20:18–21; Deuteronomy 4:11–12; 5:22–26): seven terrifying features, deliberately disorienting, fire that gives no light, darkness with a storm in it.

A voice they begged to stop. They said to Moses: “You speak to us, and we will listen; but do not let God speak to us, lest we die” (Exodus 20:19; Deuteronomy 5:25–27). Offered the direct voice of God, a nation asked for a go-between, more out of terror than reverence, and yet they were not wrong to ask.

If even a beast touches the mountain. From Exodus 19:12–13. Even an ox that wandered across a line it could not understand was killed.

I tremble with fear. Exodus does not record these words at the giving of the law; the writer draws on Deuteronomy 9:19, where Moses recalls his fear of God’s anger after the golden calf, at the same mountain. If the mediator who spoke with God face to face was shaking, what was it like at the bottom?

The request God answered with a Prophet. The LORD said they were right, and promised, “I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. And I will put my words in his mouth” (Deuteronomy 18:16–18). Peter announced that this Prophet had come in Jesus (Acts 3:22). God gave them the mediator they asked for, and far more: not another trembling Moses, but his own Son, who speaks God’s words without fear because he is “the radiance of the glory of God” (1:3).

What it does not mean. The God of Sinai is not a different God from the God of the gospel; he is the same holy God (v. 29). The difference is the covenant: at Sinai sinful people met God’s holiness without a perfect mediator; in Christ they meet the same God through the blood that brings peace.

Why did God make Sinai so terrifying? To show what his holiness means for sinners who approach him without a perfect mediator. The fire, the darkness and the boundary were not cruelty but truth: sin cannot stand in the presence of a holy God, and Israel needed to learn it to understand why a sacrifice and a priest were needed. Without Sinai we would think God easy to approach; with it we see what Christ has done in bringing us near.

verseByVerse.quote: But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable angels in festal gathering, and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and to God, the judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have already come, by faith, to the joyful city of the living God, and you stand there welcomed, not kept at a distance. Each phrase names someone you now stand among, and the list ends with the one who brought you there.

But you have come to Mount Zion. The astonishing thing is the tense: they have arrived already, by faith, above all when they gather for worship. Sitting in an ordinary room in a hostile city, they are told where they actually are. Zion was the hill of Jerusalem where God dwelt in the temple, the sign of his presence and kingship (Psalm 2:6; 48:1–2).

The heavenly Jerusalem. The city with foundations that Abraham was looking for (11:10, 16). “The Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (Galatians 4:26; Revelation 21:2). He never reached it. They have.

Angels in festal gathering. A festival crowd, like the one John hears around the throne (Revelation 5:11). At Sinai the angels attended the giving of the law amid fire and fear (Deuteronomy 33:2; Acts 7:53); here they keep festival.

The assembly of the firstborn. The “assembly” is the church, and every member is a firstborn (the word is plural): everyone has the birthright, sharing the privileges of the firstborn Son as heirs (Romans 8:29), which lands with some force a few verses after Esau, who sold his. Their names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20; Philippians 4:3; Revelation 21:27). That frees the heart from a quiet tyranny. Many of us live for a name written somewhere: on an office door, in other people’s good opinion. The one whose name is written in heaven no longer needs it written anywhere else.

God, the judge of all. The title is not softened: he is still the judge, even in the festal gathering. But we come to him through Jesus (v. 24), and the festival rejoices because his justice has been fully satisfied in Christ, so that the holy God can welcome sinners without ceasing to be holy (Romans 3:26).

The spirits of the righteous made perfect. Believers who have died, the people of chapter 11 among them, consciously alive in God’s presence and free from sin as they await the resurrection of their bodies. “Made perfect”: brought to the goal at last, as 11:40 promised, and not apart from us.

Jesus, the mediator. The climax: Jesus himself. A mediator brings two estranged parties together and guarantees the agreement. The new covenant is the one God promised through Jeremiah: “I will put my laws into their minds” and “I will remember their sins no more” (8:10, 12; Jeremiah 31:31–34). Jesus guarantees it with his own blood, and so it cannot fail. At Sinai the people begged for a mediator and got a frightened one; at Zion they have a mediator who is not afraid of God, because he is God’s Son, and not distant from them, because he is their brother.

A better word than the blood of Abel. The “sprinkled blood” is Christ’s blood, which cleanses (9:13–14, 19–22; 10:22). Abel’s blood cried from the ground for justice (Genesis 4:10; Hebrews 11:4). This blood speaks too, and says something better: it pleads mercy even for those who shed it. It cries out for his brothers; its word is mercy, and the Judge of all hears it and is satisfied.

Not by climbing. Set the two mountains side by side. There: fire, darkness, a boundary, and a voice people begged to stop. Here: a city, a festival, a family of firstborn sons, and blood that speaks in your favour. And the readers were considering going back to the first. We have been brought into the city, and not by climbing: Jesus went ahead of us as a forerunner (6:20) and brought his brothers in after him. The Judge of all looks at that assembly and sees every one of his firstborn, washed and welcomed.

Why does Sunday worship feel so ordinary if this is where we are? Because we see with our eyes, and these verses describe what is true by faith. The building may be plain, the singing thin, the sermon unremarkable; still, whenever God’s people gather in Christ’s name, they are joined to the worship of angels and of the saints in glory, before the Judge of all, through Jesus. It was true of a house church in a hostile city, and it is true of yours. Come to worship expecting to meet God, not to be entertained, and ask the Spirit to open your eyes to where you really are.

In everyday life. When you think of believing loved ones who have died, remember that they are in the same assembly you join every Sunday. Grieve, but grieve as one who belongs to the same gathering.

Where Christians differ: do the dead sleep until the resurrection? Some Christians hold that at death the whole person rests, unconscious, until the resurrection (often called soul sleep), pointing to Scripture’s frequent description of death as sleep (1 Thessalonians 4:13). This commentary’s view: no; “sleep” describes how death looks from this side, and the spirits of the righteous made perfect are already present in the heavenly assembly, consciously with Christ while they await the resurrection of their bodies (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23).
verseByVerse.note: Abel’s blood cried out for justice; Jesus’ blood speaks of pardon.

verseByVerse.quote: See that you do not refuse him who is speaking. For if they did not escape when they refused him who warned them on earth, much less will we escape if we reject him who warns from heaven. At that time his voice shook the earth, but now he has promised, “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not refuse the God who is speaking to you now from heaven; if refusing his word at Sinai was fatal, refusing it now is more serious still.

Him who is speaking. Present tense: not him who spoke, but God, who speaks now through his Son (1:1–2), through the sprinkled blood (v. 24), and in Scripture (3:7; 12:5). “Refuse” is to beg off, to ask to be excused, the word used in verse 19 of the people at Sinai begging that no further message be spoken.

Declining without disputing. Nobody at Sinai denied that God was speaking. They simply asked him to stop, because hearing him was unbearable. You can own a Bible, agree with every line, and quietly arrange your life so that it never actually speaks to you. And if you fear you have been doing this, the fear itself shows you are still listening; the voice that warns is the voice that invites.

Him who warns from heaven. At Sinai God warned them on earth, through Moses, and those who rejected him perished in the wilderness (3:16–19). Now, from lesser to greater as at 2:2–3 and 10:28–29, he speaks from heaven through his exalted Son. This is the last of the letter’s five warning passages (2:1–4; 3:7–4:13; 5:11–6:12; 10:26–39; 12:25–29), and they all say one thing: do not drift away from the Son through whom God has spoken. His warnings are mercies, and the one who speaks from heaven is the one who gave himself for us.

Yet once more. At Sinai “the whole mountain trembled greatly” (Exodus 19:18; Psalm 68:8). The quotation is Haggai 2:6, spoken to men rebuilding a modest temple after the exile and grieving over how small it was; there God promised to shake the nations and fill his house with glory. The writer sees its final fulfilment in the last great shaking at Christ’s return (2 Peter 3:10–13): the first shaking rattled a mountain; the second takes in the heavens. And it is called a promise, not a threat, which tells you on which side of it the writer expects his readers to stand.

When is this final shaking? At Christ’s return, when the present heavens and earth give way to “new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells” (2 Peter 3:13). Some apply it to the end of the old covenant order in AD 70, when the temple was destroyed; that was a foretaste, but a shaking of heaven as well as earth looks to the end. Meanwhile the kingdom that cannot be shaken is already ours (v. 28).

What it does not mean. Not that God speaks new revelation from heaven today. He speaks through his Son, whose word is recorded in Scripture, and to refuse Scripture is to refuse him. This commentary holds that, with the Son’s word delivered through those who heard him (1:1–2; 2:3–4), revelation of that kind is complete; Christians who believe God still gives prophetic words usually agree that nothing they hear may add to Scripture or overrule it, and that is the point that matters here.

How might I be refusing God without realising it? By hearing without heeding: applying sermons to other people; reading the Bible for information but never asking what it requires of me; skipping the passages that make me uncomfortable; filling every quiet moment so that there is no room to listen; agreeing with a command but postponing obedience indefinitely. None is open rebellion; all are ways of begging God to stop speaking. The remedy is simple, and hard: when God’s word touches something in your life, respond that day, in some concrete way.

verseByVerse.quote: This phrase, “Yet once more,” indicates the removal of things that are shaken—that is, things that have been made—in order that the things that cannot be shaken may remain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s final shaking will remove everything created and passing, so that only what cannot be shaken remains. It is a sifting, not mere destruction.

This phrase. The writer argues from two small words, as he did from “new” in 8:13. “Once” (hapax) is the word used of Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice (9:26–28): “yet once more” implies a last time, and a last shaking implies that whatever survives it is permanent.

The removal of things that are shaken. “Removal” is the word used of the change of priesthood (7:12). What goes is created things, everything belonging to this passing age, including the temple these readers were probably being drawn back to.

That the things that cannot be shaken may remain. The shaking leaves standing what was always going to stand: God, his Christ, his people, his word (Isaiah 40:8; 1 Peter 1:23–25), and the new creation. These readers had already been through a small version of it: their property had been shaken out of their hands (10:34), and they found they still had “a better possession and an abiding one”. If everything that can be shaken will be, you can find out in advance what your life is built on, by noticing what you cannot bear to lose.

The one who remains. What survives is anchored in the Son. Hebrews has already applied the Psalm to him: the heavens “will perish, but you remain; they will all wear out like a garment” (1:10–12), and the letter will end, “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (13:8). Whatever belongs to him, his people, his word and his kingdom, stands on the side of what remains. The God who shakes is also the God who holds, and those built on Christ will be left standing when the dust clears, in a new creation where nothing ever falls again.

An age that shakes everything. In 1848 Marx and Engels described modern society in a famous line: “All that is solid melts into air.” It has proved truer than they knew: jobs, marriages, institutions, even our sense of what a man or a woman is, almost nothing we were handed feels fixed. So modern life swings between anxiety, clutching at whatever still seems firm, and a weary irony that trusts nothing at all. Hebrews does not deny the shaking; it says God is doing it, more thoroughly than any revolution. But it names what cannot be shaken, and it is not something we build. When Jesus died, “the earth shook, and the rocks were split” (Matthew 27:51), and the one shaken to death in our place rose to a life no shaking can reach. Those who stand on him do not need the world to stand still.

Will the things I love on earth be lost? Everything belonging to the old order of sin and decay will go. But the new creation is this creation renewed, not abandoned: God is not a wasteful builder. Labour in the Lord is “not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58), believers who have died will be raised in bodies, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into the city (Revelation 21:24). We do not know every detail, and should not pretend to. But what you love rightly, in God, you will not finally lose; you will find it again, purified, in him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and thus let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we are receiving a kingdom no shaking can touch, worship God with thankful awe, for the God who welcomes us is still a holy fire.

A kingdom that cannot be shaken. The response commanded is gratitude, not what we might expect in a passage that ends with a consuming fire (on the wording, see below). “Receiving” is present tense. It is God’s eternal kingdom, promised in Daniel, where “the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom” (Daniel 7:14, 18, 27). Christ reigns now, and his kingdom grows through the gospel until it is revealed in fullness at his return (9:28).

Acceptable worship. A priest’s service, now offered by the whole congregation: a whole life of worship (Romans 12:1), expressed especially in praise and good works (13:15–16).

With reverence and awe. “Reverence” is godly fear, the word used of Jesus in 5:7. The letter has spent twelve chapters removing the barriers, opening the curtain and telling frightened people to come boldly, and it will not let that boldness (4:16) slide into familiarity.

A consuming fire. The chapter ends with Deuteronomy 4:24. Having contrasted Sinai’s blazing fire with the festival of Zion, it says the God of Zion is the same God, and still a fire. What has changed is our access: we now have the blood, the opened curtain and the priest. Anyone who concludes from the open way that God has become easy to handle has misunderstood it. For those outside Christ he is a consuming fire of judgment (10:27); for those in Christ his fire purifies (1 Corinthians 3:13–15; Malachi 3:2–3). And he is “our God”: the fire is ours, a frightening sentence or a deeply comforting one, depending on which mountain you have come to.

The kingdom given to the Son of Man. Daniel saw the kingdom given first to “one like a son of man” (Daniel 7:13–14), and then to the saints of the Most High. Jesus took that title as his own, and Hebrews shows him crowned with glory and honour, seated and waiting until his enemies are made a footstool for his feet (2:9; 10:12–13). So the kingdom we are receiving is his reign, shared with those who belong to him, and nothing can shake it, because to shake it you would have to unseat him. We did not build it, and we cannot lose it. And its King is a consuming fire, holy beyond our thought, who nevertheless lets us call him ours.

What does reverence look like in worship today? A matter of the heart, not of style: coming prepared rather than distracted; singing words you mean; hearing God’s word as God’s word; confessing sin honestly; taking the Lord’s Supper soberly. Reverence can be joyful and loud, as the Psalms are, or quiet, in a cathedral or a front room. What it is never is casual, as if God were a friend we could take or leave, or a performance we have come to judge. Come gladly, and come awed.

How can God be both a consuming fire and my loving Father? Because in Christ the fire has already fallen. God’s holiness is unchanged, a fire against sin; but for those in Christ the judgment sin deserves was borne by him at the cross, and the fire burned there, on him. What remains is the same holy God, now our Father, whose fire refines rather than destroys, burning away what is unworthy in us so that we may share his holiness (12:10). The sun that would scorch a man without shelter warms one who lives in its light. Fear him rightly, and you will find there is nothing to fear in him.

In everyday life. When you are tempted to grumble, say what you are receiving instead. A grateful person is hard to shake.

Uncertain wording. “Let us be grateful” is literally “let us have grace”, a common Greek expression for giving thanks, though some take it as “let us hold on to grace”. Thanks is the likely sense, the natural answer to a gift received, and the two belong together: grace received produces thanks, and giving thanks is how we keep hold of grace.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight, and sin which clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us,<sup>2</sup>looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God.<sup>3</sup>Consider him who endured from sinners such hostility against himself, so that you may not grow weary or fainthearted.<sup>4</sup>In your struggle against sin you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood.<sup>5</sup>And have you forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons? “My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when reproved by him.<sup>6</sup>For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives.”<sup>7</sup>It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline?<sup>8</sup>If you are left without discipline, in which all have participated, then you are illegitimate children and not sons.<sup>9</sup>Besides this, we have had earthly fathers who disciplined us and we respected them. Shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live?<sup>10</sup>For they disciplined us for a short time as it seemed best to them, but he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness.<sup>11</sup>For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.<sup>12</sup>Therefore lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees,<sup>13</sup>and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed.<sup>14</sup>Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord.<sup>15</sup>See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God; that no “root of bitterness” springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled;<sup>16</sup>that no one is sexually immoral or unholy like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal.<sup>17</sup>For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears.<sup>18</sup>For you have not come to what may be touched, a blazing fire and darkness and gloom and a tempest<sup>19</sup>and the sound of a trumpet and a voice whose words made the hearers beg that no further messages be spoken to them.<sup>20</sup>For they could not endure the order that was given, “If even a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.”<sup>21</sup>Indeed, so terrifying was the sight that Moses said, “I tremble with fear.”<sup>22</sup>But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable angels in festal gathering,<sup>23</sup>and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and to God, the judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect,<sup>24</sup>and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.<sup>25</sup>See that you do not refuse him who is speaking. For if they did not escape when they refused him who warned them on earth, much less will we escape if we reject him who warns from heaven.<sup>26</sup>At that time his voice shook the earth, but now he has promised, “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens.”<sup>27</sup>This phrase, “Yet once more,” indicates the removal of things that are shaken—that is, things that have been made—in order that the things that cannot be shaken may remain.<sup>28</sup>Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and thus let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe,<sup>29</sup>for our God is a consuming fire.

keyVerse.quote: looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God.
keyVerse.note: Everything else in the chapter, the race, the discipline, the two mountains, depends on where the runner is looking. This verse names the one place: Jesus, who began our faith and will finish it, who ran the hardest course of all for the joy ahead, and who now sits at the finish line. Tired believers are not given a technique but a person to look at.

12.reflection:
Verse 1 distinguishes weights, which may not be sinful, from sin that entangles. What are the weights in your life that slow you down in following Christ, and what would it mean to lay them aside?

Verses 5–11 teach the readers to see their hardships as a Father’s training rather than a sign that he has left them. How does this change the way you read a present difficulty? What is the difference between this and claiming that every trouble is a punishment for a particular sin?

Esau sold the unseen inheritance for relief now (vv. 16–17). In what ordinary ways are Christians tempted to make the same trade today, and how does Jesus, who endured the cross “for the joy that was set before him” (v. 2), answer that temptation?

Verses 22–24 describe where believers already stand when they gather for worship. If we really believed this, how would it change the way we come to church on Sunday, and the way we think of believers who have died?

13.title: Outside the Camp: The Unchanging Christ
13.overview:
Where we are. The sermon reached its summit at Mount Zion and the kingdom that cannot be shaken (12:22–29). Chapter 13 brings that kingdom down into ordinary streets, and then closes the letter with a benediction and greetings.

The message. People who have come to Mount Zion live differently here, in love, purity and contentment, and they can, because Jesus Christ does not change. So do not chase new teachings or creep back into the camp of the old worship for shelter. Go out to Jesus, who suffered outside the gate, carry his disgrace, and offer the sacrifices that please God now, praise and kindness. The God who raised the great Shepherd will work in you what he asks.

Why it was said. The readers had paid for their faith before (10:32–34) and were tired; their first leaders had died, teachings about food were going round, and the old faith offered a respectable home and Rome’s tolerance (see the introduction). The pull backwards was not toward vice but toward belonging.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–6: love that continues, for brothers, strangers and prisoners, in marriage and over money, resting on God’s promise never to leave. Verses 7–9: the leaders finished well and Christ is the same for ever, so teachings about food add nothing to grace. Verses 10–14, the last appeal: Christ was put outside the gate like the Day of Atonement sin offering, so go out to him, since no city here lasts. Verses 15–19: the sacrifices of praise and sharing, and a church that follows its leaders and prays for them. Verses 20–25: a benediction that gathers up the whole letter, then news, greetings and grace.

Where it leads. Two things are said of Jesus. He “is the same yesterday and today and forever” (v. 8): leaders die and cities fall, and he remains. And he “suffered outside the gate” (v. 12): the unchanging Lord of glory went to the place of the unclean to make his people holy, so the way out of the camp is the way to him. The letter ends with him as “the great shepherd of the sheep”, brought back from the dead (v. 20), and with grace.

For us. Where are you staying inside some camp for safety: a respectable silence, a comfortable belonging, rules that feel steadier than grace? Christ is outside it. Go out to him, and let the proof be ordinary: a spare bed, a letter to a prisoner, a faithful marriage, an open hand and a song.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Life in the unshakeable kingdom shows itself in love that keeps going and a heart content with God. Family love among believers must not fade (v. 1), and it widens into welcome for strangers (v. 2) and into fellow feeling with prisoners and the mistreated, whose chains believers are to feel as their own (v. 3). Marriage is to be honoured by everyone and kept pure, for God judges (v. 4). And money is to lose its grip, because God has promised himself: he will never leave, so what can man do (vv. 5–6)?
verseByVerse.theology:
Where the Argument Lands

The letter's theology ends in hospitality, prison visiting, marriage and money (see the note on vv. 1–2). Contentment rests on a promise: “I will never leave you nor forsake you.”
verseByVerse.examples:
