Then: Visiting prisoners marked a believer out publicly (see the note on v. 3).

Now: Keep loving, keep welcoming, keep remembering those in prison as though in prison with them.

verseByVerse.quote: Let brotherly love continue. Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep loving one another as family, and widen that love into welcome for strangers. After twelve chapters inside the sanctuary the letter walks out into the street, where the worship of the heavenly Zion looks like a spare bed and an open door.

Let brotherly love continue. Love of brothers and sisters (philadelphia) is family affection, and the verb is continue, remain: the love is already there. The writer is not telling a cold congregation to start loving but a tired one not to let go. They had served the saints, visited prisoners and shared each other’s losses (6:10; 10:33–34). What was failing was not their love but their stamina.

Hospitality to strangers. Love of strangers is one word in Greek (philoxenia), set beside philadelphia: family affection is to widen into welcome for people you do not know. Inns were often dirty and immoral, and the travelling teachers, missionaries and refugees of a persecuted movement depended on believers’ homes (3 John 5–8). Hospitality was not a pleasant extra; the church’s mission could not travel without it. And opening your house to an unknown Christian in a city that was confiscating Christian property had consequences.

Angels unawares. The reference is Abraham at Mamre, running out to three travellers in the heat of the day and hurrying to feed them (Genesis 18:1–8), and Lot at Sodom (Genesis 19:1–3). “Unawares” is the point: the writer does not promise angels, but says that some who opened their doors found later that they had done something far larger than they knew.

The brother at the table. Both loves rest on Christ. The church is a family because the Son took our flesh and blood and is not ashamed to call us brothers (2:11, 14); the affection we owe one another is his, continuing in us. And the welcome of strangers has a hidden guest greater than any angel: “I was a stranger and you welcomed me” (Matthew 25:35, 40). Christ came to his world as a stranger and was given no room; now he is the one who will welcome us home, to a house with many rooms. The Christian who pours tea for a tired traveller is serving the King without knowing it.

What it does not mean. Not that angels regularly come to our doors in disguise, and not that hospitality requires naivety: wisdom in protecting one’s household, especially children, is still needed.

How can I show hospitality if I am not a good host and my home is small? Hospitality is not entertaining; it is welcome. It needs no large house or good cooking, only an open door: soup at the kitchen table, a sofa for a night, Sunday lunch for the person sitting alone at church, or coffee out if your home is not suitable. Strangers become guests, guests become family, and Christ is welcomed in them.

In everyday life. Think of one brother or sister in your church with whom love has cooled, through a disagreement, a slight or simple neglect, and send them a message today.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham, Lot and others welcomed angels without first knowing who they were.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember those who are in prison, as though in prison with them, and those who are mistreated, since you also are in the body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stand by believers in prison and those who are mistreated as though their suffering were your own. You live in a body that can be chained and hurt just as theirs is.

Remember those in prison. “Remember” means keep in mind and act on it. Roman prisons gave inmates little or nothing, and a prisoner without visitors bringing food and clothing simply deteriorated. Remembering meant a basket of bread carried through a door the whole street could see you entering, identifying you publicly with the prisoner’s offence. These readers had done it before, when it was dangerous (10:34).

As though in prison with them. Literally bound together with them: not kindly from a safe distance, but as if you were in the cell yourself. A frightened community’s instinct is the opposite, to keep its distance from the members who have been arrested.

Those who are mistreated. Ill-treated, tortured: the word of 11:25 and 11:37, of Moses and the prophets. The persecuted of the present stand in the company of the heroes of chapter 11.

The prisoner who sympathises. This is what the Son of God did for us. He did not pity us from heaven; he took our flesh and blood (2:14), and was himself arrested, bound, beaten and mocked, a High Priest able to sympathise with our weaknesses (4:15). To feel another’s chains as your own is to have his mind. He still feels them. When Saul struck the church, the risen Lord asked, “why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). His suffering people’s chains are his.

What it does not mean. It does not limit care to Christian prisoners, though they are the focus. Compassion for all who suffer, including those imprisoned for real crimes, reflects Christ’s heart: “I was in prison and you came to me” (Matthew 25:36).

How can I remember prisoners when I do not know any? Start by finding out. Several organisations publish the names and stories of Christians imprisoned for their faith, with addresses for letters and guidance for prayer; choose one person and pray for them by name each week. Nearer home, prison chaplaincies and fellowships welcome volunteers and letter-writers, and prisoners’ families often need practical help. Remembering begins with knowing one name.

In everyday life. Think of anyone in your church whose suffering isolates them, a carer, a long illness, a believer cut off by family, and do one concrete thing for them this week.

Uncertain wording. “In the body” could mean the body of Christ, in which what happens to one member happens to all (1 Corinthians 12:26). More probably it means a physical body: you have a body like theirs, which can be hurt and chained. Either way, a Christian who imagines it could never happen to him is not merely unkind but mistaken.

verseByVerse.quote: Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone is to honour marriage and keep sex within it, because God himself judges sexual sin. The verse answers two opposite errors at once: despising marriage, and treating it as no barrier to anything one wants.

Marriage held in honor. “Honor” is precious, valued, and “among all” means by everybody, the single included. Marriage is God’s good gift from creation (Genesis 2:18–25). Some in the ancient world despised it as a hindrance to the spiritual life (1 Timothy 4:3); others, shaped by pagan culture, let it restrain nothing. “Marriage bed” is a polite way of speaking of sexual union, and “undefiled” is pure, unstained, the word used of Christ himself in 7:26.

What does undefiled require? Faithfulness. Sex belongs to one man and one woman within marriage and nowhere else: not in adultery, not in pornography, not in the lustful look Jesus called adultery of the heart (Matthew 5:28). Within marriage Scripture is glad and generous (Proverbs 5:18–19; the Song of Songs), and calls husband and wife to give themselves to each other freely (1 Corinthians 7:3–5). It gives no list of acts, but principles: faithfulness, mutual consent, love and care, and nothing that degrades or harms.

God will judge. The reason given is the striking part. Not that adultery damages people, though it does, nor that it is socially destructive, though it is: God will judge (1 Corinthians 6:9–10). He will judge it whether or not the wronged husband or wife ever finds out.

Pressure does not exempt. The writer sets sexual sin without comment among prison visits and hospitality. Pressure exempts nobody from ordinary temptations and often increases them: frightened, exhausted people reach for comfort.

A living picture of Christ and his church. The deepest reason to honour marriage is that God made it to show something. Paul quotes “the two shall become one flesh” and says that this mystery refers to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32). Christ is the Bridegroom who loved his bride and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25), and he has never once been unfaithful to her. So adultery breaks a promise and also tells a lie about him; and a faithful marriage, through ordinary years, is a quiet sermon on the faithfulness of Jesus.

What it does not mean. It does not mean single people are less honourable. Singleness is also a good gift (1 Corinthians 7:7–8), and the Lord Jesus himself was single. Nor does honouring marriage mean that anyone must stay in a home where they are being abused; abuse dishonours marriage, and the victim should be protected and helped.

Can I still honour marriage if I have fallen sexually in the past? Yes, and do not let shame tell you otherwise. If you have confessed your sin and turned to Christ, you are washed, sanctified and justified in his name (1 Corinthians 6:11), and God does not hold it against you. Honouring marriage now means guarding your present purity, speaking well of marriage, and, if you marry, giving yourself wholly to your spouse. There may be consequences to face or things to tell a future spouse honestly, and a pastor’s wise help is worth seeking. But your past is not the final word about you; Christ’s blood is.

Is the Bible’s sexual ethic not simply repressive? Not in a verse that begins by calling the marriage bed honourable: Scripture is not embarrassed by sex, and calls it good. The boundary is like the banks of a river, which do not stop the water but give it depth and direction. A love that makes and keeps a lifelong promise is not less free than one that keeps its options open; it is the only kind that can bear the full weight of trust, and the kind Christ has shown his bride, whom he will never leave for another.

In everyday life. If married, do one thing this week to honour your spouse: a word of thanks, an evening protected for each other, a filter put on a device. If you are struggling with sexual sin, tell one trusted Christian this week. Secrecy is where it grows.

Where Christians differ: what counts as marriage, and how should the church respond to sexual sin? Some Christians today accept sexual relationships outside marriage, or marriages other than between a man and a woman. This commentary’s view: Scripture consistently teaches that sexual union is reserved for the lifelong covenant of marriage between one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6). Jesus grounded marriage in creation, male and female joined as one flesh, and Paul sees in that union a picture of Christ and his church (Ephesians 5:31–32); the church did not invent this pattern and cannot redraw it, however sincerely others see it differently. All sexual activity outside marriage is sin. This is held with compassion: many struggle in this area, and the gospel offers full forgiveness and cleansing to all who repent (1 Corinthians 6:11). The church must uphold the standard and extend grace together.

verseByVerse.quote: Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, “I will never leave you nor forsake you.” So we can confidently say, “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear; what can man do to me?”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let money lose its grip on you, because God has promised you himself, and with him beside you no one can finally harm you.

Free from love of money. Literally “not silver-loving”. Money is not evil, but the love of it is a root of all kinds of evils (1 Timothy 6:10). The words had a sting for people who had watched their property carried out of their houses (10:34): years later the loss was presumably felt more keenly, and going back to the old ways might have won some of it back.

Content with what you have. Satisfied, having enough (Philippians 4:11; 1 Timothy 6:8). The cure for wanting more is not having more.

I will never leave you. “He” is emphatic: God himself. The words are God’s to Joshua at the border of the land (Joshua 1:5), and behind that to Israel through Moses (Deuteronomy 31:6, 8). The Greek piles up five negatives in a way English cannot reproduce: never, not ever, will I let you go; never, no never, will I forsake you. He promises not the return of their property, but himself. Money, health and in the end everything we have will leave us. He will not.

The Lord is my helper; I will not fear; what can man do to me? From Psalm 118:6. “Helper” is one who runs to another’s aid, the word used in 2:18 of Christ helping the tempted. The question is defiant, not naive. Man can do a great deal, and these people had the empty houses to prove it. The psalm asks what any of it finally amounts to, when the one who has promised never to leave is beside you. “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31; Matthew 10:28).

Forsaken so that we never would be. The promise has a price, and Christ paid it. On the cross he cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). He bore the abandonment sin deserves, so that God can say to everyone who trusts in him, I will never forsake you, without exception. He is also the pattern of contentment: though he was rich, for our sake he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9) and had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20), yet he never lacked his Father’s presence. A Christian with little money and that same presence is living as Jesus lived.

How do I know if I love money? Watch what makes you anxious, what makes you envious and what you are reluctant to give. The test is not your bank balance but whether you could lose it and still be content, because you have God.

What if I genuinely do not have enough? Contentment does not mean pretending need is not real, refusing help, or not seeking work or better provision. Paul knew hunger and need, and learned contentment in it (Philippians 4:11–13). It means trusting that God, who will never leave you, will give you what you truly need (Matthew 6:31–33), and that your worth does not depend on what you have. Pray honestly, take the practical steps you can, and let the church know (v. 16). Being content and asking for help are not opposites.

In everyday life. When a money worry wakes you at night, say the psalm back to it: “The Lord is my helper.” And give away a sum you will notice; it is one of the quickest ways to find that money’s grip on you is weaker than his.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Christ does not change, so go out to him and live as his worshipping people. The leaders who first preached to them have finished their course, but Christ is the same for ever (vv. 7–8), so new teachings about food can add nothing to grace (v. 9). Our altar is his sacrifice, which those who cling to the old tent cannot share; he suffered outside the gate like the sin offering, and believers go out to him, bearing his disgrace, because no city here lasts (vv. 10–14). Their sacrifices now are praise and sharing (vv. 15–16), and their life together means following faithful leaders and praying for them (vv. 17–19).
verseByVerse.theology:
Outside the Camp

Jesus suffered outside the gate, as the sin offering was burned outside the camp. Go to him there, bearing his reproach, and offer the sacrifices that please God: praise, doing good and sharing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: For these readers the camp was home (see the note on vv. 13–14).

Now: Leaving what is not lasting is going to where he is (see vv. 13–14).

verseByVerse.quote: Remember your leaders, those who spoke to you the word of God. Consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember the leaders who brought you the gospel and copy their faith, because the Christ they trusted has not changed.

Remember your leaders. The wording suggests leaders whose work was finished: the founding generation of that church, perhaps including apostles, who first preached the gospel to them (2:3), and quite possibly some who had died for it. They are identified not by office but by what they said: their authority was the word they preached.

Consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith. The outcome is how it ended, for some perhaps in martyrdom. Anybody can hold a belief at forty; what a man is at the close shows whether it held. And what is to be copied, as in 6:12, is not their manner, gifts or methods but their faith, the one thing every believer can copy.

The same yesterday and today and forever. “The same” echoes 1:12, “you are the same, and your years will have no end”, and here it answers a particular grief. A congregation that has buried the men who brought it the gospel feels the ground move. The leaders had an outcome, an end to their course; Christ has none. He is the same today, interceding for them (7:25), and will be the same past every leader they will ever have. He was faithful to Abraham, to Moses, to the apostles and martyrs, to our grandparents, and he will be faithful to us and our children; the whole weight of history and eternity can rest on him. And because he does not change, strange new teachings are not worth chasing (v. 9): nothing newer or better is coming after him.

Does this verse mean the miracles of the apostles continue today? It is often quoted to argue that if Jesus worked miracles then, he must do the same through his people now. But the context is about who Christ is: his character, his saving work and his word do not change. That does not mean every gift he gave in every age continues. The signs that confirmed the apostles’ message belonged to that first generation (2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12). Continuationists, who believe all the gifts continue, reply that an unchanging Christ will act as he acted. But the Christ who does not change no longer walks in Galilee either: his person stays the same while his ways of working through history move on. God still answers prayer and heals as he wills; this commentary holds, charitably, that the sign gifts of the apostolic age have ceased. Many faithful churches believe otherwise, and they worship the same unchanging Lord.

How do I imitate someone’s faith without copying their personality? Look at what they trusted and how it shaped their choices, not at their style: how they handled suffering, money, temptation, failure and death. Then ask God for the same trust in your own temperament and circumstances. A quiet person need not become loud to imitate a bold preacher’s faith; he needs to trust the same Christ as fully, where God has put him.

In everyday life. Name one person who first taught you the gospel. If they are alive, write and thank them this week; if they have died, thank God for them, and ask what one thing about their faith you could imitate.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace, not by foods, which have not benefited those devoted to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be carried off by new teachings: the heart is made steady by God’s grace, not by rules about food.

Diverse and strange teachings. “Led away” is carried aside, swept off course like a drifting ship (2:1). “Diverse” is of many kinds, and their very number counts against them, since the truth is one. “Strange” is foreign, alien to the gospel. Christ is the same; teachings are diverse.

Strengthened by grace, not by foods. “Strengthened” is made firm, and grace is God’s free favour in Christ. Whatever these teachings were exactly (see below), they concerned eating, and promised a steadiness only grace can give.

Two ways of steadying a heart. One is grace: something received from outside, on the basis of what somebody else has done. The other is food: something you manage yourself, by what you eat and avoid. The second attracts because rules are measurable: you know whether you have kept them, and they give a sense of progress that grace never does. The irreligious have their own versions: the clean diet, the morning routine, the plan that promises a steadier self. Grace is more humbling than all of them, and far more freeing.

Grace with a face. The grace that steadies the heart is not a substance, a mood or a force. It has appeared in a person: grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John 1:17). Food rules ask what you have kept; grace points to what he has done, the will of God fulfilled by the offering of his body once for all (10:10). A heart resting on its own record shifts with every good or bad week. A heart resting on Christ rests on something already finished, and cannot be moved.

Not benefited. “Devoted to them” is literally those who walk in them. The verdict comes from experience: look at the people who have given their lives to this, and ask whether it has done them any good (9:9–10; Colossians 2:16–23).

Are Christians bound by the Old Testament food laws today? No. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19; the KJV words Mark’s comment differently), Peter was told, “What God has made clean, do not call common” (Acts 10:15), and everything created by God is good (1 Timothy 4:4). Those who still keep such rules out of conscience are not to be despised (Romans 14:1–3). The danger is trusting food rules to strengthen the heart; only grace can do that.

How can I tell a strange teaching from a true one? Test it against Scripture, and above all against the Christ of Scripture (Acts 17:11; 1 John 4:1–3). Beware teaching that adds something to Christ as necessary; that promises secret knowledge or a higher Christian life through special practices; that cannot be found in the plain words of the Bible; that flatters the hearer or centres on the teacher; or that leaves you anxious about rules rather than resting in grace. Ask what it does with the cross. True teaching always makes Christ larger and grace sweeter.

Uncertain wording. We do not know exactly what the teachings about “foods” were: the Jewish food laws, meals linked with the temple sacrifices, and ascetic diets like those Paul met at Colossae have all been suggested. Verse 10, which speaks of an altar and of eating, points toward meals connected with the old sacrificial worship. The point does not depend on the details.

verseByVerse.quote: We have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat. For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians have an altar of their own, Christ’s sacrifice, which those who cling to the old worship cannot share; and like the sin offering, he was put outside the gate to make his people holy.

We have an altar. A startling sentence, after twelve chapters showing that the old altars and sacrifices are finished. This altar is not a piece of furniture but the cross, Christ’s sacrifice itself. We eat from it by faith, feeding on Christ crucified: “Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6:54).

No right to eat. “Those who serve the tent” are those who cling to the old tabernacle worship. Its priests ate portions of many sacrifices, but never of the Day of Atonement sin offering, which was wholly burned (Leviticus 6:30; 16:27). Christ is the true sin offering, and those who stay with the old system cannot share in him. You cannot hold both: the sharpest thing the letter has yet said to people considering a quiet return.

So Jesus also suffered outside the gate. Golgotha lay outside the walls of Jerusalem (John 19:17, 20), and this was no accident of Roman practice: it matched the sin offering exactly. Outside the camp was the place of the unclean, the leper and the blasphemer (Leviticus 13:46; 24:14). Jesus was not merely executed; he was put out, rejected and treated as unclean, in the place where the rubbish went.

To sanctify the people. To make holy, as in 10:10 and 10:14. Christ’s blood washes away the guilt and defilement of sin and sets his people apart as God’s own, as the priests were once consecrated with blood to serve in his house (Exodus 29:20–21). Any reader who has felt himself on the wrong side of a boundary may take that home: the one thrown outside is the one who makes his people holy.

Where the outside and the inside meet. On the Day of Atonement the blood went in and the body went out. In Jesus both happened to one person. His body was led outside the gate, and by his own blood he entered once for all into heaven itself, to appear in the presence of God for us (9:12, 24). He stands at once with the outcasts and before the face of the Father. He went outside so that we could come in.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should despise Jewish people. The old covenant system cannot give access to Christ’s benefits; only faith in him can. The gospel is for the Jew first, and many of this letter’s first readers were Jews who had found their Messiah.

What does it mean to eat from this altar? To receive by faith the benefits of Christ’s death: forgiveness, cleansing, peace with God and life. You feed on him when you trust him, meditate on his cross, hear the gospel and believe it, and in a special way at the Lord’s Supper, where bread and cup are signs and seals of his body and blood and faith receives him spiritually: not physical eating, nor mere remembering, but real communion with the living Christ who died for you.

Where Christians differ: is the Lord’s Table an altar? Roman Catholic and some Anglo-Catholic traditions identify this altar with the communion table, on which the sacrifice of the Mass is offered. Others take it as the Lord’s Supper understood as a meal. This commentary’s view: the New Testament never calls the Lord’s Table an altar. The altar here is Christ’s sacrifice on the cross, which this letter says again and again was offered once for all and is never repeated (7:27; 9:25–28; 10:12–14), so the verse gives no support to a sacrifice in the Mass. We eat from the altar by faith in his finished work, especially as we receive the Lord’s Supper, where Christ is spiritually present and we feed on him by faith; but no new sacrifice is offered.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured. For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So leave the shelter of the old camp and go out to Jesus, sharing his disgrace, because nothing here lasts and the city to come does. This is the letter’s whole appeal in a single line.

Outside the camp. For these readers, very probably Jewish Christians, the camp was not paganism. It was the temple, the synagogue, the festivals, the family table, everything that had made them who they were. Going out meant being cut off from their own people and losing the shelter Judaism enjoyed under Roman rule (see the introduction). The pull backwards was not toward sin but toward home.

Let us go to him and bear the reproach. The invitation is not into nothing but to him: he is not inside the camp any more, and the appeal is less to be brave than to be where he is. Nor does the writer pretend the cost is small. “Reproach” is disgrace, insult, as of Moses in 11:26: the shame Jesus despised (12:2).

No lasting city. Verse 14 answers the unspoken objection that going out means losing everything: what you have was never permanent. Jerusalem itself would be rubble in AD 70, probably within a few years of this letter. No earthly city, nation or institution is our permanent home.

The city that is to come. The heavenly Jerusalem (11:10, 16; 12:22), the city Abraham looked for while he lived in tents. You are not asked to trade a permanent home for homelessness, but to stop pretending a temporary one is permanent, and to go and find the man standing outside it. He went out first. Nor is he a fugitive in the wilderness: he is the King of the city to come, whose foundations cannot be shaken. Going out to him, we lose a camp that was always going to fall, and find a Saviour who will bring us home.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should withdraw from society or stop caring about their earthly cities. We are to seek the welfare of the city where we live (Jeremiah 29:7), but we do not put our ultimate hope there.

What does outside the camp look like for me? Wherever loyalty to Christ costs you belonging: the family that thinks your faith an embarrassment, the workplace where honesty marks you out, the friends who drift away when you stop joining in, the culture that calls biblical convictions hateful. You go out not by being needlessly odd or harsh, but by refusing to deny Christ to keep your place. And outside the camp is where he is. You never go out alone.

verseByVerse.quote: Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name. Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through Christ, offer God the sacrifices that please him now: constant praise that names him openly, and good done and shared with others. If Christians have an altar (v. 10), these are what they bring to it, and anybody can bring both.

A sacrifice of praise. Praise goes up through Christ our High Priest (1 Peter 2:5), so the worship of a struggling Christian is acceptable for the same reason his forgiveness is: because of Christ. And “continually” is deliberate in a letter that insists the sacrifice for sin was made once for all. That one is finished; this one never stops.

The fruit of lips. The phrase comes from Hosea 14:2 in the Greek translation; most English Bibles, following the Hebrew, speak there of paying with bulls the vows of our lips, but either way the offering is what the lips give. “Acknowledge” is confess, profess: the very thing the readers were tempted to stop doing. Praise is not only singing in church; it is saying his name aloud in a world that would prefer you kept quiet.

To do good and to share. Then the surprise. “Share” is koinōnia: fellowship, generosity, sharing possessions. Practical kindness is put on the altar beside praise, and both are called sacrifices: praise offered to God and good done to people are both worship (Romans 12:1). After chapters on blood and sanctuaries, one of the two things Hebrews finally asks us to offer is sharing what you have.

He leads the song. Our praise does not climb to God alone. The Son who sat down at the right hand is not ashamed to call us brothers, and says to the Father, “in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise” (2:12). Every halting hymn and every quiet act of sharing is taken up into the worship of the great High Priest and carried into the Father’s presence as though it were his own.

How can I praise God continually when life is hard? By remembering that praise is a sacrifice: it costs something, and it is often offered through tears. The psalmists praised God in caves and exile, and Paul and Silas sang in prison at midnight (Acts 16:25). Praise does not require you to feel happy, but to say what is true about God when your circumstances say otherwise. Start small: thank him for one thing each hour, read a psalm aloud. Praise offered through Christ is always acceptable, and it often lifts the heart that offers it.

In everyday life. A meal left on a new mother’s doorstep and a hymn hummed over the washing-up are, by this passage, the same kind of thing: sacrifices God is pleased with.

verseByVerse.quote: Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they are keeping watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account. Let them do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be of no advantage to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Follow your present leaders and make their work a joy, because they keep watch over your souls and must answer to God for you.

Obey your leaders. These are the present leaders, in contrast with the former (v. 7). “Obey” is be persuaded by, follow; “submit” is yield, defer. The command is real and should not be softened, but the reason given is not their rank: they watch over you and must answer for you.

Keeping watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account. Literally staying awake, losing sleep: the sentry at his post, the shepherds keeping watch over their flock by night (Luke 2:8). These elders will stand before God and be asked about the people entrusted to them (James 3:1; Ezekiel 34). Submission is owed not because they are senior but because they are answerable, and that cuts both ways. It tells a congregation to be led, and it tells leaders that the job is to keep watch and answer to God, not to hold a position. On accountable leadership in every sphere, see on Ephesians 5:21.

Not with groaning. Sighing, grieving: the sound a man makes when the weight is more than the encouragement. A congregation that exhausts its leaders damages itself, because a discouraged man watches less well. There is no version of this where the church wins and the leaders lose.

Under the great Shepherd. Over every under-shepherd stands the great Shepherd, who never sleeps and never groans over his sheep, though he has every reason to. The flock belongs to Christ, who obtained it with his own blood (Acts 20:28), and its elders will answer to the chief Shepherd when he appears (1 Peter 5:2–4). So following faithful leaders is finally a way of trusting him, who cares for his sheep through such men and will hold them to account.

Why trust a leader at all? A fair question, after presidents who lie, institutions that cover up, and church leaders who harm the people they were meant to protect. There is truth in the reflex of distrust: power without accountability corrupts. But distrust cannot build anything, and a person led by no one is usually led by his own moods, which are not kind masters. Hebrews grounds authority in answerability, not rank or charisma, and measures every leader against a Shepherd who spent himself for the flock rather than the flock for himself, and laid down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). Only he can be trusted without reserve. Because he can be, we are free to follow lesser shepherds gladly as they follow him, and free to refuse them when they do not.

What it does not mean. It does not support a single ruling bishop: “leaders” is plural. Christians differ over church government, and this verse does not settle every question.

How far must I obey? The leaders in view speak the word of God (v. 7) and are to be followed as they lead by it. Their authority is real but not unlimited. Where they command what Scripture forbids, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29); the Bereans were commended for checking even an apostle’s teaching against the Scriptures (Acts 17:11); and elders are not to domineer over those in their charge (1 Peter 5:3). A leader who uses this verse to control, silence or exploit people has left the ground it stands on. He should be confronted, and if he will not listen, brought before the other elders (1 Timothy 5:19–20); a believer harmed by him may seek help and, if need be, leave. Where abuse is a crime, it should be reported to the authorities.

What if I disagree with my elders on something? Most disagreements concern judgment, not sin: a decision, a style, a priority. Speak to them directly and respectfully, listen to their reasons, and if they still decide otherwise, defer gladly unless conscience is at stake. Do not gather a faction or complain to others; that is exactly how leaders come to groan. If it concerns the gospel or a clear command of Scripture, press it humbly, and if necessary seek help from outside. And pray for them.

In everyday life. Make your elders’ work a joy this week: tell them specifically how God has used their teaching or care, and bring problems to them rather than talking about them to others.

verseByVerse.quote: Pray for us, for we are sure that we have a clear conscience, desiring to act honorably in all things. I urge you the more earnestly to do this in order that I may be restored to you the sooner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer, whose conscience is clear, asks his readers to keep praying for him, so that he may be given back to them sooner.

Pray for us. The verb is keep praying, and “us” is the author and his companions. The man who has taught them with such authority now asks for their help. In a healthy church help runs both ways: a teacher who only gives and never receives is not really sharing life with anybody.

A clear conscience. Literally a good conscience. The claim sounds slightly defensive, as if someone had questioned his motives, perhaps people who resented the letter’s pressure. He states it and moves on, usually the right way to handle an accusation you cannot disprove, claiming not to be sinless but to aim at acting honourably in everything.

A conscience Christ has cleansed. In this letter a good conscience is not a boast but a gift. The old sacrifices could not perfect the conscience of the worshipper (9:9), but the blood of Christ purifies our conscience from dead works to serve the living God (9:14), so that we draw near with hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience (10:22). When this writer says his conscience is clear, he stands where every forgiven believer stands: nothing hidden, and nothing the blood of Jesus has not already covered.

Restored to you the sooner. “Restored” is given back. Something he does not explain, illness, imprisonment or distance, has kept him from them, and he believes their prayers will make a real difference. He asks to be given back to these particular people. He misses them.

A name nobody recorded. One of the most polished writers in the New Testament is a man whose name has not come down to us (see the introduction). That fits a letter which tells its readers to seek a city that is to come: the work outlasts him, and his name was never the point.

Does my prayer really make a difference to whether God acts? Yes. God has ordained to work through the prayers of his people, and he answers them (James 5:16–18); the writer expected their prayers to hasten his return. God’s sovereignty does not make prayer pointless; it makes it effective, because we are asking the one who rules everything. He may answer differently from what you asked, but no prayer offered in Christ’s name is wasted, and the prayers of ordinary believers have upheld missionaries, pastors and persecuted churches across the centuries.

How do I pray for my leaders? This verse gives the outline. Their conscience: that they stay honest in private as well as in public, “desiring to act honorably in all things”, kept clean by the blood of Christ rather than propped up by a reputation. Their words: Paul asked for prayer “that words may be given to me in opening my mouth boldly to proclaim the mystery of the gospel” (Ephesians 6:19); pray that for whoever preaches to you next Sunday. Their bodies and homes: leaders get tired, ill and discouraged, and their families carry the cost. That they finish well: many start well. And tell them: a short message saying you prayed will strengthen them more than most compliments. You are not holding them up alone. The great shepherd of the sheep (v. 20) always lives to make intercession for his people (7:25), as he prayed for Peter, “that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What God asks, he gives. The letter closes by praying that the God of peace, who raised the great Shepherd by the blood of the eternal covenant, will equip his people and work in them what pleases him, through Jesus Christ (vv. 20–21). Then come a plea to receive the sermon patiently, news of Timothy, greetings to everyone, and the letter’s last word: grace (vv. 22–25).
verseByVerse.theology:
The God Who Works in Us

The God of peace, who brought again from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, equips his people and works in them what pleases him (see the note on vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The writer calls his letter a “word of exhortation” (see vv. 22–25).

Now: After its hardest warnings, the letter ends with grace for all (see vv. 22–25).

verseByVerse.quote: Now may the God of peace who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, by the blood of the eternal covenant, equip you with everything good that you may do his will, working in us that which is pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The letter ends by praying that the God who raised Jesus will make his people whole and work in them all that pleases him, through Christ. Every phrase of this benediction gathers up something the letter has argued.

Now may the God of peace. The God who has made peace with sinners through Christ’s blood and gives peace (Romans 15:33; 1 Thessalonians 5:23): apt for a congregation under strain, whose leaders are groaning.

Brought again from the dead. The only explicit mention of Jesus’ resurrection in the letter, though it is assumed on every page: a seated priest is necessarily a living one, whose priesthood rests on the power of an indestructible life (7:16).

The great shepherd of the sheep. The one pastoral image in a letter full of priests, echoing Isaiah 63:11, where in the Greek translation God brought up from the sea the shepherd of the sheep, Moses. A new exodus and a greater shepherd, brought up not out of water but out of death: the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, the chief Shepherd who will appear (John 10:11; 1 Peter 5:4).

By the blood of the eternal covenant. Most likely the ground on which God raised him (see below). The blood was not the power that raised Jesus but the reason he was raised: his sacrifice had been accepted, and the covenant it sealed could not have a dead mediator. The resurrection is the Father’s seal on the covenant. And “eternal” answers everything the readers were tempted back toward. The old covenant was growing old, ready to vanish away (8:13); this one never grows old and will never be replaced (Jeremiah 32:40).

Equip you. The verb means to put right, make complete, fit out, mend; it is used of setting a broken bone and of fishermen mending their nets (Mark 1:19). The God of peace, who raised the Shepherd, bends to mend his broken people into working order. And as Christ came to do God’s will (10:7, 9), so his people do it by his equipping.

Working in us. God does not merely equip them to work; he works in them: “it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13). That is why the letter’s demand, to go outside the camp and bear the reproach, is not crushing: what he requires, he supplies. Our obedience is real but flawed, and it is pleasing in his sight through Jesus Christ, whose perfect obedience is counted as ours, so that our imperfect works are accepted for his sake (1 Peter 2:5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we are passive. God equips us by the Spirit he has put within us, so that we do his will: his work is the cause of our obedience, not a replacement for it.

If God works in me what pleases him, why do I struggle so much? Because his work in you is real but not yet finished, and it works through your struggle, not around it; mending takes time and sometimes hurts. Your hatred of sin, your desire to please him, your getting up after falling, are evidence that he is at work. Do not wait to feel equipped: obey, trusting that he is working in you as you do, and when you fail, return to the great Shepherd who was brought back from the dead for you.

In everyday life. Pray this benediction by name over one person who is struggling. And when a task this week feels beyond you, ask him to work in you what is pleasing in his sight, and then step into it.

Uncertain wording. Two phrases can be read more than one way. “By the blood of the eternal covenant” may say on what ground God raised Jesus, or why he is the great Shepherd, whose flock was bought with his blood; both are true, and the first fits the sentence best. “To whom be glory” may refer to Jesus Christ, the nearest name, or to God, the subject of the prayer; doxologies to Christ are found elsewhere (2 Peter 3:18; Revelation 1:5–6), so either is possible. Either way, the letter that has exalted Christ above angels, Moses and Aaron ends in glory for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, bear with my word of exhortation, for I have written to you briefly. You should know that our brother Timothy has been released, with whom I shall see you if he comes soon. Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Those who come from Italy send you greetings. Grace be with all of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer asks his readers to take his hard sermon patiently, sends news and greetings, and ends with grace.

My word of exhortation. “Bear with” is listen patiently, for the warnings have been severe. “Word of exhortation” is how Acts describes a synagogue sermon, when Paul was invited at Antioch: “if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it” (Acts 13:15), with the same Greek word. Hebrews is a sermon sent as a letter: it closes like a letter, has no opening greeting, and argues like a preacher (see the introduction).

Briefly. Either dry humour or an honest estimate: Hebrews takes under an hour to read aloud, and for the vastness of its subject it is brief (9:5; 11:32).

Timothy has been released. The one living companion the letter names, and a tantalising one. Timothy had evidently been in prison, the only mention of it in the New Testament, perhaps after Paul’s death in Rome. And the writer means to come with him if he arrives soon: the sermon would be followed by the preacher.

All your leaders and all the saints. The leaders are the elders (v. 17), and “the saints” are all believers, holy in Christ. “All” comes twice. A letter whose warnings have frightened readers for two thousand years ends by including everybody. The greeting from “those who come from Italy” probably comes from Italians abroad sending greetings home (see below).

Grace be with all of you. The letter has warned, exhorted and taught, and its last word is grace. In Hebrews grace always has Christ at its centre: by the grace of God Jesus tasted death for everyone (2:9), and the throne of grace is reached through him, the great High Priest who has passed through the heavens (4:14–16). So the letter closes not with a demand but with the one who makes every demand possible.

A better hope, and he is ours. Hebrews began with God speaking by his Son, the radiance of his glory, who made purification for sins and sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. Everything since has unfolded that grace: a better priest, a better covenant, a better sacrifice, a better hope, and he is ours. The writer’s name is lost, but his Saviour’s name is above every name. Grace be with all of you, and glory to the one who gives it, for ever and ever.

Who wrote the letter? Probably not Paul, since the writer received the gospel from those who heard the Lord (2:3), which Paul insisted he did not (Galatians 1:12). Apollos, Barnabas, Luke and Priscilla have been suggested, and none can be proved (see the introduction): most likely a gifted teacher in Paul’s circle whose name God has not preserved. The letter’s authority rests not on its author but on the God who speaks in it, and the church received it as Scripture.

How should I respond to a hard word from Scripture or a preacher? Bear with it, as this writer asked. Do not dismiss it because it stings, and do not be crushed by it as if it were God’s rejection. If it is true to Scripture, receive it as the loving word of a Father who disciplines his children, pray over it, and act on it. The warnings of Hebrews were written by a man who loved his readers and wanted them to arrive. Hard words in Scripture are always spoken inside grace, and they end, as this letter does, with grace.

Uncertain wording. “Those who come from Italy” (literally “those from Italy”) can mean Italians living abroad, sending greetings home, or people in Italy sending greetings elsewhere. The first is more natural, and fits other evidence that the letter went to Rome: the earliest known use of Hebrews is by Clement of Rome, around AD 95. But the phrase alone cannot settle where the letter was sent.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy had evidently been in prison. “Those who come from Italy” may be Italians abroad sending greetings home, or believers in Italy itself.

Those who come from Italy send you greetings.<sup>25</sup>Grace be with all of you.

keyVerse.quote: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter leans on this verse. Leaders die, teachings shift and earthly cities fall (vv. 7, 9, 14), but the Christ who saved the founders is the same Christ who keeps their children, so there is nothing newer to chase and no one safer to go out to. Spoken to a congregation that had stood at its leaders’ graves, it is not a slogan about timelessness but a promise.

13.reflection:
Verses 1–6 describe love for brothers, strangers, prisoners and a spouse, and a heart content with God. Which of these is hardest for you or for your church at present, and what is one concrete step you could take this month?

The readers’ first leaders had died, and verse 8 answers that loss with the unchanging Christ. Whose faith has shaped yours, and how does it help to know that the Christ they trusted is the same for you and for those who come after you?

For the first readers, going “outside the camp” (v. 13) meant losing a respected religious home. Where does loyalty to Christ cost you belonging today, and how does it change things to know that he is already there, outside?

Verses 15–16 call both praise and sharing “sacrifices”, and verses 20–21 pray that God will work in us what pleases him. How does it change ordinary kindness and Sunday singing to see them as offerings God is pleased with through Jesus Christ?
